beads.title: Filed no asks this turn
beads.body: The live strategic tension — whether continued narrow closed-form autoSplit extensions satisfy vision item 1 or whether the general multi-hop LP is still the actual ask — is already captured by unanswered ask lp-15f7f9. A second ask on the same question would spend attention without adding a new soThat.

beads.title: autoSplit(): extend the shared-sink case when the OTHER supplier is a plain single-edge source
beads.body:
autoSplit()'s condition (c) refuses ANY fan-out group whose destination sink is fed by more than one edge in the whole network — production.selftest.mjs's 'a sink fed from more than one edge in the whole network is left untouched' CONTROL pins this exactly (the sharedSinkNet fixture). That refusal is broader than it needs to be for one common, still-closed-form sub-case: the sink's one OTHER supplier is a plain source with no fan-out of its own (whole-network out-degree exactly 1), so its contribution to that sink is an unambiguous constant — its full `rate` — nothing needs solving for it, only subtracting.

Extend the qualification: a group's edge to sink S still qualifies if S has AT MOST one edge outside the group, and when it has exactly one, that outside edge's `from` is a `source` node whose whole-network out-degree is exactly 1, AND that source's `rate` is strictly less than S's `demand` (so the group still has positive effective demand left to fill — if the lone outside source alone already meets or exceeds demand, exclude that sink from the group the same way a non-qualifying member is silently excluded today, and split only over the remaining qualifying sinks). For each qualifying sink compute `effectiveDemand = demand - outsideContribution` (0 if there is no outside edge, i.e. today's case, which must keep behaving exactly as it does now) and split proportional to effectiveDemand instead of raw demand — same max-min-fair proof autoSplit()'s header already works for the plain case, with effectiveDemand standing in for demand.

This is a distinct axis from the already-ready lp-9be387, which relaxes condition (b) (destination kind: processor vs sink), not condition (c) (supplier count). Both tickets edit autoSplit() but in physically separate parts of its qualifying-predicate logic and grouping loop, so promoting both should rebase cleanly.

Tests: extend the existing 'sharedSinkNet' fixture in production.selftest.mjs (currently only proves the old refusal) with a variant where 'other' has out-degree 1 and rate less than demand — hand-compute the effectiveDemand-proportional shares and check them exactly, plus a new CONTROL where the outside source's rate alone already meets or exceeds demand (that sink excluded from the group; the group's other, still-qualifying member's math is unaffected — same shape as the existing 'no-mutation' and 'byte-identical when untouched' CONTROLs in this file). No existing assertion changes.

Bounded paths: plant/production.mjs, plant/test/production.selftest.mjs.

[turn 28 — done] Extended autoSplit()'s condition (c) in plant/production.mjs from an all-or-nothing whole-group check to a per-sink one: a sink with a single outside supplier that is a plain (whole-network out-degree 1) source whose rate is strictly less than the sink's demand now qualifies for the split, with effectiveDemand = demand - outsideRate standing in for demand in the same proportional-to-effectiveDemand allocation the plain case already used. A sink that fails the extended check (more than one outside supplier, an outside supplier that isn't a plain source, or one whose rate alone already meets/exceeds demand) is excluded from the split rather than voiding the whole group -- its edge is left untouched, and the split runs over whatever qualifying sinks remain; fewer than two remaining leaves the whole group untouched, preserving every existing test's behavior byte-for-byte. Conditions (a) (no pre-existing explicit share) and (b) (destination is a sink) stayed whole-group checks, unchanged from before. Added two new test blocks to production.selftest.mjs: one exercising the new qualifying case (source rate chosen so total effectiveDemand equals it exactly, reproducing the same zero-margin equalized-ratio optimal signature as the original plain-case test), and one CONTROL where the outside source's rate alone already covers demand -- that sink is excluded and left share-less, the other two (still-qualifying) sinks in the group split normally between themselves unaffected by the exclusion, and feasible() on the result is asserted to still throw with 'fan-out' in the message since the excluded sink's edge has no share inside an otherwise partially-split group. Every existing assertion in the file, including the untouched 'sharedSinkNet' CONTROL this ticket referenced, was hand-traced against the new code path and confirmed unchanged. I could not execute node plant/test/production.selftest.mjs myself (no Bash in this turn's tool grant) -- see the recorded finding below, which is now well past twenty instances of this identical structural gap.

beads.title: feasible(): report per-sink margin and unrouted output as new, purely-additive fields
beads.body:
feasible() already computes, per sink, `(achieved - demand) / demand` inline while reducing to the single aggregate `margin` — and throws that per-sink number away. LEVEL_5's and LEVEL_6's own header comments hand-derive exactly this number in prose right now (level5.mjs: 'margin 0.25 on BOTH sinks'; level6.mjs: 'margin 1/9 on BOTH sinks') because the oracle does not expose it — that is a fact the oracle should supply, not something a level's comment should restate by hand.

Add `sinkMargins` to feasible()'s return: `{ sinkId: margin }` for every sink, the exact same formula already computed inline for the aggregate, just retained instead of discarded.

Also add `wastedSupply`: an array of `{ nodeId, resource, amount }`, one entry per (node, resource) pair where that node's computed `out[resource]` exceeds what its outgoing edges for that resource actually route (`out[resource] * sum of shares over edges carrying that resource from that node`), mirroring `deficits`'s existing array shape and only including entries where the leftover amount is above the file's existing 1e-9 tolerance. Scope is OUTPUT-side waste only — emitted-but-unrouted supply, from a partial share (sum < 1) or a resource with no outgoing edge at all. Input-side waste (a capacity-bound processor leaving offered-but-unconsumed input) needs tracking each input's offered-vs-used rate separately and is deliberately out of scope.

Both fields are purely additive: `ok`, `achieved`, `deficits`, `margin` are untouched byte-for-byte, so every existing assertion in production.selftest.mjs keeps passing unmodified. New known-answer cases: the file's own 'a single partial share is legal, not an error' fixture already leaves 0.4 of a 10-unit source unrouted on purpose (share 0.6, sink demand 5) — that becomes the first wastedSupply known-answer case (`{ nodeId: 'src', resource: 'x', amount: 4 }`) for free. Add a sinkMargins case against the basic feasible chain fixture (margin 0.25, one sink, sinkMargins.snk === 0.25) and against the fan-out-with-explicit-shares fixture (two sinks, two different margins, checked individually rather than just their min).

Bounded paths: plant/production.mjs, plant/test/production.selftest.mjs.

beads.title: level-view.js: buildOrderLines(level) — surface gate 6's already-built construction order, level-agnostic and unwired
beads.body:
buildOrder() (production.mjs, gate 6's non-spatial half — built and pinned, though FACTORIO.md/vision.md's tables still call gate 6 wholly 'to build', a stale FINDING already on record) has never been consumed by anything a player-facing file touches; every level only ever calls feasible()/band().

Add `buildOrderLines(level)` to level-view.js: calls `buildOrder(level)` (import from './production.mjs', alongside the existing `feasible` import) and returns an array of one string per node in order, 1-indexed and using the node id as declared — e.g. `['1. ore', '2. smelterA', '3. smelterB', '4. depotA', '5. depotB']` for a five-node level. Throws exactly when buildOrder() throws (a cycle) and does no validation of its own — a thin formatting wrapper, same posture as `withSourceRate`/`withProcessorCapacity` already in this file. Pure and level-agnostic: takes the same `level` shape every existing level already provides, so it works unmodified against LEVEL_1 through LEVEL_6 with zero level-specific code.

Deliberately NOT wired into index.html or any level's SVG/DOM this turn — same precedent as LEVEL_5 and LEVEL_6 both shipping their level module before a separate wiring ticket picked them up. This ticket is level-view.js plus its selftest only, so a later, independent ticket can choose which level(s) to surface it in without this one guessing.

Tests (new cases added to the existing plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs, which already covers drawLevel/verdictLine): check buildOrderLines(LEVEL_1) against LEVEL_1's known straight three-node chain, and check buildOrderLines(LEVEL_6) matches `buildOrder(LEVEL_6).map(...)` formatted the same way — call the real buildOrder() to get the reference order rather than hand-guessing LEVEL_6's five-node topology, since this ticket is testing formatting fidelity, not re-testing buildOrder()'s own correctness (already pinned in production.selftest.mjs). Add one CONTROL: a hand-built two-node cycle throws with 'cycle' in the message, same as buildOrder()'s own CONTROL.

Bounded paths: plant/level-view.js, plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs.

beads.title: Conditions (a)/(b) stay whole-group; only (c) became per-edge
beads.body: Considered making all three conditions per-edge (exclude any single disqualifying edge and split over the rest), but that would let a group with one edge carrying an already-explicit share plus two newly-splittable sinks produce shares that could sum past 1 when combined with the pre-existing explicit share -- an untested, ambiguous interaction. Keeping (a) and (b) as all-or-nothing at the group level (exactly as before this ticket) avoids that entirely: a group either has zero pre-existing explicit shares and is entirely sink-destined, or autoSplit leaves it completely alone. Only (c) -- how confounded a sink's demand may be by outside supply -- is checked per-edge, which is the specific relaxation the ticket asked for. This keeps every prior test's behavior identical without needing to reason about a compound case nobody has asked for yet. Reversible: if a future ticket wants per-edge (a)/(b) too, the total-share-sums-to-1 validation in analyse() already catches the over-allocation case safely (it throws rather than silently producing a wrong split), so relaxing further later is not blocked by anything built here.

beads.title: This turn's own gate is unverifiable in-turn -- the structural gap is now well past twenty tickets deep
beads.body: Tool grant was Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only, no Bash, and the GATE is `node plant/test/production.selftest.mjs`, a shell command this turn cannot run. Every new number (effectiveDemand 20 and 70, shares 20/90 and 70/90, achieved 30 and 70, margin 0 for the extension case; effectiveDemand exclusion and shares 0.3/0.7 for the CONTROL case) was hand-traced step by step through analyse()'s and feasible()'s exact algorithm -- including the Kahn's-algorithm processing order and the supplyIn accumulation across two source nodes feeding the same sink -- and every pre-existing assertion in the file was independently re-traced against the new code to confirm zero behavior change. Confidence is high but this is inference, not execution. This is now well past the twentieth class-a/creates-gate ticket in this ledger with this identical structural gap (lp-dfad42, lp-138b76, and roughly two dozen subsequent tickets, each re-noting the same standing recommendation). Repeating it once more because nothing has changed at the source: either grant Bash to turns whose gate is a shell command, or make explicit in the ticket body that gate execution happens downstream (CI/judge) rather than in-turn. Given the count, every turn that re-notes this instead of the loop-work.yml workflow being fixed is spending ledger space restating an established fact -- this is the last time I intend to restate it rather than proposing the fix directly, but I have no bounded path into .github/workflows/ from this ticket to do so myself.

beads.body:

Both are scoped to production.mjs and its existing selftest only, independent of each other and of every open ticket.

beads.title: Scoped this turn to two production.mjs-oracle-only tickets, not a new level or UI wiring
beads.body: Fan-out's remaining closed-form extension (processor destinations) is already lp-9be387 and real-pocket placement is already lp-39d6e7 — proposing either again would duplicate open work. Both new tickets touch only plant/production.mjs and plant/test/production.selftest.mjs, deliberately not level-view.js or index.html, so neither creates a hidden ordering dependency on a future rendering ticket (R4).

beads.title: feasible() has no visible metric for unrouted fan-out output
beads.body: production.mjs's own header and the 'a single edge with a partial share leaves the remainder simply unrouted, not an error' CONTROL test both document that a fan-out group summing to <1 (or a processor output with zero consuming edges) is legal and silently drops output. feasible()'s return has margin/achieved/deficits for the SINK side but nothing for the SOURCE/PROCESSOR side, so this consequence is invisible to any caller, including a future level.

beads.title: production.mjs's zero-sink branch is self-documented as untested
beads.body: The docstring above feasible()'s margin computation says the vacuous margin-0 case for a sinkless network is 'not exercised by any ticket case, recorded as a decision rather than left to fall out silently' — the code admits its own coverage gap. Confirmed by reading test/production.selftest.mjs in full: no fixture there omits every sink.

beads.title: Should unrouted fan-out output (the new waste metric) become a visible in-level failure state, or stay an oracle-only fact?
beads.body:
This turn proposes adding a `waste` field to feasible()'s return — how much of a source's or processor's output goes nowhere because a fan-out group's shares sum to less than 1, or a processor output has no consuming edge at all. It is scoped oracle-only (production.mjs + its selftest) on purpose, so it does not preempt this question: today a level can only fail by a SINK falling short of demand (the red-box treatment in level-view.js's drawLevel). Wasted output is a different kind of failure — nothing downstream is short, but the player made a choice that throws resources away for no reason, which is arguably closer to 'an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for' than a sink shortfall is, since it is entirely self-inflicted rather than a capacity fight.

DO: Once this turn's waste-metric ticket ships, open plant/index.html locally, pick any fan-out level (4, 5, or 6), and drag a share slider so the two shares sum to noticeably less than 1 (e.g. LEVEL_5's shareA far from its valid window in the direction that leaves both destinations under-fed AND leaves headroom unrouted, if such a setting exists in that level's current wiring — otherwise imagine the SVG showing a third, amber state alongside the existing green/red boxes).

WATCH FOR: Whether 'some of my ore just vanished, nobody consumed it' reads as a real decision cost the moment you see the number, or whether it needs a visual (an amber box, a leak icon, a line in verdictLine) before it registers as a failure at all — i.e. whether the NUMBER alone is enough or whether it needs level-view.js's rendering treatment.

SO THAT: If the number alone reads as meaningful, a follow-up ticket wires `waste` into verdictLine()'s existing sentence (a small, additive change). If it needs a visual treatment to register, the follow-up instead extends drawLevel()'s red/normal styling to a third state, which is more UI work and should be sized and proposed as its own ticket rather than assumed free.

beads.title: feasible(): add a waste metric for unrouted fan-out/processor output
beads.body:
BOUNDED PATHS (R3): plant/production.mjs and plant/test/production.selftest.mjs only. Nothing else changes — no level, no level-view.js, no index.html wiring.

WHY (R5): production.mjs's own header states fan-out's group-sum-<1 case 'leaves that much of the output unrouted, not an error', and test/production.selftest.mjs's 'a single edge with a partial share leaves the remainder simply unrouted' CONTROL proves the oracle already computes this correctly for margin purposes. But nothing in feasible()'s return says HOW MUCH was unrouted, or names the node/resource it happened to. That is exactly the invisible-consequence gap vision.md's playability bar rules out: right now a fan-out whose shares sum to 0.7 is indistinguishable, from the return value alone, from one that sums to 1.0 and simply has smaller sinks — the only clue is re-deriving it from the edges by hand. It also silently covers a second, currently-undetectable case: a processor output resource with literally zero outgoing edges (a dead-end recipe output) reports no waste today because nothing ever asked.

WHAT (R2, the gate): extend feasible()'s return with a new `waste` array: `{ id, resource, produced, wasted }` for every (node, resource) pair the node actually emits (source rate, or a processor's `out[resource]` after scaling) where the TOTAL share committed across that node's outgoing edges for that resource is less than 1 (by more than 1e-9) — including the zero-edges case, where committed share is 0 and `wasted === produced`. `produced` is the node's emitted amount for that resource before any edge share is applied; `wasted = produced * (1 - totalShareCommitted)`. Nodes/resources with full (>= 1-1e-9) commitment are simply absent from the array — same 'absence means nothing wrong' convention `deficits` already uses. A sink emits nothing (per `emits()`) so sinks never appear. Compute this inside feasible()'s existing walk: `outEdges.get(id)` already carries `{ to, resource, share }` per resolved edge, so summing `share` grouped by `resource` for a given node's outgoing edges is a few lines next to the existing delivery loop, using data `analyse()` already resolved — no new validation, no change to `analyse()`'s contract, no change to any existing field's meaning.

TEST (append to plant/test/production.selftest.mjs, do not rewrite existing sections): (a) reuse the file's own 'a single edge with a partial share leaves the remainder simply unrouted' fixture (source rate 10, one edge share 0.6, sink demand 5) and assert `waste` contains exactly one entry for `{id: 'src', resource: 'x'}` with `produced` 10 and `wasted` 4 (10*0.4); (b) a CONTROL using that same file's basic fully-routed fan-out fixture (shares 0.3/0.7 summing to 1) asserting `waste` is empty; (c) a new small fixture: a processor with an output resource that has zero outgoing edges, asserting one waste entry with `wasted === produced` (the full emitted amount); (d) a CONTROL chain (source->processor->sink, no fan-out, single edges throughout, share defaulting to 1 everywhere) asserting `waste` is empty, so the new field is a pure addition and does not flag the ordinary case. Existing assertions in the file must keep passing unmodified — no waste-shaped changes to any existing return-value snapshot check (several existing tests do `JSON.stringify(result) === ...` style byte comparisons on `autoSplit()`'s edges, not on `feasible()`'s return, so they are unaffected).

beads.title: production.mjs: cover the zero-sink vacuous-feasibility case its own docstring flags as untested
beads.body:
BOUNDED PATHS (R3): plant/test/production.selftest.mjs only — this is a pure coverage addition, no production.mjs code change (the behavior is already implemented at the `if (margin === Infinity) margin = 0;` line; only the test is missing).

WHY (R5): the docstring directly above feasible()'s margin loop reads: 'A network with no sinks is vacuously feasible and reports margin 0 (no sink to have headroom over) — not exercised by any ticket case, recorded as a decision rather than left to fall out silently.' I read the full 676-line test/production.selftest.mjs to confirm: every fixture in the file has at least one sink node. This is the codebase naming its own gap in plain language, which is the cheapest, lowest-risk kind of ticket to pick up — no design judgment call, just closing a documented hole.

WHAT (R2, the gate): add one new `console.log` section to plant/test/production.selftest.mjs (matching the file's existing house style — see its header's own description of paired positive/CONTROL cases) with at least these fixtures, each fed through `feasible()`: (a) a source-only network (one source node, zero edges, zero sinks) asserting `ok === true`, `margin === 0`, `deficits.length === 0`, and `achieved` is `{}` (no sink ever wrote an achieved entry); (b) a source -> processor network with no sink downstream of the processor (processor's output edge omitted entirely) asserting the same `ok === true, margin === 0, deficits.length === 0` — this is the CONTROL that proves the vacuous case holds even with upstream production happening, not just for a totally inert single-node network; (c) a CONTROL that reuses the file's own existing basic chain fixture (source->processor->sink, margin 0.25) run through the SAME assertions as (a)/(b) to prove `margin === 0` is not simply a variable that always reads 0 — the sink-having case must show its real 0.25, not 0, so the two code paths are genuinely distinguished. Existing assertions elsewhere in the file are untouched.

beads.title: Planning run 2026-08-05T12:51:06Z
beads.body:
A plan seat was staffed because the ready queue was starved. Output: proposals, born proposed, awaiting human promotion.

[turn ? — done] Read vision.md verbatim and cross-checked it against plant/production.mjs, plant/test/production.selftest.mjs and plant/level-view.js before proposing anything. The two most obvious gaps in production.mjs's own comments — the visible waste metric and the zero-sink branch — turn out to already be exactly what the immediately-prior planning turn proposed (its own recorded decision was 'two production.mjs-oracle-only tickets' addressing those same two findings), so proposing them again would duplicate work already sitting in the proposed pool. All five already-open beads (lp-f25c2f, lp-b80b67, lp-39d6e7, lp-484b7f, lp-e8d94e, lp-9be387) and all twelve already-waiting asks cover the rest of the obvious surface — fan-out's closed-form processor extension, real-pocket placement, frame budget, the cron PAT. Cosmetic UI (the svg#lvl2-6 CSS gap) and a seventh level are both things the vision and the ledger's own DECISION trail already say to avoid this turn. So I went looking for what none of that already claims: genuinely untested refusal branches that already exist in shipped, passing code. I found three in production.mjs's analyse()/autoSplit() validation logic (processor input/output rate positivity, edge share (0,1] bounds, and three of autoSplit's four condition-(c) exclusion sub-cases) and one in level-view.js's HTML-escaping path (esc(), which stands between a level literal's node id and the live innerHTML of an internet-facing page, and has never been asserted against HTML-special input). Both proposals are pure test-file additions against existing gates, closing coverage gaps rather than adding behavior — no source file changes, so both are trivially reversible and carry zero risk to the live page.

beads.title: Did not re-propose the waste metric or zero-sink coverage
beads.body: The ledger's own FINDING/DECISION trail ('feasible() has no visible metric for unrouted fan-out output', 'production.mjs's zero-sink branch is self-documented as untested', 'Scoped this turn to two production.mjs-oracle-only tickets') shows the immediately-prior planning turn already proposed work against exactly these two findings. Proposing them again would duplicate a ticket already sitting in the proposed pool awaiting promotion — worse than not proposing at all per the standing rule that a rejected duplicate costs more than an unwritten ticket.

beads.title: Bundled three untested production.mjs branches into one ticket, not three
beads.body: All three (processor input/output rate positivity, edge share bounds, autoSplit condition-c exclusions) live in the same gate file, plant/test/production.selftest.mjs. Splitting them into separate proposals would have two tickets leasing the same file with no real independence (R4) — bundling avoids the conflict outright rather than hoping the lease mechanism serializes them.

beads.title: Scoped the second ticket to esc()'s own coverage, not to a security claim about attacker-controlled input
beads.body: Every level id shipped today is a hand-written literal, not user input, so this is defense-in-depth coverage of a zero-tested utility function on the one path (drawLevel's innerHTML write) where a broken escape would be invisible to every other gate in the repo, not a claim of an active vulnerability.

beads.title: Did not propose a new level, the svg#lvl2-6 CSS fix, or a binding-constraint diagnostic
beads.body: The vision explicitly closes the level curve at three-plus-fan-out ('a fourth straight-line level teaches nothing new'), the CSS fix appears to be the previously-rejected 'cosmetic UI change' the ledger's own open ask (lp-c436ee) is asking a human to explain, and a binding-constraint diagnostic has been explicitly declined by name in at least two prior turns' DECISION records.

beads.title: Close production.mjs's untested refusal/exclusion branches: processor rate positivity, edge share (0,1] bounds, autoSplit condition-(c) exclusions
beads.body:
production.mjs's own validation and autoSplit()'s own condition-(c) exclusion logic each have refusal/exclusion branches that exist in shipped, currently-passing code but are exercised by zero test cases in plant/test/production.selftest.mjs — a real gap in the file whose own header states the discipline it is supposed to meet ('a self-authored gate certifies absence-of-regression, not presence-of-correctness... every positive case below carries a paired CONTROL that must fail'). Three distinct gaps, bundled into one ticket because all three live in this one gate file and a second ticket touching the same file risks a lease conflict with this one (R4 independence).

(1) Processor input/output rate positivity. analyse() calls `positive(i.rate, ...)` for every processor input and `positive(o.rate, ...)` for every output (production.mjs's node-validation block), producing messages of the shape `processor "x" input "iron" rate must be positive` and `processor "x" output "gear" rate must be positive`. The file's existing 'other refusals' block tests source rate, sink demand and processor capacity going non-positive, but skips these two entirely — grep for 'input.*rate' / 'output.*rate' assertions in the file finds none. Add one throws()+messageOf() pair for each (input rate 0, output rate -1), with the message checked for the distinguishing substring, plus a CONTROL using a valid positive rate that must NOT throw — same shape as every existing entry in that block.

(2) Edge share bounds (0, 1]. Two call sites in analyse() throw `edge "X"→"Y" share must be in (0, 1]` — one when a single (non-fan-out) edge's explicit share is out of range, one when a fan-out group member's share is out of range. Neither is exercised anywhere in the file today: every existing share-related test either omits share, uses an in-range value, or targets the distinct 'over-allocate' (sum > 1) and 'fan-out without explicit share' messages. Add cases for share = 0, share = -0.1 and share = 1.5, once on a lone edge and once on a group member (two members whose shares are otherwise valid), each paired with a boundary-valid CONTROL (share = 1 on a lone edge; two group members summing to exactly 1) that must NOT throw.

(3) autoSplit()'s condition (c): its own doc comment names four exclusion sub-cases for a sink with exactly one outside supplier plus the base 'more than one outside edge' case, but only two are exercised today (the 'extension' block: outside rate < demand; the 'extension CONTROL' block: outside rate already meets/exceeds demand). Untested: 'more than one outside edge' (outside.length > 1), 'outside supplier not a plain source' (e.g. it is a processor), and 'outside supplier itself fans out' (its own out-degree is not exactly 1). Add three small fixtures, one per sub-case, each a 3-4 node network reusing the shape of the existing excludedNet fixture (a qualifying pair that splits normally, plus one excluded sink), asserting the excluded sink's edge keeps `share === undefined` — exactly the assertion the existing excluded-sink CONTROL already makes for its own sub-case.

Bounded paths: plant/test/production.selftest.mjs only. No changes to production.mjs — every branch under test already exists and already passes; this only proves it, so a failed attempt leaves the tree exactly as it found it (R6). Carries production.selftest.mjs's own header discipline and the standing findings 'a self-authored gate certifies absence-of-regression, not presence-of-correctness' and 'a checker that fails correct work is worse than no checker' (solids.mjs's header) — every new assertion here is paired with a CONTROL that must still pass, closing coverage rather than asserting new behavior.

beads.title: Prove level-view.js's HTML-escaping (esc()) actually escapes, via drawLevel on a level with HTML-special node id
beads.body:
level-view.js's drawLevel() writes directly to `svg.innerHTML` on plant.minomobi.com — a live, internet-facing page with no human between a loop turn and the publish (plant/CLAUDE.md: 'What you write here reaches the internet... there is no human between your turn and the publish'). Its local `esc()` helper is the only thing standing between a level literal's node id / line2 text and raw HTML landing in that innerHTML sink. It has never been asserted against actual HTML-special input: every existing drawLevel test in level-view.selftest.mjs and the index-level*-wiring selftests uses plain alphanumeric ids ('ore', 'smelter', 'depot', 'src', 's1', 's2', 'a', 'b', 'p', 's'). production.mjs's analyse() places no character restriction on node.id — it is used only as a Map key and echoed into error messages — so nothing in the type system stops a future level literal from carrying an id containing `<`, `>`, `&` or `"`.

Add one test block to plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs: build a minimal level (one source, one sink, one edge — the smallest shape already used elsewhere in this file) whose source id is a string containing HTML-special characters, e.g. `a<b>&"c`. Call `drawLevel(svg, level, feasible(level))` against the plain-object svg stub this file already uses everywhere (`{ innerHTML: '' }` — drawLevel only ever writes to `.innerHTML`, per this file's own existing comment). Assert three things: (a) `feasible()` on the level succeeds first, so the test is fixture sanity, not accidentally exercising production.mjs's own id validation on an unusual string; (b) the escaped form (`a<b>&"c`) appears somewhere in `svg.innerHTML`; (c) the CONTROL — the raw, unescaped substring `<b>` does NOT appear anywhere in `svg.innerHTML`. (c) is what actually proves the escaping ran: (b) alone would still pass if esc() were accidentally a no-op that happened to leave the escaped-looking text in some other unrelated spot, so the negative check on the raw tag is the one that catches a broken or bypassed esc() call, same 'checker that fails correct work is worse than no checker' discipline this repo already applies elsewhere (solids.mjs's header).

This is defense-in-depth coverage, not a claim that any level shipped today is attacker-controlled — every id currently in plant/levels/*.mjs is a hand-written literal. The value is closing the one untested path between a level's data and the page's live HTML output, on the one file in this repo where a broken escape would be invisible to every other gate (production.selftest.mjs never touches rendering; view.selftest.mjs covers the summon inspector's SVG, not a level's).

Bounded paths: plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs only. No changes to level-view.js — esc() already escapes correctly by inspection ('&','<','>','"' are all in its replacement map); this proves it rather than changing it, so a failed attempt leaves the tree exactly as it found it (R6). Independent of the production.mjs ticket above: different file, no shared fixtures, no ordering between them (R4).

beads.title: A bead could never change class: --tag unioned, and classOf takes the first class tag
beads.body:
The three highest-priority beads in the ready queue were all class-b, all
well-written, and all unreachable — and the reason was a missing verb, not a
missing decision.

classOf() returns the FIRST class-[a-d] tag on a bead, and `beads.mjs set --tag`
could only UNION tags. So a bead tagged class-b could never become class-a: the
union keeps class-b, classOf keeps returning 'b', and the bead stays
undispatchable regardless of what else is added. Reclassification — an ordinary
operation on any ticket system — was structurally impossible, and the only route
was to drop the bead and file a replacement, discarding its edges and history to
change one word.

The tick was therefore correct every time it reported "6 ready, none class A" and
staffed a plan seat. It was correct about the queue and wrong about the world:
there WAS next-phase work sitting in front of it, correctly specified, that no
sequence of loop actions could reach.

Fixed by adding `--untag` to `beads.mjs set`, applied before `--tag` so
`--untag class-b --tag class-a` reads left to right.

The general shape, which this repo keeps rediscovering: a queue can be starved by
its own vocabulary. Before concluding there is no work, check whether the work is
merely unsayable.

beads.title: foamworld ported into plant/ — the pocket primitive the next phase was blocked on
beads.body:
`plant/foamworld.js` is a port of `foam/foamworld.js`, byte-identical at the time of
the port, plus a header noting the provenance. `plant/test/foamworld.selftest.mjs`
came with it and passes: 184 checks over 8 seeds.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A FILE COPY. `generatePocket` and `reformPocket` are the
only code in the repo that knows what a real pocket is — seeds, closure, navigation,
the indestructible hull. Without them in plant/, "placement in a real pocket" was
not merely unscheduled, it was unbuildable: the loop cannot write foam/, so any
ticket needing a pocket was pointed at a tree its worker could not reach. Two of the
three next-phase beads were in that state.

Note the shape of what that absence produced: plant/solids.mjs's seedGap() was
written by READING foam/foamworld.js:721-722 and reimplementing it, because the file
could not be imported. That duplication is now removable, and until it is removed
the two must be changed together.

The port was done by the operator rather than by a turn, deliberately.
Transcription is mechanical, has no judgement in it, and a model turn spent copying
798 lines is a turn not spent on anything a model is for.

beads.title: reformPocket does not refuse an out-of-bounds point — it CLAMPS it and plants somewhere else, silently
beads.body:
foamworld.js:734-738 runs the requested point through Math.min/Math.max into x in [1,W-1], y in [0.8,H-0.8], z in [1,D-1] BEFORE the seed-gap check, and then plants the clamped point. The return value is a perfectly good pocket. Nothing in the signature, the return, or the existing selftest says the seed is not where you asked for it.

For navigation that is a harmless convenience. For a SUMMON it is a bug wearing a success: a constellation whose centre moved is no longer the solid that solids.mjs verified, and every neighbour moved with it. Worse, the seed-gap check runs against the CLAMPED point, so a verdict computed at the requested position is a verdict about a position the kernel is never going to use — which is why placement.mjs checks hull first and treats out-of-hull as a refusal rather than mirroring the clamp.

TWO CONSEQUENCES BEYOND THIS FILE.

1. ANY test of reformPocket that asserts `!== null` is asserting something weaker than it reads. The honest oracle is "did the seed land where it was asked": q.seeds[q.seeds.length-1] compared componentwise against the request. placement.selftest.mjs uses that form throughout, and one of its assertions (the foam does not plant [0.5, 18.9, 38] as asked) is TRUE under both branches — refused, or clamped and relocated — which is what makes it safe to assert unconditionally.

2. THE MARGINS ARE ASYMMETRIC BETWEEN AXES: 1 on x and z, 0.8 on y. That reads as a typo and is not. It is pinned in the gate now so it cannot drift silently.

General shape, and this repo has the pattern already: a function that SILENTLY REPAIRS its input is indistinguishable from one that accepted it, and the caller that needed to know cannot find out from the return value. Clamping is a repair. The only fix from outside is to compare what came back against what you asked for.

beads.title: The anisotropic constellation is an INVERSION — w = 2r·v/|v|², which gives closed-form self-gaps and proves all five solids clear at r=1.6
beads.body:
Needed to know whether every solid is self-compatible at r=1.6 without being able to run anything. Deriving it turned out to be worth more than the answer.

Work in the metric-transformed space where the anisotropic gap is an ordinary Euclidean length: let M = diag(1, aniso, 1), and map a point p to w = M^(1/2)·p. Then seedGap(a,b) = |w_a − w_b| exactly.

constellation() places a neighbour for unit face-normal u at p = 2r·M⁻¹u/(uᵀM⁻¹u). Put v = M^(−1/2)u = (ux, uy/√aniso, uz), so uᵀM⁻¹u = |v|², and

    w = 2r · v / |v|²

which is the INVERSION of v in a sphere of radius √(2r). Two facts fall straight out of the standard inversion identity |v/|v|² − v'/|v'|²| = |v−v'|/(|v||v'|):

    gap(centre, i)      = 2r / |v_i|
    gap(neighbour i, j) = 2r · |v_i − v_j| / (|v_i|·|v_j|)

Everything follows. |v|² = 1 − uy²(1 − 1/aniso), so |v| ≤ 1 always ⇒ every centre-to-neighbour gap is ≥ 2r, with equality exactly when uy = 0 — which is the already-recorded 'cube's minimum self-gap is EXACTLY 2r' result, now as a corollary rather than a special case, and it says WHY: only the uy=0 pairs achieve the bound, for every solid.

And since |v_i − v_j| ≥ |u_i − u_j|/√aniso while |v_i||v_j| ≤ 1,

    min neighbour gap ≥ 2r · |u_i − u_j| / √aniso ≥ 2r · 2·sin(θ_min/2) / √aniso

for θ_min the smallest angle between two face normals of the solid. At r=1.6, aniso=2.2 the tightest solid is the icosahedron (20 normals = dodecahedron vertices, θ_min = 41.81°, |Δu| = 0.7136): bound = 3.2·0.7136/1.4832 = 1.540 ≥ 1.5. It clears, and the four sparser solids clear by much more (dodecahedron 2.27, octahedron 2.49, cube 3.05, tetrahedron 3.52). Spot-checking three actual icosahedron pairs numerically gives ~2.28, so the bound is loose by ~50% and the real margin is comfortable.

WHY THIS IS WORTH KEEPING. selfCompatible() is an O(n²) loop that answers yes/no for one r. This says min-self-gap is LINEAR in r with a per-solid constant, so 'what is the smallest r at which a dodecahedron can exist at all' is division, not search — and any future placement UI that wants to scale a summon down to fit does not need to probe. It also explains the shape of the trap solids.mjs warns about: the inversion is what maps a uniform sphere of normals to a NON-uniform set of seed distances, and the cube is exempt only because all six of its normals sit at the two extremes (uy ∈ {0, ±1}) where |v| takes its boundary values.

beads.title: Some pocket seeds sit OUTSIDE the placeable hull — generation clamps to 0.3, placement clamps to 0.8
beads.body:
buildPocket clamps generated seeds to y in [0.3, H−0.3] (and x,z to [0.4, W−0.4]); reformPocket clamps a PLANTED point to y in [0.8, H−0.8] and x,z to [1, W−1]. The two are different, so a pocket legitimately contains seeds at positions where nothing can be planted.

It bit while writing the gate. The obvious way to test 'a refusal names its colliding seed' is to ask about a point standing exactly on a pocket seed — but for a ramp seed on the bottom or top layer (jitterY 0.75 at layerH 9 puts layer-0 seeds as low as the 0.3 clamp), the predicate correctly answers 'hull', not 'seed', and an assertion expecting 'seed' fails against correct behaviour. The gate filters to comfortably-interior seeds first and says why.

Worth knowing for anything that reasons about seeds and placement together: the seed set is NOT a subset of the placeable region, and the two clamps are unrelated constants that were never written to agree.

beads.title: Out-of-hull is a REFUSAL, not a clamp — the predicate deliberately diverges from reformPocket here
beads.body:
reformPocket clamps and succeeds. placement.mjs refuses and names the wall. That is a divergence, chosen, and it changes what 'agreement with the real refusal' can even mean — so the gate's oracle is 'did the seed land where it was asked', not 'did reform return non-null'.

WHY. A summon is a shape with a verified geometry and a position the player chose. Clamping moves the centre and every neighbour with it, producing a solid at a place nobody asked for; accepting that as success would make the predicate agree with the kernel and disagree with the player. The alternative — mirror the clamp, report ok:true for out-of-bounds points, and let the caller notice the relocation — was rejected because it pushes a silent-repair bug onto every future caller, and the whole point of this predicate is that the caller does not have to attempt the insert to find out.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT. A UI that wants drag-to-place with the summon sliding along the wall rather than going red at the boundary. That is a legitimate feel, and it is buildable on top of this rather than instead of it: clampToHull() is exported precisely so the divergence is inspectable and a caller can opt into the kernel's behaviour explicitly.

beads.title: The predicate claims a NECESSARY condition only, and the gate asserts the two directions asymmetrically
beads.body:
reformPocket returns null for three different reasons: the point is too close to a seed, the reformed complex fails the closure gate, or the target chamber loses its floor. Only the first is decidable without doing the rebuild — and the rebuild is the whole cost the predicate exists to avoid. So a predicate that claimed 'ok:true means it will work' would be lying about two of the three.

What is claimed: ok:false ⇒ certain refusal. That is the direction a UI needs (never offer a placement the foam will reject) and it is a theorem, so the gate asserts it unconditionally on every sample, with live reformPocket calls.

The converse is asserted only on points foamworld.selftest.mjs ALREADY PROVES are reformable at this seed and these opts. That is deliberate and it is the part I would defend hardest: I could have sampled a dozen predicate-legal points and asserted they all plant, and it would probably have passed — but a closure failure at any one of them would fail the gate for a reason that is not the predicate's fault, and I would have had no way to tell the two apart from inside. Borrowing an existing passing assertion converts a probabilistic check into a certain one at no loss of strength, because the pair still pins both degenerate answers: constant-false dies on the accept direction, constant-true dies on the refusal direction.

REJECTED: weakening the existence search at the end of section 4 into 'at least N of M plant'. That is exactly the shape the judge is told to look for — a gate made to pass by loosening an assertion. It is written as an existence claim instead, which is what it honestly is, with the reason stated in the file.

beads.title: Self-compatibility is pinned against a seedless STUB pocket, not against the real one
beads.body:
Whether a constellation's own seeds fight each other has nothing to do with any particular pocket — it asks whether the shape could be planted anywhere. Testing it inside the real pocket would mean finding a centre with enough clearance that no seed or hull refusal masks the self refusal, which makes the assertion depend on the fixture's geometry for no gain.

So the boundary is pinned against { W, H, D, seeds: [], faces: [], opts: { aniso } } — exactly the fields legalSummon reads — where hull and seed refusals are impossible by construction and only the self rule can fire. That makes r=0.74 (min self-gap 1.48, refused) and r=0.76 (1.52, allowed) an exact two-sided pin on the 1.5 threshold, using the already-proven fact that a cube's minimum self-gap is EXACTLY 2r with no floating-point slack.

What would make this dishonest: if the stub let the test avoid the real pocket entirely. It does not — every hull, seed and agreement assertion runs against generatePocket(seed 2) and real reformPocket calls. The stub is used for the one property that is genuinely pocket-independent, and the file says so.

beads.title: When a player aims at ground that will not take a summon, should the game refuse, snap, or never let the click happen?
beads.body:
The predicate can now answer "is this legal" before anything is attempted, which means the design question is no longer blocked by the maths — it is blocked by taste, and it is the next fork in wiring this into something playable.

Three honest options, and they build different things. (1) REFUSE THE CLICK and say why — the constraint is a failure the player can actually hit, which is what the bar for "playable" in vision.md asks for, but a refusal with no guidance is just a wall. (2) SNAP to the nearest legal position — generous, always succeeds, and it removes the failure entirely; the constraint stops being a mechanic and becomes a formatting rule. (3) SHOW BUILDABLE SPACE as an overlay so the illegal click is never available — what most factory games do, and it turns the constraint into information rather than into a refusal.

I cannot decide this from here because all three are correct implementations of the same predicate and the difference is entirely in how it FEELS to be told no. I have deliberately not guessed: placement.mjs supports all three (refusals carry their cause, clampToHull is exported, and the coarse sphere test exists to make sweeping a whole grid cheap enough for an overlay).

DO: Open any factory or builder game you already have — Factorio, Satisfactory, Dorfromantik, Minecraft, whichever is nearest — and deliberately try to place something on ground that will not take it. Do it three or four times in a row rather than once.

WATCH FOR: Whether being refused taught you where you COULD build, or only that you could not build there. And whether you noticed the refusal at all, or whether the game had already made the bad click impossible before you reached for it.

SO THAT: REFUSE: I build refusalLine() (proposed above) and a rejection the player can read, and the next level is designed around ground that runs out. SNAP: I build nearestLegal() — a search over the buildable set for the closest legal centre — and stop treating placement as a failure state at all, which also means the "something that can fail" in the playable bar has to come from somewhere else and I need to know that early. OVERLAY: I build the buildable-space sweep into a drawable mask first, which is a different and larger piece of work than either of the others, and it should be scheduled before any level that needs it rather than after.

beads.title: Gate 6, the build certificate: is there a legal ORDER to build this factory in this pocket?
beads.body:
FACTORIO.md §4 and vision priority 2. A factory can be satisfiable (gate 5 says so) and still impossible to BUILD, because the pieces go into a real pocket one at a time and each one changes what space is left. Until now this was unbuildable: nothing could say whether a pocket had room for one summon, let alone a sequence. That is fixed — plant/placement.mjs decides one summon and plant/production.mjs already exports buildOrder(), a topological construction order over the recipe network.

WHAT TO BUILD: plant/buildcert.mjs, exporting certify(pocket, network, layout) where layout maps each network node to a { solid, centre, r }. Walk buildOrder(network); for each node in turn, ask whether its constellation is legal against the pocket state AS IT WILL BE after the previous steps — not against the empty pocket. The state that matters is the accumulated seed set, so this is legalSummon against a running seed list plus pairGap between the new constellation and every already-placed one (pairGap exists in solids.mjs and placement.mjs does not use it, precisely because a single summon never needs it).

The answer must be constructive in both directions, the same way feasible() is: on success return the order and each step's clearance margin; on failure name the STEP that could not be placed, what it collided with (placement.mjs's refusal records carry this already), and whether a different order would have helped — a step blocked by the hull or by a pre-existing pocket seed is unfixable by reordering, a step blocked by an EARLIER step in the same build is exactly the case where order matters. That distinction is the whole content of the certificate; without it this is just legalSummon in a loop.

DELIBERATELY OUT OF SCOPE: searching for a layout. Given positions, decide. Choosing positions is a placement problem and a separate ticket — conflating them turns an exact decision procedure into a search, which is the mistake production.mjs correctly refused to make with fan-out.

THE GATE IT CREATES: plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs, which must (a) certify a two-node chain in a real generatePocket at a fixed seed and verify the certificate by ACTUALLY planting every seed in the certified order via reformPocket, asserting each insert lands where the certificate said it would — agreement with the real kernel is the claim, exactly as in placement.selftest.mjs; (b) exhibit a layout that is feasible() -ok but NOT buildable, so the two oracles are shown to be independent rather than one implying the other; (c) exhibit a layout that fails in one order and succeeds in another, and assert the certificate distinguishes the reorderable failure from the unfixable one. Note that (a) is the expensive assertion — one reformPocket per seed — so use the MACRO opts (nx 4, nz 4, layers 3, subLayers 1, cell 20, layerH 9) that foamworld.selftest.mjs and placement.selftest.mjs both use to keep it fast.

Depends on nothing that does not exist. Bounded to plant/buildcert.mjs and plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs.

[turn 38 — done] IMPORTANT AND STATED FIRST: plant/buildcert.mjs and plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs ALREADY EXISTED on disk, committed and complete, before this turn began. I did not write them and I will not claim I did. Grepping .github/loop/ for 'buildcert' returns exactly one hit — the bead text itself — so the ledger has no record of the work that produced them. The loop dispatched a turn to build an artifact it had already built and forgotten. So what I actually did was AUDIT the existing deliverable against the ticket and then strengthen its gate. The audit was by hand-trace only (no Bash in this tool grant, so I could not run the gate): I verified the fixture facts (80x36x80, 64 seeds, aniso 2.2) are copied verbatim from placement.selftest.mjs's already-passing assertions rather than derived; that buildOrder's Kahn queue is FIFO over nodes order, so the two pinned orders ['ore','depot'] and ['a','b','sa','sb'] are right; that analyse() does NOT require a source to have an outgoing edge, so section 4's single-node SOLO network is accepted rather than throwing; that all five BLAME_PRECEDENCE kinds are genuinely reachable (I recomputed the cube hull case — the -x neighbour sits at exactly centre-2r = -1.2, outside [1,W-1], wall B4 — and the r=0.74/0.76 self-gap boundary, which is exactly 2r=1.48 vs 1.52 by the ledger's own proof that a cube's minimum self-gap is exactly 2r); that every throw message matches its regex; and that the order-invariance claim is a real theorem, not a hope (cert.clearance is the min over cross-owner seed pairs, each counted at the later of its two steps, so the multiset of measured gaps is identical under every topological order). Then two changes, both to the gate. (1) Removed an assertion conjunct that could never fail: line 330 read JSON.stringify(h.blames) === undefined, but blames lives on h.failure, so it compared undefined to undefined on every run. The real check was already on the next line. (2) The substantive one: the certificate's headline constructive output — clearance and margin — was only ever asserted SELF-consistently (positive, and margin === clearance - 1.5). Every such assertion is satisfied by whatever number the walk returns, including one from a nearest() that took the max, or that measured against the pocket alone and ignored the seeds the earlier step had just committed — which is precisely the behaviour that separates this file from legalSummon in a loop. I pinned it against an independent re-derivation from solids.mjs primitives (step 0 against the 64 pocket seeds; step 1 against those AND step 0's five), pinned cert.clearance as the tightest step, and added a check on the owner bookkeeping (a nearest pointing into the pocket must report owner null, one pointing at a planted seed must name its node) because the pocket-vs-step failure taxonomy that section 3 rests on is built on that distinction and nothing tested it. HONESTY ON THE GATE: I could not execute it. My additions are exact re-derivations using the same primitives in the same argument order (seedGap is bit-symmetric — it squares its differences through Math.hypot — so the min is bit-identical), and they are written with 1e-12 tolerances rather than ===, so a rounding surprise cannot redden them; the mutations they exist to catch move the number by metres.
evidence: revived by operator 2026-08-05: rejected with no reason recorded; this is FACTORIO.md gate 6 and vision.md priority 2

beads.title: Make a refused placement legible to a player: refusalLine() over placement.mjs's verdicts
beads.body:
Vision item 1 says the bar for playable is "an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for". placement.mjs now produces real refusals with everything needed to explain them — the seed index and the actual gap, or the hull wall and how far outside — and every one of them is currently a JavaScript object nobody can read.

WHAT TO BUILD: a pure function refusalLine(verdict) in plant/level-view.js, alongside the existing verdictLine(), turning a legalSummon result into one sentence a person understands, with no jargon. Not "seed 41 at gap 1.21 < 1.5" but something closer to "too close to the rock on your left — about half a metre short". Three shapes to cover, because they are three different player mistakes: a collision with existing ground, a piece of the shape poking through the pocket wall, and a shape too small to hold itself apart (the self case, which is a property of the summon rather than the place, and should read that way).

TWO THINGS IT MUST GET RIGHT, both learned the hard way in this tree. First: report EVERY refusal, not just the first — verdictLine() shipped with exactly that bug (it read deficits[0] and dropped the rest) and legalSummon deliberately returns the full list so the same mistake is not available here. A summon fouling three seeds should say three, or say "and two more", never silently pick one. Second: the sentence must not contradict the predicate. The bug that failed turn 9's gate was a test asserting a band the implementation did not produce; here the equivalent is a sentence claiming a distance the verdict does not carry. Derive every number in the string from the verdict object, never recompute it.

THE GATE: node plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs, which exists and passes today. Add a block that builds refusals with the real predicate against a real generatePocket fixture — not hand-written verdict literals, which would let the sentence and the predicate drift apart — and asserts the sentence names the right count and the right cause for each of the three shapes, plus a CONTROL that a legal summon produces no refusal line at all.

Bounded to plant/level-view.js and plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs. No new file, no new gate: this is class-a against an existing green test, which is the cheap half of connecting the predicate to something a person can meet.

[turn 41 — done] Added refusalLine(verdict) to plant/level-view.js — a pure function turning a legalSummon refusal into one jargon-free sentence — and a six-part block in plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs that builds every verdict with the real predicate against the real generatePocket macro fixture (seed 2, the same one placement.selftest.mjs uses). It groups refusals by reason in the order the predicate produced them and emits one clause per reason, so a summon that fouls three seeds says 'in 3 places' and a summon that both collides and pokes out gets both sentences; within a group it names the WORST (largest shortfall / deepest protrusion), earliest-wins on a tie. Every distance is read off the verdict (need/gap/depth) and the only arithmetic is need-gap, mirroring verdictLine's demand-achieved; the gate parses the number back OUT of the sentence and compares it to the verdict within rounding, which is the check that stops the sentence claiming a distance the predicate did not measure. The three shapes the ticket names are covered by fixtures whose refusal counts are provable rather than hoped for: a cube centred on a pocket seed at least 6 m from every wall (so every refusal is provably a seed collision), a cube at [1.2,18,1.2] whose -x and -z neighbours land exactly 3.0 m outside (exactly two hull refusals, hand-derived from 2r=3.2), and a cube at r=0.74 on a coarselyClear centre (exactly four self refusals at gap 1.48 vs need 1.5 — derived pair by pair from the cube's six axis normals). Plus a CONTROL that a legal summon returns null, a CONTROL that the floor gets its own word so 'the wall' is not a constant, a CONTROL that r=0.76 is not refused at all, the metric branch pinned so no refusal can fall through to an empty clause, and a sweep over placement.selftest.mjs's own 784-centre lattice asserting the property (every distinct reason named, every count>1 stated, no undefined/NaN) on every refusing candidate rather than on three chosen ones. HONESTLY: I could not run the gate — this turn had Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep and no Bash — so every fixture count above is hand-derived, not executed. I deliberately made each one derivable from constants rather than from where the generator happened to put its seeds, and both search loops (the coarselyClear centre and the legal centre) use placement.selftest.mjs's exact lattice so their existence is inherited from a test that passes today rather than being a fresh bet. refusalLine is NOT wired into index.html — that is outside this ticket's bounded paths, and it is proposed below.

beads.title: The frame budget's dominant term is not the rebuild cost — it is that ONE SUMMON IS 13 REBUILDS, and lp-f25c2f is the whole lever
beads.body:
Measuring gate 7 turned up something bigger than the number it was asked for.

`reformPocket` plants ONE seed. `constellation()` returns 13 seeds for a dodecahedron, and its own docstring says the array is there 'to hand to an atomic multi-insert' — which does not exist. `placement.mjs`'s `legalSummon` states the consequence plainly in its `self` refusal: 'a multi-insert plants them one at a time and the kernel checks each new seed against the ones already down'.

So TODAY, one summon costs |seeds| full lattice rebuilds:

    tetrahedron   5 rebuilds
    cube          7
    octahedron    9
    dodecahedron 13
    icosahedron  21

And each rebuild is Θ(n²) in the TOTAL seed count, which the summon is itself raising as it goes. A dodecahedron summoned into the 294-seed shipping pocket is thirteen rebuilds of a ~300-cell complex, back to back, while the player waits.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE PER-REBUILD NUMBER. Every micro-optimisation of `buildComplex` is bounded by what a constant factor can buy. Batching the insert is a 13× win on the exact workload the game is made of, and it is already specified: `lp-f25c2f`, 'Atomic multi-insert: reformPocket for a constellation', which has been sitting in the ready queue tagged class-b. It was scoped as a CORRECTNESS ticket (a constellation lands or nothing does). This says it is also, and probably mainly, THE performance ticket — and gate 7 now exists to price it, which is exactly the argument that justified building gate 7 in the first place.

The generalisable bit: a per-operation cost measurement answers 'how expensive is the operation'. It does not answer 'how many operations does one user action cost', and that second number was the larger one here by an order of magnitude. Measure the unit the PLAYER experiences, not the unit the API exposes. This gate currently measures the API's unit and says so; it cannot measure the player's until the multi-insert exists.

beads.title: The budget that FAILS this gate is 2× the budget the product actually needs, and the product number is reported instead of asserted
beads.body:
The ticket requires a named constant with a documented provenance that the gate fails on. Two candidates, and I took neither on its own.

THE PRODUCT NUMBER is 1000 ms — the one-second limit (Miller 1968; Card, Robertson & Mackinlay 1991; Nielsen's middle response-time threshold), the longest delay over which a person still feels they are manipulating the thing rather than waiting for a machine. Below ~0.1 s feels instantaneous and is simply not reachable for a full voronoi rebuild; above ~10 s attention is gone. A plant is a turn and the player is waiting on it, so 1000 ms is the right requirement.

I did NOT assert it. The measurement is taken on a two-core shared CI runner, which is neither the target device nor a stable one. A gate that fails on runner weather is the gate someone deletes, and a deleted gate protects nothing — which is the exact failure mode the ticket names in requirement (c). So `FLOW_LIMIT_MS = 1000` is REPORTED, along with the thing the game actually needs to know (how many summons fit inside it), and `PER_TURN_BUDGET_MS = 2000` is what fails the gate.

WHAT I GIVE UP BY DOING THAT, stated rather than hidden: at 2× headroom the absolute threshold only catches roughly a 7× regression at the largest fixture. That is why it is not the only assertion. The exponent ceiling (2.75, against an expected 2.0–2.4) catches an algorithmic class change that no absolute threshold on a fast machine would ever see, and the normalised ms-per-(100 seeds)² ceiling catches a constant-factor blow-up independently of which fixture sizes happened to get measured.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE THIS: one real measurement. Once the gate has run on CI even once, the honest constant is 'N× the number it printed', and every threshold here should be re-derived from that instead of from my estimate. I would rather ship a gate with defensible-but-loose constants than no gate, and the file says which constants are which.

REJECTED: a machine-independent ratio (reform cost ÷ generation cost) as the primary assertion. It is genuinely immune to machine speed, and that is also its flaw — a regression inside `buildComplex` slows both sides equally and the ratio does not move. It would have been a gate that could not see the most likely defect.

beads.title: A benchmark can stay inside its own time budget by using its own fit to decide what it can afford to measure
beads.body:
Requirement (c) — run in under ten seconds — is in tension with the most valuable measurement in the file, which is a plant at the SHIPPING density (294 seeds). That one call is predicted to cost more than the entire rest of the benchmark, and its cost is the thing being measured, so it cannot be known in advance.

The resolution, which I have not seen written down elsewhere in this repo and which generalises: the benchmark fits its curve on the cheap fixtures FIRST, then uses that fit to predict what the expensive measurement will cost, and only takes it if the prediction fits in the remaining budget. A skipped check logs SKIPPED and says explicitly that the extrapolation is unverified on that run.

Three guards, staggered on purpose, and the stagger is the part that matters: entry to a new fixture is gated ~2.5 s before the sampling deadline, because GENERATING a fixture is itself unbudgeted work and a machine that crawls must decline to start a pocket it cannot afford rather than discover that halfway through. The out-of-sample plant is additionally capped at exactly one rebuild attempt, so a late refusal loses the check instead of starting a second unbudgeted rebuild.

Net effect: on a machine ~10× slower than the estimate this file was written against, the gate loses the 6×6 fixture and the out-of-sample check, still fits an exponent over a 1.57× span of n, and finishes inside ~8 s. On a machine ~20× slower it fails — and it fails with 'at least two fixture sizes were measured' rather than with a timeout, which is the correct message, because at that point the kernel really is slower than gate 7 assumes.

beads.title: Do not assert a timing residual on individual samples — it is a flake generator wearing a goodness-of-fit label
beads.body:
The ticket asks, correctly, that a shape claim be checked by fitting and asserting the residual rather than by checking one N. My first version asserted that no single timed plant was more than 3.5× off the fitted curve.

That assertion cannot survive contact with a real runner. A rebuild at the small fixture is tens of milliseconds; one GC pause inside it is a 3–4× outlier all by itself, and the voronoi build allocates heavily (a fresh mesh per cell, Maps keyed by strings in the weld pass). The assertion would have failed on garbage collection and been read as a regression.

The residual is now asserted on FIXTURE MEDIANS — one point per pocket size — with the worst single sample printed alongside for information. A median over three samples absorbs a GC pause; a fixture whose median sits 2× off the curve means the model is genuinely wrong, which is the thing worth failing on.

The general shape, and it applies to any timing gate anyone adds here: aggregate before you assert. The statistic you assert on must be one that noise cannot move much and a real regression moves a lot. Individual wall-clock samples fail both halves of that test, and the fact that they are the raw data makes them look like the honest thing to assert on.

beads.title: Is a one-second pause after placing a factory piece a hitch, or is it the world reforming around you?
beads.body:
I asserted the budget from literature, not from taste, and taste is what actually decides it. Gate 7's product number is 1000 ms — the classic one-second limit, below which a person still feels they are directly manipulating the thing. That is the right number for a BUTTON. A plant is not a button: the whole lattice visibly reforms around the seed, and in that context a pause can read as weight and consequence rather than as a hitch. Games trade on exactly that difference and no benchmark can tell them apart.

This is not decidable from here for two reasons. I cannot run anything this turn, so I have no number at all; and even with the number, whether 900 ms of foam reforming feels good is not a property of the measurement. What I already did instead: picked 1000 ms with its provenance written into the file, and made the ASSERTED threshold 2x that so a runner's weather cannot fail the gate — so nothing is blocked on this answer, only calibrated by it.

DO: Once this gate has run on CI, open the run log and read the block headed 'what this means for the game' — it prints the predicted per-turn cost at the shipping pocket and, for each solid, how many summons fit inside the 1000 ms limit. Then judge the number against the feel you want: is a pause of that length after clicking 'summon' acceptable, welcome, or unacceptable?

WATCH FOR: Whether the number is in the hundreds of milliseconds or the seconds, and whether the answer changes between a small summon (tetrahedron, 5 seeds) and a big one (icosahedron, 21). A budget that a tetrahedron meets and an icosahedron blows is a DESIGN lever, not just a performance problem — it prices the big solids in real time.

SO THAT: If a second or so is fine, gate 7's thresholds stand as written and no optimisation work should be scheduled at all — I close the performance thread and the proposal above stays unpromoted. If it is too slow, the atomic multi-insert (lp-f25c2f) becomes the highest-value performance ticket in the backlog by roughly an order of magnitude, and the proposal above should be promoted first to give it a before-number. If you want the pause to be LONGER for weight, say so and I will stop treating this as a cost at all and start treating it as an animation budget, which is a different ticket entirely.

beads.title: Price the sequential-summon path, so the atomic multi-insert has a number to beat
beads.body:
Gate 7 (`plant/test/frame-budget.selftest.mjs`) now prices ONE PLANT. It does not price one SUMMON, and the gap between those is the largest single term in the frame budget: with no atomic multi-insert, a summon is |seeds| sequential `reformPocket` calls — 5 for a tetrahedron, 13 for a dodecahedron, 21 for an icosahedron — each a full Theta(n^2) rebuild, against a seed count the summon is itself raising as it goes.

WHAT TO BUILD: extend `plant/frame-budget.mjs` with `summonSeries(pocket, con, opts)` — plant every seed of a constellation in order, timing each rebuild — and a gate that reports the TOTAL wall clock of one complete summon, per solid, at the proven 4x4 MACRO fixture (seed 2, the one `foamworld.selftest.mjs` and `placement.selftest.mjs` both already use). Screen each seed with `legalSummon` first so a refusal is never mistaken for a cheap sample. Report the per-solid total and the ratio against a single plant at the same n.

WHY IT IS WORTH A TURN. `lp-f25c2f` (atomic multi-insert) is already specified as a CORRECTNESS ticket — a constellation lands or nothing does. This measurement says it is also the performance ticket, and a ~13x claim with no before-number is a claim nobody can check. This produces the before-number, and it does it against work that already exists rather than waiting on work that does not.

THE GATE IT CREATES: `plant/test/summon-cost.selftest.mjs`, which must (a) report a total-summon cost for at least three solids and FAIL if any exceeds a named constant with its provenance in a comment; (b) assert the deterministic part separately from the timing — that the number of rebuilds a summon costs is exactly `SUMMON_SEEDS[solid]` (5/7/9/13/21), which is exact arithmetic and is the claim the whole ticket rests on; and (c) run in under five seconds, using the same deadline-guard pattern gate 7 uses, so the two together stay inside a suite anyone will keep running.

RANKING, honestly: this is vision item 4 work (the frame budget), and vision item 1 (turning six levels into one game) outranks it. Promote it only when there is capacity that is not going to item 1.

NOTE FOR WHOEVER PROMOTES: this is class-a plus creates-gate. `plant/test/summon-cost.selftest.mjs` must NOT exist at promotion time, and the turn is judged on the file appearing, passing, and breaking nothing that passed before.

beads.title: The relay must be fed by nothing else in the whole network — a guard the ticket did not ask for, and without which the closed form is simply wrong
beads.body: The ticket's relay conditions require the SINK behind P to be fed by nothing else, but say nothing about P itself. That gap is fatal to the algebra. The whole derivation rests on P's supply being exactly R*share: that is what makes the headroom precondition (capacity*inputRate >= R) sufficient to guarantee P is supply-bound at every share in (0,1], and it is what makes delivered rate linear in share. If P has any other incoming edge, its supply is R*share + outside, so (a) the headroom bound no longer covers the worst case and P can silently become capacity-bound, and (b) effectiveDemand = S.demand/k over-states what this group has to deliver. Added `inDegree(P) === 1` and a paired CONTROL (4b). I also added `outgoing[0].share === undefined` — a relay that already splits its own output explicitly is not handing its WHOLE output to S, so k is not the right conversion factor. Both fail closed, which is this file's standing discipline: refusing a case is a legitimate answer for an oracle, silently approximating it is not. What would reverse either: nothing short of solving the general LP, at which point autoSplit is the wrong function to be extending.

beads.title: `from.kind === 'source'` is required only when the group CONTAINS a relay, not for every group — otherwise the extension would silently narrow existing behaviour
beads.body: The ticket states the source requirement as group-level and unconditional. Applied literally that would break something already shipped: production.mjs's own header documents autoSplit as handling 'a direct source-or-processor -> sink fan-out', so a PROCESSOR fanning out to several private sinks is a case that works today. Making from.kind === 'source' unconditional would stop splitting those groups — a regression dressed as an extension, and the existing suite would not have caught it because no fixture exercises a processor `from` with implicit shares. So the rule is: R is computed as fromNode.rate when `from` is a source and null otherwise, and qualifyingRelay() refuses a null R. An all-sink group never calls qualifyingRelay, so it never asks, and a processor `from` keeps splitting into sinks exactly as before. This is a strict superset of prior behaviour, which is the only shape an 'extension' should have. The ticket's own WHY supports this reading: the reason given for the source requirement is that R must be constant for the HEADROOM precondition, and headroom only exists for relays.

beads.title: The relay extension's headroom precondition needs a supply-bound/capacity-bound distinction that feasible() computes and then throws away
beads.body:
qualifyingRelay() has to answer 'is P supply-bound at share=1 or capacity-bound' and can only do it by reimplementing the comparison from feasible()'s inner loop (`scale = min(capacity, min supply/inputRate)`) as the algebraic precondition `capacity*inputRate >= R`. feasible() computes exactly which term won that Math.min for every processor on every call, and returns nothing about it — the result carries `achieved`, `deficits` and `margin`, all sink-side.

That is the second consumer to need it (the first is recorded in the ledger as 'feasible() has no visible metric for unrouted fan-out output', which is the same shape one node kind over). It also matters for vision item 1, and that is the bigger point: a player told 'depot is short by 12' has been told the symptom. A player told 'the smelter is at capacity, not starved of ore' has been told what to change. The distinction is already computed and thrown away, on every call, for every processor.

Proposed as a bead below with the existing gate. Deliberately NOT done here: it is outside this ticket's bounded paths in spirit (it changes feasible()'s return shape, which every level and level-view.js reads) and mixing it in would make this turn's diff unreviewable.

beads.title: This turn's own gate is unverifiable in-turn — and unlike the previous ~20 instances, this one had a real chance of a silent regression rather than just an unrun new assertion
beads.body:
Tool grant was Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep, no Bash; the GATE is `node plant/test/production.selftest.mjs`.

What is different this time, and why it is worth one more note rather than a bare tally: most turns in this streak ADDED a new file or a new block, so an unrun gate risked only the new assertions being wrong. This turn REWROTE the condition-(a)/(b) block of a function with five existing CONTROLs depending on its exact refusal behaviour. The realistic failure mode was not 'my new test is wrong', it was 'I silently narrowed autoSplit and the old tests catch it — in CI, one turn later'.

So the mitigation was different in kind: every pre-existing autoSplit fixture in the file was re-traced by hand through the NEW code path, not just the new ones. The one that mattered is the 'destinations are not all sinks' CONTROL, whose processor `p` has whole-network out-degree ZERO — under the new code it is refused by `outgoing.length !== 1` rather than by `to.kind !== 'sink'`, so it still passes, but for a different reason. I updated its comment to say so; a control that passes for a reason nobody wrote down is a control that will be deleted as redundant by someone eventually.

Still inference, not execution. The standing recommendation is unchanged and I am not restating it at length: it is a loop-work.yml fix, and I have no bounded path into .github/workflows/ from this ticket.

beads.title: Does an auto-computed split that accounts for recipe ratios read as helpful, or as the game doing the interesting part for you?
beads.body:
Level 5's header made exactly this critique of autoSplit() and the ledger records it as the best thing this loop has produced: an optimal split computed for you is not a decision, and 'splitting a shared output between competing consumers' is the genre's central decision. This turn made autoSplit STRONGER — it now sees through a processor to the sink behind it and corrects for the recipe ratio, which is precisely the calculation a player would otherwise have to do in their head.

I cannot decide from here whether that is a good tool or a spoiler. The algebra says the answer is right; nothing in the repo says whether being handed it is fun. Both readings are defensible and they point at opposite next tickets, which is why I am spending an ask rather than guessing.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, go to LEVEL_5 (the player-chosen split, two sliders, narrow winnable band) and play it to a win. Then imagine a button labelled 'balance it for me' that instantly sets the correct split — including through a machine that converts 1 ore into 0.6 ingots, so the right answer is not the one the demand numbers suggest.

WATCH FOR: Whether you would press that button, and whether pressing it would end your interest in the level. Specifically: is working out that 0.6 conversion the part that felt like solving something, or the part that felt like arithmetic homework?

SO THAT: If it reads as a SPOILER: autoSplit stays an internal oracle used to author and validate levels, never exposed to the player, and the next ticket is a level where the ratio conversion is the puzzle — a machine whose recipe ratio the player must reason through to set the split.
