If it reads as a HELPFUL TOOL: the next ticket surfaces it as an in-game hint or assist button, and difficulty moves up a layer to constraints autoSplit cannot solve (capacity limits, competing sinks), which is also a concrete ticket. If it reads as NEITHER — interesting maths, boring to meet — that is the strongest possible answer, because it says stop extending the oracle and spend the remaining windows entirely on vision item 1, turning the six levels into one game.

beads.title: feasible() should report WHICH term bound each processor — capacity or a named starved input
beads.body:
feasible()'s inner loop computes `scale = min(capacity, min over inputs of supply/inputRate)` for every processor and discards which term won. Two callers now need it and a third would use it.

WHAT TO BUILD: add a `bound` field to feasible()'s return — `{ processorId: { by: 'capacity' | 'input', resource: string|null, scale: number, headroom: number } }` for every processor in the network, where `by` names the winning term, `resource` names the starved input when `by === 'input'` (null otherwise), and `headroom` is `capacity - scale` (>= 0; zero exactly when capacity-bound). Ties (capacity exactly equal to the binding supply ratio) resolve to 'capacity', and that tie rule must be pinned by an assertion because it is the only judgement call in the change.

WHY, three reasons in ascending order of value:
(1) autoSplit()'s new relay HEADROOM precondition (`capacity*inputRate >= R`) is a hand-derived restatement of that same Math.min comparison living in a second place. Duplicated invariants drift.
(2) The already-recorded finding that feasible() has no visible metric for unrouted fan-out output is the same gap on the output side; this is the input side of it.
(3) VISION ITEM 1. A player told 'depot is short by 12' has been told the symptom. A player told 'the smelter is at capacity — a bigger smelter, not more ore' has been told what to do. level-view.js's verdictLine() currently can only report sink deficits, which is exactly why every level's failure message describes the end of the chain rather than the cause. This is the smallest oracle change that makes a genuinely diagnostic verdict possible, and it needs no new module.

CLASS AND GATE: class-a, gate `node plant/test/production.selftest.mjs` — the file exists and passes today, so this is certified against an existing gate, no createsGate. Bounded paths: plant/production.mjs and plant/test/production.selftest.mjs only. Do NOT change level-view.js in the same ticket; making the UI use it is separate work with its own gate (plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs), and mixing them makes the oracle diff unreviewable.

REQUIRED ASSERTIONS, each with a paired CONTROL in the file's house style:
 · the existing capacity-cap fixture (capacity 0.3, both input ratios 2) reports by:'capacity', resource:null, scale 0.3, headroom 0;
 · the existing convergence CONTROL (a=6/rate3, b=1/rate2, capacity 10) reports by:'input', resource:'b', scale 0.5, headroom 9.5 — it must name the STARVED input 'b', not the ample 'a', which is the assertion that catches an implementation returning merely 'not capacity';
 · a tie fixture where capacity exactly equals the input ratio resolves to 'capacity' (pins the judgement call);
 · every processor in the network appears in `bound`, including one whose scale is 0, and no sink or source does;
 · a no-regression check that the existing `achieved`/`deficits`/`margin` values are byte-identical to what the same fixtures produce today — additive only.

R4 (independence): touches only feasible()'s return, additively. It does not interact with autoSplit(), which reads the network and never calls feasible(). R5: follows directly from the finding filed with the autoSplit relay extension, and from the already-recorded unrouted-output finding.

[turn 33 — done] Added a `bound` field to feasible()'s return: for every processor (and nothing else), which term of `min(capacity, min supply/inputRate)` actually won — `{ by: 'capacity'|'input', resource: string|null, scale, headroom }`. The implementation unrolls the existing Math.min into a strict-`<` scan so the winning term is kept rather than discarded; strict `<` is exactly what makes a tie resolve to 'capacity' and makes the first input achieving the minimum win among inputs. `headroom` is `capacity - scale`, always >= 0 and exactly 0 iff capacity-bound. The change is additive: `ok`/`achieved`/`deficits`/`margin` are computed by the identical arithmetic and `bound` is appended last. New test section covers all five required assertions — the capacity-cap fixture (by 'capacity', resource null, scale 0.3, headroom 0), the convergence CONTROL naming the STARVED input 'b' rather than merely 'not capacity' (scale 0.5, headroom 9.5), the tie pinned from BOTH sides (capacity exactly 2 against ratio 2 -> 'capacity'; a hair above -> 'input'; a hair below -> still 'capacity'), coverage including a processor with no incoming edge at all (scale 0, headroom = full capacity) with sources and sinks asserted absent, and a no-regression block pinning the result's key list and order plus a literal byte-comparison of the pre-existing fields on the integer-valued chain fixture. HONEST LIMITS: (1) this turn had no Bash, so `node plant/test/production.selftest.mjs` was NOT executed — every expected value was hand-traced through the walk (6/3=2 and 1/2=0.5 and 10-0.5=9.5 are all exact in binary floating point, which is why those fixtures were chosen over e.g. the -0.7 margin case) and the one literal JSON comparison deliberately uses only integers and a quarter so float printing cannot bite. (2) I did NOT change autoSplit(), per the ticket — only added a comment at its headroom precondition explaining why it restates the same comparison (it must decide before shares exist, so it cannot call feasible(), which throws on an unsplit fan-out) and pointing at the de-duplication proposal. (3) level-view.js is untouched, per the ticket. I grepped every other consumer of feasible() in plant/: none compares a whole result against a literal or enumerates its keys, so the added field cannot break another selftest.

beads.title: Ties resolve to 'capacity' because that is the only choice that keeps `headroom === 0 iff by === 'capacity'` exactly true
beads.body:
The ticket mandates the tie rule; it does not say why, and the why turns out to be load-bearing. When capacity exactly equals the binding supply ratio, BOTH statements are true, so either answer is defensible on its own. But `headroom` is `capacity - scale`, which at a tie is exactly 0 — so reporting 'input' would produce a processor with zero headroom that claims not to be capacity-bound, and a caller branching on `headroom === 0` would disagree with a caller branching on `by === 'capacity'`. Two fields describing one fact must never disagree. Resolving to 'capacity' makes the invariant exact in both directions, and the selftest asserts it as a biconditional over every processor in the fixture rather than as two separate one-way checks. What would reverse it: if a caller ever needs 'which input is at the edge of binding' at a tie, that is a different question and wants a separate field (e.g. a list of all terms achieving the minimum), not a change to this one.

Second, smaller call, not specified by the ticket: among INPUTS, the FIRST input achieving the minimum wins, in the processor's own `inputs` declaration order. This is what strict `<` gives for free and it matches the determinism discipline analyse()'s Kahn queue already follows (declaration order breaks every tie in this module). It is pinned by a fixture with two inputs at ratio 2 exactly. The alternative — reporting all starved inputs — is strictly more information and is proposed as follow-up rather than smuggled in here, because it changes the field's type.

beads.title: `bound` names ONE starved input even when several are equally starved — the same under-reporting shape as verdictLine's single-deficit bug
beads.body:
The coverage fixture is a processor with no incoming edge at all: every input's supply is 0, so every input's ratio is 0 and they are ALL equally binding. `bound` reports the first one. For a single-input processor that is the whole truth; for a multi-input processor whose supply chain has collapsed, a diagnostic verdict built on this field will tell the player to fix one input when fixing it changes nothing, because the sibling input is equally short.

This is structurally identical to the already-recorded finding that verdictLine()'s fail path reads `v.deficits[0]` and drops every deficit but the first — and it is worth noting that BOTH were introduced by choosing the simplest correct-looking shape (a scalar where the domain has a set). The oracle side is now the second instance in the same file family.

It is not a defect in this ticket: the ticket specifies `resource: string|null`, a scalar, and a scalar is the right first version — the multi-starvation case needs a UI decision (name all of them? name the cheapest to fix?) that no gate can settle. But anything that renders this field should be written knowing it is a representative, not an exhaustive answer. The clean fix, if it is ever wanted, is an additional `starved: string[]` alongside `resource`, keeping `resource` as `starved[0]` so nothing that reads it today breaks.

The fixture that makes this visible is already in the gate (`starved`, scale 0, headroom = full capacity); what is NOT asserted is which of several equally-starved inputs is named, because that would pin a behaviour I have just argued is arbitrary.

beads.title: autoSplit()'s headroom precondition cannot be replaced by a feasible() call — it has to decide BEFORE the shares exist
beads.body:
Reason (1) in this ticket's body is that `qualifyingRelay`'s `capacity*inputRate >= R` is a hand-derived restatement of feasible()'s own Math.min comparison living in a second place, and duplicated invariants drift. Now that `bound` exposes the comparison, the obvious de-duplication is to have autoSplit ask feasible(). IT CANNOT: autoSplit runs on a network whose fan-out group is still unsplit, and feasible() THROWS on an unsplit fan-out ('without an explicit share'). So the caller that most needs the answer is precisely the one that cannot obtain it from the function that computes it.

The honest de-duplication is therefore a small shared pure helper — `boundBy(capacity, inputs, supplyOf)` returning the same `{ by, resource, scale }` — called by feasible()'s walk with real supply and by qualifyingRelay with the hypothetical worst-case supply `R * 1`. That is a real refactor with a real risk of changing autoSplit's refusal set, which is why it is proposed as its own bead rather than folded in here; the ticket's R4 explicitly says this change must not interact with autoSplit.

Recorded because the next person to look at this will have the same idea I did and should not have to rediscover why the direct call is impossible. A comment saying so now sits at the precondition itself.

beads.title: Gate unverifiable in-turn again (no Bash) — noting only what is NEW about this instance
beads.body: The standing recommendation is already in the ledger past twenty times and I am not restating it. What is worth one line is the risk PROFILE of this particular unrun turn, which is unusually low and for a specific reason: every expected number in the new assertions was chosen to be exactly representable in binary floating point (6/3 = 2, 1/2 = 0.5, 10 - 0.5 = 9.5, 0.3 - 0.3 = 0), so the assertions use `===` rather than a tolerance and cannot fail on a rounding surprise. The one place a tolerance would normally hide a mistake — the literal JSON byte-comparison in the no-regression block — was restricted to the chain fixture whose values are 5, [] and 0.25, all exact. I deliberately did NOT pin the starved chain's `achieved: 3` as a literal even though I believe 0.6*5 rounds to exactly 3, and pinned that deficit's KEY ORDER instead: the regression it needs to catch is a changed field set, and betting the gate on a float-printing argument to catch it would have been a bad trade.

beads.title: Make every level's failure message say the CAUSE, not just the symptom, using feasible().bound
beads.body:
VISION ITEM 1, and it is now a small change rather than a new module. `feasible()` returns `bound` as of this ticket: for every processor, whether it was held back by its own capacity or by a named starved input, plus `headroom`. `level-view.js`'s `verdictLine()` still builds its whole failure message from sink deficits, so every level tells the player 'the depot is short by 12' — the end of the chain — when the oracle already knows 'the smelter is at capacity' or 'the smelter is starved of ore'.

WHAT TO BUILD: extend `verdictLine()` so a failing verdict names the upstream cause alongside the deficit. Concretely, for the first deficit, walk back to the processor(s) that feed it and append one clause derived from `bound`: capacity-bound -> 'the <id> is at capacity' (the actionable reading: a bigger machine, not more input); input-bound -> 'the <id> is short of <resource>'. A network with no processors between source and sink keeps today's wording exactly.

WHY IT IS NOT COSMETIC: 'a slider that turns a label red' is precisely what the vision says is NOT a game. A player who is told what to change has been given a decision; one told the score has been given a readout. LEVEL_2 (a discrete machine choice) and LEVEL_3 (two independent bottlenecks) are the two levels where the distinction changes what the player would do next, and both already have passing gates that pin their exact bound-relevant numbers.

CLASS AND GATE: class-a, gate `node plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs` — the file exists and passes today, so this is certified against an existing gate, no createsGate. Bounded paths: plant/level-view.js and plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs only. Do NOT touch production.mjs (bound is already there) or any level literal.

REQUIRED ASSERTIONS, each with a paired CONTROL in that file's house style: (1) a capacity-bound fixture's verdict string contains the processor id AND the word 'capacity', and does NOT contain the word for starvation; (2) an input-bound fixture's verdict contains the processor id AND the starved resource name, and does NOT say 'capacity' — this pair is the assertion that catches an implementation that always prints one branch; (3) a FEASIBLE fixture's verdict is byte-identical to what it produces today, so the success path is untouched; (4) a fixture with no processor at all still produces today's exact wording, pinning that the new clause is conditional; (5) the existing multi-deficit fixture (the LEVEL_4 CONTROL A shape already in that file) still names every deficit — the recorded regression there must not be undone by this change.

R4 (independence): reads `bound` and writes only presentation. It cannot affect the oracle, and no level literal changes. R5: follows directly from this ticket, whose body names exactly this as the separate follow-up with exactly this gate.
evidence: rejected: This is the attractor the vision warns about, and it is a good ticket pointed at the wrong target. It is well formed — class-a against plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs which exists and passes, tightly bounded to two files, and the required assertions are the right ones (a capacity-bound and an input-bound fixture that must NOT contain each other's wording, which is precisely the pair that catche

beads.title: De-duplicate the bound-by comparison: one pure helper shared by feasible()'s walk and autoSplit()'s headroom precondition
beads.body:
`qualifyingRelay()` decides `p.capacity * p.inputs[0].rate >= R` — an algebraic restatement of the same `min(capacity, supply/inputRate)` comparison `feasible()` makes per processor and now reports as `bound[id].by`. Two expressions of one invariant, in one file, and the ticket that added `bound` named this as reason (1) for adding it.

IT CANNOT BE FIXED BY CALLING feasible(), and that is the trap this ticket exists to stop someone falling into: autoSplit runs on a network whose fan-out group is still unsplit, and feasible() THROWS on an unsplit fan-out. The caller that needs the answer is exactly the one that cannot get it from the function that computes it. A comment saying so now sits at the precondition.

WHAT TO BUILD: a module-private pure helper `boundBy(capacity, inputs, supplyOf)` returning `{ by, resource, scale }`, where `supplyOf(resource)` yields available supply. `feasible()`'s walk calls it with the real `inc` map. `qualifyingRelay()` calls it with the worst case the precondition is stated against — supply `R` on the relay's single input, i.e. share = 1 — and qualifies the relay iff the result is `by === 'input'` (supply-bound, so delivered rate stays LINEAR in share, which is the entire justification for the closed form). Export nothing new.

WHY THIS IS THE RISKY ONE, said plainly: `capacity * inputRate >= R` and `by === 'input' at supply R` are equal as real arithmetic and may differ at the boundary in floating point, because one multiplies and the other divides. The existing gate pins that boundary from both sides on purpose (`capacity*inputRate = 99.9 < R = 100` refuses, `= 100` qualifies), so any drift shows up there — but the turn taking this MUST check that pair specifically rather than assuming, and if the two forms genuinely disagree at the boundary the correct outcome is to record that as a finding and leave the duplication in place, which is a legitimate 'done'.

CLASS AND GATE: class-a, gate `node plant/test/production.selftest.mjs` — exists and passes today. Bounded paths: plant/production.mjs and plant/test/production.selftest.mjs only.

REQUIRED ASSERTIONS: (1) every existing autoSplit CONTROL in that file passes UNCHANGED — the refusal set must not move, and the headroom boundary pair (99.9 refuses / 100 qualifies) is the specific one to check; (2) every existing `bound` assertion passes unchanged; (3) a new direct assertion that the helper agrees with the algebraic form at the exact boundary, so a future change to either cannot silently separate them; (4) no new export appears in the module's public surface.

R4 (independence): pure refactor inside one file, no signature changes. R5: follows from this ticket's reason (1) and from the finding filed alongside it explaining why the direct call is impossible.
evidence: rejected: A pure refactor with no player-visible effect, taken while item 1 is unstaffed. It is honest and technically careful — it correctly explains why the duplication CANNOT be removed by calling feasible() (autoSplit runs on a network whose fan-out group is still unsplit, and feasible() throws on an unsplit fan-out, so the caller that needs the answer is the one that cannot get it), and it flags the fl

beads.title: The brief hit MAX_ARG_STRLEN at 133,003 bytes and the agent silently never ran
beads.body:
The brief is composed by loop-work/plan/review, written to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and
read back through the workflow's `env:` block — which puts the entire brief into
the child process's ENVIRONMENT. Linux caps a single env string at
MAX_ARG_STRLEN = 32 * PAGE_SIZE = 131072 bytes. Not ARG_MAX (2 MB here); the
per-string limit, which is 16x smaller and is the one that bit.

Measured at the failure: 133,003 bytes. Over by roughly 2 KB.

HOW IT FAILED IS THE POINT. exec() returns E2BIG, the runner reports "An error
occurred trying to start process '/usr/bin/bash' ... Argument list too long",
and because `Run the agent` is deliberately continue-on-error — correct, so a
timeout still keeps whatever landed on disk — the step goes GREEN IN ZERO
SECONDS. The agent never ran. No outbox, no diff, and the workflow carried on to
write a verdict and bank turn 34 and turn 35 as real turns that produced
nothing. Budget spent, gauge advanced, every check green.

Fixed by writing the brief to /tmp/brief.txt and running `claude -p <
/tmp/brief.txt`. A file has no such limit and stdin is what the agent wanted
anyway. Guarded by asserting the transcript is non-empty: an empty
/tmp/agent.jsonl now fails the job loudly instead of being recorded as a turn.

THE DEEPER PROBLEM IS NOT FIXED AND IS WORTH A TICKET. The brief embeds EVERY
finding and dead-end verbatim, and those only accumulate — 82 at the time of
writing, one or more per turn, forever. The file fix removes the hard cliff, so
the next symptom will not be an error: it will be a brief that quietly eats the
model's context and its budget, and a turn that reads two hundred old findings
to write forty lines. Memory in the brief is the whole reason the graph exists
(CLOSED-LOOP.md's opening example), so the answer is not truncation by age; it
is relevance. Somebody has to decide what a turn actually needs to remember.

beads.title: The brief grows without bound: select memory by relevance, not by everything
beads.body:
Every brief embeds every finding and every dead-end, verbatim, forever. 82 today,
+1 or more per turn. The env-var cliff that made this fail loudly is gone (the
brief is a file now), so the next symptom is silent: context spent on two hundred
old findings, most irrelevant to the ticket in hand.

Truncating by age is wrong — the oldest findings include the ones that cost the
most to learn. The question is relevance to THIS ticket.

Cheapest thing that could work, and it needs no model call: select by overlap
between the finding's text and the ticket's own text/paths/tags, keep the top N
by that score, and ALWAYS keep dead-ends (a dead-end is a thing that does not
work; re-attempting it is the specific failure the memory exists to prevent).
State N and the scoring rule in the file.

THE GATE IT CREATES: scripts/loop-brief.selftest.mjs, which must (a) assert the
composed brief for a known ticket stays under a stated byte budget with a memory
of 500 synthetic findings; (b) assert that a finding whose text overlaps the
ticket survives selection while an unrelated one does not — i.e. that selection
discriminates rather than just truncating; (c) assert EVERY dead-end survives
regardless of score, and say in the message why that asymmetry exists.

[turn ? — blocked] TURN 3 ON THIS BEAD. First, the thing that matters most: turn 2's outbox — which itself carried turn 1's — was STILL ON DISK, UNAPPLIED, when I opened it. I read it before writing, exactly as turn 2 did, and everything from both earlier turns is carried forward below marked [CARRIED]. Had I written blind I would have erased two complete turns' diagnoses. Second: I did NOT re-litigate the containment problem or rewrite the mechanism. plant/tools/loop-brief.mjs and its 11-section gate were already complete and I judged that re-deriving them would waste the turn. Instead I HAND-TRACED all eleven existing sections against the module — every tokenizer case, every field weight, the RELEVANT/UNRELATED scores (25 vs 0), star/noise/weak (30/9/1), the top-24 outcome, the ~85KB composition against the 131072 budget, the middle-clip offsets (896/704 at 1600) and the 82-byte marker, and the created-desc tie-break that makes the no-ticket fallback correct without a second sort. All sound; I changed no behaviour. Then I spent the turn on the two branches the implementation genuinely HAS and nothing tested. NEW SECTION 12 — THE ANSWER EXEMPTION. selectMemory partitions three ways (dead-end / answer / finding) and only two were tested. isAnswer reads the `answer` TAG, not the `decision` kind. The load-bearing CONTROL is a decision tagged ['learned'] — verbatim what loop-apply-outbox.mjs stamps on every agent-filed decision, one or more per turn forever — which must appear in NO bucket and not in the composed text. Drop the tag half of that conjunction, an easy simplification for anyone who reads 'answers are decisions', and the entire decision log becomes unconditionally exempt and blows the very budget this file defends, while every assertion about answers surviving still passes. Verified the tags against scripts/loop-apply-outbox.mjs:213 and scripts/beads.mjs cmdAnswer. NEW SECTION 13 — THE EXEMPT HALF'S CAPACITY. Dead-end BODIES are clipped so each costs bounded bytes, but nothing bounds how many there are; the budget therefore has a finite dead-end capacity that nothing anywhere stated. Section 13 measures it by varying ONLY the dead-end count against a byte-identical findings half, with a control that the budget must be REACHABLE by dead-ends alone (if that fails, something began bounding the exempt half by count, which section 7 forbids) and a stated tripwire whose message carries its own remedy: tombstone superseded dead-ends, never score them. I deliberately deleted two draft assertions that could not fail — `size(capacity) <= budget` is definitional given the scan — and replaced them with one that can: that the measuring harness reproduces section 6's composition to within the fixtures' newline variance. Also documented the parked pair in plant/CLAUDE.md, because a committed file is the only durable channel a turn on this bead has. HONESTLY, WHAT IS UNVERIFIED: no Bash, so NOBODY HAS EVER EXECUTED EITHER FILE — not turn 1, not turn 2, not me. My additions' numbers are hand-derived: the answer fixture's score of 0 was checked token by token against the ticket's full term list, and the ~25 capacity estimate comes from per-dead-end cost (3200 clip + 82-byte marker + ~94 bytes of newline re-indentation + label and title) against a ~44KB findings half — which is why the tripwire is set at DEAD_ENDS+4 and not at a tighter multiple. Outcome is `blocked`, not `done`: the gate file does not exist at the path the ticket names, no seat can create it, and no brief anywhere is yet composed by this module.
