beads.title: The multi-insert REFUSES an out-of-hull point where reformPocket clamps it — and that divergence is the reason it exists
beads.body:
reformPocket runs a requested point through Math.min/Math.max into [1,W-1] x [0.8,H-0.8] x [1,D-1] BEFORE the gap check and then plants the CLAMPED point, returning a perfectly good pocket. For navigation that is a harmless convenience. For a summon it is a bug wearing a success, and worse for a constellation than for a single seed: clamping only SOME of the seeds does not move the shape, it DEFORMS it, so what lands is not the solid solids.mjs verified and not any solid at all.

reformPocketAll therefore refuses, with reason 'hull', naming the wall (B0..B5, boxMesh's own ids), the axis, the depth and where the kernel WOULD have put it. placement.mjs made the identical call for the identical reason, so the predicate a UI greys the ground out with and the transaction that does the planting now agree — and the gate asserts that agreement (same wall, same axis, same depth) rather than trusting it.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a caller that genuinely wants clamp-and-plant for a single navigation node. That caller should use reformPocket, which is unchanged, or clampSeed (now exported precisely so the divergence is inspectable rather than implicit) and then hand the clamped point in. Nothing was taken away.

Two smaller calls recorded here rather than in their own beads. (1) An EMPTY batch is a refusal ({reason:'empty'}) rather than a silent success: succeeding would hand back a 'new' pocket identical to the old one and hide a caller bug. (2) EVERY refusal is reported, not just the first, following placement.mjs and the level-view.js verdictLine bug this repo already shipped once; `first` is refusals[0] for callers that only want a sentence.

beads.title: Extracted rebuildWith/clampSeed/seedGapSq so the two insert paths share one copy of every rule, rather than writing the multi-insert alongside
beads.body:
The ticket's stated worry is drift: reformPocket's refusal compares a squared anisotropic distance against 2.25 and solids.mjs's seedGap() is the un-squared form of the same thing, and 'they must not drift'. Writing reformPocketAll as a sibling of reformPocket would have made a THIRD copy of the clamp and a THIRD copy of the gap arithmetic.

So instead: MIN_SEED_GAP_SQ (2.25), seedGapSq(a,b,aniso) and clampSeed(pocket,p) are now module-level, reformPocket calls them, and the whole rebuild-and-assemble tail — append seeds, derive layerOf, buildComplex, buildNav in fixed mode, re-derive the dais face, assemble the pocket object — is a private rebuildWith(pocket, pts) that BOTH paths call with 1 or n points.

This is a PURE EXTRACTION. Every expression and every evaluation order is unchanged, so reformPocket returns bit-identical results (the ported foamworld selftest is the check that says so). What it buys is that 'a one-point transaction equals reformPocket' stops being a claim someone has to re-verify after each edit and becomes structurally true — the gate asserts it anyway, as the tripwire for a future edit that breaks the sharing.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: if the two paths ever need genuinely different rebuild semantics (say, a multi-insert that tolerates a nav failure the single insert refuses). At that point rebuildWith grows an options argument rather than being forked, or the sharing is abandoned deliberately and both copies get a comment saying so.

COST, stated plainly: plant/foamworld.js is no longer byte-identical to foam/foamworld.js, so a future port from foam is now a merge rather than a copy. That is recorded in the file's own header, where the byte-identity promise was made, and in plant/CLAUDE.md. The ticket named this file as where the work lives, and the private buildComplex/buildNav/allCandidates leave no alternative.

beads.title: A rollback test is only worth something if the naive path would really have half-applied — so the gate proves that first
beads.body:
The obvious way to write requirement (b) is: force a mid-constellation collision, assert the pocket is unchanged. That assertion PASSES TRIVIALLY for an implementation that does nothing at all, and — worse — it passes for the real implementation whether or not a half-apply was ever possible, because reformPocketAll copies rather than mutates. The test would be asserting a property of the copy, not of the transaction.

So the gate first runs the naive path explicitly: reformPocket on batch[0], then on the result with batch[1], asserting both succeed and leave a two-seed fragment, and only THEN asserting reformPocket refuses batch[2]. That is the bug, executed, in the same file that then shows the transaction refusing the same batch and leaving nothing behind. The rollback assertion now has something to be about.

Second thing the same section needed and would have been wrong without: JSON.stringify IS NOT A DEEP COMPARE for a pocket. It renders pocket.basinOf (a Map of every basin) as {} and every vertical membrane's slope:Infinity as null. A comparator built on it is blind to two whole classes of mutation, and would have called a mutated pocket unchanged while reading like the strictest check in the file. The gate carries its own serializer that handles Map, Set, Infinity, NaN and -0, plus a CONTROL asserting that serializer really does distinguish the reformed pocket from the original — without which every rollback assertion in the file would pass for a comparator stuck on 'equal'.

General shape, and it is the same one this ledger keeps recording: a check that cannot fail is indistinguishable from a check that passes. Both halves — 'the failure mode is reachable' and 'the comparator can see it' — have to be asserted, or the assertion between them is decoration.

beads.title: The commit assertion is an EXISTENCE claim over 6 candidates, deliberately — the closure gate is not decidable in advance
beads.body:
reformPocketAll can refuse for reasons that no predicate can anticipate: buildComplex's per-cell Euler gate rejects an unstitchable degeneracy, and buildNav refuses when the target chamber loses its floor. So 'this specific constellation plants at this specific centre' is not a safe assertion to hard-code — a single failing candidate would be evidence about voronoi degeneracy, not about the transaction.

The gate therefore pre-filters ~900 (solid, centre) pairs with placement.mjs (pure arithmetic, cheap), keeps only those where every seed is a comfortable 2.2m clear of any pocket seed, spreads 6 attempts across the resulting lattice so one bad neighbourhood cannot decide the run, and asserts that at least one lands — then runs every closure and nav assertion on the one that did. This mirrors placement.selftest.mjs's own reasoning for the same fixture, which is what makes it a precedent rather than an excuse.

THE RESIDUAL RISK, stated because I could not run it: if all 6 attempts refused, the gate fails. I judge that unlikely — placement.selftest.mjs already proves for this exact pocket (seed 2, the MACRO opts) that predicate-legal cube centres at r=1.6 plant for real, and the tetrahedron/cube/octahedron constellations here are 5-9 seeds at mutual gaps of 2.5m and up, which is a generic rather than a degenerate configuration. But it is a probabilistic argument about voronoi stitching, not a proof, and it is the one assertion in the file I would look at first if the gate goes red.

The 2.2m clearance filter (rather than the 1.5m legality threshold) exists for a second reason worth recording: section 4 perturbs a constellation seed by 0.5m to force a batch self-collision, and section 4's 'exactly one refusal is reported' assertion would break if that perturbation strayed within 1.5m of a pocket seed. Requiring 2.2m up front makes the perturbed point provably >= 1.7m clear by the triangle inequality. Likewise the victim seed for the mid-batch collision is filtered to seeds no OTHER pocket seed is within 1.5m of — the generator's jitter (+/-7.6m on x/z, up to +/-6.75m on y against 20m/9m spacing) genuinely can place two pocket seeds close together, and standing on one of a close pair would produce two correct refusals and fail an assertion that has nothing to do with the transaction.

beads.title: Atomic and sequential land on the byte-identical pocket when both succeed — so atomicity is a failure mode and a cost, not a different geometry
beads.body:
buildComplex is a pure function of (seeds, layerOf, opts, W/H/D, candidate order) and allCandidates derives its order from the seed list itself. So planting a constellation one seed at a time and planting it in one transaction produce the SAME final seed list in the SAME order, and therefore the same complex, the same nav graph, the same everything — provided the sequential path survives all n steps.

The gate asserts exactly that (section 7), with the honest branch: if the sequential path refuses part-way, it says so and that is a more damning result rather than a skipped test.

Why this is worth recording rather than just testing: it pins down what reformPocketAll actually buys, which is easy to overstate. It does NOT produce a better lattice. It buys two things and only two. (1) THE FAILURE MODE: n-1 committed seeds and a broken pocket becomes zero committed seeds and a named refusal. (2) THE COST: one Theta(n^2) rebuild instead of |seeds| of them, on a seed count that the summon is itself raising as it goes — the ledger's frame-budget finding measured a dodecahedron at 13 rebuilds of a ~300-cell complex and called lp-f25c2f 'the whole lever' for that reason. Anyone who later wonders whether the transaction changed the geometry has a test that says no.

beads.title: Summon a constellation into a real pocket from the page — the first thing a stranger can do that can fail
beads.body:
Everything under the summon is now built and gated: solids.mjs makes the constellation, placement.mjs says whether it fits and names what it hits, and reformPocketAll plants it as one transaction or refuses with a named cause. NOTHING CONNECTS THEM TO A CLICK. plant/index.html is still the inspector — you can orbit a wireframe, you cannot place one.

This is vision item 1's bar, and it is now one wiring ticket away rather than a phase: a stranger opens the page, picks a solid, picks a spot in a real generated pocket, and either it lands or it is refused for a reason they can see (that seed there, that wall there).

SCOPE, deliberately small: a pure controller module, plant/summon-session.mjs, with no DOM in it — start(seed) generates a pocket, candidates() or preview(point) returns the placement verdict, place(solid, point) calls reformPocketAll and returns {ok, refusal} plus the new pocket, and history()/undo() are NOT in scope. The page wiring is a sibling ticket; a controller a test can drive without a browser is the part that can be gated, and vision item 1 says so explicitly ('the game's control logic lives in a module, not in event handlers').

THE GATE IT CREATES: plant/test/summon-session.selftest.mjs, which must (a) drive a scripted session that reaches A REFUSAL THE PLAYER CAUSED in a bounded number of moves, and assert that bound — not merely that a refusal is possible; (b) assert a refusal leaves the session's pocket byte-for-byte unchanged, so a refused placement cannot corrupt the run (reuse multi-insert.selftest.mjs's serializer approach: JSON.stringify is not a deep compare here, it drops Maps and Infinity); (c) assert that a successful placement is visible in the session state afterwards and that the placed seeds are exactly where they were asked for. A weaker gate that only checks ok/!ok would pass for a controller that discards the pocket on every call.

Bounded paths: plant/summon-session.mjs, plant/test/summon-session.selftest.mjs. Nothing else — index.html is the sibling.

[turn 44 — done] Built plant/summon-session.mjs — a DOM-free controller with start(seed) / candidates(opts) / preview(point, opts) / place(solid, point, opts) / state() / ownerOf(i), composing generatePocket, solids.mjs's constellation, placement.mjs's summonAt predicate and reformPocketAll's transaction. history()/undo() are out of scope as the ticket says, and the module header records why undo is NOT one line (membrane open/closed state is the caller's, so restoring a pocket without it would silently reset the level). The controller's real content beyond wrapping the transaction is ATTRIBUTION: it holds originCount (the seed index boundary between the generated foam and what the player built), so every refusal is classified blame: player | pocket | hull | self | foam | caller, with blameMove/blameSolid/blameCentre when the player is at fault. That distinction is not derivable from reformPocketAll's return value and it is the whole reason this is a session and not a function. Also wrote the gate, plant/test/summon-session.selftest.mjs. Its (a) fixture is exact arithmetic rather than a search: two cubes at r=1.6 whose centres are 5m apart in x collide on exactly ONE of their fourteen seed pairs — solids.mjs puts an axis-aligned neighbour at exactly 2r=3.2 (q=1 for a unit axis normal, so the anisotropy cannot move it), so A's +x neighbour is at +3.2 and B's -x neighbour at 5-3.2=1.8, gap 1.4 against a 1.5 refusal radius, and every other pair is >= 1.8. So the gate asserts spot B previews LEGAL on the freshly generated pocket, previews ILLEGAL after one cube lands 5m away, and is refused on move 2 — G.moves === 2, asserted, with the blamed pocket seed index asserted to be exactly placed.first+1 and independently re-checked with the kernel's own seedGapSq against a constellation the test rebuilds itself. (b) deep-compares a snapshot with multi-insert.selftest.mjs's serializer (JSON.stringify renders basinOf as {} and Infinity slopes as null), with a control proving the serializer sees exactly those two things and JSON.stringify does not. (c) asserts every planted seed componentwise === where it was asked for, which is the assertion that matters because reformPocket clamps rather than refuses. HONESTLY: I could not run the gate. This turn's tools were Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep, no Bash. I hand-traced everything, and that caught TWO real defects in my own gate before writing this — a backtick nested inside a template literal (a syntax error; the file would not have parsed at all) and a fixture that would have been shadowed (testing the 'self' refusal at a spot where the player's own cube already stood, where legalSummon reports the per-seed refusal first). Both are fixed. The residual risk is concentrated in two existence claims, both guarded by assertions that fail legibly: that a predicate-legal cube actually commits (up to 6 spread attempts, exactly multi-insert.selftest.mjs's argument — closure and nav are not decidable in advance), and that spots 3.5m clear of every seed exist in the macro pocket for the r=0.5 self-collision fixture.

beads.title: Price the multi-insert: extend the frame-budget gate to summons, so '13 rebuilds became 1' is a number and not a claim
beads.body:
The ledger's gate-7 finding says the dominant term in a summon's cost is not the per-rebuild time but that ONE SUMMON IS |seeds| REBUILDS — 5 for a tetrahedron, 13 for a dodecahedron, 21 for an icosahedron — and it explicitly says gate 7 'currently measures the API's unit and says so; it cannot measure the player's until the multi-insert exists'. It exists now.

So: extend plant/frame-budget.mjs with a summon measurement — the wall-clock cost of reformPocketAll for a whole constellation, against the cost of the same constellation planted seed-by-seed through reformPocket — and report the ratio at the shipping pocket density.

WHY THIS IS NOT A VANITY BENCHMARK: the multi-insert was scoped in this ticket as a CORRECTNESS change (a constellation lands or nothing does) and the frame-budget finding argues it is mainly a PERFORMANCE change. Nobody has measured which. If the ratio comes out near |seeds| the claim is confirmed and the number belongs in the vision; if it comes out near 1 — plausible, since buildComplex is Theta(n^2) in the TOTAL seed count and the sequential path's early rebuilds are over a smaller n — then the sequential path is cheaper than the naive multiplication suggests and the honest claim shrinks to correctness alone. Either answer is worth knowing and neither is currently known.

CRITICAL CONSTRAINT, from the ledger's own frame-budget finding: DO NOT ASSERT ON INDIVIDUAL TIMED SAMPLES. A GC pause inside one rebuild is a 3-4x outlier by itself. Aggregate before asserting — medians per fixture size — and keep the existing file's budget discipline (it fits its own measurements inside a 10s ceiling by fitting on cheap fixtures first and only then deciding whether it can afford the expensive one).

THE GATE: node plant/test/frame-budget.selftest.mjs, which already exists and already passes. This ticket adds to it rather than creating it, so it is a plain class-a — but note the self-certification exposure: the same turn writes the measurement and the assertion about it. The assertion worth making is a SHAPE claim (the atomic path is not slower than the sequential one, at every fixture size measured) rather than a magic constant, because a constant pins the machine the turn happened to run on.

Bounded paths: plant/frame-budget.mjs, plant/test/frame-budget.selftest.mjs.
evidence: rejected: Rejected purely as throttle, and it deserves to be said plainly: this is a good ticket and I am the constraint, not it. It is correctly class-a against plant/test/frame-budget.selftest.mjs which exists and passes, it is bounded to two files, and it respects the hard-won ledger findings rather than rediscovering them — it explicitly forbids asserting on individual timed samples (a GC pause is a 3-4

beads.title: The loop dispatched a turn to build gate 6 — and gate 6 was already on disk, complete, with no ledger record of it
beads.body:
plant/buildcert.mjs (368 lines) and plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs (400+ lines) were both committed and complete before this turn started. `grep -r buildcert .github/loop/` returns exactly one hit: beads.jsonl line 527, which is the bead TEXT. No turn record, no evidence entry, no done status.

This is the inverse of the already-recorded dead-end 'lp-dfad42 turn 1's claimed port never actually existed on disk'. That one was a bead marked done whose files were absent. This is files present whose bead reads ready. Both are the same underlying defect — THE LEDGER AND THE WORKING TREE DISAGREE — and the loop has now been bitten in both directions.

The cost here is a whole dispatched turn. The bead's own evidence says 'revived by operator 2026-08-05: rejected with no reason recorded', so the sequence was plausibly: agent proposes at run 29, review rejects with no cause recorded, some later turn builds it anyway (or built it under another bead), the ledger never learns, the operator revives the bead from the rejection list, and the reactor dispatches it as fresh work. Every component behaved correctly and the system still paid for the same artifact twice.

THE CHEAP FIX, and it is cheap: a bead whose gate file already EXISTS is not creates-gate work. `beads promote` already refuses a creates-gate bead whose named file is present (lp-4d3aa1's fix put an existence check at promotion, where a filesystem is available). That check is not being applied on REVIVAL — the operator revived this bead straight past it. Revival should run the same predicate promotion does. More generally: any path that moves a bead INTO ready — promote, revive, untag — needs the same existence check, or the check only guards the one door somebody thought of.

GENERAL SHAPE, and it is this repo's most-repeated one: a ticket's status is a CLAIM about the tree, and nothing periodically reconciles the two. Both failures were found by a human or an agent noticing in passing, not by a check. The tree is cheap to interrogate — a turn that verifies its ticket's deliverables are absent BEFORE building them costs one Glob.

beads.title: buildcert's headline number was asserted only against itself — clearance/margin passed for a nearest() that ignored the accumulated seeds entirely
beads.body:
The whole content of a build certificate is that step N is judged against the pocket AS IT WILL BE after steps 0..N-1, rather than against the empty pocket. If that is wrong the file is legalSummon in a loop, which its own header says it exists not to be.

The gate asserted `cert.margin > 0`, `|cert.clearance - (cert.margin + 1.5)| < 1e-12`, and `every step margin > 0`. All three are SELF-consistency: they relate the returned numbers to each other and to nothing outside. They are satisfied by any positive number the walk cares to return. Specifically they all pass for a `nearest()` that measures only against the ORIGINAL pocket seeds and never sees what earlier steps committed — the exact mutation that would gut the file's purpose — because in the passing fixture the two constellations are 14m apart and both are comfortably clear of the pocket, so every candidate number is positive and the internal arithmetic still agrees with itself.

This is a sharper instance of the pattern already recorded in lp-c46a0c ('a self-certifying turn tests what it BUILT and under-tests what it CLAIMED'). Here the docstring's claim — 'clearance is the real anisotropic distance to the closest committed seed' — and the assertions had drifted apart in exactly that way: the assertions test the arithmetic, the docstring claims the SOURCE SET, and only the second one is the interesting half.

Closed by recomputing both steps' clearance in the test from solids.mjs primitives alone (step 0 over the 64 pocket seeds; step 1 over those plus step 0's five, via pairGap) and pinning cert.clearance as the min of the two. Also pinned the `owners` array, which nothing read: owner must be null exactly when seedIndex < the original seed count. The 'pocket' (unfixable) vs 'step' (possibly reorderable) taxonomy that all of section 3 rests on is computed from `r.seedIndex < base`, so an off-by-one there would silently reclassify every refusal in the file while every existing assertion stayed green.

THE TRANSFERABLE RULE: an assertion that relates a function's outputs only to its other outputs measures the arithmetic between them, never the input set they were computed over. When the interesting claim is WHICH DATA was consulted — and for an accumulating walk it always is — the only assertion that bites is an independent recomputation from a different direction.

beads.title: Left reorderable's 'and then it lands' overclaim in place rather than fixing it blind; proposed it as a ticket instead
beads.body:
buildcert.mjs's header states that when a step is blocked only by non-ancestor earlier steps, 'scheduling it first is a legal topological order AND IT LANDS'. `reorderable: true` is returned on that reasoning and `suggestedOrder` is handed back, but the suggestion is never executed before being asserted.

It is not sound in general. blockedBy can only ever contain steps that preceded the failing node in the ORIGINAL order; a node that came AFTER it was never in the pocket state when it was judged, so a collision with that node was never detected. orderPreferring() places the wanted node as early as legally possible but may insert arbitrary ready non-avoid nodes ahead of it while it waits for its ancestors, and one of those may be a node that originally came later — and may collide.

I spent real effort trying to build a counterexample and could not: the greedy rule plus the dodge set is robust across every 3- and 4-node shape I traced, because Kahn's FIFO tends to place any early-ready node before the failing node anyway, which puts it in blockedBy and therefore in the dodge set. So the claim is probably true for small networks and is definitely not PROVEN, and the header states it as a certainty.

WHY I DID NOT FIX IT: the honest fix is to verify the suggestion by re-running the walk under it, which means certify() calling itself and needs a recursion guard (explain -> certify -> explain -> certify would otherwise chase suggestions indefinitely). That is a real semantic change to a 100+ check gate I have no way to execute, on a turn whose remit was to audit. The ledger is emphatic that the expensive failure mode here is turning a green gate red from inference. Proposed as its own bead against the now-existing gate.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE THIS: a counterexample. If someone builds a 5+ node network where the suggested order also refuses the same node, the field is actively misleading rather than merely unproven and it should be fixed immediately rather than scheduled.

beads.title: Make buildcert's `reorderable` verify its own suggestion instead of arguing for it
beads.body:
certify()'s failure record returns `reorderable: true` and a `suggestedOrder` on the argument that a step blocked only by non-ancestor earlier steps will land if scheduled before them. The suggestion is never executed before being asserted, and the reasoning has a hole: `blockedBy` can only contain steps that PRECEDED the failing node in the original order, so a node that came after it was never in the pocket state when the node was judged and a collision with it went undetected. orderPreferring() can place such a node ahead of the wanted one (it inserts ready non-avoid nodes while the wanted node waits for its ancestors), so `reorderable: true` can in principle be returned for a suggestion that also fails.

I could not construct a counterexample by hand across 3- and 4-node shapes — Kahn's FIFO tends to put any early-ready node before the failing node, which lands it in blockedBy and therefore in the dodge set — so this is UNPROVEN rather than known-broken, and the header states it as a certainty either way.

WHAT TO BUILD: have explain() verify rather than argue. Re-run the walk under suggestedOrder and set `reorderable` from whether the failing node is actually certified in it. certify() calling itself needs a recursion guard — an internal `{ suggest: false }` option — because otherwise each suggestion's own failure would generate another suggestion without bound. Keep `reorderable: false` when the suggestion is not verified, and add a field distinguishing 'no legal order exists' from 'the suggested order also failed', because those are different facts for a caller repositioning a factory.

WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK, and the first is the one that makes this worth doing: (a) a network where the naive argument is WRONG — the failing node is blocked only by a non-ancestor earlier step, yet the suggested order still refuses it because a node that originally came later now precedes it. If that fixture cannot be constructed after real effort, say so in a finding and assert the invariance instead, because 'I could not build the counterexample' is itself the answer to whether the claim holds. (b) The existing TWIN CLASH assertions must still hold exactly: 'b' reorderable under the default order, 'a' reorderable under the suggested one, the CHAIN dependency case still not reorderable. (c) A cost assertion that the recursion guard works — certify() on a deep chain of collisions must not blow the stack or issue more than one suggestion per call.

Bounded to plant/buildcert.mjs and plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs. The gate already exists and already passes, so this is class-a against it: the new assertions land in the existing file and everything currently green must stay green.

[turn 46 — done] certify()'s failure record no longer ARGUES that a reordering would work — it runs it. explain() now constructs the candidate order (as before), then re-enters certify() under it with an internal { suggest: false } recursion guard and sets `reorderable` from whether the failing node is actually certified in that run. New fields: `reorderCheck` ('none' | 'verified' | 'refuted' | 'unchecked') which is the ticket's requested distinction between 'no legal reordering exists' and 'the suggested one was tried and also failed'; `attemptedOrder` (what was constructed, always reported); `reorderRuns` (nested runs behind the record, 0 or 1, the observable that pins the guard). `suggestedOrder` is now non-null ONLY when verified, so a caller that reads it without checking reorderable cannot follow a bad suggestion. Requirement (a) is satisfied with a real counterexample rather than an invariance fallback: a fixture of two strands of DIFFERENT DEPTH (d0->d1->z and a0->w) plus a loose node c0, where Kahn's level-order puts z AFTER w while orderPreferring — told to dodge c0 and stuck waiting for a0 — walks the other strand and schedules z (originally later, therefore invisible to blockedBy) onto the exact spot w wanted. The control is the same network, same layout, same blocker, same gap, with z DELETED: it comes back 'verified'. One node's existence is the only difference. The refuted verdict is additionally re-executed from outside the module by hand and asserted to fail on 'z' specifically. Requirement (b): the TWIN CLASH and CHAIN dependency assertions are untouched and I hand-traced every one of them through the new code path — 'b' verifies under the default order, 'a' verifies under the suggested one, the dependency case still has no candidate at all. Requirement (c): the guard is pinned three ways — reorderRuns === 1 on the fixture where an unguarded version would report 2, an explicit { suggest: false } call reporting 'unchecked' with 0 runs and a null suggestion, and a 30-node pile-up that still costs exactly one nested run. HONESTLY: no Bash this turn, so nothing was executed. Every fixture order (buildOrder and orderPreferring alike) was hand-traced step by step against the actual algorithms in production.mjs's analyse() and buildcert.mjs's orderPreferring, and the geometry rests on SPREAD centres the file already proves are mutually clear. I also could NOT build a fixture that forces deep recursion (see the finding) — the cost assertion is a bounded-work claim, not a stack-depth stress test, and the comment in the file says so.

beads.title: Reconcile bead status against the working tree before dispatch — a ready bead whose deliverables already exist should not be dispatched
beads.body:
This turn was dispatched to build plant/buildcert.mjs and plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs. Both already existed, committed and complete. `grep -r buildcert .github/loop/` returns one hit: the bead text. The ledger had no record of the work, so the reactor dispatched a full turn to rebuild an artifact the loop already owned.

The loop has now been bitten in BOTH directions by the same underlying defect — the ledger and the working tree disagree, and nothing reconciles them. The other direction is already recorded: a bead marked done, with evidence paths listed, whose files were never on disk (lp-dfad42).

The existing partial fix is at promotion: cmdPromote refuses a creates-gate bead whose named gate file already exists, because a gate already present proves nothing about new capability (lp-4d3aa1). That check guards ONE door. This bead reached ready by REVIVAL — the operator un-rejecting it from the rejected-by-review list — which does not run it. Any transition into ready needs the same predicate, or the check only ever guards the door somebody happened to think of.

WHAT TO BUILD: a reusable predicate in scripts/lib/beads.mjs answering 'do this bead's declared gate files already exist?', applied at EVERY transition into ready (promote, revive, and any --untag that changes class from non-dispatchable to class-a), plus a `beads audit` verb that reports every ready or in-progress bead whose gate file is already present. Conservative in the same way lp-4d3aa1's check is: only tokens ending in a source extension count as paths, so a grep pattern containing a slash is not mistaken for a missing file. A rule that cries wolf gets --forced past every time and then it is not a rule.

WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK: a creates-gate bead whose file exists is refused at promote AND at revive (two separate assertions — the whole point is that guarding one door is what failed); a bead whose gate file is genuinely absent passes both; `beads audit` finds a planted inconsistency in a fixture ledger and exits non-zero; and a CONTROL that a class-a bead naming an EXISTING gate is still promotable, since for plain class-a an existing gate is the requirement rather than a defect. That control is the one that stops this becoming a rule that blocks ordinary work.

No gate file exists for beads.mjs today, so this is creates-gate: it must land scripts/test/beads.selftest.mjs (or the repo's nearest convention), pass, and break nothing. NOTE THE BOUNDED-PATH PROBLEM, stated plainly because it decides whether this is dispatchable at all: this work is in scripts/ and .github/loop/, OUTSIDE the loop's declared writes, which are plant/**. As specified it is human-only or needs config.json's writes extended first. I am proposing it anyway because the cost is a whole turn per occurrence and it has now happened twice.
evidence: rejected: R3 FAILS AND THE BODY SAYS SO. The work is in scripts/lib/beads.mjs and its gate lands at scripts/test/beads.selftest.mjs — outside plant/**, which is the loop's entire declared write surface, enforced twice (config.json's write paths and loop-work.yml's containment gate, which reverts any diff that escapes them). A turn dispatched on this would have its whole diff reverted and report success. The

beads.title: Dropping a refused SINK makes the surviving network VACUOUSLY satisfiable — network.ok goes TRUE on a level that just failed
beads.body:
The ticket asked that a refused object be dropped from the production network, and named the trap it was avoiding: keeping the edge would let a level pass on a factory it could never stand. Doing the drop correctly opens the OPPOSITE trap, which nothing in the ticket anticipated and which I only saw while hand-tracing the CONTROL.

Collide the sink with the processor. The sink's node is dropped and both its edges go with it. What survives is source -> processor, which has NO SINKS AT ALL — and production.mjs's own docstring says a network with no sinks is vacuously feasible and reports margin 0. So:

    verdict.network.ok  === true      <- the factory 'passes'
    verdict.network.margin === 0
    verdict.ok          === false     <- only because placement failed

A caller that reads network.ok as the verdict reports SUCCESS on a level whose sink is sitting inside another building. That is not a hypothetical: it is the natural thing to render, because network.ok is the field that sounds like the answer.

So `ok` requires BOTH halves and level.mjs says so in its docstring, and the gate asserts the whole vacuous shape explicitly (network.ok true, margin 0, no 'snk' key in achieved, verdict false) rather than just asserting the verdict — because asserting only the verdict would pass for an implementation that got there by accident.

TWO THINGS WORTH CARRYING FORWARD. First, this is the same under-reporting shape the ledger already has twice (verdictLine reading deficits[0]; `bound` naming one starved input of several): a scalar summary standing in for a structure. Here it is a BOOLEAN standing in for two independent verdicts, and the failure direction is the dangerous one — it reads as a pass.

Second, and more cheerful: the ledger records that production.mjs's zero-sink branch is 'self-documented as untested — no fixture omits every sink'. This gate now exercises it, from a caller that reaches it by accident rather than by construction, which is the honest way to find out that branch matters.

beads.title: A refused summon must not block what comes after it — and the discriminating test is a one-number pair, not an assertion
beads.body:
placementReport checks each object against every EARLIER object THAT WAS ITSELF LEGAL. The rule is obvious once stated (a summon that was refused was never placed, so it occupies nothing) and it is exactly the kind of rule a self-authored test asserts vacuously, because every well-separated fixture passes whether or not the rule is implemented.

The fixture that actually discriminates is a pair of runs differing in ONE NUMBER:

    cubes at z = 0, 5, 10   ->  A ok | B refused by A (gap 1.0) | C OK
    cubes at z = 0, 6, 10   ->  A ok | B ok (gap 2.0)           | C REFUSED by B (gap 0.0)

In the first, C is ~1.0 from B and must still be legal, because B is not there. In the second, the only thing that changed is B moving 1m — and now B is legal, so it blocks C. An implementation that checks against all earlier objects rather than all earlier LEGAL ones fails the first and passes the second; an implementation that never checks earlier objects at all passes the first and fails the second. Neither run alone can tell you anything; the pair pins the rule from both sides.

The general shape, and it is the same argument as the surviving-mutant lesson in lp-c46a0c: when the interesting claim is about WHICH DATA a walk consulted, no single positive case can test it. You need two runs whose only difference is membership of that data set.

beads.title: Four judgement calls the ticket left open, and what would reverse each
beads.body:
1. THE REFUSAL CARRIES `gap`. The ticket's shape is { id, ok, reason, blockedBy? }; refusals also carry the actual anisotropic distance that fell short. Why: placement.mjs already argues that a refusal returning only `false` throws away the interesting half, and — the reason that mattered here — it lets the gate grade the verdict against an INDEPENDENTLY recomputed number instead of re-calling pairGap and proving nothing. Purely additive; reversed by deleting one field if a caller is ever confused by it.

2. WHEN SEVERAL EARLIER OBJECTS COLLIDE, THE FIRST IN PLACEMENT ORDER IS NAMED. Deterministic, and the same first-wins tie-break production.mjs uses for its binding input. This is the same scalar-for-a-set compromise the ledger already flagged twice (verdictLine's deficits[0], `bound`'s single starved input) and I made it knowingly — a `blockedByAll: string[]` alongside is the clean fix if a UI ever wants to light up every offender. Reversed additively; nothing has to change shape.

3. AN EDGE NAMING AN ID THAT IS NOT AN OBJECT AT ALL IS **NOT** DROPPED. The ticket says drop edges referencing an ILLEGAL object; an id that names no object is a typo in a level literal, not a refused placement. Dropping it would silently shrink the network and pass. It is passed through so feasible() raises its own 'edge names unknown node'. Reversed only if level literals ever become machine-generated in a way that makes stray ids legitimate.

4. `node.id` MUST EQUAL THE OBJECT'S `id`, ENFORCED BY A THROW. Otherwise `edges` address two namespaces that happen to overlap, which is a footgun with no upside. The check is scoped to LEGAL objects only — an illegal object is never asked for a node, because demanding one would refuse levels that are merely losing. That scoping has its own CONTROL in the gate.

beads.title: Gate unverifiable in-turn (no Bash) — recording only the ONE float risk I engineered out rather than restating the standing recommendation
beads.body:
The standing recommendation is in this ledger past twenty times and the previous turn said it would stop restating it. Agreed. What is worth one entry is the single place where an unrun gate could have gone red for a reason that has nothing to do with the code under test.

The boundary test wants to pin that a gap EXACTLY equal to minSeedGap is legal (the rule is `refuse when gap < threshold`). Cubes at z=0 and z=5.5 give a binding pair of (0,0,2) vs (0,0,3.5) — dy = 0, every value exactly representable, difference exactly 1.5. My first version asserted `report[1].ok === true` at the default threshold of 1.5, which stakes a pass/fail boundary on Math.hypot(0, 0, 1.5) returning bit-exactly 1.5. It almost certainly does (max-scaling gives sqrt(1)*1.5), but 'almost certainly' is not a thing to hang a gate on, and a checker that fails correct work is worse than no checker.

Rewritten to run the boundary against the MEASURED gap: `placementReport(objs, measured)` must be legal and `placementReport(objs, measured * (1 + 1e-9))` must refuse. That pins the thing actually under test — `>=` is legal, anything strictly below is not — with no floating-point assumption at all. The literal-1.5 case is still asserted, but as an informational hand-check with a 1e-12 tolerance, so if hypot ever surprises anyone the failure names the arithmetic rather than the verdict.

General shape for anyone writing a boundary assertion: assert the RELATION between the measured value and the threshold, not the identity of the measured value with a literal. The literal is the hand-check; the relation is the test.

beads.title: When a placement is refused, should the level read as LOST or as UNFINISHED?
beads.body:
levelVerdict returns a single boolean `ok`, and it is false for two situations that feel completely different to play: (1) you placed a building somewhere illegal, and (2) everything you placed is legal but the factory does not meet demand. Right now both are just 'not ok'.

I cannot settle this from here because it is not a correctness question — both readings are implementable, both are self-consistent, and no gate can tell me which one a person experiences as fair. It is exactly the class the vision says is worth an ask rather than a guess. I DID decide and ship: `ok` stays a single boolean because it is the smaller, more reversible choice, and the two causes are already distinguishable by inspecting `placement` vs `network`. Adding a third state later is additive; removing one is not.

DO: Open plant/test/level.selftest.mjs and read the 'END TO END' CONTROL section (the sink recentred onto the processor). Then imagine that state on screen: a building is visibly overlapping another one, and the verdict line says you have not won.

WATCH FOR: Whether your instinct is 'I lost' or 'I have not finished placing things yet'. Specifically: would you expect the game to let you keep going and fix it, or to tell you the attempt failed?

SO THAT: If LOST: `ok: false` is the whole story, the game shell shows a fail state, and nothing changes. If UNFINISHED: the proposed game.mjs needs a third status ('illegal' distinct from 'short'), the refused object should probably not even be committed to the placement list, and 'place() returns a refusal you can retry' becomes the interaction rather than 'place() records a loss'. That is a different state machine, and it is much cheaper to know before game.mjs is written than after.

beads.title: game.mjs — the playable shell: one level at a time, a win you are told about, and a next level offered
beads.body:
Vision item 1, and level.mjs (this turn) is the piece it was missing: something that can answer 'is what the player just did legal, and does the factory work' in one call.

Build plant/game.mjs — a pure state machine with NO event handlers and NO DOM, so a test can drive it without a browser. That separation is the whole reason this is gateable; the vision names it explicitly.

API, exactly four verbs:
  · start(levelId) -> state        enter one level; nothing else is on screen
  · place(objectSpec) -> state     append to the ordered placement list and re-run levelVerdict
  · verdict() -> { status, ... }   status is one of 'playing' | 'illegal' | 'short' | 'won'
  · next() -> state | null         advance to exactly one successor; null on the last level

'illegal' vs 'short' is the distinction level.mjs makes and a page currently cannot: a placement that was REFUSED is a different failure from a factory that is merely under-supplied, and conflating them is what makes the current page read as documentation.

Gate (creates it): plant/test/game.selftest.mjs, asserting the four claims the vision names as executable, every one a claim about the state machine rather than about a feeling:
  (a) a scripted playthrough reaches a refusal THE PLAYER CAUSED in a bounded number of moves, and the test asserts that bound — three place() calls or fewer from start();
  (b) completing a level advances to EXACTLY ONE successor, and the last level's next() returns null rather than wrapping;
  (c) the level order is monotonic in a stated difficulty measure — feasible().margin at each level's designed solution, which already exists — so '1, 3, 2, 5, 6 is roughly the curve' stops being an opinion. If the measured order contradicts the assumed one, REORDER THE LEVELS and say so; do not weaken the assertion;
  (d) start() twice on the same level gives byte-identical state (no hidden accumulation across entries).

Deliberately NOT in scope: any HTML. Wiring the module into index.html is a separate ticket with its own regex-wiring gate, the same split the existing index-levelN-wiring selftests already use. Doing both in one turn produces a diff nobody can review.

What this ticket cannot prove, stated plainly: that a stranger enjoys it. (a)-(d) are the part of 'playable' that can be written down; the rest waits for a human.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED ON A FALSE PREMISE ABOUT THE TREE, not on priority — this is vision item 1 and I wanted to approve it. The body says place(objectSpec) appends to a placement list and re-runs levelVerdict, and that difficulty is measured by 'feasible().margin at each level's designed solution, which already exists'. Neither is true of plant/levels/. All six levels are network literals — {nodes, edges} wit

beads.title: Compose level.mjs with placement.mjs — session legality AND pocket legality against a real foam pocket
beads.body:
level.mjs (this turn) answers 'are these objects legal with respect to EACH OTHER'. placement.mjs's legalSummon answers 'is this ONE object legal in THIS pocket' (hull + the 1.5 seed gap against existing pocket seeds). Nobody calls both. That composition is vision item 3 — the bridge between production.mjs's rates and a real pocket — and the blocker it used to have is gone, because plant/foamworld.js now exists in the loop's own tree.

Build plant/pocketLevel.mjs exporting pocketPlacementReport(pocket, objects, opts) and pocketLevelVerdict(pocket, objects, edges, opts), with the SAME return shapes level.mjs uses plus the pocket refusal reasons legalSummon already names ('hull', 'seed', 'metric'). Reuse both modules; reimplement neither.

THE ONE REAL DESIGN QUESTION, and the reason this was not folded into lp-7b7f04: a pocket-illegal object must be dropped from the production network exactly as a session-illegal one is, which means the vacuous-satisfiability trap recorded in this turn's findings applies here too and has to be asserted, not assumed.

Second decision to make and record: ORDER. legalSummon checks against the pocket's ORIGINAL seeds; a real multi-object placement means each object also has to clear the seeds the EARLIER objects planted. Deciding whether pocketPlacementReport simulates that accumulation (correct, and what buildcert.mjs already does for a single constellation's steps) or checks against the static pocket (cheap, and WRONG in exactly the way the buildcert ticket exists to prevent) is the substance of this ticket. Take the accumulating version; the cheap one is the bug.

Gate (creates it): plant/test/pocket-level.selftest.mjs, on a real generatePocket fixture with a fixed seed, asserting: a set of well-separated legal placements verdicts ok with the hand-computed production numbers; CONTROL, one object moved onto a pocket seed is refused with reason 'seed' naming the seed index, and its edges are dropped; CONTROL, one object moved outside the hull is refused with reason 'hull' (NOT clamped — the divergence placement.mjs already made, for the reason the ledger records); CONTROL, two objects legal against the static pocket but colliding with each other's planted seeds are caught, which is the assertion that proves the accumulation is real and not assumed.

[turn 43 — done] Built plant/pocketLevel.mjs — pocketPlacementReport(pocket, objects, opts) and pocketLevelVerdict(pocket, objects, edges, opts) — and its gate plant/test/pocket-level.selftest.mjs. It composes and reimplements nothing: each object's geometric verdict is ONE legalSummon call against a {W,H,D,seeds,faces,opts} state view whose seed list grows as legal objects commit (the same technique buildcert.mjs already uses for the steps of one build), and the production half is level.mjs's own drop-the-refused-object rule. I took the ACCUMULATING version as the ticket directed. A consequence I derived and recorded rather than assumed: the accumulated seed check SUBSUMES level.mjs's pairGap check exactly, so pocketLevel calls pairGap nowhere — pairGap is the min of seedGap over the two constellations' seed pairs under conA.aniso, the accumulated check is the min of seedGap over the same pairs under pocket.opts.aniso, and a constellation whose aniso differs is refused for 'metric' before it can commit a seed. Blame precedence is IMPORTED from buildcert.mjs (BLAME_PRECEDENCE) rather than restated, then mapped onto reason strings that are level.mjs's own words for the session refusals ('self-collision', 'collides with existing summon') and placement.mjs's own words for the pocket ones ('hull', 'seed', 'metric'), so a UI written against either module keeps working. To avoid a second copy of the fifteen-line drop-the-edge rule I extracted networkFrom() out of level.mjs's levelVerdict and exported it — a pure extraction, same code, byte-identical error messages, levelVerdict now three lines. The gate asserts all four things the ticket named, and the headline one (accumulation is real) proves the failure mode is REACHABLE first: it asserts legalSummon(P, conB).ok === TRUE, i.e. the cheap static implementation really would have said yes, before asserting the accumulating one refuses, names the earlier object, and reports the independently recomputed gap. It also pins the vacuous-satisfiability trap in full (refused sink dropped -> surviving network has no sinks -> network.ok TRUE, margin 0, 'snk' absent from achieved, verdict FALSE). HONESTLY: I could not run the gate — no Bash in this turn's grant — so this is hand-traced, not executed. The specific residual risk is the three fixture-health assertions, which depend on where generatePocket(seed 2) actually put its 64 seeds: roomy.clear >= MIN_SEED_GAP+SHIFT+0.1, far.length === 2, and inner.length >= 1. I derived those thresholds from the geometry rather than picking them (a 1 m translation on x changes any anisotropic gap by at most 1 m, so clear >= 2.5 is exactly sufficient for the shifted copy to stay pocket-legal) and every claim they support is ALSO asserted directly, but if the fixture is denser than I estimate those three are where it would go red.

beads.title: legalSummon's docstring says 'every refusal carries summonSeed' — the metric refusal does not, and a renderer is the first thing that notices
beads.body:
placement.mjs's legalSummon header states: 'Every refusal carries `summonSeed` — the index within `con.seeds`, where 0 is the centre — so a caller can light up the offending part of the shape.' The metric refusal, pushed twelve lines below that sentence, carries only `{ ok, reason, conAniso, pocketAniso }`. No summonSeed, no role, no at.

It is not a bug in the predicate — a metric mismatch is a property of the whole constellation and there is no single seed to blame, so omitting the field is the right call. It is a bug in the SENTENCE the file tells its callers, and the cost lands on exactly the caller the docstring was written for: a UI that trusts the claim and writes `refusals.map(r => highlight(r.summonSeed))` lights up seed `undefined` and shows nothing, silently, on the one refusal a caller is least likely to have a test for.

This is the same shape lp-c46a0c recorded from the other direction ('a self-certifying turn tests what it BUILT and under-tests what it CLAIMED — the gap is between the docstring and the assertions'). placement.selftest.mjs's metric block asserts only that the refusal exists; nothing there reads summonSeed, so nothing could catch the drift. refusalLine handles it by branching on reason and never touching summonSeed, and by rendering metric with its own words rather than letting it fall through to an empty clause — a refusal with no sentence being the one outcome the function exists to prevent.

The cheap fix is one word in the docstring ('every PER-SEED refusal'), or an assertion in placement.selftest.mjs pinning which fields each reason carries. The second is better: a field list that no test reads is a field list that drifts, and this is the second consumer (after level.mjs) to build a walk over refusals from that paragraph.

beads.title: refusalLine returns null for a legal summon, and refuses to import placement.mjs
beads.body:
TWO CALLS, both easy to reverse, recorded so a later reader does not have to re-litigate them.

1. NULL RATHER THAN ''. A caller writing `if (line)` behaves identically either way. A caller that renders the value unconditionally shows the string 'null' — visible, reported, fixed in a minute — where '' shows an empty box, which is invisible and ships. This tree has already recorded (lp-a4030e and its four siblings) that its recurring failure mode is a channel that carries nothing and throws nothing; given a choice between two silences and a noise, take the noise. Reversing it is one `return ''`.

2. NO IMPORT OF placement.mjs. level-view.js is loaded in a browser by index.html, and placement.mjs imports solids.mjs while the verdicts it produces come from foamworld.js — pulling the predicate in to get a type or a constant would drag the pocket kernel into the page for a function that only reads fields. refusalLine takes a plain object instead. The side effect is the useful part: the gate can build verdicts with the REAL predicate in node and hand them straight to a renderer that has never heard of it, which is precisely what makes 'the sentence and the predicate cannot drift' checkable rather than asserted. The cost is that MIN_SEED_GAP is not imported and not needed — every number comes off the verdict.

What would reverse either: a caller that needs refusalLine to VALIDATE its input rather than render it. That caller wants the predicate, not this function.

beads.title: The sentence names the WORST refusal in each group and counts the rest, rather than listing them all
beads.body:
verdictLine's fail path enumerates every deficit in full ('a wanted 5 and got 3; b wanted 8 and got 7'). I did not copy that shape here and the reason is that the two verdicts are different in kind.

A production deficit is per-SINK, and a sink is a thing the player named and can point at — so listing them all reads as a list of places to go fix. A summon refusal is per-SEED of a constellation, and a seed is an internal part of a shape the player thinks of as one object. 'Seed 3 is 0.4 m short and seed 5 is 0.2 m short and seed 6 is 0.9 m short' is three facts about one mistake, and enumerating them buries the only thing the player can act on — which is that the whole shape has to move.

So each reason gets one clause: the cause, the COUNT ('in 3 places'), and the worst measurement. The count is what satisfies the ticket's first hard requirement — report every refusal, never silently pick one — without pretending the parts are separately fixable.

Worst is defined per reason (largest need-gap for seed and self, largest depth for hull) and ties keep the EARLIEST refusal, so the sentence is stable across runs. That mattered immediately: the hull fixture in the gate has two refusals at exactly equal depth, so a max that kept the last would have named a different wall on a different day.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a UI that highlights the offending seeds in 3D. Then the sentence is a caption for something the player can already see part-by-part, and enumerating becomes useful. The verdict carries everything needed for that (summonSeed, seed coordinates, per-refusal gap) and refusalLine deliberately does not consume it, so building the enumerated version alongside costs nothing this function did.

beads.title: A sentence-rendering gate is only worth something if it parses its own numbers back out — includes() would have passed for a renderer that invents distances
beads.body:
The obvious way to check 'the sentence does not contradict the predicate' is `line.includes(String(expected))`. That is weaker than it reads, in a way that matters here.

The verdict for a cube standing on a pocket seed carries gap 0 and need 1.5, and the sentence has to say the shortfall is 1.5. `line.includes('1.5')` passes for a renderer that hardcodes the threshold and never looks at the gap at all — which is EXACTLY the bug the ticket names, since a hardcoded 1.5 is right for a coincident seed and wrong for every near miss. It also passes on the substring of an unrelated number: '11.5', '1.52'.

So the gate extracts the number with a clause-specific regex ('about ([0-9.]+) m short of clear', 'by about ([0-9.]+) m', 'the tightest by about ([0-9.]+) m') and compares it to a value computed from the verdict, within 0.005 — the rounding the formatter is allowed. That permits the sentence to round and forbids it to invent, which is the actual contract. It also survives a change to the prose around the number, so the gate does not go red for a wording edit.

The general shape, and it is the same argument lp-8c9d1e made for build certificates: an assertion that relates a rendered string to a literal you chose measures your literal. Recomputing the expected value from the SOURCE OBJECT, in the test, by a different route than the renderer took, is the only version that bites.

The cheap and non-obvious companion check that came out of the same reasoning: assert `!/undefined|NaN/.test(line)` on every sentence the sweep produces. A missing field renders as the string 'undefined' inside a template literal and every includes() check in the file still passes, because the words around it are intact.

beads.title: Should a refusal say what is WRONG, or say what to DO about it?
beads.body:
refusalLine currently describes the fault: 'Too close to the rock already here in 3 places — the tightest is about 0.29 m short of clear.' The alternative is to describe the remedy: 'Move it about 0.3 m to your left.'

This is not decidable from here and it is not decidable by a gate, because both sentences are true and both are derivable from the same verdict — placement.mjs's seed refusals carry the offending seed's coordinates and the verdict carries the constellation's centre, so a direction and a distance are one subtraction away. What a gate can check is that the number matches the verdict. What it cannot check is which sentence a person can act on, and they pull in opposite directions: the fault version is honest about the whole obstruction (three seeds, worst 0.29 m) while the remedy version has to pick ONE move, and a move that clears the worst seed may not clear the other two — so the helpful-sounding sentence is the one that can lie.

I went with the fault version because it is the one that cannot be wrong, and because 'easier to reverse' favours it: adding a remedy clause to an existing fault sentence is additive, while removing a remedy players have learned to trust is not.

DO: Open the page once it renders a real pocket (the proposal above wires it), drag a summon into occupied ground, and read the refusal out loud. Then imagine the same moment with 'Move it about 0.3 m to your left' instead.

WATCH FOR: Whether you look at the sentence and then look at the screen to work out where to go, or whether the sentence alone is enough to make the next move. And whether being told a direction that turns out not to work feels worse than being told nothing.

SO THAT: If the fault version is enough: nothing changes, and the direction data in the verdict stays unused. If the remedy version is wanted: I file a bead adding a direction clause derived from the offending seed's coordinates and the summon centre, gated on a fixture where the suggested move is asserted to ACTUALLY produce a legal placement — which is the assertion that stops it lying, and it is buildable today because summonAt can just be asked.

beads.title: Wire refusalLine into the page: a refused summon must say why, on screen, not in a console
beads.body:
refusalLine() now exists in plant/level-view.js and is pinned by plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs against the real predicate. NOTHING CALLS IT. index.html renders the summon inspector and never asks placement.mjs anything, so the sentence a player is supposed to read is currently reachable only from node.

This is vision item 1 work, not inspector polish: the bar is 'an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for', and the refusal is the half that is missing. Everything needed is built — generatePocket, summonAt, refusalLine — and the remaining work is wiring plus one gate.

WHAT TO BUILD: in plant/index.html, a section that holds a real pocket (generatePocket with the MACRO opts already used by placement.selftest.mjs and level-view.selftest.mjs: nx 4, nz 4, layers 3, subLayers 1, cell 20, layerH 9, parMin 3, parTarget 6, seed 2), a control that moves a summon centre, and a live verdict line: summonAt(pocket, solid, centre) then refusalLine(verdict), rendered where verdictLine's output is rendered for the levels. A legal placement must say so; an illegal one must show the sentence.

THE GATE, and it must be a NEW file — plant/test/index-refusal-wiring.selftest.mjs — following the precedent already in this tree (index-level4-wiring.selftest.mjs, index-level5-wiring.selftest.mjs). It reads index.html as text and asserts: the pocket is built with those exact opts (so the page and the gates share a fixture); refusalLine is imported and called; its return value reaches the DOM rather than console.log; and the control's min/max bound the centre to values the module can actually evaluate. Then — the part the existing wiring tests do NOT do and this one should — it imports summonAt and refusalLine directly and asserts that at least one reachable control value produces a refusal and at least one produces a legal placement, so the page cannot ship a slider whose whole range is legal (nothing can fail, so it is not a game) or whose whole range is refused (nothing can succeed, so it is broken).

WHY A WEAKER GATE WILL NOT DO: asserting only that the string 'refusalLine' appears in index.html passes for a page that imports it and never renders it, which is exactly the state this bead leaves the tree in. The discriminating assertion is the reachability pair — one legal value and one refused value inside the control's own bounds — because that is the claim 'a player can cause a refusal' reduced to arithmetic.

Bounded to plant/index.html and plant/test/index-refusal-wiring.selftest.mjs. Note for whoever takes it: plant/CLAUDE.md records that svg#lvl's CSS rule targets Level 1's SVG by exact id and levels 2-6 render unstyled by it; do not fix that here, it is a separate pre-existing gap across five levels.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED ON DESIGN, and its factual claims all check out — refusalLine really is at plant/level-view.js:189 and really is called by nothing. Two reasons, and the first is the operator's own sentence. (1) What this builds is a control that MOVES A SUMMON CENTRE and re-renders a verdict. The pocket never changes; nothing is committed; there is no act, only a preview. The vision names that exact arti

beads.title: Pin which fields each legalSummon refusal reason carries — the docstring already promises one that metric does not have
beads.body:
placement.mjs's legalSummon header states 'Every refusal carries summonSeed — the index within con.seeds, where 0 is the centre — so a caller can light up the offending part of the shape.' The metric refusal, constructed twelve lines below that sentence, carries only { ok, reason, conAniso, pocketAniso }. No summonSeed, no role, no at.

The omission is CORRECT — a metric mismatch is a property of the whole constellation and there is no single seed to blame — so this is not a request to add the field. It is a request to stop the file promising it, and to make the promise checkable so it cannot drift again.

WHY IT MATTERS: the cost lands on the caller the docstring was written for. A UI doing refusals.map(r => highlight(r.summonSeed)) highlights seed `undefined` on the one refusal it is least likely to have a fixture for, silently. level.mjs and level-view.js's new refusalLine are both walks over that array built from that paragraph; refusalLine sidesteps it by branching on reason and never reading summonSeed, but the next consumer will not know to.

WHAT TO BUILD, in plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs (which exists and passes today): a block asserting the field contract per reason — hull carries at, wall, axis, depth, value, limit, clamped, summonSeed, role; seed carries at, seedIndex, seed, gap, need, summonSeed, role; self carries summonSeed, otherSummonSeed, gap, need and NO at; metric carries conAniso, pocketAniso and NO summonSeed. Assert both presence and ABSENCE, because a contract that only checks presence permits the fields to grow silently and it is exactly the absent one that bit here. Every fixture must come from the real predicate against the existing seed-2 macro pocket — the file already produces all four reasons, so no new fixture is needed. Then correct the header sentence to say 'every per-seed refusal'.

WHY THE EXISTING GATE IS NOT ENOUGH TODAY: placement.selftest.mjs's metric block asserts only that a refusal with reason 'metric' exists. Nothing in the file reads summonSeed off a metric refusal, so nothing could have caught the drift, and nothing will catch the next one.

Bounded to plant/placement.mjs (the docstring line only) and plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs. class-a against the existing green gate, no new file.

The drift is real and the diagnosis is right: the legalSummon header promises 'every refusal carries summonSeed', the metric refusal carries only { ok, reason, conAniso, pocketAniso }, and the omission is CORRECT because a metric mismatch is a property of the whole constellation with no single seed to blame — so the fi

beads.title: ACCUMULATE, and the accumulated seed check subsumes level.mjs's pairGap check EXACTLY — so pairGap is not called
beads.body:
The ticket named the order question as the substance of the work and said to take the accumulating version. I did. What is worth recording is that once you accumulate, the session-local pairwise check DISAPPEARS rather than sitting alongside the pocket one, and that is a derivation rather than a convenience.

pairGap(conA, conB) is the minimum of seedGap over every pair of their seeds, taken under conA.aniso. The accumulated check is the minimum of seedGap over exactly those same pairs, taken under pocket.opts.aniso, because conA's seeds are IN the seed list legalSummon is walking by the time conB is asked. Those are the same number, and they are the same number for a reason that has to hold: a constellation whose aniso differs from the pocket's is refused for 'metric' before it can ever commit a seed, so every committed seed was placed under the pocket's own metric.

So pocketLevel.mjs calls pairGap nowhere. Calling it too would be a second copy of a check already being made, and the two copies would be free to disagree the moment either metric moved. The gate does not take my word for it: the collision it forces is graded against a min-gap recomputed in the test file from reformPocket's own formula, never read back from pairGap or seedGap.

What would reverse this: if a future caller ever needed to compare two constellations built for DIFFERENT metrics without refusing them — at which point the subsumption argument breaks at its one load-bearing step and the pairwise check has to come back explicitly.

beads.title: Extracted networkFrom() out of level.mjs rather than copying fifteen lines into pocketLevel.mjs
beads.body:
pocketLevelVerdict needs exactly level.mjs's rule — a refused object contributes no node, every edge naming it is dropped, an edge naming a non-object is passed through so feasible() raises its own unknown-node error — applied to a DIFFERENT placement report. Three options: copy it, call levelVerdict (impossible, it computes its own session-local report), or export the half that does the work.

I exported it. levelVerdict is now `feasible(networkFrom(objects, placement, edges))` and nothing else changed: same code, same order, byte-identical error strings including the `level:` prefix, so level.selftest.mjs's message assertions are untouched. pocketLevel.mjs's own validation errors say `pocketLevel:` and its networkFrom-sourced ones say `level:`, which is honest — they are level.mjs's checks and re-badging them would hide where they live.

Why not copy: the drop-the-edge rule is the one place the vacuous-satisfiability trap can be reintroduced, and this repo's most-repeated failure is two copies of a rule drifting. Fifteen lines is exactly the size that feels too small to share and is not.

What would reverse it: if the pocket layer ever needs to drop objects on a different rule than the session layer does, at which point they are genuinely two rules and should be two functions.

beads.title: buildcert.certify and pocketPlacementReport are now two accumulating walks over the same state view — close enough to look like duplication, and they are not
beads.body:
Both build `{ W, H, D, seeds, faces, opts }` from the real pocket with committed seeds appended, both hand it to legalSummon, both split a 'seed' refusal on `seedIndex < base` into pocket-owned versus step-owned, and both use BLAME_PRECEDENCE. pocketLevel imports that constant from buildcert precisely so the split cannot drift. The next reader will see the rest and want to merge them.

They should not be merged as they stand, and the reason is the ORDER each walks:

  · certify walks buildOrder(network) — the TOPOLOGICAL order, derived from the
    factory's own edges. It is answering 'is there a legal order to build this',
    and it goes on to compute reorderability, dependency blocking and a
    suggestedOrder, none of which mean anything without a network.
  · pocketPlacementReport walks the order the OBJECTS ARE GIVEN IN — the player's
    placement order. It is answering 'is what has been put down legal', and it
    runs before any network exists (an object may be refused and never contribute
    a node at all).

The honest de-duplication, if anyone wants it, is a shared `accumulate(pocket, items, minSeedGap)` returning per-item verdicts plus the seed/owner arrays, with each caller keeping its own explanation layer. That is a real refactor of two files that both have passing gates, and it is worth doing only when a third accumulating walk appears — two is a coincidence, three is a pattern.

beads.title: The gate's only fixture-dependent assertions are three, and their thresholds are derived rather than picked
beads.body:
Nobody can know where generatePocket(seed: 2) put its 64 seeds without running it, so every centre in this gate is CHOSEN BY SWEEP over a 1445-point lattice rather than hard-coded — a hand-picked coordinate that happened to be occupied would fail the gate for a reason that has nothing to do with pocketLevel.mjs. That leaves exactly three assertions that are claims about the FIXTURE rather than about the module:

  roomy.clear >= MIN_SEED_GAP + SHIFT + 0.1   (2.6 m)
  far.length === 2                            (two more clear centres, 20 m apart)
  inner.length >= 1                           (a comfortably-interior pocket seed)

The first is the one that took thought, and stating the derivation is the point. Section 4 needs two constellations that are EACH legal against the static pocket and yet collide with each other. It builds the second by translating the first SHIFT metres along x. A translation of SHIFT changes any anisotropic gap by at most SHIFT — x is the unscaled axis and the triangle inequality holds in the scaled metric — so `clear >= MIN_SEED_GAP + SHIFT` is exactly sufficient, and the threshold is written as that expression rather than as a number so it moves if SHIFT does.

SHIFT is 1 rather than 2 for the same reason: at 1 m the matched seed pairs are exactly 1 m apart (dy = 0, no sqrt(aniso) enters at all) and the fixture only has to be 2.6 m open; at 2 m the collision is 1.2 m and the fixture has to be 3.6 m open. Halving the demand on the fixture cost nothing, because both values are comfortably under the 1.5 threshold the section needs.

And every claim those three support is ALSO asserted directly — clearOf(conB) >= MIN_SEED_GAP and legalSummon(P, conB).ok are checked on the actual constellation, not inferred from the sweep — so a fixture-health failure names itself instead of surfacing as a mysterious verdict.

beads.title: A pocket-illegal object opens the vacuous-satisfiability trap from a SECOND direction, and only one of the two is visible in the verdict
beads.body:
The ledger already records that dropping a refused SINK leaves a network with no sinks, which production.mjs documents as vacuously satisfiable at margin 0 — so network.ok goes TRUE on a level that just failed. That was found for session-local collisions. It transfers to pocket refusals unchanged, and the gate asserts the whole shape (network.ok true, margin 0, no 'snk' key in achieved, verdict false) rather than just the verdict, because asserting only the verdict passes for an implementation that reached it by accident.

What is new is the CONTRAST the two pocket CONTROLs now draw, and it is worth knowing before anyone builds a UI on this:

  · refuse the SINK  -> the factory goes VACUOUS. network.ok true, margin 0,
    deficits empty. The production half reports success on a broken level.
  · refuse the PROCESSOR -> the factory DEGRADES. network.ok false, achieved 0,
    margin -1, one deficit naming the sink and its resource. The production half
    reports the failure in useful detail.

Same severity of mistake, opposite legibility. A player who parks a depot in a rock gets a factory that says it is fine; a player who parks a smelter in a rock gets a factory that says exactly what is starving. Any renderer built on this must take the placement half's refusals as the primary message and treat network.* as secondary, or the first case will read as a win. Both cases are pinned in plant/test/pocket-level.selftest.mjs sections 2 and 3.

beads.title: LEVEL_7: the first level played IN A POCKET — pocketLevelVerdict driving a real generatePocket fixture
beads.body:
Vision item 1 says stop making the explainer and make the game, and item 3 says the bridge between rates and a real pocket is the missing link. pocketLevel.mjs (this turn) is that bridge as a LIBRARY; nothing plays it. Every one of levels 1-6 is an abstract network literal with a slider — there is no pocket, no position, and nothing a player can put anywhere.

Build plant/levels/pocket1.mjs exporting a fixed pocket (generatePocket with a pinned seed and the MACRO opts already used by three selftests), a fixed set of node RATES, and a small set of candidate CENTRES the player chooses between — so the decision is WHERE a machine goes, not what number a slider reads. The verdict is one pocketLevelVerdict call. Deliberately NOT in scope: rendering, and any new oracle work — the oracle is done.

The level must be barely satisfiable in the sense level1.mjs established (a narrow winnable band with a DIFFERENT failure on each side), and the design constraint that makes it a level rather than a diagram is that at least one candidate arrangement must fail on PLACEMENT while its rates are perfectly fine, and at least one must fail on RATES while every placement is legal. If both failure modes cannot be reached by moving one object, it is a diagram.

Gate: creates plant/test/pocket1.selftest.mjs, asserting (a) the winning arrangement verdicts ok with hand-computed achieved/margin; (b) a CONTROL arrangement whose placements are all legal and whose network is infeasible, with the deficit naming the right sink; (c) a CONTROL arrangement whose rates are identical to the winner's and whose verdict is false purely because one object is refused — and asserting WHICH refusal reason, so 'it failed' is not confused with 'it failed for the reason the level is about'; (d) the vacuous-satisfiability shape if the refused object is the sink, since that is the case a renderer will get wrong.
evidence: rejected: The vision rejects this by name. 'A SEVENTH LEVEL' is listed under what does not matter right now, with the reasoning spelled out: 'Six is a curve; seven is tiling. If you find yourself writing another network literal with different numbers, the ticket you actually want is item 1.' This is a seventh level, and it says so in its own title. The pocket framing is a real distinction and I weighed it —

beads.title: Give feasible() a per-processor bound report so a pocket verdict can say WHY, not just WHAT
beads.body:
Two consumers now need something feasible() computes on every call and throws away, and this is the third time it has been recorded. Its inner loop evaluates `scale = min(capacity, min supply/inputRate)` and knows exactly which term won; the return carries only achieved, deficits and margin, all sink-side.

The ledger already records two callers that had to reimplement the comparison: qualifyingRelay's `capacity*inputRate >= R` precondition, and the note that `bound` names one starved input where several may be equally starved. pocketLevel.mjs is now a third context where it bites, and the reason is specific rather than general: when a level fails, the placement half can already say 'the smelter is standing in a rock' with a seed index and a real gap, and the production half can only say 'the depot is short by 12'. The two halves of one verdict are wildly uneven in how actionable they are, and the missing half is already computed.

Scope: extend feasible()'s result with a per-processor entry naming which term bound it ('capacity' or 'supply'), the resource if supply-bound, and the scale — WITHOUT changing any existing field, because level.mjs, level-view.js, buildcert.mjs, pocketLevel.mjs and six levels all read the current shape. The no-regression half of the gate is the important half: every existing assertion in production.selftest.mjs must still pass unchanged, and the new fields must be pinned on at least one capacity-bound and one supply-bound fixture that already exist there.

Explicitly NOT in scope, and this is the trap: do not try to make autoSplit() call it. The ledger records why that is impossible — autoSplit runs on a network whose fan-out group is still unsplit, and feasible() throws on an unsplit fan-out, so the caller that most needs the answer cannot obtain it from the function that computes it. Attempting the de-duplication inside this ticket would change autoSplit's refusal set, which is a separate risk with a separate gate.
evidence: rejected: It proposes to build something that already exists, and I checked before saying so. plant/production.mjs already returns `bound`: it is documented at lines 222 and 232, populated at line 288 as bound[id] = { by, resource, scale, headroom: node.capacity - scale }, and returned at line 314 — which is field-for-field what this ticket asks a turn to add ('which term bound it, the resource if supply-bo

beads.title: placement.mjs's legalSeed ACCEPTS a NaN point — the predicate and the kernel disagree on exactly the input a UI produces most often
