beads.body:
legalSeed(pocket, [NaN, 18, 40]).ok === true. The kernel refuses the same point. So the predicate a UI greys the ground out with and the transaction that does the planting disagree on a raycast that missed — the single most common bad input a placement UI can produce.

THE MECHANISM, and it is two independent silences stacked:

1. hullViolation computes `depth = v < lo ? lo - v : (v > hi ? v - hi : 0)`. Every comparison against NaN is false, so BOTH branches fall through to the literal 0, and `if (depth <= 0) continue` then skips the axis. No hull violation is found for a coordinate that is not a number.

2. nearestSeed then returns `{ gap: NaN }` (the first seed wins because `NaN < NaN` is false for every subsequent one), and `near.gap < minSeedGap` is false. No seed refusal either.

So legalSeed returns ok:true with `nearest.gap === NaN` — a green light, carrying a NaN in the field a caller would inspect. summonAt inherits it: a constellation centred on NaN has NaN everywhere and every seed passes.

The kernel does NOT have this hole, and the reason is worth noting because it is luck rather than design: foamworld.js's hullRefusal compares the CLAMPED coordinate against the original (`if (c[i] === p[i]) continue`), and `NaN !== NaN`, so the axis is not skipped and the point is refused as a hull violation. The comment there even says 'NaN also lands here'. Two files implementing the same predicate, one of which happens to be written in a form that catches it.

GUARDED IN summon-session.mjs rather than fixed at the source, because placement.mjs is outside this ticket's bounded paths: preview() and place() both refuse a point that is not three finite numbers, with reason 'point' and blame 'caller'. That guard is load-bearing, not defensive tidiness, and the module header says so.

THE CHEAP REAL FIX is one line in hullViolation — compute depth from the clamp the way foamworld.js does, or test Number.isFinite explicitly — and it is proposed as its own bead against the existing placement.selftest.mjs gate. The gate written here deliberately does NOT pin placement.mjs's current behaviour: asserting `legalSeed([NaN,...]).ok === true` would turn a future fix of it into a red gate. It asserts the KERNEL's answer (which is correct and stable) and logs the predicate's, which is the right split when you are recording a bug you are not allowed to fix.

GENERAL SHAPE: a predicate written with `<` and `>` has a third outcome nobody wrote a branch for. Every ordered comparison against NaN is false, so a chain of them falls through to whatever the final `else` says — and the final else in a validator is almost always 'fine'. NaN does not fail a range check; it passes one.

beads.title: A self-collision fixture is silently shadowed by a seed collision — refusal ORDER decides what a test is actually testing
beads.body:
Caught while hand-tracing my own gate, and it would have gone red for a reason that had nothing to do with the code under test.

The block asserts that a cube summoned at r=0.5 fights ITSELF (its neighbours land 1.0m from its centre, inside the 1.5m refusal radius) and that the session normalises placement.mjs's 'self' and the kernel's 'batch' to one blame value. My first version ran that at FIX.c1 — the centre where the scripted playthrough had just planted a cube. Of course it did: it was the one point already in scope and already known legal.

But legalSummon pushes refusals in a fixed order — metric, then PER-SEED (hull/seed) in summonSeed order, then self pairs — so with the player's own cube centre sitting exactly on that point, `first` is a 'seed' refusal blamed on 'player'. The assertion `first.reason === 'self'` fails, and the failure says nothing about self-collision detection, which works perfectly.

THE FIX IS A CLEARANCE BOUND, not a different point picked by eye. The anisotropic gap is a genuine metric (a linear rescale of Euclidean), so the triangle inequality applies: if the centre is `clear` from every pocket seed, and a tiny neighbour is at most `2r*sqrt(aniso)` from the centre, then that neighbour is at least `clear - 2r*sqrt(aniso)` from every pocket seed. For r=0.5, aniso=2.2 that is `clear - 1.483 > 1.5`, i.e. clear > 2.983. The gate asks candidates() for clear=3.5 and states the arithmetic in a comment.

TWO THINGS TRANSFER. (1) When a function reports MULTIPLE refusals in a defined order and a test reads `first`, the test is implicitly asserting an ORDERING as well as a verdict — and a fixture that can trigger an earlier-ranked reason is testing something else entirely, silently. (2) The convenient fixture is the dangerous one. FIX.c1 was in scope and known-good, which is exactly why it was the worst possible choice: it was known-good BECAUSE something had already been built there.

beads.title: The session classifies blame (player / pocket / hull / self / foam / caller) rather than passing the kernel's refusal through
beads.body:
WHAT I CHOSE. Every refusal returned by preview() and place() is a copy of the underlying refusal plus a `blame` field, and when blame is 'player' it also carries blameMove, blameSolid and blameCentre.

WHY. A thin wrapper over reformPocketAll would have been worth nothing — the transaction already exists and already names what it hit. What it names is 'seed 71 is 1.4m away', and a player cannot use that. The session is the only layer that knows seed 71 is the east face of the cube THEY summoned on move 1, because it is the only layer that holds originCount (the index boundary between the generated foam and what the player built) and the per-placement seed ranges. That distinction — 'you did this' versus 'the world is like that' — is not derivable from the transaction's return value, and it is the difference between a message a player can act on and a number.

It also made the gate's requirement (a) sharply testable rather than vaguely so. 'A refusal the player caused' is otherwise a judgement; with blame it is `refusal.blame === 'player' && refusal.blameMove === 1`, cross-checked against an independently recomputed seed index.

WHAT I REJECTED. (i) Returning the raw kernel refusal and letting the UI work it out — that pushes the one piece of state only the session has into every caller, and the level-view verdictLine bug in this repo's ledger is what happens when refusal rendering is left to a consumer. (ii) A boolean `playerCaused` — the ledger already records three separate instances in this project of a scalar standing in for a structure and under-reporting (verdictLine's deficits[0], `bound` naming one starved input, network.ok standing for two verdicts). Six named classes cost nothing and do not collapse.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT. If a renderer ends up switching on `reason` anyway and never reads `blame`, the field is decoration and should go. BLAME is exported as an array precisely so that a renderer can be checked for exhaustiveness against it.

beads.title: A malformed point is a REFUSAL; an unknown solid THROWS — and a bad point does not count as a move
beads.body:
WHAT I CHOSE. preview([NaN, 1, 1]) and place('cube', null) return an ordinary refusal, `{ reason: 'point', blame: 'caller' }`, and place() returns `move: null` without incrementing the move counter. select('trapezohedron') and place('trapezohedron', p) throw.

WHY THE ASYMMETRY. A solid name comes from a fixed enum inside the program — SOLID_NAMES has five entries and a caller who passes a sixth has a bug that should be loud and immediate. A point comes from the world: a raycast, a click, a slider, a level file. Bad points are a normal runtime event and a controller that throws on one turns a missed click into a crashed page.

WHY IT IS NOT A MOVE. The gate asserts a bound — 'a player-caused refusal in exactly 2 moves' — and that assertion is only meaningful if `moves` counts things the player actually did. A refused summon IS a move (they aimed, they clicked, the foam said no; that is the mechanic). A malformed argument never reached the foam, and counting it would let a caller's bug inflate the number the gate is asserting on. So refusals increment, malformed arguments do not, and both halves are pinned in the gate.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT. If a level format ever lets a designer write a solid name as data rather than as code, the solid check becomes the same kind of runtime input as the point and should become a refusal too — reason 'solid', blame 'caller'.

beads.title: candidates() returns { list, found, truncated, scanned } — never a bare array, because a cap that is not reported reads as completeness
beads.body:
WHAT I CHOSE. candidates() caps `list` at `limit` (default 64) but counts every legal placement in `found` and sets `truncated` outright. It also reports `scanned`, and the gate asserts scanned >= found >= list.length, that truncated is exactly (found > list.length), and — as a control that the `clear` filter is applied at all — that an impossible clearance finds zero while a relaxed one can never find fewer.

WHY. The ledger's standing rule is that a workflow which bounds coverage must log what it dropped, because silent truncation reads as 'covered everything'. The same argument is stronger for an API than for a log: a UI handed a bare array of 64 highlights has no way to know whether that is all of them or the first page, and 'these are the legal spots' is precisely the kind of claim a player will treat as exhaustive.

WHAT I REJECTED. Returning a plain array (idiomatic, and the ticket's phrasing 'candidates() ... returns' invites it) with the count attached as a property or logged to the console. Both hide the cap in a place a caller can ignore by accident. An object forces the destructure.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT. Nothing about the shape; if it turns out no caller ever wants a cap, `limit` could default to Infinity and `truncated` would simply always be false.

beads.title: Hand-verification without a shell caught a SYNTAX error and a shadowed fixture — the two failure classes are different and only one of them is about arithmetic
beads.body:
Recording what was actually productive, rather than restating the standing 'gate unverifiable in-turn' recommendation, which is in this ledger past twenty times and which the previous two turns agreed to stop repeating.

The hand-verification pass on my own gate found two defects, and they are worth distinguishing because the ~20 prior instances of this note all reason about ARITHMETIC risk (is my expected number right?) and neither of these was arithmetic.

1. A SYNTAX ERROR. I had written ``ok(x, `... relaxing `clear` cannot find fewer ...`)`` — a backtick nested inside a template literal. The file would not have parsed. NOT ONE ASSERTION would have run, and the failure would have been a parse error naming a line in a message string, which reads like a typo rather than like the gate never executing. Found by grepping the file for lines carrying three or more backticks; also grepped for an ASCII apostrophe inside a single-quoted string, which is the same class and the reason this repo's test files use the typographic apostrophe in prose.

2. A SHADOWED FIXTURE (filed separately in full): a 'self'-refusal assertion aimed at a point where an earlier-ranked refusal fires first.

THE TRANSFERABLE PART. When you cannot run the file, arithmetic is the risk you naturally worry about and it is not the only one, or even the worst one — a wrong number fails one assertion loudly, a syntax error fails all of them in a way that looks unrelated. The two cheap mechanical passes that do not require a shell, and that I would run again on any unrun test file:

  · grep for quote-nesting hazards (backticks inside template literals, ASCII apostrophes inside single-quoted strings) — a pure lexer problem a human eye slides straight over;
  · for every assertion that reads `first` or `[0]` of a list the code builds in a defined ORDER, ask what else could rank ahead of the thing being tested.

Neither is about whether the code is correct. Both are about whether the test will run and whether it will test what it says.

beads.title: Does highlighting every legal spot destroy the failure the whole thing is for?
beads.body:
candidates() exists so a UI can show the player where a summon fits. But vision.md's bar is that within thirty seconds a stranger DOES SOMETHING THAT CAN FAIL — 'an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for'. A page that highlights every legal cell removes exactly that: the player clicks a green square, it works, and the constraint that is supposed to BE the mechanic is never felt. The two designs are in direct tension and I cannot settle it from here, because it is a question about what a person feels in the first minute and every check I could write would pass for both.

I have decided the reversible half and shipped it: candidates() is a controller method with a `clear` margin, not a UI decision, so the page can use it for a full highlight, for a subtle hint (highlight only after a refusal), or not at all, without any change to the module or its gate. What I cannot decide is which the page should do.

This is item 1 of the vision and the first thing a stranger meets, which is why it is worth a person's two minutes rather than a guess.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com once the summon panel ships. Play it twice: once with every legal spot highlighted before you act, once with no highlight at all and only a refusal message when you get it wrong. Two minutes each.

WATCH FOR: Whether the un-highlighted version makes you look at the pocket and form a theory about where things fit, or just makes you click at random until something sticks. And whether the highlighted version feels like a puzzle or like colouring in.

SO THAT: If the un-highlighted version produces a theory, the page ships with no highlight and candidates() stays a debug/level-design tool — and the next ticket is a better refusal sentence, since the refusal becomes the only teacher. If it produces random clicking, the page ships with the highlight on and the difficulty has to come from somewhere else (which solid fits where, or a limited budget of summons), and that is a different next ticket. If both feel flat, the problem is that placement has no CONSEQUENCE yet — nothing is produced or consumed — and the next ticket is wiring production.mjs to placed objects, i.e. level.mjs's levelVerdict against a real pocket rather than a session-local list.

beads.title: Wire summon-session.mjs into plant/index.html — the click that reaches the foam
beads.body:
The sibling this ticket deliberately excluded. plant/summon-session.mjs now exists and is gated: start(seed) generates a real pocket, candidates() says where a summon fits, preview(point) gives the verdict without planting, place(solid, point) plants it as one transaction or refuses with a named, ATTRIBUTED cause (blame: player | pocket | hull | self | foam | caller). Nothing on the page calls any of it — index.html is still the inspector.

SCOPE: a summon panel on plant/index.html driven entirely by the controller. Solid picker, a point chosen by the player (the simplest honest version is three numeric inputs or a click on a 2D top-down plan of the pocket — NOT a 3D raycast, which is a much bigger ticket and not needed to clear the bar), a Summon button, a live verdict line, and a running list of what has been placed. Event handlers must contain NO placement logic: they read inputs, call the controller, render what comes back. That is vision item 1's explicit requirement ('the game's control logic lives in a module, not in event handlers') and it is also what keeps this ticket gateable.

THE REFUSAL SENTENCE IS THE POINT, not decoration. blame:'player' must read differently from blame:'pocket' — 'that is 1.4m from the cube you placed' versus 'there is already foam there' — because the whole bar in vision.md is that a stranger does something that CAN FAIL and understands why. A refusal rendered as 'refused' throws away everything the module computed.

THE GATE IT CREATES: plant/test/index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs, following the established precedent of index-level4/5/6-wiring.selftest.mjs — read plant/index.html as text and assert the wiring exists. It must check (a) that the page imports ./summon-session.mjs and calls start/preview/place, (b) that every solid in SOLID_NAMES the picker offers is a real name from solids.mjs rather than a hand-typed list that can drift, (c) that the verdict renderer branches on all six BLAME values, exported from the module as an array precisely so exhaustiveness is checkable, and (d) that no literal 1.5 / 3.2 / 2.2 threshold appears in the page's own script — a placement constant re-typed into the page is the drift this whole module exists to prevent. A weaker gate that only greps for the word 'summon' would pass for a page that imports the module and never calls it.

WARNING for whoever takes this: plant/index.html's CSS keys svg#lvl by exact id, and levels 2-6 already ship unstyled by that selector (recorded finding). Do not fix that here; it is pre-existing and a separate ticket.

[turn 53 — done] Wired summon-session.mjs into plant/index.html and created the gate. The page now carries a summon panel: a top-down SVG plan of a real generatePocket pocket (every pocket seed drawn, the player's own summons in a different colour), a height slider, a solid picker built from SOLID_NAMES, a live verdict line, a running list of what has been placed, and a 'start a new pocket' button. Click the plan to choose a point, press summon to plant. Every placement decision belongs to the controller — the handlers read a control, call session.start/preview/place/candidates, and render what comes back; the page never calls legalSummon, summonAt, legalSeed, constellation or reformPocket*, and contains no placement threshold. Refusals render one sentence per BLAME value from a table keyed on refusal.blame, and the page throws at startup if the module ever grows a blame the table has no sentence for. The gate, plant/test/index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs, reads index.html as text and checks (a) the imports and all four controller calls plus the negative 'no placement in the page' assertions, (b) the picker comes from SOLID_NAMES and no solid name is hand-typed in the block, (c) exhaustiveness DERIVED from the module's own BLAME export — every value has an entry, all six sentence bodies are pairwise distinct, and player/pocket are asserted to differ in the specific way the ticket names, (d) no literal 1.5/2.2/3.2 in the summon block. HONESTLY: I could not run anything — this turn had Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only, so neither the gate nor the page has been executed. Every regex in the gate was hand-traced against the exact bytes I wrote, and I grepped index.html to confirm no forbidden literal, solid name or placement call exists after the summon banner (all such hits are at lines 321-378, well before it). Untested by construction: that a browser paints the plan, that getScreenCTM maps a click to the world point the player aimed at, and how long generatePocket takes on a phone — pocket generation is deferred one tick so it cannot block first paint, but its cost is unmeasured.
evidence: raised to P0 by the operator 2026-08-06: this is vision item 1, and it sat at P1 behind oracle work I promoted to P0. Fifteen turns produced seven backend modules and not one line of plant/index.html.

beads.title: placement.mjs's legalSeed accepts a NaN point — close it, and pin the whole finite-input contract
beads.body:
legalSeed(pocket, [NaN, 18, 40]).ok === true today. The kernel refuses the same point. So the predicate a UI greys the ground out with and the transaction that plants disagree on a raycast that missed, which is the most common bad input a placement UI can produce.

MECHANISM (full detail in this turn's finding): hullViolation computes `depth = v < lo ? lo - v : (v > hi ? v - hi : 0)`; both comparisons are false for NaN so depth is the literal 0 and `if (depth <= 0) continue` skips the axis. nearestSeed then returns gap NaN and `NaN < 1.5` is false. Two silences, and ok:true falls out with a NaN sitting in `nearest.gap`.

foamworld.js does NOT have the hole, and by luck rather than design: hullRefusal compares the clamped coordinate against the original (`if (c[i] === p[i]) continue`) and `NaN !== NaN`, so the axis is not skipped. Two implementations of one predicate, one of which happens to be written in a form that catches it.

SCOPE, small and additive: make hullViolation (or legalSeed) refuse a non-finite coordinate explicitly. Prefer an explicit Number.isFinite test over mimicking foamworld's clamp comparison — the clamp form works by accident and the next person to refactor it will remove the accident. Decide and document whether the refusal is `reason:'hull'` (matching the kernel exactly, so the two agree byte for byte, which is what multi-insert.selftest.mjs's hull-agreement block already asserts for finite points) or a new `reason:'point'`. I would take 'hull' for agreement; either is defensible and the choice belongs in the bead's evidence.

Bounded paths: plant/placement.mjs, plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs.

CLASS-A against the EXISTING gate — plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs exists and passes today, and it is the right one because the real risk here is a REGRESSION: hullViolation is called by legalSeed on every seed of every summon and by candidates() hundreds of times per sweep. The new assertions belong in the same file: NaN, Infinity and -Infinity on each of x, y, z; that the predicate's answer matches reformPocketAll's for those points (the file already has the machinery to compare the two); and a CONTROL that finite points are entirely unaffected.

NOTE for whoever takes it: plant/summon-session.mjs currently guards this itself, refusing a non-finite point before the predicate sees it, and its gate deliberately does NOT pin placement.mjs's buggy answer — it asserts the kernel's and logs the predicate's, so fixing this cannot turn that gate red. Once this lands, summon-session's guard becomes redundant rather than wrong; leave it, or remove it in a follow-up, but do not remove it in this ticket without re-running summon-session.selftest.mjs.

[turn 54 — done] Closed the hole in plant/placement.mjs's hullViolation: a coordinate that is not a finite number is now refused explicitly (Number.isFinite, not the NaN !== NaN accident foamworld.js relies on), with reason:'hull' so the predicate and reformPocketAll agree on reason, axis and wall, plus a new nonFinite:true flag and depth:Infinity. The nonFinite key is added ONLY on the non-finite branch, so a finite refusal record is byte-identical to what this file has been asserting since it was written — the real risk in this change was a regression, since hullViolation runs on every seed of every summon and hundreds of times per sweep. Added a section 7 to plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs (~58 new checks): NaN, +Infinity and -Infinity on each of x, y and z, each cross-checked against reformPocketAll (the transaction refuses non-finite points arithmetically before rebuildWith, so it is a safe oracle where attempt()/reformPocket would clamp to NaN and rebuild); the x-y-z tie-break between two non-finite axes; a two-element point and a string coordinate, which fell in the same hole; propagation through summonAt (a cube centred on NaN is refused at all 7 seeds); and controls that the finite path is unchanged. HONESTLY: I could not execute the gate — this turn had no Bash. Every assertion was hand-traced against both implementations' source, including each of the 18 (value, axis) pairs' wall and depth on both sides; the two edits are small and the finite branch is unchanged logic. Still inference, not execution.

beads.title: The reorderable hole is REAL, and the fixture that exposes it needs two strands of DIFFERENT DEPTH plus a declaration order pulling both ways
beads.body:
The ticket said the counterexample was UNPROVEN — the author could not build one across 3- and 4-node shapes because "Kahn's FIFO tends to put any early-ready node before the failing node, which lands it in blockedBy and therefore in the dodge set". That diagnosis is exactly right, and it is also the recipe for beating it. Here is the construction, because it took most of the turn and nobody should have to re-derive it.

TWO FACTS IN TENSION:

  1. FIFO Kahn (production.mjs's analyse) emits in LEVEL ORDER — every node at longest-path-depth k precedes every node at depth k+1. So for the colliding node z to come AFTER the failing node w in the default order, z must be DEEPER than w. That is the only lever; no amount of declaration-order fiddling moves a depth-0 node after a depth-1 one.

  2. orderPreferring picks the first READY non-avoid node in NODE DECLARATION order while the wanted node waits for its ancestors. So z's whole strand must sit EARLIER in the nodes[] array than w's ancestors, or the greedy races straight to w and z never gets in.

Those two are satisfiable simultaneously because Kahn's queue only seeds itself from the declaration order of the ROOTS. So:

    d0 -> d1 -> z        (z at depth 2)
    a0 -> w              (w at depth 1)
    c0                   (loose, depth 0, the blocker)

    nodes[] = [d0, d1, z, a0, c0, w]

  · Kahn: roots d0, a0, c0 in that order -> d0, a0, c0, then d1, then w, then z.
    buildOrder = [d0, a0, c0, d1, w, z]. z is AFTER w. Its seeds are not in the
    pocket when w is judged, so a collision with it CANNOT appear in blockedBy.
  · w fails, blamed on c0 alone — a non-ancestor earlier step, the textbook
    reorderable:true shape.
  · orderPreferring(w, avoid=[c0]) then spends the wait for a0 on the cheapest
    ready non-avoid nodes, which are d0, d1 and then z — because they are
    earlier in nodes[] than a0. Suggested order = [d0, d1, z, a0, w, c0], and z
    lands on the exact centre w wanted.

WHY EVERY SMALLER ATTEMPT FAILS, so nobody retries them: if w is ready at step 0 the greedy takes it first and nothing can precede it; if w has exactly one initially-ready ancestor the greedy takes that ancestor and then w, in two picks, and the other strand never advances; if z is at the same depth as w or shallower, Kahn puts z before w and z is in blockedBy (hence dodged) after all. Depth(z) > depth(w) AND z-strand-before-w-ancestors-in-nodes[] are both necessary.

So the claim in buildcert.mjs's header was not merely unverified, it was FALSE, and it is false on a six-node network.

beads.title: The recursion the guard prevents is naturally SHALLOW — the dodge set converges in about two rounds, and that is why the guard is a bound rather than a bugfix
beads.body:
Requirement (c) asked for a cost assertion that the guard works on "a deep chain of collisions". I tried to build a fixture that forces an unguarded implementation to recurse N deep and could not, and the reason is structural rather than a failure of effort.

Each round's avoid set is built from blockedBy — every node that ACTUALLY collided in that round's order. So the avoid set grows monotonically, and orderPreferring dodges strictly more nodes each time. On the fixture built here: round 1 dodges {c0} and pulls z in (refuted); round 2 dodges {z} and produces [d0, d1, a0, w, c0, z], where w lands. Two rounds, converged. To get three you would need a THIRD node that is deeper than w, later in the default order, and earlier in nodes[] than w's ancestors, and that survives being dodged — each extra round costs a whole extra strand, and every strand you add is one more node the next round's dodge set eliminates.

I am NOT claiming unguarded recursion terminates; I am claiming I could not exhibit a deep case, and the gate says so in a comment rather than pretending the assertion is a stress test. What the gate does assert is the honest version: reorderRuns === 1 on the fixture where an unguarded implementation would report 2 (the trial fails and would suggest again), an explicit { suggest: false } call reporting 'unchecked' with zero runs, and a 30-node pile-up costing exactly one nested run — so the cost is not a function of how many things collide.

The transferable bit: "prove the guard by making the unguarded version blow up" is the instinct, and when the unguarded version turns out to be self-limiting, the honest substitute is an assertion on the COUNT at the smallest fixture where guarded and unguarded differ. 1 vs 2 is a real difference and it is testable; 1 vs 400 was not available.

beads.title: suggestedOrder is nulled when the suggestion is refuted, and the tried order moves to attemptedOrder
beads.body:
The alternative was to keep suggestedOrder pointing at the constructed order regardless of the verdict and let callers consult reorderCheck. I rejected it: a field called suggestedOrder that holds an order which does not work is a trap for exactly the caller the field exists for, and this repo has already recorded two under-reporting bugs of that shape (verdictLine reading deficits[0], `bound` naming one starved input of several). So suggestedOrder now means "an order that was RUN and works", full stop, and attemptedOrder means "what was constructed", non-null whenever a candidate existed — including under the recursion guard, which is what makes 'unchecked' mean constructed-and-not-run rather than not-considered.

What would reverse it: a caller that wants to show the player the near-miss order. It can read attemptedOrder, so nothing is lost — only the default reading changed, and it changed toward the safe one.

Also decided: `suggest` is a documented option rather than a private module flag. A private one could not be pinned by the gate, and the guard is the kind of thing that gets refactored away by someone who cannot see a test naming it. The docstring says plainly that callers should leave it alone.

beads.title: Make orderPreferring schedule ONLY the wanted node's ancestors ahead of it — then 'refuted' becomes provably unreachable
beads.body:
This turn made certify() VERIFY its suggestion instead of arguing for it, and immediately found the argument was false: the constructed order can put a node that originally came LATER ahead of the node it is rescuing, and that node collides. The fix is to stop constructing an order that can do that.

THE CHANGE: orderPreferring(network, wanted, avoid) currently fills the wait for `wanted` with the first READY node not in `avoid`, in declaration order — any node at all. Change it to prefer, among ready nodes, those that are ANCESTORS of `wanted` (buildcert.mjs already computes the transitive closure in ancestors()), falling back to the current rule only once `wanted` is placed.

WHY IT IS PROVABLE, and this is the reason to do it rather than a preference: if the only nodes preceding `wanted` in the suggested order are its ancestors, then the committed seed set when `wanted` is judged is a SUBSET of the set it was judged against in the original order — every ancestor preceded it there too, in every topological order, by definition. A collision cannot appear in a subset that was absent from the superset. So `wanted` lands, always, whenever dependencyBlocked is empty. The verification stops being a check that sometimes says no and becomes a check that can only ever confirm.

WHAT THIS COSTS, stated because it is the interesting part: section 3b's fixture would no longer be refuted, and `reorderCheck: 'refuted'` would become unreachable by construction. That is a GOOD outcome and a BAD test situation — a branch no fixture can reach is a branch nobody can prove correct. The ticket must therefore keep the refuted branch (as a defensive fallback; the proof is about orderPreferring, and a future change to it must not silently re-open the hole) AND replace section 3b's refuted assertions with the invariance the proof gives: over every fixture in the file, and over the LATE fixture in particular, a failure with dependencyBlocked empty must come back 'verified'. Assert the property, not the counterexample. Keep the LATE fixture — it is the thing that would go red if the ancestor preference were ever removed.

BOUNDED PATHS: plant/buildcert.mjs and plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs. The existing gate covers it and the file's other consumers (pocketLevel.mjs imports BLAME_PRECEDENCE only) are untouched.

WHAT MUST STAY GREEN, exactly: the TWIN assertions that sug.indexOf('b') < sug.indexOf('a') and that the suggested order is a legal topological order; the CHAIN dependency case still producing no candidate; and the recursion-guard assertions, whose reorderRuns counts do not change (one nested run, still executed — the proof is a reason to expect 'verified', not a licence to skip running it).

[turn 52 — done] Changed orderPreferring so that while the wanted node is unplaced it takes only the wanted node itself or a ready ANCESTOR of it, falling back to the old any-ready-non-avoid rule only after the wanted node is placed. That makes the committed seed set when the wanted node is re-judged exactly its ancestors' seeds — a subset of the set it already faced in the original order — so, given the condition under which an order is constructed at all (every refusal blamed 'step', no blocker among the ancestors), the step provably lands. Kept the trial run and kept the 'refuted' branch as the fail-closed landing site, since the proof is a property of orderPreferring and a future edit there must not be able to make certify wrong in silence; both are documented as such in the header. In the gate, replaced section 3b's refuted assertions with the property: the prefix of every constructed order contains nothing but ancestors of the wanted node (re-derived in the test from the network's edges rather than importing buildcert's own ancestors(), so a wrong closure cannot agree with itself), and dependencyBlocked-empty implies verified — swept over nine failure shapes (late, its z-deleted control, the moved failure, the guarded run, the 30-node pile, twin and its re-suggestion, the dependency case and a hull case; the last two must construct no order at all). The LATE fixture is retained deliberately and is now the regression detector: its node declaration order is such that removing the ancestor preference reconstructs the old ['d0','d1','z','a0','w','c0'] and goes red. HONESTLY, AND IT MATTERS HERE: I had no Bash, so nothing was executed. Every new expected value was hand-traced through orderPreferring's new loop and certify's forward pass — attemptedOrder ['a0','w','d0','d1','z','c0'] for late, ['a0','w','d0','d1','c0'] for the control, the re-run failing at 'z' step 4 blocked by 'w' at gap 0, and 'z''s own rescue ['d0','d1','z','a0','c0','w'] — and every pre-existing assertion in the file was re-traced against the new code path, including the reorderRuns counts (still 1 for late, none and pile), the TWIN suggested order (unchanged, because 'b' is ready at step 0 so the ancestor branch is never entered), the CHAIN dependency case (unchanged, no order is constructed) and the guarded run. The risk profile is worse than a typical add-only turn: this rewrote a function five existing assertions depend on, so the realistic failure mode is a silently changed refusal set rather than a wrong new number.

beads.title: pocketLevel.mjs and buildcert.mjs are two accumulating walks over the same state view — extract accumulate() now that a third caller is in sight
beads.body:
Already recorded as a finding in the ledger ('buildcert.certify and pocketPlacementReport are now two accumulating walks over the same state view — close enough to look like duplication, and they are not'), which concluded: two is a coincidence, three is a pattern, do not merge yet. This turn is the reason to revisit, because certify() now calls ITSELF a second time to verify a suggestion, so the walk runs twice per failing certificate and any future third caller inherits both copies.

WHAT TO BUILD: a shared pure helper `accumulate(pocket, items, minSeedGap)` returning per-item verdicts plus the seeds/owners arrays, with each caller keeping its own explanation layer — buildcert's topological-order-plus-reorderability layer and pocketLevel's placement-order-plus-network layer are genuinely different questions and must NOT be merged. Only the state construction, the legalSummon call, and the seed/owner bookkeeping move.

HOW IT IS CHECKED: both existing gates, unchanged, must still pass — `node plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs` and `node plant/test/pocket-level.selftest.mjs`. This is a pure refactor with no new behaviour, so a new gate would be the wrong shape; the whole point is that nothing observable changes. The risk to watch, and a reviewer should look for it specifically: buildcert splits a 'seed' refusal on `seedIndex < base` into pocket-owned vs step-owned and pocketLevel imports BLAME_PRECEDENCE from buildcert precisely so that split cannot drift — the extraction must not put that logic in the shared helper, or the two callers' taxonomies fuse and a change for one silently changes the other.

I am NOT confident this is worth doing yet and say so plainly: it is a maintenance-cost ticket with no user-visible effect, and vision item 1 (one game, not six demos) outranks it. File it, let a reviewer weigh it against the queue.
evidence: rejected: The author does not think it is worth doing yet, says so in the body ('I am NOT confident this is worth doing yet... vision item 1 outranks it'), and asks the reviewer to weigh it against the queue. Weighed: it loses. It is a maintenance-cost refactor with no user-visible effect, and the ledger finding it cites already reached the correct conclusion — two accumulating walks are a coincidence, thre

beads.title: Fifteen turns, seven modules, zero lines of index.html — priority, not the vision, is what the scheduler reads
beads.body:
Fifteen Opus turns (36-50) produced seven backend modules and NOT ONE LINE of
plant/index.html, which has been untouched since turn 26. Eight of the twelve
modules in plant/ are not imported by the page: buildcert, foamworld,
frame-budget, level, loop-brief, placement, pocketLevel, summon-session. The
oracle stack went 5/7 -> 7/7 and a visitor saw no change at all.

THE CAUSE WAS THE QUEUE, AND I WROTE THE QUEUE. Reviving gate 6 (lp-574eb2) and
the level certificate (lp-7b7f04) at P0 put vision items 2 and 3 above item 1,
which had no P0 bead at all. The loop worked the queue in priority order and did
exactly what it was told. The vision's own warning — "an explainer is the natural
attractor... legible, gateable, provable, and safe" — describes the trap, and
the way I sprang it was by promoting the gateable work to the top of the queue
and leaving the page work at P1.

Worth noticing what the loop got RIGHT: at turn 44 it wrote lp-a59b0f itself, and
it is the best-specified ticket in the graph — a summon panel driven entirely by
the controller, no placement logic in event handlers, refusal sentences that
distinguish blame:'player' from blame:'pocket'. It is precisely vision item 1. It
was P1, so it was not reached until turns 48 and 50 — the exact minutes the model
quota ran out. The loop identified the right work and the priority order starved
it.

THE LESSON, stated so the next window does not repeat it: priority is the only
part of the vision the scheduler can actually read. Prose at the top of vision.md
saying item 1 outranks items 2-4 does nothing if the beads are numbered the other
way round. If ONE GAME matters most, exactly one bead should be P0 and it should
be the one that changes what a visitor sees.

beads.title: A creates-gate bead whose gate lives outside the agent's write paths can never pass — five turns lost
beads.body:
lp-14c7f5 was attempted five times and failed five times — a third of a fifteen-
turn window — and it was unsatisfiable at the moment it was promoted.

Its gate was `node scripts/loop-brief.selftest.mjs`. The agent is contained to
the loop's `writes` paths (loop/, .github/loop/, plant/) by loop-work's
containment gate, so it could not create a file under scripts/ no matter what it
did. It did the work anyway, correctly, three separate times — as
plant/tools/loop-brief.mjs plus a selftest that passes 106/106 — and each time
the ticket gate looked in scripts/, found nothing, and failed the turn.

Nothing in the system could tell it why, because nothing had checked that the
promised gate was somewhere the agent could reach.

I wrote that bead. Fixed at the source: `beads.mjs promote` now refuses a
creates-gate bead whose gate file falls outside config.writes, and says so in
those words. Verified against the real bead — it is rejected.

The general shape, and it is the third instance in this repo: a requirement the
system states, that the system also makes impossible to satisfy, with silence as
the only symptom. Every one of them was caught by asking "could the thing being
asked have succeeded?" rather than by reading the failure.

beads.title: Kept 'refuted' as a branch no fixture can reach, and asserted the property instead of the counterexample
beads.body:
The ancestor preference makes reorderCheck: 'refuted' unreachable by construction. Two options: delete the branch (no dead code, but a future weakening of orderPreferring then silently produces a wrong 'verified'), or keep it (a branch nobody can prove correct, which this ledger has repeatedly called out as the shape a vacuous test hides in).

I kept it, and paid for it by changing what the gate asserts. The branch is now documented in buildcert.mjs's header as UNREACHABLE BY CONSTRUCTION and as the fail-closed landing site if the preference is ever weakened — fail-closed is the right behaviour there, and it is exactly the case where nobody would be watching. In exchange the gate stopped asserting the counterexample and started asserting the invariant: over nine failure shapes, dependencyBlocked-empty implies verified, and the prefix of every constructed order is ancestors-only.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: if a later change makes 'refuted' reachable again on purpose (for instance if orderPreferring is widened to search rather than construct), the branch stops being dead and needs its own fixture. If instead somebody wants the dead branch gone, the honest replacement is a throw — 'orderPreferring returned an order in which the wanted step was refused' — which converts a silent wrong answer into a loud one and is strictly better than the current false. I did not do that here only because it changes certify's contract from total to throwing on an internal invariant, which is a bigger call than this ticket's paths cover.

I also rejected deleting the nested trial run. It is now provably redundant for its verdict, and running it is the entire reason a future edit to orderPreferring would be caught by this gate rather than by a wrong certificate in production.

beads.title: The LATE fixture survives the fix by changing job: it was the counterexample, it is now the only regression detector — and its node ORDER is what arms it
beads.body:
The instinct on closing a hole is to delete the fixture that exhibited it, because the fixture no longer exhibits anything. That would have been wrong here and the reason generalises.

LATE's node declaration order is [d0, d1, z, a0, c0, w]. Two consumers read it and they pull in opposite directions: analyse()'s Kahn queue seeds itself from it, which is why z ends up AFTER w in the default build order and therefore invisible to blockedBy; and orderPreferring scans `ready` in it, which is why the OLD rule picked d0/d1/z ahead of a0 while w waited, constructed [d0,d1,z,a0,w,c0], and got refused.

With the ancestor preference in place the second consumer no longer reaches declaration order for the prefix — a0 is picked because it is w's ancestor, not because of where it sits in the array. So the fixture now passes. But it is the ONLY fixture in the file whose two strands have different depths AND whose deeper strand sits earlier in nodes[], which is precisely the pair of conditions needed to make the old greedy misbehave. Delete the ancestor preference and this one fixture reconstructs the old order and goes red; every other fixture in the file has the wanted node ready at step 0, where both rules agree.

The transferable rule: WHEN YOU CLOSE A HOLE AT THE SOURCE, THE FIXTURE THAT EXHIBITED IT BECOMES THE REGRESSION TEST, and it is usually the only one you have, because it was built to satisfy conditions no ordinary fixture meets. Deleting it because it 'no longer shows the bug' removes the only thing that would notice the bug coming back. I left a comment at the fixture saying that reordering `strand` disarms the section WITHOUT failing it — a silent disarm is the failure mode a reader needs warning about, not the loud one.

beads.title: The rescue and the impossibility theorem are now visible in one fixture: 'w' lands and the failure moves to 'z'
beads.body:
Before this change the LATE fixture's re-run refused 'w' again, so the section could only demonstrate the hole. Now, running the suggested order ['a0','w','d0','d1','z','c0'] by hand certifies 'w' AND fails at 'z' step 4, blocked by 'w' at gap 0 — the exact mirror of the original failure.

That is section 3's invariance theorem (the build as a whole is doomed under EVERY topological order, because the constraint set is a property of the seed SET and not of the sequence) and the per-step rescue (this piece is fine, the layout is not) exhibited in a single pair of runs rather than argued in two separate places. And it continues: 'z' is itself reorderable, behind its own ancestors d0 and d1, giving ['d0','d1','z','a0','c0','w'] — the same shape one level down.

Why this is worth recording rather than just testing: a caller repositioning a factory needs both halves, and the two halves read as contradictory if you only see one of them ('reorderable: true' next to 'ok: false' looks like a bug). The certificate is saying two different true things about two different questions, and the LATE fixture is now the clearest place in the repo where both are on screen at once.

It also suggests the field the certificate does not yet have: WHERE the failure moves to. certify() computes it — it is trial.failure.node — and throws it away, so a caller who wants to tell the player 'move w's neighbour, not w' has to re-run the suggested order themselves, which is what the gate now does by hand. Proposed as a follow-up rather than folded in, because it changes the failure record's shape and every consumer reads that.

beads.title: certify() throws away where the failure MOVES to — surface it as failure.movesTo
beads.body:
When a step is rescued by reordering, certify() runs the trial, reads trial.steps to decide `reorderable`, and DISCARDS trial.failure. That discarded record is the answer to the caller's actual next question.

Concretely, on the LATE fixture in plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs: 'w' is refused, the suggested order is run, 'w' lands — and the trial then fails on 'z', blocked by 'w' at gap 0. The certificate today reports `reorderable: true` and `suggestedOrder`, and says nothing about 'z'. A caller told 'build w first and it works' will build w first, hit a failure on z, and have to re-derive from scratch what certify already computed and dropped. The gate currently re-runs the suggested order BY HAND, from outside, precisely to see that fact — which is a good independent check and also a sign the information is being recomputed because it is not exposed.

THE CHANGE: add `movesTo` to the failure record, populated only when `reorderCheck === 'verified'`, as `{ node, step, blame, blockedBy }` copied from the trial's own failure — or `null` when the trial certified the whole build (possible in principle: the rescue may complete it). Null when reorderCheck is 'none' or 'unchecked'. No new computation at all; the trial already runs.

WHY IT IS WORTH A TICKET AND NOT A DRIVE-BY: the failure record is read by pocketLevel.mjs and by the gate, and any new field has to be pinned or it drifts — this ledger already records `legalSummon`'s docstring promising a `summonSeed` on every refusal that one refusal does not carry, found only when a renderer trusted the sentence. So the new field must be asserted, not merely added.

GATE: `node plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs`, which exists and passes. class-a. The assertions it needs, and each names a value that can be hand-computed from fixtures already in the file:
  · LATE: failure.movesTo.node === 'z', step 4, blame 'step', blockedBy names 'w' at gap 0 — and it is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the failure record you get by re-running failure.suggestedOrder from outside, which the gate already does and calls `direct`. That equality is the assertion that bites: it says movesTo is the trial's real record and not a re-derivation that could drift.
  · NOLATE control: movesTo.node === 'c0'.
  · The dependency case (CHAIN stacked) and the hull case: movesTo === null, because no order was run.
  · The guarded run ({ suggest: false }): movesTo === null — fail closed, same rule as suggestedOrder.
  · determinism: the existing JSON.stringify comparison covers the new field for free.

BOUNDED PATHS: plant/buildcert.mjs and plant/test/buildcert.selftest.mjs. pocketLevel.mjs imports only BLAME_PRECEDENCE and is untouched.

WHAT MUST STAY GREEN: everything in the existing file, in particular the reorderRuns counts (this adds no nested run) and the ancestors-only sweep added by lp-0b1bc5.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED ON PRIORITY, NOT ON QUALITY — and I want that recorded precisely, because this is one of the better-specified beads on this desk and it should come back the moment its premise is true. It meets all six DoR criteria. I checked the technical claim rather than taking it: plant/buildcert.mjs:465-472 runs the trial, reads trial.steps for `reorderable` and trial.failure.reorderRuns for the coun

beads.title: A click on a 2D top-down plan, not three numeric inputs — and the height is a separate slider
beads.body:
The ticket offered both and called three numeric inputs 'the simplest honest version'. I took the plan.

WHY. The bar in vision.md is that a stranger forms an intention, acts on it, and is refused. Typing 34, 12, 51 into three boxes is not an intention about a place; it is data entry, and a refusal for it reads as a validation error rather than as the ground being occupied. The plan makes the pocket visible — 64 rock seeds, drawn — so 'there is already rock there' is a sentence about something the player can SEE, and the green candidate dots make the whole thing an invitation instead of a form.

COST, stated plainly: the plan is FLAT and the pocket is not. Two dots on top of each other can be far apart vertically, and the foam's metric scales y by sqrt(aniso) anyway, so a spot that looks clear can be refused for a reason the picture cannot show. I did not hide that — there is a note under the panel saying it in those words, and the height slider is right there. A 3D raycast is the honest fix and the ticket explicitly excludes it.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: if the flat plan turns out to mislead more than it invites (see the ask), the cheap next step is not numeric boxes, it is a side elevation next to the plan — same controller, one more pure-view function.

REJECTED ALSO: making the plan a drag/hover preview. preview() is cheap, but a hover verdict changing under the cursor on every mousemove is noise; a click is a decision and the verdict answers a decision.

beads.title: The page throws at startup if a BLAME value has no sentence — belt behind the gate's brace
beads.body:
BLAME_SENTENCE is checked against the module's BLAME export at module scope, and a missing entry throws, which takes the WHOLE PAGE down including six working levels. That is a real cost and I chose it deliberately.

THE ARGUMENT: the gate asserts the same property from outside, and loop-work runs the whole plant suite before deploy-plant publishes. So a seventh blame that outruns the page fails in CI and never reaches the internet; the runtime throw is a second line that should never fire in front of a visitor. The failure it prevents is worse than it looks — a blank or 'refused' verdict is exactly the outcome this ticket exists to prevent, and it fails SILENTLY, which is this repo's most-recorded failure shape.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: if plant/index.html ever ships something a visitor needs more than the summon panel, downgrade the throw to a console.error plus a loud fallback sentence. The gate keeps the real guarantee either way.

beads.title: Requirement (d)'s no-threshold check is scoped to the summon block, not to the whole script
beads.body:
The ticket asks that no literal 1.5 / 3.2 / 2.2 appear in 'the page's own script'. Applied to the whole script it fails IMMEDIATELY on code twenty turns older than this ticket: line 342 is `const state = { solid: 'dodecahedron', r: 1.5, aniso: 2.2, ... }` — the starting positions of the INSPECTOR's own sliders, whose entire subject is varying them, plus `value="2.2"` and `value="1.5"` in its markup and a `Math.min(1.5, ...)` pitch clamp that is an unrelated 1.5.

So the gate scopes the check to everything after the `// ── Summon` banner, and the header says why in full. That keeps it a real constraint on the code this ticket writes — a placement threshold retyped next to a placement call — without failing on state that is not a placement constant at all. A check that fails correct pre-existing work would have been reverted or --forced past, and then it would not be a rule.

VERIFIED rather than assumed: grepped index.html for 1.5|2.2|3.2 — every hit is at line 378 or earlier, and the summon block starts at 504.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a ticket that makes the inspector take its own defaults from a module (they are arguably the same constants) would let the check widen to the whole script. That is inspector work, not placement work, and the vision says stop making the explainer better.

beads.title: The summon verdict names only the FIRST refusal — the third instance of the same under-reporting shape in this codebase
beads.body:
The renderer reads `res.refusal || res.first` and builds one sentence from it. legalSummon and reformPocketAll both report EVERY refusal, and legalSummon's order is fixed: metric, then per-seed (hull/seed) in summonSeed order, then self pairs.

CONSEQUENCE: a summon that both pokes out through a wall AND stands on rock says only 'part of the X pushes out through the west wall'. Move it in, and the second refusal appears — two moves to learn what one verdict knew. Worse for blame: if the constellation touches BOTH the generated foam and something the player built, whichever has the lower summonSeed index wins, so 'there is already rock there' can be shown when 'too close to the cube you summoned on move 2' was the more useful half.

This is structurally identical to two things already in the ledger — verdictLine()'s fail path reading `v.deficits[0]`, and `bound` naming one starved input when several are equally starved. Three instances now, all from choosing a scalar where the domain has a set, and all in the render layer rather than the oracle. The oracle got it right in every case: it returns the whole list.

I did NOT fix it here, deliberately. The right fix is to group refusals by blame the way level-view.js's refusalLine groups by reason — and refusalLine is in a MODULE with a real selftest, while this sentence table is inside index.html where only a regex can reach it. Fixing the under-reporting first would put more untestable logic in the page. Proposed the extraction first, the fix second, in that order.

beads.title: summon-session's two verbs name the same field differently — preview() returns `first`, place() returns `refusal`
beads.body:
preview() returns `{ ok, solid, centre, r, con, refusals, first }`; place() returns `{ ok, move, ..., refusals, refusal }`. Both are 'the first refusal, or null'. A renderer that wants one function for both verdicts has to write `res.refusal || res.first`, which is what the page now does, and which is silently wrong the moment either verb gains the other's field.

It is a small thing and it is exactly the seam class this ledger keeps recording: not a bug in either component, a mismatch in the channel between them. Anything that consumes both verdict shapes — the summon-view module proposed below, a future undo, a level built on the session — will have to know this. Cheapest fix is one line in summon-session.mjs (have place() set both, or have preview() set both) plus one assertion in its selftest pinning the field name per verb. Not done here: summon-session.mjs is outside what this ticket should be touching, and a renaming that misses a caller is worse than the asymmetry.

beads.title: The new plan SVG carries an inline style attribute on purpose — svg#lvl's CSS is keyed by exact id and levels 2-6 already ship unstyled by it
beads.body:
The ticket warned not to fix the pre-existing `svg#lvl` selector problem here. The panel's SVG therefore does NOT rely on the page's stylesheet at all: width, height, display, touch-action and cursor are inline on the element. So the plan is styled regardless of how that pre-existing gap is eventually resolved, and this ticket adds nothing new to it — no seventh id waiting for a CSS rule.

Worth knowing for whoever does fix it: the shared selector list will need `svg#plan` too, or the inline attribute removed in the same change, or the plan keeps its inline style and is simply exempt. Any of the three is fine; picking one silently and leaving two is not.

beads.title: Does clicking a FLAT plan of a 3D pocket read as fair, or as the game hiding the thing that refuses you?
beads.body:
This is the one judgement I could not settle by writing a check, and I made the call anyway rather than stalling: the panel maps a click on a top-down plan to a world point, with height on a separate slider.

The worry is specific and structural, not a matter of polish. The plan CANNOT show the reason for a large fraction of refusals: two seeds that overlap on the plan may be far apart vertically, and the foam scales vertical distance by sqrt(aniso) on top of that, so 'there is already rock there' will sometimes be said about a dot the player cannot see near their cursor. I mitigated it three ways — every pocket seed is drawn, green dots mark spots that look clear at the CURRENT height, and a note under the panel says the plan is flat in plain words — but mitigation is not the same as the thing being legible, and no test I can write distinguishes 'honest and demanding' from 'arbitrary'.

It is not decidable from here because it is a question about what a person infers from a picture, and the loop has no instrument for that.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, scroll to 'Summon — put one of these into real ground', and try to place three shapes without reading the note underneath. Then drag the height slider to the bottom and try again.

WATCH FOR: Whether a refusal ever feels arbitrary — specifically whether you look for the thing that refused you and fail to find it on the plan. Also whether you touch the height slider at all unprompted.

SO THAT: If refusals read as arbitrary, the next ticket is a side elevation beside the plan (same controller, one more pure-view function) and NOT a 3D raycast. If they read as fair but the height slider goes untouched, the panel should pick the height itself from the clearest candidate at that x/z and the slider becomes an override. If both are fine, the next ticket is the one that turns this into a level with a goal — which is where vision item 1 actually ends.

beads.title: Lift the summon refusal sentences out of index.html into summon-view.js, where a test can read them
beads.body:
The summon panel's refusal sentences are the whole point of the panel — 'too close to the cube you summoned on move 2' versus 'there is already rock there' — and they currently live inside plant/index.html, where the only thing that can check them is a regex asserting six table entries exist and differ. index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs does exactly that and it is the strongest check available from outside the page. It cannot check that a sentence says something TRUE.

The precedent is already here and it is the right one: level-view.js holds drawLevel/verdictLine/refusalLine as pure functions with plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs driving them on real fixtures. Do the same.

SCOPE: a new plant/summon-view.js exporting (1) `summonSentence(res)` — the ✓/✗ line for any preview() OR place() result, blame-branched, and (2) `planShapes(pocket, bounds, cands, cursor, originCount)` returning an array of plain shape descriptors the page turns into SVG. index.html imports both and keeps only the DOM plumbing. No behaviour change is intended: the sentences move verbatim.

THE GATE IT CREATES: plant/test/summon-view.selftest.mjs. It must drive a REAL session (startSession on a fixed seed, the same MACRO fixture the other gates use) rather than hand-built verdict objects, and for each blame value it can reach — pocket, player, hull, self, caller — assert BOTH that the sentence is produced and that its NUMBERS come from the verdict, by re-extracting them with a clause-specific regex and comparing to a value recomputed from the refusal (the method the ledger already established for refusalLine: `includes(String(x))` passes for a renderer that hardcodes the threshold, which is precisely the bug worth catching). Assert `!/undefined|NaN/` on every sentence produced across the sweep. 'foam' (closure/nav) may not be reachable on a fixture — if so the gate must say so out loud rather than skip silently.

WHY THIS IS THE NEXT THING RATHER THAN MORE PANEL: everything else anyone wants to do to the refusal text — report every refusal instead of the first, name the offending seed, colour it on the plan — is currently ungradeable because it lives in an HTML file. This makes it gradeable, and it is a move, not new behaviour, so the diff is reviewable.

[turn 56 — done] TURN 55 ALREADY BUILT THIS TICKET IN FULL AND ITS GATE FAILED, so its outbox was never applied, the bead stayed 'ready', and it was re-dispatched to me as turn 56. I found plant/summon-view.js, plant/test/summon-view.selftest.mjs, the index.html import and the rewritten index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs all committed and complete before I wrote a line. My first act was to open .github/loop/outbox/lp-250e23.json rather than write it, because the ledger records that a second turn on a bead silently destroys the first turn's unapplied record at that path — turn 55's four learnings, two well-formed proposals and one ask were sitting there. THEY ARE CARRIED VERBATIM BELOW, marked as carried. WHAT I ACTUALLY DID. (1) Tried to find the gate failure by static analysis, since I have no Bash. I verified against the real sources that every field each sentence prints exists on the refusal it comes from (placement.mjs: hull carries wall/depth, seed carries gap/need, self carries gap/need), that summonAt takes aniso from the pocket so a 'metric' refusal is unreachable and cannot displace the refusal each section reads as `first`, that low-x really is B4 in the AXES table section 2 asserts, that legalSummon's push order makes the centre's refusal first in sections 1/2/5b, that the r=0.4 self-collision shortfall provably differs from both gap and need for a cube, that toPlan's corners are exactly representable so === is safe, and that the whole of index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs still passes against the moved code (its (a2)/(b)/(d)/(e) regexes all check out against the actual bytes of both files). I ALSO SCANNED FOR THE TWO NON-ARITHMETIC HAZARDS THE LEDGER NAMES — nested backticks inside template literals, and ASCII apostrophes inside single-quoted strings — and found none. I COULD NOT IDENTIFY THE FAILURE. I am not claiming I fixed it. (2) I did find and fix a real weakness, and it is precisely the one turn 55's own summary flagged as 'the assertion I would look at first if the gate goes red': section 5's 'a constellation actually planted' tried CANDS.list.slice(0, 3), and candidates() sweeps ascending x, then z, then ys, so the first three entries are THE SAME COLUMN AT THREE HEIGHTS — three samples of one neighbourhood deciding a run whose outcome (does the rebuild close) is not decidable in advance. Sections 5b and 9 both hard-depend on that landing. I replaced it with an index-strided spread across the whole candidate list, gave section 6 the attempts section 5 did not spend so a foam probe is never a re-try of an occupied centre, and made the failure detail print each attempt's reason/blame instead of a fixed sentence — a red gate whose cause is invisible is the exact failure shape this repo keeps paying for. The new spread assertion is deliberately CONDITIONAL on the sweep having found more than one column, because a pocket tight enough to offer only one is a legitimate fixture and must not fail a gate about a renderer. HONESTLY: no assertion was weakened and nothing was executed — I have Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only. This is strictly more fixture coverage than the slice it replaces, so it cannot make the gate fail where it previously passed; whether it makes it PASS where it previously failed is unknown, because I never established why it failed.

beads.title: The summon verdict must report every refusal, not just the first — group by blame like refusalLine groups by reason
beads.body:
DEPENDS ON the summon-view.js extraction above; do not schedule it first, because the change belongs in a module with a selftest and not in index.html.

THE DEFECT (recorded as a finding this turn): the panel renders `res.refusal || res.first`, one sentence from one refusal. legalSummon reports all of them, in a fixed order — metric, then per-seed in summonSeed order, then self pairs. So a summon that both pushes through a wall and stands on rock reports only the wall; fix that and the rock appears, two moves to learn what one verdict already knew. And when a constellation touches BOTH the generated foam and something the player built, the lower seed index wins, so the less useful half can be the half shown.

This is the third instance of one shape in this repo — verdictLine reading deficits[0], `bound` naming one starved input of several, and now this. All three are render-layer scalars standing in for a set the oracle correctly returned whole.

SCOPE: `summonSentence` groups refusals by blame in first-appearance order and emits one clause per group, with a count and the WORST member of the group (deepest hull violation, tightest gap) — exactly the shape level-view.js's refusalLine already uses for reasons, so read that function before writing this one rather than inventing a second convention.

THE GATE: the existing plant/test/summon-view.selftest.mjs, extended. The assertion that bites is a fixture producing TWO different blames at once (a centre near a wall and near rock is reachable by sweeping candidates for one) and asserting BOTH clauses appear with their own numbers — plus a CONTROL with exactly one refusal asserting the sentence did not grow a spurious second clause. A single-refusal fixture alone proves nothing here: it passes identically before and after the change.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED for two independent mechanical reasons, either of which is sufficient. The underlying defect is real and worth fixing — repropose it next round, after lp-250e23 has landed. R2, and this is the one that would have burned a turn visibly: the bead is tagged class-a ONLY — it does NOT carry creates-gate, unlike its sibling lp-250e23, which carries both — and its gate is `node plant/test/summo

beads.title: Non-finite is reason:'hull' with a nonFinite flag and depth Infinity — not a new reason, and not the kernel's depth:NaN
beads.body:
Three choices were open and the ticket left all three to this turn.

1. REASON. Took 'hull', as the ticket recommended, over a new 'point'. Decisive argument: every consumer of a refusal branches on the four published reasons — level-view.js's refusalLine, summon-session.mjs's _attribute, buildcert.mjs's BLAME_PRECEDENCE, pocketLevel.mjs — and a fifth reason would fall through every one of them to an empty clause. refusalLine's own docstring says a refusal with no sentence is the outcome it exists to prevent. 'hull' also makes the predicate and reformPocketAll agree on the field they are most often compared on. REVERSED BY: a caller that must distinguish 'the player aimed outside the cave' from 'the caller handed me garbage' — but that is what the nonFinite flag is for, and it costs no consumer anything.

2. DEPTH. Chose Infinity over mimicking the kernel's NaN. Infinity is TRUE (no finite move fixes a NaN), it is comparable, and it makes the deepest-violation rule pick the non-finite axis deterministically. depth:NaN would have reproduced inside placement.mjs exactly the incomparability that caused this bug — `NaN > worst.depth` is false, so the rule silently degrades to first-wins. The cost is one pinned divergence from the kernel on mixed points, filed as a separate finding and asserted from both sides in the gate rather than hidden.

3. THE FLAG, and why it is only on one branch. `nonFinite: true` is added on the non-finite branch alone, so a finite hull refusal has the same five keys in the same order as before. That was deliberate: several files JSON-compare or snapshot verdicts, and a new key on every record is a regression surface for no gain. A caller tests `r.nonFinite === true`, and absence means finite.

WHAT I DID NOT DO: left nearestSeed and coarselyClear alone. Both have NaN-shaped weak spots (nearestSeed returns gap NaN; coarselyClear returns true because `NaN <= R` is false) but legalSeed refuses at the hull before reaching either, and coarselyClear's stated soundness claim — accept implies no 'seed' refusal — remains literally true for a NaN centre, since the refusal it gets is 'hull'. Documented in nearestSeed's docstring instead of changed. Reversed by anyone calling those two directly on unvalidated input.

beads.title: The kernel's OWN deepest-violation rule is order-dependent for a mixed point — depth:NaN is incomparable, so `NaN > 0.5` is false and the finite axis wins
beads.body:
The ticket described foamworld.js's hullRefusal as catching NaN by luck rather than design ('c[i] === p[i]' is false for NaN). That is right, and there is a second consequence nobody had noticed: the luck stops at the refusal and does not extend to the BLAME.

hullRefusal computes `depth: Math.abs(c[i] - p[i])`, which is NaN when the clamp is NaN, and then ranks axes with `rec.depth > worst.depth`. Every comparison against NaN is false, so:

    [0.5, NaN, 40]  ->  x checked first, depth 0.5, becomes worst
                        y is NaN, `NaN > 0.5` is false, worst stays x
                        KERNEL BLAMES x — the 0.5 m violation

    [40, NaN, 0.4]  ->  y is NaN, becomes worst (nothing before it)
                        z depth 0.6, `0.6 > NaN` is false, worst stays y
                        KERNEL BLAMES y — the NaN

Same class of point, opposite answers, decided entirely by which axis the loop reached first. That is exactly the failure mode the 'deepest violation wins, ties break x-y-z' rule was written to prevent, and it is silently absent whenever a NaN is involved.

placement.mjs now reports depth Infinity, which is comparable, so it blames the non-finite axis in BOTH cases — 'no finite move fixes this' outranks 'move half a metre', which is also the more useful thing to tell a caller. That is a real divergence from the kernel and it is pinned from both sides in section 7 of the gate rather than left to be discovered: the predicate must blame y and the kernel must blame x on [0.5, NaN, 40]. Both refuse, which is the property that matters for safety; only the attribution differs.

I did NOT fix the kernel. foamworld.js is outside this ticket's bounded paths, the divergence is now asserted rather than latent, and changing the kernel's blame would move a field multi-insert.selftest.mjs pins. Proposed as a follow-up.

The transferable shape, and it is the same one the original finding recorded one level up: NaN does not merely slip past a comparison, it POISONS every comparison it participates in. A validator that catches NaN in its guard can still be wrong about NaN in its ranking, and the second failure is invisible because the verdict is still correct.

beads.title: The same hole swallowed `undefined` and un-coerced strings — and those are likelier in practice than NaN
beads.body:
The ticket is framed entirely around NaN from a missed raycast. Number.isFinite closes strictly more than that, and the extra cases are worth knowing because they are more ordinary:

    legalSeed(P, [40, 18])          // z is undefined
    legalSeed(P, [40, 18, '40'])    // z is a string

Both returned ok:true before this change, for exactly the reason NaN did: `undefined < 1` and `'40' < 1` are both false, `undefined > 79` and `'40' > 79` are both false, so the ternary fell through to the literal 0 and the axis was skipped. Note the second one is not even a numeric failure — the comparison operators coerce '40' to 40 and it compares perfectly well, so the range check genuinely passed; it was seedGap's arithmetic downstream that would have silently coerced too, and the point would have been treated as legal at a position nobody typed.

A missing third coordinate is what an object destructure that names the wrong key produces, or a two-element screen coordinate handed to a three-dimensional API. Neither requires a raycast to miss. Both are now refused as hull violations naming the offending axis, and both are pinned in the gate.

The general form: `!Number.isFinite(v)` is a stronger and cheaper guard than `Number.isNaN(v)` for anything that is about to do geometry, because it is a TYPE test as well as a value test. Guarding only against NaN closes the case you thought of and leaves the two next to it open.

beads.title: Two files now carry prose asserting this bug is present, and neither is reachable from this ticket
beads.body:
The fix lands with its own documentation already contradicted in two places, both outside the bounded paths (plant/placement.mjs, plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs) and therefore deliberately untouched:

  · plant/summon-session.mjs lines 66-70 — the module header states, in bold, '**legalSeed therefore ACCEPTS a NaN point.**' and justifies its own guard by that. The guard is still correct and still worth keeping (it also catches a null or a string PASSED AS THE WHOLE POINT, which placement.mjs cannot see because legalSeed does p.slice() on it), but the reason given is now false.

  · plant/test/summon-session.selftest.mjs line 362 — a console.log, NOT an assertion, printing `legalSeed([NaN,...]).ok === ${...}` followed by 'every comparison against NaN is false, so the predicate has no hull violation and no seed gap.' It will now print `false` alongside a sentence explaining why it is `true`. No gate goes red — I checked that this is the only place either file mentions the predicate's NaN answer, and its one real assertion (line 360) is about the kernel, which is unchanged. That care was taken deliberately by whoever wrote it: the comment above says pinning placement.mjs's behaviour there 'would turn a future fix of it into a red gate', and it worked exactly as intended.

Worth recording as a small success rather than only as debt: a turn that knowingly recorded a bug it was not allowed to fix chose to LOG the buggy value and ASSERT only the correct one. That is the right split, and it is why this fix could land without touching a second gate. The residual cost is two stale paragraphs, which is a much better trade than a red gate.

beads.title: summon-session: retire the prose that says legalSeed accepts a NaN, and decide the guard's fate on its real merits
beads.body:
lp-1921ff fixed placement.mjs's legalSeed so a non-finite coordinate is refused (reason 'hull', nonFinite: true, depth Infinity). Two pieces of prose still say otherwise and both are outside that ticket's bounded paths:

  · plant/summon-session.mjs lines 66-70 — the module header asserts '**legalSeed therefore ACCEPTS a NaN point.**' and justifies the session's own point guard with it.
  · plant/test/summon-session.selftest.mjs line 362 — a console.log that will now print `false` next to a sentence explaining why it is `true`. It is NOT an assertion, so nothing is red today; it is simply misleading output on every run.

THE WORK IS NOT JUST A COMMENT EDIT, and that is why this is a ticket rather than a nit. The guard at summon-session.mjs:111 is now redundant AGAINST placement.mjs but is NOT redundant overall, and the header should say which:

  · it refuses a point that is not an array at all (null, 'nowhere'), which legalSeed cannot survive — legalSeed calls p.slice() on the hull-refusal path and would throw;
  · it refuses without counting a move, and it reports reason 'point' / blame 'caller', which is a genuinely different taxonomy entry from 'hull' / blame 'hull'. A UI wants to distinguish 'you aimed outside the cave' from 'my raycast returned nothing', and after lp-1921ff placement.mjs conflates them under 'hull' (the nonFinite flag is the only discriminator).

My read, offered rather than imposed: KEEP the guard, rewrite the header to justify it by the two reasons above instead of by the now-fixed predicate bug, and change the console.log into a real assertion that legalSeed now REFUSES a NaN — turning a note that documented a bug into a check that the fix stays fixed. Whoever takes it may decide otherwise; the deliverable is that the file no longer describes behaviour that does not exist.

CLASS-A against the existing, passing gate: node plant/test/summon-session.selftest.mjs. That is the right gate because the risk here is a regression in the taxonomy assertions (lines 341-374 pin every blame the session emits), not a new capability. Bounded paths: plant/summon-session.mjs, plant/test/summon-session.selftest.mjs. Do not touch plant/placement.mjs — its behaviour is settled and pinned by placement.selftest.mjs section 7.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED AS A TURN, NOT AS A CLAIM — the claim is correct and I confirmed every part of it. plant/summon-session.mjs:62-75 does assert '**legalSeed therefore ACCEPTS a NaN point.**' and placement.mjs:114/131-142 shows lp-1921ff made that false (hullViolation now tests Number.isFinite explicitly and returns nonFinite:true at depth Infinity). The console.log at plant/test/summon-session.selftest.mjs

beads.title: foamworld's hullRefusal ranks axes with a NaN depth, so which axis it blames depends on loop order — make the ranking comparable
beads.body:
Found while pinning the predicate/kernel agreement for lp-1921ff, and it is a defect in the kernel rather than in the predicate.

foamworld.js's hullRefusal (around line 784) computes `depth: Math.abs(c[i] - p[i])`, which is NaN when the clamp is NaN, and then ranks axes with `if (!worst || rec.depth > worst.depth)`. Every comparison against NaN is false, so the ranking silently degrades to first-wins whenever a NaN is involved:

    [0.5, NaN, 40]  ->  blames x (the 0.5 m violation), because `NaN > 0.5` is false
    [40, NaN, 0.4]  ->  blames y (the NaN), because `0.6 > NaN` is also false

Same class of point, opposite attribution, decided by which axis the loop reached first. The 'deepest violation is named; ties break x, y, z' rule that hullRefusal's own docstring promises is simply absent for these points. The REFUSAL is correct in every case — nothing plants — so this is about which face a UI lights up, not about safety.
