WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK: for a real session (not hand-built objects), assert on a preview refusal AND on a place refusal AND on both success paths that `res.first === res.refusal` — including that both are `null` together on a success, which is the case an implementation setting only the failure path would get wrong. Also assert the value is the SAME OBJECT or deep-equal to `res.refusals[0]`, so the two names cannot drift to two different refusals. A per-verb field-list assertion would be worth adding at the same time: the ledger records that `placement.mjs`'s docstring claims 'every refusal carries summonSeed' while the metric refusal does not, and a field list no test reads is a field list that drifts.

WHY class-a: plant/test/summon-session.selftest.mjs already exists and passes, so this is certified against an existing gate; the taker adds assertions to it.

[turn 62 — done] Both verbs now set BOTH names for the first refusal, to the SAME OBJECT, on every path. preview() gained `refusal`; place() gained `first`; on a success both are null together. Nothing was renamed or removed, exactly as the ticket scoped it, so every existing caller keeps working and summon-view.js's `res.refusal || res.first` becomes redundant rather than load-bearing. The module header gained a section explaining why both names exist and why neither is going away; both verb docstrings now list the full field set. The gate gained section 10, which drives a REAL session (not hand-built objects) over six cases — a preview refusal, a preview bad point, a preview success, a place refusal, a place bad point, and the successful place() section 9 already paid for — and for each asserts (i) first === refusal, (ii) that value IS refusals[0] by identity so the two names cannot drift to two different refusals, (iii) the exact sorted key set for that verb, and (iv) on the two success paths that both are null TOGETHER. Point (iii) is load-bearing rather than tidiness and the header says so: `first === refusal` passes for an implementation that sets NEITHER, so the key set is the only assertion proving the names exist at all; and on a refusal `first.reason` is asserted to be a real string and `first.blame` to be in BLAME, so the identity is not two undefineds agreeing. A second block pins the SECOND asymmetry the ticket did not ask me to fix — preview refusals name `summonSeed`, place refusals name `point` — with a guard asserting both loops actually ran against a refusal, so they cannot silently assert nothing. HONESTLY: I could not run the gate. This turn had Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only, no Bash. Every key set was derived by reading all five return statements; every fixture reuses one already proven in an earlier section of the same file (FIX.c2, [NaN,18,40], and section 9's landed result, hoisted into a module-level LANDED for the purpose); and the one new fixture (a spot that still previews legal on S) is justified by S's seed set being a strict subset of G's, where section 9 already asserts such spots exist.

beads.title: Difficulty is the WIN FRACTION over the page's own control range — shipped margin would have made the tutorial the hardest level
beads.body:
vision.md suggests ordering the campaign by feasibility margin, and that measure is wrong here in a way worth writing down because it is the obvious choice.

LEVEL_1 ships at margin 0.02 ('barely satisfiable by design', its own header says so), LEVEL_5 and LEVEL_6 both ship at margin 0, and LEVEL_3 at 1/44. Sorting on the shipped margin therefore sorts on HOW TAUT THE DESIGNER LEFT THE KNOB, which is a property of the opening position, not of the puzzle. It would put the one-slider tutorial last.

The measure used instead: sweep the FINITE DECLARED DOMAIN of the level's control and count what fraction of the settings win. A level where two settings in three succeed is one you can stumble into; a level where one in eight does is one you have to reason about. It is deterministic, needs no search and no model, and it is a property of the puzzle AND of the control — which is right, because the difficulty of a puzzle played through a slider is partly a property of the slider.

THE PART THAT KEEPS IT HONEST, and the part I would defend hardest: each knob's `samples` is exactly the range and step of that level's control in index.html today. I could have picked any domain and got any order; taking the page's own bounds means the number is not chosen. It also creates a real coupling the follow-up must respect — the wiring ticket has to take its control bounds FROM campaign.mjs rather than keeping a second copy, or the measure silently stops describing what the player is offered. That is written in plant/CLAUDE.md and in the module header.

Computed result, all six distinct:
  level1 71/111 = 0.6396
  level4 41/81  = 0.5062
  level3 3249/8281 = 0.3923
  level2 1/3    = 0.3333
  level5 21/91  = 0.2308
  level6 11/91  = 0.1209

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a level whose control is not a scalar the page sweeps (a placement level, once pocket work reaches the campaign) has no finite declared domain, and win fraction stops being computable for it. At that point the measure needs replacing rather than extending, and the pinned ORDER in the gate is the thing that will force the conversation.

beads.title: The computed order independently reproduces the operator's guessed curve — 1, 3, 2, 5, 6 — for the five levels the guess covered
beads.body:
vision.md says '1, 3, 2, 5, 6 is roughly the curve they already form; check it rather than assuming'. That is a guess made by eye, and it names five of the six levels (LEVEL_4 is absent from it).

The win-fraction sweep, which knows nothing about that sentence, produces:

    level1, level4, level3, level2, level5, level6

Delete level4 — the one the guess did not mention — and what remains is 1, 3, 2, 5, 6. Exactly. Including the non-obvious half: level3 (two capacities, both of which can starve) is EASIER than level2 (three buttons, one right answer), which reads backwards until you notice that level2 offers three settings and only one wins, while level3's grid is 39% winning.

Why this is worth recording rather than just enjoying: it is the closest thing this run has to an external check on a measure the loop invented for itself. The measure was chosen for structural reasons (it is computable, it is a property of the puzzle rather than of the opening position) and it agrees with a human's independent read of the same six levels. That is weak evidence — one sample, and the human was ordering by feel — but it is evidence from OUTSIDE the loop, which is the resource this programme is short of.

Where it disagrees is also informative: level4 lands SECOND, and the operator's list has no opinion about it. level4 is the autoSplit level, whose split is computed for the player — the loop itself wrote, at turn 15/16, that this 'removes exactly that decision from the player's hands'. A level that makes the interesting choice for you being the second-easiest thing in the game is consistent with that critique, arrived at by a completely different route.

beads.title: won requires a MOVE; an out-of-domain value is refused not thrown; next() does not require a win; and move() returns `accepted`, never `ok`
beads.body:
Four judgement calls the ticket left open, recorded together because they are one design stance: the module is MECHANISM and the page is POLICY.

1. `won = ok && moves > 0`. FIVE OF THE SIX LEVELS OPEN ALREADY FED (only LEVEL_2 ships broken, on purpose). If `won` were just `ok`, a player would arrive at level 1 having already won it, and the campaign would be five screens of being congratulated for scrolling. Vision item 1's bar is 'an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for' — the player has to have ACTED. This is one clause and deleting it reverses the decision. The gate pins both halves: at start, ok is true and won is false; one move — even to the same setting — wins it.

2. AN OUT-OF-DOMAIN VALUE IS REFUSED, NOT THROWN, AND COSTS NO MOVE. A rejected setting was never applied, so charging a move for it would punish a caller bug as though it were a player mistake; and a throw would put a try/catch in every event handler the follow-up writes. Reversal: if a level ever wants wasted attempts as a mechanic, count them in a separate field rather than conflating them with moves.

3. `next()` DOES NOT REQUIRE A WIN. Tempting to gate it — 'completing a level advances' — but a module that refuses to advance leaves a stuck stranger with no way out and, this run, nobody to ask. The page offers the button when `won`; the module will always let you leave. Reversal: `next({ requireWin: true })`, an argument rather than a rewrite.

4. `move()` RETURNS `{ accepted }`, NEVER `{ ok }`. There are two senses of 'ok' here — did the game take this setting, and does the factory work — and a shared field name would be misread exactly once, in the page, silently. This ledger already records the same seam one module over: summon-session's preview() returns `first` where place() returns `refusal`, so a renderer has to write `res.refusal || res.first`. Naming them apart up front costs nothing.

Also, smaller: knob membership is by a `key(value)` STRING, not identity, because LEVEL_3's setting is an object (two capacities at once) and a float setting must not match a value that drifted off the grid. So `move({miner:44,smelter:44})` is accepted from a freshly-built object, and `move(0.1+0.2)` is refused rather than rounded to 0.3. The domain is declared and finite; a value that is not in it is a bug worth surfacing.

beads.title: index.html's level-1 slider carries value="1000" against max="120" — the browser silently clamps it, and the campaign had to decide what 'as shipped' means
beads.body:
plant/index.html line 166 is `<input type="range" id="ore" min="10" max="120" step="1" value="1000">`. LEVEL_1's literal ships at rate 1000 (deliberately far above anything the smelter can consume, so its capacity is what binds), and whoever wired the slider copied that number into `value` while bounding the control at 120.

HTML clamps an out-of-range range value to the max, so the control actually opens at 120 and always has. Nothing is visibly wrong — 120 and 1000 both leave the smelter capacity-bound at 51, so the page shows the same verdict either way — which is exactly why it has survived.

It mattered here because campaign.mjs has to declare an OPENING SETTING that is a member of the level's finite domain, and 1000 is not in 10..120. I took 120, the value the page effectively opens at. campaign.mjs throws at import if a start value is outside its own domain, so the contradiction cannot be introduced silently again.

For the wiring follow-up: the slider's `value` attribute should become 120 (or be taken from campaign.mjs's knob start), and the bounds should come from `knob.samples` rather than being retyped. The general shape is one this tree keeps meeting — two copies of the same fact, drifted, with no symptom.

beads.title: Four win-count boundaries turn on IEEE-754 rounding, and two of them are already proven by passing gates — the other two are hand-derived
beads.body:
Every pinned win fraction in this gate is a COUNT, and a count is decided by whether the boundary sample wins. Four of the six boundaries are exact-equality cases where the achieved rate lands precisely on the demand, so each one turns on whether a product rounds to the integer or one ulp below it. Recording the analysis because a future turn retuning a level will face the same question and should not have to redo it.

The rule used throughout: if the exact real product differs from the integer by less than half an ulp at that magnitude, the correctly-rounded double IS the integer.

  LEVEL_5 at shareA 0.30: 100 x fl(0.3). Exact product is 30 - 1.11e-15; half-ulp at 30 is 1.78e-15. Rounds to exactly 30 = demand -> WINS.
  LEVEL_6 at shareA 0.40: supply 100 x fl(0.4) -> exactly 40; then 40 x fl(0.6), exact product 24 - 8.88e-16 against a half-ulp of 1.78e-15 -> exactly 24 = demand -> WINS.
  LEVEL_4 at rate 100: 100 x fl(0.3) -> 30 (as above) and 100 x fl(0.7), exact product 70 - 4.44e-15 against a half-ulp of 7.11e-15 -> exactly 70 -> WINS.
  LEVEL_1 at rate 50 and LEVEL_3 at 44/44 are integer-only arithmetic, no rounding involved.

TWO OF THESE ARE ALREADY EMPIRICALLY PROVEN and that is the useful part. LEVEL_5 SHIPS at shareA 0.3 and LEVEL_6 SHIPS at shareA 0.4, and plant/test/level5.selftest.mjs and level6.selftest.mjs both assert 'feasible as shipped' — those gates pass today, so 100 x fl(0.3) >= 30 and 40 x fl(0.6) >= 24 are facts about this engine rather than facts about my arithmetic. LEVEL_4's rate-100 case has no existing gate and rests on the derivation alone; if it were wrong, level4's fraction would read 40/81 instead of 41/81 and ORDER WOULD BE UNCHANGED (0.4938 still sits between level1 and level3), so the risk is confined to one pinned count and it would fail with a message naming the boundary.

The transferable habit: when a gate pins a COUNT over a swept domain, the count is only as sound as the boundary case, and the boundary case is usually the one place floating point can bite. Assert the two bracketing samples individually BEFORE asserting the count — then a miscount fails with 'rate 100 should have won' rather than with '41 != 40', and the difference is an hour of somebody's time.

beads.title: Is win fraction the right difficulty measure — specifically, does LEVEL_4 belong second?
beads.body:
The campaign's order is computed rather than claimed, and it reproduces your '1, 3, 2, 5, 6' exactly once LEVEL_4 (which your note did not mention) is removed. So the measure agrees with you on the five levels you had an opinion about, which is the best evidence available from inside the loop.

The one place it makes a call nobody has checked is LEVEL_4, which lands SECOND — easier than everything except the tutorial. The measure says so because 41 of the 81 rates the slider offers win. But LEVEL_4 is the autoSplit level: the split is computed FOR the player, and the loop's own turn-15 critique was that this 'removes exactly that decision from the player's hands'. A level that decides the interesting thing for you being nearly the easiest is either the measure working (it is easy because there is nothing to decide) or the measure missing something (it is not easy, it is empty, and easy is the wrong word for it).

I cannot settle it from here: it is a question about what a person experiences, and every instrument I have counts winning settings.

DO: Once the campaign is wired to the page, play it straight through in the computed order — level1, level4, level3, level2, level5, level6 — without reading any of the code.

WATCH FOR: Whether LEVEL_4 in second place feels like a step UP from level 1 or like a rest stop, and whether you notice that its split is being decided for you.

SO THAT: If it feels like a step up, win fraction stands and the pinned ORDER stays as is. If it feels empty rather than easy, the fix is not to reorder — it is that LEVEL_4 needs a lever (its own module says as much), and I would propose replacing the source-rate knob with an explicit share, which turns it into a genuine choice and moves it down the curve on the same measure. If it feels HARDER than level 1 despite winning more often, the measure is wrong and the next thing to try is win fraction weighted by how far a losing setting is from a winning one.

beads.title: Wire campaign.mjs into index.html — one level at a time, a win state, and a next, replacing the six scrolled sections
beads.body:
campaign.mjs exists and is gated; the page does not use it. This is vision item 1's remaining half and it is the ONLY proposal here that changes what a visitor sees, which is why it is at priority 0 — the vision's own box says a planner about to propose something at P0 that does not change the page should propose it at P2 instead.

SCOPE: plant/index.html and plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs (new). Do NOT touch campaign.mjs, the level modules, production.mjs or level-view.js — if the wiring needs something the controller does not expose, that is a second bead, not an edit to a gated module.

WHAT TO BUILD. One <section> that shows ONE level: its title, its blurb (campaign.mjs exports it; do not retype it), a control built FROM `entryOf(id).knob` rather than a hand-written <input>, the board drawn by level-view.js's drawLevel (campaign's verdict() is deliberately a valid drawLevel verdict — it spreads feasible()'s own result), the verdict line from `verdict().line`, and a next button that appears only when `verdict().won`. On the last level, next() returns null and the panel says the run is over rather than wrapping.

THE CONTROL BOUNDS MUST COME FROM `knob.samples`, NOT BE RETYPED. This is the whole reason the knob domains were declared as the page's own ranges: a slider is `min=0 max=samples.length-1 step=1` over the INDEX, and `move(samples[i])`, so a drifted float can never be produced and the difficulty measure keeps describing what the player is offered. The existing level-1 slider currently carries `value="1000"` against `max="120"` (silently clamped by the browser, see the finding on this bead) — that duplication is exactly what this removes.

THE GATE IT CREATES: plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs, reading index.html as text, in the style of index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs — which derives its expectations from the MODULE's own exports rather than from a copied list, and that is the property to reproduce. It must assert: (1) the page imports campaign.mjs and constructs a Campaign; (2) NO level id, blurb, title or control bound is hand-typed in the campaign block — derive the forbidden literals from LEVELS and knob.samples and assert none appears as a literal there; (3) the six old per-level sections are gone (assert the count of level SVG ids, so a leftover section fails loudly); (4) the handlers call move/verdict/next and contain no feasible(), no autoSplit() and no level literal — the page must decide nothing.

USE EXPLICIT BLOCK MARKERS around the campaign block rather than relying on position: the existing index-summon-wiring gate finds its block POSITIONALLY (its closing note says 'all such hits are at lines 321-378, well before it'), so restructuring the page around it can break a currently-correct gate. A checker that fails correct work is worse than no checker.

[turn 60 — done] Wired campaign.mjs into plant/index.html and built the gate it names. The page now opens on ONE campaign panel — title and blurb read from the module, a control built over knob.samples BY INDEX (min=0, max=samples.length-1, move(samples[i]), so an off-grid setting is unrepresentable), the board drawn from the verdict the controller already returned, the sentence from verdict().line, and a next button shown only on `won` that terminates rather than wrapping. The six scrolled per-level sections and their six sliders, six oracle calls and six copies of a level's bounds are gone; the page now contains no feasible(), no autoSplit(), no level id and no threshold. THE PART THE TICKET DID NOT SCOPE, AND THE REASON IT WAS REJECTED LAST ROUND: this change breaks FOUR passing gates it never named — index-level4/5/6-wiring.selftest.mjs assert the six sections exist, and index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs's closing section asserts six direct level imports. I rewrote all four rather than deleting them or leaving them red, following this ledger's own MOVE precedent (absence at the source, presence at the destination); the three level gates now import the real modules and assert by IDENTITY (entry.base === LEVEL_4) and by EXECUTION (feasible() really does refuse LEVEL_4 unsplit, really does accept LEVEL_5/6) what the old regexes could only infer from call order, which is stronger than what they replaced. HONESTLY UNVERIFIED: this turn had Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep and no Bash, so not one of the five test files was executed and the page was never rendered. Every regex in the new gate was hand-traced against the exact bytes of the block I wrote (line by line, including the numeric-bound lookarounds), and the two mechanical passes this ledger recommends for unrun files were run — grep for quote-nesting hazards, and a check of every assertion that reads the front of an ordered list. Two behavioural risks I could not close are named in the learnings.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED ON R2/R3, and it is the ticket I most want back next round — this is the game loop and I am rejecting the spec, not the idea. IT BREAKS A PASSING GATE IT NEVER NAMES. plant/test/index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs:224-237 has a section headed 'levels 1-6 are untouched' that asserts, against index.html, six direct imports: LEVEL_1 from ./level-view.js, and ./levels/level2.mjs through level6.m

beads.title: Move withSourceRate and withProcessorCapacity out of level-view.js — they are pure level transforms living in a view file, and five modules import them from there
beads.body:
level-view.js is the renderer: drawLevel writes SVG, verdictLine and refusalLine write sentences. It also exports withSourceRate and withProcessorCapacity, which are pure level-literal transforms with nothing to do with rendering, and they are imported from there by plant/test/level2.selftest.mjs, level3.selftest.mjs, level4.selftest.mjs, level-view.selftest.mjs and now campaign.mjs.

The smell is concrete rather than aesthetic: campaign.mjs is a headless controller that imports a VIEW module to get two pure functions, so anything that ever puts DOM at level-view.js's top level breaks the controller and its gate. Today there is none, which is exactly why this is cheap to do now.

SCOPE: create plant/levels/transforms.mjs holding the two functions verbatim; have level-view.js import and RE-EXPORT them so no existing importer changes in this bead (level-view.js already re-exports LEVEL_1 and feasible, so the pattern is established); update nothing else. A follow-up can migrate the importers one at a time.

WHY class-a WITH NO NEW GATE: every one of the five importers has a passing selftest that exercises these functions against known answers, and level-view.selftest.mjs pins withSourceRate directly. A move that breaks them cannot pass. The gate list below is the full set that must still pass — a re-export that quietly changed a signature would fail level-view.selftest.mjs first.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE in the campaign bead: it touches five importers and would have made that diff unreviewable. Noted in plant/CLAUDE.md at the time.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED on vision priority, not on correctness — the ticket is technically well-formed and that is exactly the case the operator's brief tells me to reject and say so. It meets R1, R2, R3 and R6 cleanly, and the re-export strategy is the right conservative shape (level-view.js already re-exports LEVEL_1 and feasible, so the pattern is established and no importer changes in this bead). But it chan

beads.title: A first screen: one sentence saying what you are doing, before the first level
beads.body:
Vision item 1 asks for 'a first screen that says what you are doing in one sentence, without the words oracle, feasibility, margin or anisotropy'. campaign.mjs shipped the vocabulary rule (a BANNED array, enforced on every level blurb by its gate) and the per-level blurbs, but there is no game-level sentence and no entry point — a stranger still lands mid-page. SCOPE: plant/campaign.mjs (add an exported INTRO: a title and one sentence) and plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs (extend). Nothing else — the page half belongs to the wiring bead above, and this deliberately lands first so the wiring has something to render. WHY IT IS SEPARATE from the wiring: the wiring bead is already large, and this is the piece with actual writing in it. Splitting them means the sentence can be rewritten without touching the page and vice versa. THE GATE ALREADY EXISTS — plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs — and the assertions to add are the ones it already makes about blurbs, applied to INTRO: one sentence, no word from BANNED, and non-empty. Also assert INTRO does not name a level id or a number, since it must survive a reordering of ORDER. WHAT NO GATE CAN CHECK, said plainly: whether the sentence is any GOOD. A machine can only confirm it is one sentence in plain words. That is a real limit and the reason this is small — one sentence is cheap to replace when a person finally reads it. [turn 61 — done] Added an exported INTRO { title, blurb } to plant/campaign.mjs and a new section 2b to plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs asserting it. The sentence is 'Each puzzle is a small factory that is not quite working, and you get a single control - move it until everything downstream gets what it asked for.' under the title 'Get everything fed'. The gate applies the two rules a level blurb already gets (exactly one sentence by the same /^[^.!?]+[.]$/ regex, no word from BANNED) plus the two the ticket asked for (names no level id, contains no number), each paired with a CONTROL that must fail so a broken matcher cannot pass as clean text. IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE TICKET'S PREMISE: it says 'there is no game-level sentence and no entry point', and that is stale - index.html already ships a hand-typed

and an

Plant

, and index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs section (8) already asserts an intro paragraph exists and is BANNED-free. So the real remaining gap was not 'no sentence' but 'the sentence is a second copy the module does not own', which is what this closes; the page is still not wired to INTRO and that is out of scope by the ticket's own words. I did NOT run the gate - no Bash in this turn's tool grant - so every assertion was hand-traced against the exact bytes written, including each regex character by character. Two things I checked specifically because this file family has been bitten by them: no backtick nested inside a template literal and no ASCII apostrophe inside a single-quoted string, and countRe carries no /g flag so repeated .test() calls cannot alternate on lastIndex. I also grepped the four other gates that read index.html or import campaign.mjs to confirm a new export breaks none of them.

beads.title: The ticket's step 2 was already complete when it was dispatched — a ticket written from a finding can go stale before it is worked
beads.body:
lp-3d2c8e asked for assertions in plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs pinning that legalSeed refuses a NaN, an undefined and the string '40'. All of them were already there, in a well-argued §7 that also pins +/-Infinity on all three axes, the mixed finite/NaN blame divergence between predicate and kernel, the x->y->z tie rule, propagation through summonAt, and four CONTROLs proving the finite path is byte-identical. The turn that fixed placement.mjs clearly wrote the gate at the same time, which is exactly right.

The ticket was authored from the recorded finding 'Two files now carry prose asserting this bug is present, and neither is reachable from this ticket' — and by the time it was dispatched, one of the two things it asked for had been done by the fixing turn itself. Nothing in the system could tell it: a bead's body is a snapshot of the tree at authoring time, and nothing re-reads the tree before dispatch.

This is the same shape as the already-recorded 'The loop dispatched a turn to build gate 6 — and gate 6 was already on disk', one notch smaller: there it was a whole artefact, here it is one of three steps. The cheap defence is the same and it cost one Grep: BEFORE writing anything, grep the bounded paths for the thing the ticket says is missing. If it is already there, the honest turn is to strengthen it rather than duplicate it, and to say so.

What I did with the freed budget is the part worth copying. §7 asserted `wall` ONLY as `k.first.wall === r.wall` — agreement between two implementations, which is a strong check and cannot catch both of them being wrong together. `wall` is the field a UI highlights, so a wrong wall is a visible defect, and it is now pinned to literals (B5/B3/B1 for anything not-finite that is not -Infinity; B4/B2/B0 for -Infinity) derived from the AXES table and the `v < lo` branch. A step that turns out to be done is an invitation to find the assertion next to it that is weaker than it looks.

beads.title: A deliberately-not-asserted console.log outlived the bug it described — the choice was right and the staleness is the price nobody costed
Kept summon-session's badPoint guard and justified it on BLAME, not on redundancy
beads.body:
The ticket said not to delete the guard and I agree, but 'two checks are safer than one' is a bad reason and would have left the next reader free to delete it. The header now gives the reason that survives the redundancy: placement.mjs answers 'this point is outside the hull', which is true and useless to a player, while the session answers blame:'caller' — a bug in the code rather than a move somebody made — and that is why place() returns move:null and does not advance the move count. No hull refusal can express that distinction, so the guard is not duplication even though the check is.

Second, narrower reason, verified against the source rather than assumed: legalSeed calls p.slice() and indexes p, so `null` and a non-array passed as the WHOLE point throw a TypeError there. The session's Array.isArray check catches those; placement.mjs structurally cannot. The selftest's bad-point list already includes `null` and the string 'nowhere'.

What would reverse it: if placement.mjs ever grew its own caller-vs-player taxonomy, the guard would be pure duplication and should go. That is unlikely — placement.mjs is a pure predicate with no notion of a player — so I do not expect this to be revisited.

beads.title: Strengthened placement.selftest.mjs's wall check instead of duplicating step 2's already-present assertions
beads.body:
Step 2 was done (see the finding above). Adding a second set of NaN/undefined/'40' assertions would have grown the file and detected nothing. Instead I pinned the one field §7 left implicit — `wall`, asserted only as equal to the kernel's — to literals from the AXES table, and added reason/axis/wall to the string case which had only asserted nonFinite.

Rejected: adding nothing at all and reporting step 2 as already-satisfied. That would have been honest and would have left the turn with one edit; the wall pin is small, derivable without running anything, and closes a real (if narrow) hole where both implementations could drift together.

Rejected: asserting `limit` too. It is `lo` or `hi` for the blamed axis and no consumer reads it; pinning unread fields is how a gate becomes brittle without becoming stronger.

What would reverse it: if the wall naming ever becomes derived from pocket geometry rather than a fixed table, the literals become the wrong shape and should go back to kernel-agreement only.

beads.title: legalSummon's docstring claims every refusal carries summonSeed — the metric refusal does not. Fix the sentence and pin the field set per reason.
beads.body:
plant/placement.mjs's legalSummon header states, in the sentence a UI author reads before writing their highlight code: 'Every refusal carries `summonSeed` — the index within `con.seeds`, where 0 is the centre — so a caller can light up the offending part of the shape.'

The metric refusal, pushed twelve lines below that sentence in the same function, carries only { ok, reason, conAniso, pocketAniso }. No summonSeed, no role, no at.

Omitting it is CORRECT — a metric mismatch is a property of the whole constellation and there is no single seed to blame — so this is not a bug in the predicate. It is a bug in the sentence, and the cost lands on exactly the caller the sentence was written for: `refusals.map(r => highlight(r.summonSeed))` lights up seed `undefined` and shows nothing, silently, on the one refusal a caller is least likely to have a fixture for. This is a recorded finding (see the ledger entry naming refusalLine as the second consumer to build a walk over refusals from that paragraph) and it has not been acted on.

BOUNDED PATHS: plant/placement.mjs (the legalSummon docstring ONLY — no executable change; the field sets are already right) and plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs.

WHAT TO DO.
1. Change the docstring sentence to say every PER-SEED refusal carries summonSeed and role, and state explicitly that a `metric` refusal carries neither because it is about the constellation rather than about one of its seeds — so a caller branches on reason before reading summonSeed.
2. Add a section to plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs pinning THE FIELD SET OF EACH REASON, which is the part that makes the docstring stop drifting. For each of the four reasons reachable on a fixture — metric, hull, seed, self — assert the exact key set of the refusal object, sorted, with === against a literal array. Section 6 already produces a metric refusal and sections 3/5 produce seed and hull ones; `self` is produced by a cube at a small r (see summon-session.selftest.mjs §8's fixture and the clearance argument in its comment for how to pick a centre that does not shadow it with a seed refusal).
3. The load-bearing assertion is the NEGATIVE one, and it must be written as such: assert that a metric refusal has NO summonSeed key at all (`!('summonSeed' in rf)`), not merely that it is undefined. A missing key and a key holding undefined read the same through `rf.summonSeed` and only one of them is what the code does; pinning the key set is what catches a future turn 'helpfully' adding summonSeed: 0 to the metric refusal, which would make every UI light up the centre for a whole-constellation problem.

WHY class-a AND NOT PROSE: plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs exists and passes today, so the docstring correction becomes an executable claim rather than an unverifiable comment edit. This is the same shape as lp-3d2c8e and for the same reason.

WHAT COULD GO WRONG, stated so the turn does not have to rediscover it: the key sets include fields added by the spread in legalSummon (`...v, summonSeed, role`), so a hull refusal's set is legalSeed's hull set PLUS those two. Derive each expected array by reading legalSeed and legalSummon rather than by guessing, and sort before comparing — key order is insertion order and a spread changes it.

R1: one docstring paragraph and one test section, no algorithm. R4: independent of anything touching production.mjs or the page. R6: fully reversible.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED BY THE THROTTLE, NOT ON MERIT — this one is ready and it is the first bead I would take next round. Re-propose it unchanged. I am allowed three approvals and this was fourth. It meets all six: R1 (one docstring paragraph, one test section, no algorithm), R2 (plant/test/placement.selftest.mjs exists and passes, so a prose correction becomes an executable claim), R3, R4 (independent of inde

beads.title: The ticket was rejected for breaking gates it never named — and there were FOUR of them, not the one the rejection found
beads.body:
The recorded rejection says: 'IT BREAKS A PASSING GATE IT NEVER NAMES. index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs:224-237 has a section headed levels 1-6 are untouched that asserts six direct imports.' That is correct and it is an undercount. Grepping every file in plant/test/ for readFileSync of index.html returns FOUR readers, and three of them are worse than the one the reviewer found:

  index-level4-wiring  asserts id="lvl4", id="ore4", drawLvl4, autoSplit(withSourceRate(LEVEL_4,
  index-level5-wiring  asserts id="lvl5", id="shareA5", withShareA(LEVEL_5,
  index-level6-wiring  asserts id="lvl6", id="shareA6", withShareA6(LEVEL_6,
  index-summon-wiring  asserts six direct level imports  <- the one that was found

So the P0 ticket for vision item 1 was, as written, unsatisfiable: 'replace the six scrolled sections' and 'break nothing that passed before' cannot both hold while three gates assert those sections by id. Nothing in the system could tell it — a bead's body is a snapshot of the tree at authoring time, and no promotion check asks whether the paths a ticket proposes to delete are asserted by an existing gate.

THE RESOLUTION, and it is the ledger's own MOVE precedent rather than an invention: when work relocates code, the old location's guard is not collateral damage to be repaired, it is the only artefact that can prove the relocation happened. All four were REWRITTEN to assert absence at the source and presence at the destination. The three level gates came out stronger, and the reason is worth keeping: a regex over a page can only see call ORDER, so `autoSplit(withSourceRate(LEVEL_4, ...))` was asserted as a SPELLING. Importing the real modules lets the gate assert the property that spelling existed to guarantee — `entry.base === LEVEL_4` by identity, and `feasible()` genuinely throwing on the unsplit level, run rather than inferred. The same swap made the LEVEL_5/6 'must not be routed through autoSplit' check into 'the oracle accepts it with no split step', which is the reason rather than the symptom.

THE CHEAP CHECK, and it belongs at promotion next to the existing gate-file-exists rule: a ticket that says it will DELETE or REPLACE a file's contents should be checked against the gates that read that file. `grep -l <path> plant/test/*.selftest.mjs` is the whole of it. This is the second bead in a row whose real cost was a gate nobody had connected to the work.

beads.title: The control is one index slider for every knob, buttons only for a domain small enough to see — and level 3 gets an 8281-position slider as a result
beads.body:
The ticket mandates a slider over the INDEX of `knob.samples`. Applied literally that gives LEVEL_3 — whose knob is a 91x91 grid of {miner, smelter} pairs — a single slider with 8281 stops sweeping lexicographically: miner 10 with every smelter, then miner 11, and so on. It works, it is winnable, and it is a bad control.

WHAT I REJECTED. Branching on the knob's `kind` ('capacities' -> two sliders) puts level vocabulary back in the page, which is the entire thing this ticket removes. Hand-writing a second control for the one level that needs it is the six-sections problem returning at a smaller scale.

WHAT I CHOSE. The page makes exactly one judgement about a control and it is about SIZE, not about which level it is: a domain of ALL_AT_ONCE (8) or fewer members gets one button per member, anything larger gets the index slider. LEVEL_2's three smelters therefore stay a discrete choice with no dragging toward the answer — which was that level's whole design — and a future level offering four options is laid out as buttons without editing a line. Nothing in the page knows a level id.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a `knob` that declares its own components (a multi-part knob offering one control per part) would let LEVEL_3 have two sliders with no level knowledge in the page at all. That is an edit to campaign.mjs, which this ticket forbids, so it is proposed as its own bead. Until then the honest statement is that level 3's control is playable and ugly, and the vision says ugly and playable beats elegant and inert.

beads.title: Two behavioural risks this turn could not close, and neither is arithmetic
beads.body:
The ~25 prior 'gate unverifiable in-turn' notes all reason about whether a hand-computed number is right. Neither of this turn's residual risks is of that kind, and recording the difference is more useful than restating the standing recommendation.

1. THE PAGE WAS NEVER RENDERED. Every assertion in the new gate is a claim about TEXT, and text is the only thing a gate reading index.html can check — so 'the slider is wired' means the string `$('gameKnob').addEventListener('input',` is present, not that dragging it moves anything. Three specific things are unverified and a browser would settle all three in seconds: that `element.hidden = true` really removes the range input given `.ctl input[type=range] { width: 100% }` (it should — that rule sets no `display`, so the UA's `[hidden] { display: none }` is unopposed); that an 8281-stop range input is usable on a phone; and that `campaign.mjs`'s ~8,600-call win-fraction sweep at MODULE LOAD does not put a visible stall in front of the first paint. The summon panel's pocket generation is deferred one tick for exactly that reason and the campaign import is NOT, because it happens at import and cannot be.

2. FOUR GATES WERE REWRITTEN AND NONE WAS RUN. That is the larger risk, and it is the one a reviewer should read first: a turn that edits the checks that grade it is the specific shape this ledger warns about. What I can say is what I did rather than that it is right — every relocated assertion kept its wording and its intent and changed only its subject; nothing was removed without a replacement that makes a strictly stronger claim (identity and execution in place of regex); and each rewritten file states in its header WHY it was rewritten and what the old form asserted, so the diff is reviewable rather than 'I updated some tests'. The three level gates now genuinely exercise the oracle, so if they pass they have proved more than the versions they replace ever could.

The standing recommendation is unchanged and I am not restating it at length: this is a loop-work.yml fix, and I have no bounded path into .github/workflows/ from this ticket.

beads.title: One board fixed the five-level CSS gap by making it unreachable rather than by fixing it
beads.body:
The ledger records that `svg#lvl { ... }` and its two descendant rules were keyed to the exact id of LEVEL_1's mount, so LEVEL_2 through LEVEL_6 rendered unstyled by them — a pre-existing gap across five levels that a previous turn correctly declined to fix inside its own ticket.

One level at a time deletes the failure mode rather than repairing it: there is now exactly one board, `svg#gameBoard`, and the four rules were repointed at it. `drawLevel` emits `class="ln"` and `class="ls"`, so those descendant rules are load-bearing rather than decorative — a board without them renders unstyled text, which is precisely what levels 2-6 have been doing.

Worth noticing as a general shape, because it is cheerful and it is rare: a bug whose cause is 'N copies of a thing, one of which was configured' is closed for free by any change that makes N equal to one. The proposed fix at the time was a shared selector list, which would have had to be maintained; this needs nothing maintained. A comment at the rules says so, so nobody re-adds a second board without noticing what it costs.

beads.title: Does the page now read as a game, or as a game bolted to the top of an explainer?
beads.body:
This turn made the page open on one level with a title, a blurb, a control, a verdict and a next button — vision item 1's remaining half. What it did NOT do is remove the summon inspector, the summon panel and the two essays underneath, because they are the surface's stated job (making the primitive judgeable by a stranger in thirty seconds) and deleting them is a decision about what the page is FOR rather than about wiring. So a visitor now meets a game and then scrolls into documentation about a different thing. No gate can tell whether that reads as generous or as unfinished, and I have no way to look at it.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com on a phone. Do not scroll. Play the first level to a win and press next. Then scroll once and stop.

WATCH FOR: Whether the first screen made you want to press something, and whether the moment you scrolled past the game you felt you had left it or finished it.

SO THAT: If the game reads as the page, the next tickets are inside it — a first-run line, a completion screen, an undo. If it reads as bolted on, the inspector and the summon panel should move to a second page and the vision's item 1 becomes 'the game is the whole surface', which is a bigger and more valuable ticket than any of those. If it reads as unfinished specifically because there is no ending, the completion screen is the one to do first and the rest can wait.

beads.title: A multi-part knob: let campaign.mjs declare a knob's COMPONENTS so LEVEL_3 gets two sliders instead of one 8281-position index
beads.body:
LEVEL_3's knob is a 91x91 grid of {miner, smelter}, and the page — correctly forbidden from knowing which level it is showing — renders it as a single index slider with 8281 stops sweeping lexicographically. It is playable and it is the worst control on the page. The decision recorded on lp-6c88fb explains why the alternatives available inside that ticket were worse.

THE FIX, and it is small: give `knob()` an optional `parts` descriptor — an array of `{ name, samples }` — for a knob whose settings are objects, plus a `compose(values)` that turns one member of each part's domain into a setting. `key` already exists and already handles object membership, so nothing about the domain, the win-fraction measure or `move()`'s refusal changes: `parts` is a presentation of the SAME finite declared domain, and the gate must assert that (every composition of members is a member of `samples`, and the count matches).

The page then renders one index slider per part with no new level knowledge — it iterates `knob.parts` if present and falls back to today's single slider if not, so nothing about LEVEL_1/4/5/6 changes.

SCOPE: plant/campaign.mjs, plant/index.html, plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs, plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs.

WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK, beyond the obvious: (a) the cartesian product of the parts' domains equals `samples` as a SET (compare by `key`, and assert the sizes match — a `parts` that offers fewer combinations than the domain silently removes settings the difficulty measure counted); (b) `WIN_FRACTION` is byte-identical before and after, since the domain did not change and the measure must not move; (c) the page reads `knob.parts` and still hand-types no bound, which the existing derived-literal check in index-campaign-wiring already covers and must keep covering.

[turn 63 — done] Gave knob() an optional `parts` descriptor and wired LEVEL_3's page control to it, so the 91x91 grid is now two sliders of 91 stops instead of one index slider of 8281. The one design call I made differently from the ticket's letter: a knob with `parts` DERIVES `samples` from the cartesian product and REFUSES to be given them, rather than declaring both and checking they agree. That makes requirement (a) — 'a parts that offers fewer combinations than the domain silently removes settings the difficulty measure counted' — impossible by construction instead of merely detectable, which is the same move this tree keeps wishing it had made (the level-1 slider shipped value="1000" against max="120" for weeks because a fact had two homes). The cost is that the ticket's literal assertion becomes vacuous, so the gate asserts a STRONGER thing in its place: it rebuilds the expected 8281-key set from a double loop over literals typed in the test file and compares it as a set, which catches a wrong compose, a swapped part order, a truncated part domain and a changed key function alike. The knob also returns `compose(values)` and `positions(value)` (a setting -> per-part indices, null for a non-member) so the page needs no product arithmetic of its own; `positions` inverts the odometer by division rather than by searching, and the product order is unchanged from the hand-written double loop it replaced, so every slider index still means the setting it meant before. The page picks between three control shapes on the SHAPE OF THE KNOB (parts / small domain / anything else) and still names no level, no bound and no part name. Requirement (b): the gate re-counts the win fraction by sweeping the two PART domains directly and asserts it equals the exported WIN_FRACTION.level3, which is still pinned at 3249/8281, and ORDER is still pinned as a literal. HONESTLY: I have no Bash, so NEITHER GATE WAS RUN. Every number was hand-derived (flat index 60*91+35 = 5495 for the opening setting; samples[1] = 10x11, samples[91] = 11x10, samples[8280] = 100x100 pin the odometer) and every new regex was traced character-by-character against the exact bytes I wrote into index.html. The page was never rendered — 'the part sliders are wired' means the string is present, not that dragging one moves anything.

beads.title: The vision's thirty-second bar as an executable gate: a scripted playthrough reaches a player-caused refusal within an asserted bound
beads.body:
vision.md names four executable claims for item 1 and lp-6c88fb's gate now covers three of them: the control logic lives in a module a test can drive; completing a level advances to exactly one next and the last terminates rather than wrapping; and the order is monotonic in a stated measure (campaign.selftest.mjs pins ORDER as a literal). THE FOURTH IS NOT COVERED: 'a scripted playthrough reaches a refusal the player caused in a bounded number of moves, and the test asserts that bound.'

That is the only one of the four that is about the EXPERIENCE rather than the state machine, and it is the closest a machine gets to the thirty-second bar. index-campaign-wiring asserts a weak proxy — every level's win fraction is strictly between 0 and 1, so some offered setting loses and some wins — which proves a refusal EXISTS and says nothing about how far a player has to walk to meet one.

WHAT TO BUILD: plant/test/playthrough.selftest.mjs. Drive a real `Campaign` with a scripted policy that only ever does what a stranger can do (pick a member of `knob.samples`, read `verdict()`, press `next()` when `won`), and assert, for EVERY level in ORDER: (a) starting from `knob.start`, a losing state is reachable within N moves, N asserted as a literal; (b) a winning state is reachable within M moves from the opening, M asserted as a literal; (c) the whole campaign is completable — a policy that always moves toward a win finishes all six and terminates. The literals are the point: 'reachable eventually' is true of any finite domain and worth nothing.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT WORTHLESS, and the gate must guard it: a policy that SEARCHES the domain for a losing setting proves only that the domain contains one, which is already known. The policy must be blind — a fixed rule such as 'move one step down the index' — so the bound it measures is a property of the level's shape rather than of the search. State that in the file header, and include a CONTROL: a policy that moves one step in the WRONG direction must NOT find a win within the same bound, or the bound is not measuring anything.

[turn 64 — done] Built plant/test/playthrough.selftest.mjs, the gate this ticket names. It drives a real Campaign with three BLIND policies — YANK_FLOOR (move 1 is samples[0]), STEP_DOWN and STEP_UP (one index per move, clamped at the ends) — each a pure function of (samples, openingIndex, moveNumber) that never receives a Campaign and never calls grade()/verdict()/feasible(). Requirement (a): a refusal the player caused is reached in 1 move on EVERY level by yanking the control to its floor, and the fine STEP_DOWN bound is pinned per level as a literal (level1 71, level2 1, level3 2, level4 3, level5 1, level6 1; worst 71) with TIGHTNESS asserted from below — the move before the bound must still be fed. Requirement (b): STEP_UP wins in a pinned literal per level (all 1 except level2 at 2), tightness coming from won = ok && moves > 0 so zero moves can never win. Requirement (c): one blind up-stepping player completes all six levels in exactly 7 moves, visits ORDER once each, and terminates rather than wrapping. The ticket's anti-search requirement is enforced STRUCTURALLY, not claimed: §2 stringifies each policy and fails on any mention of an outcome, carrying a deliberately-cheating policy as a CONTROL so the regex cannot pass by matching nothing; §3 computes each policy's whole move sequence before the Campaign exists, replays it, recomputes and asserts it did not change. The ticket's wrong-direction CONTROL is split in two because neither covers all six levels and I say so in the header: §6 (STEP_UP finds no refusal within the STEP_DOWN bound) bites on five levels and provably cannot bite on level2, which opens broken; §7 (STEP_DOWN never wins while STEP_UP wins at 2) bites only on level2, for the mirror reason. That 5/1 split is pinned as a table so a level retuned across the line fails here. HONESTLY: I had no Bash, so the file was never executed — every bound was derived by hand from the level literals and cross-checked against boundaries campaign.selftest.mjs already pins as passing (rate 50 wins, 44x44 wins, rate 100 wins, 0.30 and 0.40 win, golden is the only winning smelter). Nothing outside plant/test/playthrough.selftest.mjs was touched, so no previously-passing gate can regress.

beads.title: Check a ticket's deletions against the gates that read the file, at promotion
beads.body:
lp-6c88fb was rejected once and nearly unsatisfiable twice for the same reason: it proposed to replace the six per-level sections of index.html, and FOUR gates assert those sections exist. The reviewer found one of the four by reading; the other three were found by this turn grepping `readFileSync` across plant/test/ before writing anything. A ticket that says 'replace X' while a passing gate asserts X is a ticket that cannot satisfy both its own body and the creates-gate rule ('breaks nothing that already passed'), and nothing between the planner and the executor compares the two.

This is the same shape as lp-4d3aa1's fix, which put a gate-file-EXISTS check at promotion because the outbox validator must stay pure and cannot see a filesystem. This is the mirror image: a gate-file-READS check, at the same boundary, for the same reason.

SCOPE: scripts/beads.mjs (cmdPromote) and its selftest — NOTE THIS IS OUTSIDE THE FLEET'S WRITE PATHS, so it is human work or it needs the containment set widened first. That is stated deliberately rather than discovered: the ledger records a bead attempted five times because its gate lived somewhere no seat could reach, and this proposal must not become the sixth.

WHAT IT WOULD DO: when a bead's `paths` name a file, grep the repo's test files for that path and WARN (not refuse) listing every gate that reads it, in the same conservative spirit as the existing existence check — a rule that cries wolf gets forced past every time. The warning is enough: the cost here was never that the collision was unfixable, it was that nobody knew about it until a turn was spent.
evidence: rejected: R3, and it is not close: the scope is scripts/beads.mjs (cmdPromote) plus its selftest, which is OUTSIDE plant/ and outside the fleet's declared write paths, so no seat can write it. R2 also fails — gate: NONE, class-d, not fleet-dispatchable, which the body itself states. THE REJECTION IS NOT A DISAGREEMENT WITH THE IDEA. The diagnosis is correct and I hit it myself this turn: I checked lp-056d80

beads.title: The count rule forbids ALL numbers, not just counts of levels - stricter than its own justification, on purpose
beads.body:
The ticket asks that INTRO 'does not name a level id or a number, since it must survive a reordering of ORDER'. The hazard being guarded is a sentence like 'six levels' or 'start on the ore line' becoming false when ORDER is recomputed from win fractions.

But no regex can distinguish 'six levels' (a claim that expires) from 'one setting' (a claim that does not). I had three options: forbid every number, forbid only numbers adjacent to level-ish nouns, or forbid only digits.

I took the broadest. COUNT_WORDS is one..ten plus first/second/third, matched on word boundaries, plus any digit.

WHAT IT COSTS, stated because it is not free and because a future writer will hit it: index.html's own shipped intro, 'Each level gives you one setting to move', WOULD FAIL THIS CHECK. My sentence says 'a single control' precisely to dodge it. So the rule does reject phrasing that is perfectly correct, which is the shape the ledger already warns about ('a checker that fails correct work is worse than no checker').

WHY I TOOK IT ANYWAY: INTRO is ONE SHORT SENTENCE. Rewording it costs nothing, and the adjacency version needs a noun list that is itself a guess and is gameable. The asymmetry decides it - a false positive costs a writer one reword and says so out loud in the failure message; a false negative is a stale count on a live page that nobody notices.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a real sentence somebody wants that the list rejects and that carries no structural claim. Then delete 'one' from COUNT_WORDS (cardinals two..ten are the realistic level-count hazard; 'one' is almost always article-like). That is a one-line edit. The comment in the test says this in those words, and says explicitly not to delete the assertion instead - making a gate pass by weakening it is the specific cheat this shape permits.

beads.title: INTRO uses a LEVELS entry's field names (title, blurb) rather than title/sentence
beads.body:
The ticket says 'add an exported INTRO: a title and one sentence', which invites `{ title, sentence }`. I used `{ title, blurb }` instead, matching what every LEVELS entry already carries.

Reason: index.html's render() already does `$('gameTitle').textContent = entry.title; $('gameBlurb').textContent = entry.blurb;`. With matching field names the wiring follow-up can render the intro screen and a level screen with the SAME two lines and no adapter, and any future helper that formats 'a screen' takes either object.

It also makes the gate's job obvious: section 2b is literally section 2's blurb rules applied to one more object, so if the blurb rules are ever tightened, the diff that tightens them is visibly the same shape in both places.

Cost: 'blurb' is a slightly odd word for a game-level sentence, and someone reading INTRO alone might expect 'sentence'. Reversing it is a rename in two files with no logic change.

beads.title: The ticket's premise was stale before it was worked - #gameIntro already exists, hand-typed, and the real gap was ownership not absence
beads.body:
lp-ffddc7's body says 'there is no game-level sentence and no entry point - a stranger still lands mid-page'. Both halves are out of date: · index.html:82-86 ships `

Plant

` and `

A little factory that has to feed everything it promised. Each level gives you one setting to move; get nothing short and the next one opens.

` · plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs section (8) already asserts that paragraph exists, is under 400 chars, and contains no BANNED word - deriving BANNED from campaign.mjs rather than re-typing it. The wiring bead the ticket calls 'the wiring bead above' has already landed (lp-6c88fb, per plant/CLAUDE.md). So the ticket was authored from a true observation about a tree that then moved, which is the already-recorded shape 'a ticket written from a finding can go stale before it is worked' and 'the loop dispatched a turn to build gate 6 - and gate 6 was already on disk'. This is the milder version: the artefact was not already built, but the problem statement was wrong about why it was needed. The cheap defence is the same one the ledger already names and it cost me one Grep: before writing anything, grep the bounded paths AND the paths the ticket describes for the thing it says is missing. Doing that here changed the work - not what I built, but what I claimed. Without it this outbox would have said 'a stranger now has a first screen', which is false; they always had one. What they now have is a first screen whose words the module owns and a gate that checks them. The genuinely useful reframing for whoever picks up the follow-up: the intro is currently the ONLY text on the campaign panel that is not module-owned. Level titles and blurbs are asserted absent from the page (section 4 checks `!block.includes(e.blurb)`); the intro is asserted only to exist and to be clean. That asymmetry is the whole remaining bug.

beads.title: Section (8) of the wiring gate cannot catch intro drift - it checks a property of the text, never that it is the RIGHT text
beads.body:
index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs section (8) reads the page's `#gameIntro` and asserts: it exists, it is non-empty and under 400 chars, and it contains no BANNED word. Every one of those is a property the string has ON ITS OWN.

So it passes for any plain-English paragraph whatsoever. It would pass for an intro describing a completely different game, for one naming 'level 2' as the opener after ORDER was recomputed, or for one that says 'six levels' after a seventh was added. That is exactly the class of check the ledger keeps recording as weaker than it reads - `line.includes(String(x))` passing for a renderer that hardcodes the constant, assertions that relate a function's outputs only to its other outputs.

It is not a defect in that gate: when it was written the intro was the page's own text and there was nothing external to compare it to. There is now. The comparison that bites is one line, `intro.trim() === INTRO.blurb`, and it is only available because the words moved into the module - which is the argument for doing the wiring follow-up beyond tidiness.

Note the ordering constraint this creates and why proposal 1 must change the page's wording rather than the module's: the shipped paragraph says 'one setting to move' and is two sentences, so it violates both the count rule and the one-sentence rule that section 2b now enforces on INTRO. A turn that wires the page by copying the page's wording INTO campaign.mjs would go red in campaign.selftest.mjs and might then be tempted to relax section 2b. The correct direction is module wins, page changes.

beads.title: A section of only NEGATIVE assertions needs controls more than a normal one, and the level-id control is guarding an empty array rather than a regex
beads.body:
Every substantive assertion in section 2b is a negation: no banned word, no level id, no number. A negation over one short clean string is the easiest thing in the world to pass by accident - an empty BANNED array passes, a `LEVELS.map(...)` that came back empty passes, a regex with a typo that matches nothing passes. All of them print a tick.

So each predicate is fed something it MUST catch. Two of those controls are ordinary (a string containing 'feasibility'; strings containing '6', 'six', 'first'). The third is worth pointing at because it looks tautological and is not:

    LEVELS.map((e) => e.id).some((id) => `start on ${id} and work down.`.includes(id))

The template embeds the id, so per-element it can never be false. What it actually tests is that the ARRAY IS NON-EMPTY - `.some()` on `[]` returns false. That is the only realistic way the level-id check silently stops working, since the ids themselves are pinned in section 1. A reader who mistakes it for a redundant tautology and deletes it removes the only guard on that failure mode.

There is also a control in the other direction, which I nearly left out: `!countRe.test('everything downstream is stone.')`. Without it, someone 'simplifying' the word-boundary regex to a bare substring test would still pass all five positive controls while making the check fire on 'stone', 'everything', 'atone' - i.e. unusable for any real sentence, discovered only by the next person trying to write one. A boundary-sensitive matcher needs a control proving it does NOT overmatch, not just that it matches.

beads.title: Gate unverifiable in-turn (no Bash) - recording only what is specific to a prose gate, since the standing recommendation is past twenty entries
beads.body:
The standing recommendation is in this ledger well over twenty times and the last several turns agreed to stop restating it. I am not restating it. What is worth one entry is that the risk profile of an unrun PROSE gate is different from the ~25 prior instances, which almost all reason about whether a hand-computed number is right. There is no arithmetic here at all.

The three things that could actually have gone wrong, and what I did about each:

1. LEXICAL. A backtick inside a template literal or an ASCII apostrophe inside a single-quoted string makes the file fail to PARSE, and then not one assertion runs - a failure that reads like an unrelated typo rather than like the gate never executing. Checked: the only template literals I added are `${INTRO.title} ${INTRO.blurb}`, `\\d|\\b(${COUNT_WORDS.join('|')})\\b` and `start on ${id} and work down.`, and the inner join uses single quotes, not backticks. No added string contains an apostrophe; INTRO's blurb says 'is not' rather than 'isn't' partly for this reason.

2. REGEX STATE. `countRe` is used for six separate `.test()` calls plus one `.match()`. With a /g flag that is a classic bug - `lastIndex` persists and alternate calls return false. It carries only /i. This is the one defect that would have produced a confidently wrong PASS rather than a red gate.

3. THE MATCH ITSELF. Traced by hand over the exact bytes: introText lowercased is 'get everything fed each puzzle is a small factory that is not quite working, and you get a single control - move it until everything downstream gets what it asked for.' No BANNED substring; no 'level'; no digit; and no COUNT_WORD at a word boundary - 'control' does not contain 'one', and 'everything' does not contain 'ten'. The one-sentence regex holds because the only . ! ? in the string is the final period, the em dash and comma being ordinary members of [^.!?].

The transferable half: for a gate with no arithmetic, the failure modes are lexical and stateful, not numerical - and the stateful one (a stray /g) is the only one of the three that fails silently in the passing direction.

beads.title: Is the first sentence any good? A machine can only confirm it is one sentence in plain words
beads.body:
The gate proves INTRO.blurb is one sentence, uses none of the jargon, names no level and counts nothing. It cannot say whether it makes a stranger want to touch the control, and I have no way to find out from here - there is no reader in this turn and the page is not yet wired to it.

The sentence: 'Each puzzle is a small factory that is not quite working, and you get a single control - move it until everything downstream gets what it asked for.' Title: 'Get everything fed'.

Two specific doubts I could not settle. (1) 'not quite working' may undersell it - on five of the six levels the opening state is already FED, so the honest framing might be 'working, but you have not proved it' rather than broken. I chose the punchier reading because a stranger who thinks nothing is wrong has no reason to move anything. (2) The word 'puzzle' commits to a framing the page never uses elsewhere ('level' is used throughout the module and the markup), and I deliberately avoided 'level' in the intro because the count rule and the level-id rule made every phrasing with it read awkwardly.

I decided both ways rather than waiting, per the standing instruction. This is a note, not a request.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com once the wiring follow-up has landed, read only the top of the page, and stop. Do not scroll.

WATCH FOR: Whether you know what you are supposed to DO before you touch anything - and specifically whether 'not quite working' makes you look for something broken on a level that opens already fed.

SO THAT: If it reads fine, INTRO is done and nobody spends another turn on wording. If 'not quite working' misleads, the fix is one string in campaign.mjs and the gate re-checks it for free - and the finding worth recording is that the intro must describe the ACT (move the control until you have proved it) rather than the STATE. If 'puzzle' jars against 'level', that is a vocabulary decision for the whole panel and wants its own small bead rather than an edit to this one sentence.

beads.title: Render INTRO from campaign.mjs into the page, and assert the page's intro EQUALS it
beads.body:
The campaign panel's intro is now the only text on it that the module does not own. Level titles and blurbs are set from `entry.title`/`entry.blurb` and index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs section (4) asserts they are absent from the page source; the intro is hand-typed at index.html:82-86 and section (8) checks only that SOME plain paragraph exists and is BANNED-free. That check passes for any English at all - including an intro naming a level as the opener after ORDER is recomputed, which is precisely what INTRO's new gate forbids in the module and nothing forbids in the page.

SCOPE: plant/index.html and plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs.

THE WORK: import INTRO alongside the other campaign exports; set `$('gameIntro').textContent = INTRO.blurb` and the `<h1>` from `INTRO.title` (or leave the h1 as the site name and use INTRO.title as the panel heading - either is fine, but pick one and assert it); ship both mount points EMPTY in the markup, the way `#gameTitle` and `#gameBlurb` already do, so there is no second copy to drift.

THE GATE, which already exists: extend section (8) to `intro.trim() === INTRO.blurb` and add the absence check the other module-owned text already gets - `!html.includes(INTRO.blurb)` outside the mount, mirroring section (4)'s `!block.includes(e.blurb)`. Keep the existing BANNED loop; it becomes cheap redundancy rather than the only defence.

ONE TRAP, and it is the reason this needs saying rather than being obvious: the shipped page wording is TWO sentences and says 'one setting to move'. Both violate rules campaign.selftest.mjs section 2b now enforces on INTRO. The fix direction is MODULE WINS, PAGE CHANGES - do not copy the page's wording into campaign.mjs and then relax section 2b to accommodate it. If the module's sentence is genuinely worse, change the module's sentence and let both gates judge the new one.

What this does NOT do: improve the writing. That needs a person and is filed as an ask.
evidence: rejected: R2 FAILS: the gate it names cannot pass as specified, and I checked the file rather than inferring. The body asks to 'ship both mount points EMPTY in the markup' AND to extend section (8) to `intro.trim() === INTRO.blurb`. In plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs:184-186, `intro` is the regex capture from the raw text of index.html — with an empty mount it is the empty string, so that equa

beads.title: `first` was already the name TWO layers down — place() was the sole renamer, which is why the asymmetry read as arbitrary
`res.first === res.refusal` passes for an implementation that sets NEITHER — the field-list assertion is what makes the section non-vacuous
beads.body:
The obvious gate for this ticket is `ok(res.first === res.refusal)` on a handful of results. That assertion is satisfied by `undefined === undefined`, so it passes for the pre-fix code on any verb/path combination where NEITHER name happens to be set — and more importantly it would pass for a future refactor that deleted both. It measures agreement, not existence, and the two are different claims.

Three things close it, and only the first is obvious in hindsight:

  1. THE KEY SET. Each verb's exact sorted `Object.keys()` is pinned as a literal, identical across all its paths (preview 8 keys, place 12). This is the only assertion in the section that proves the names exist at all, and it is also what catches the pre-fix code directly — preview lacked `refusal`, place lacked `first`, so both literals fail.
  2. ON A REFUSAL, `first.reason` must be a string and `first.blame` must be in BLAME. Two undefineds cannot agree past that.
  3. ON A SUCCESS, both must be `null` — not one null and one undefined. This is the case an alias applied only to the failure branches gets wrong while passing everything else, and it is the dangerous one in practice: `undefined || null` is still null, so `summon-view.js` renders correctly and nothing looks wrong until a stale refusal is sitting in the other name.

THE TRANSFERABLE SHAPE, and this ledger has it from other directions: an assertion that two expressions are EQUAL is not an assertion that either is DEFINED. Any test pinning an alias, a mirror field, a cached copy or a denormalised value needs a separate existence check, or it is satisfied by the absence of both things it is about.

beads.title: The SECOND asymmetry is worse than the one this ticket fixed: preview refusals name `summonSeed`, place refusals name `point`
beads.body:
Fixing the result-level name surfaced the same disagreement one level down, in the field a UI needs most.

  preview -> legalSummon pushes `{ ...legalSeed(...), summonSeed: i, role }`, and its
             self refusals carry `summonSeed` / `otherSummonSeed`.
  place   -> reformPocketAll pushes `{ reason, point: i, ... }`, and its batch
             refusals carry `point` / `otherPoint`.

Both mean the same thing — the index within `con.seeds`, 0 being the centre — because place() hands `con.seeds` straight to the kernel in order. Neither ever carries the other's name (verified by reading every push site in both files: `legalSeed` returns `at/seedIndex/seed/gap/need` with no `point`, and `hullRefusal` returns `axis/wall/depth/value/limit/clamped` with no `summonSeed`).

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN THE ONE JUST FIXED. `first` vs `refusal` was visible the moment anyone tried to write one renderer, and it produced an obviously-suspicious `||`. This one is invisible: a renderer that does `highlight(rf.summonSeed)` works perfectly against every preview and lights up `undefined` — i.e. nothing at all, silently — for exactly the summons that were actually attempted. That is the recorded `legalSummon` docstring failure ('every refusal carries summonSeed', which the metric refusal does not) with a wider blast radius.

Also note the third spelling in the same family: a closure/nav refusal carries `points` (plural, the whole batch) and no index at all, because the rebuild cannot attribute a closure failure to one seed.

PINNED, NOT FIXED. Section 10 asserts which name each verb uses, with a guard that both loops actually ran against a real refusal so they cannot pass while asserting nothing. Proposed as its own bead below: `_attribute` can set `summonSeed` from `point` on the kernel's per-seed refusals while keeping `point`, which is the same conservative both-names move this ticket just made and for the same reason.

beads.title: Kept both names as aliases of the SAME OBJECT, and accepted that place() now has `first` at two levels meaning two things
beads.body:
WHAT I CHOSE. Both verbs return both names, assigned from one local so they are identity-equal, not deep-equal. Identity rather than a copy because the gate can then assert `res.first === res.refusals[0]`, which is a strictly stronger claim than deep equality and rules out the two names drifting to two different refusals — the failure the ticket is actually about.

WHAT I REJECTED, and why:

  · RENAMING `refusal` to `first` (or vice versa). The ticket forbids it and it is right to: a rename that misses a caller is strictly worse than the asymmetry, and `summon-view.js` and `index.html` are both outside this ticket's bounded paths, so I could not have followed through even if I wanted to.
  · Setting only the failure branches. That is the version that passes almost every plausible test and is still wrong — see the finding above.
  · Making `refusal` a getter over `refusals[0]`. Cleaner in principle; rejected because these are plain data objects that get spread, snapshotted and serialised elsewhere in the tree, and a getter does not survive `{ ...res }` as a getter.

THE COST I ACCEPTED AND WROTE DOWN AT THE SITE. `place()` now has `first` at the top level (the first refusal, null on a success) AND `placed.first` one level in (the index of the summon's first seed in the pocket). Two meanings, one word, two nesting levels. I took it because `placed` is `null` on exactly the paths where the top-level `first` is non-null, so the two are never both live, and because inventing a third name for the alias would have defeated the entire point of the ticket. A comment on `place()`'s docstring says this explicitly rather than leaving the next reader to find it.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: if `placed.first` is ever renamed to `firstSeed` or `baseIndex` — which would be an improvement on its own merits — the collision disappears and this note can go.

beads.title: summon-view.js's header now describes a fixed bug in the present tense, and it is outside this ticket's bounded paths
beads.body:
`plant/summon-view.js` lines 86-88 read: 'The two verbs name the first refusal differently — `preview` returns `first`, `place` returns `refusal` — so both are read. That asymmetry is in `summon-session.mjs` and is not this file's to fix.'

The second sentence is now false and the first is now merely historical. Line 99's `const rf = res.refusal || res.first` still WORKS — both operands are now the same object, so the `||` is a no-op rather than a hazard — and no gate goes red, which is why I did not reach for it.

I did not touch it: `summon-view.js` is outside the bounded paths this ticket names, and its own gate (`summon-view.selftest.mjs`) is outside them too, so a prose-only edit there would be an uncontained diff for zero verified benefit.

This is the exact debt shape the ledger already recorded from the placement.mjs NaN fix — a file that correctly documented a bug it could not fix, and then the bug was fixed elsewhere and the paragraph became a lie. The collector this time is a proposal below rather than a comment, because the ledger's own lesson was that a note in a comment is not a queue.

beads.title: Normalise `summonSeed` across both verbs' refusals — a renderer that highlights the offending part of the shape currently works on preview and silently highlights nothing on place
summon-view.js documents a fixed asymmetry in the present tense, and its `res.refusal || res.first` is now a no-op — correct the prose and pin the alias from the consumer side
beads.body:
`plant/summon-view.js` lines 86-88 assert, in its only header paragraph about verdict shape: 'The two verbs name the first refusal differently — `preview` returns `first`, `place` returns `refusal` — so both are read. That asymmetry is in `summon-session.mjs` and is not this file's to fix.'

lp-aabb74 fixed it. Both verbs now set both names to the same object on every path, so line 99's `const rf = res.refusal || res.first` is a no-op rather than a hazard and the paragraph is a description of history written as a statement of fact. Nothing is red — this is prose debt, and prose debt in this tree is collected by a bead rather than by a comment, because the ledger has already recorded that a note left in a file is not a queue.

SCOPE, and it is small:
  · rewrite the paragraph to say both names are aliases and that `res.first` is read for that reason, with one sentence of history so the `||` is not re-added by someone who reads the git log;
  · simplify line 99 to `const rf = res.first`. This is a REAL behaviour question, not a tidy-up, and it is the reason the ticket needs a gate rather than a proofreader: if any producer ever regresses to setting only one name, the `||` hides it and a bare read exposes it. Taking the bare read is deliberately the LESS forgiving option.

WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK, added to `plant/test/summon-view.selftest.mjs`, which already drives a real session on the MACRO fixture and therefore has both verbs' results to hand:
  · `summonSentence` produces the IDENTICAL string for a `place()` refusal and for the `preview()` of the same point — the property the shared renderer exists to have, and one no assertion in either file makes today;
