  · it produces the same string for a synthetic result carrying only `first` and for one carrying only `refusal`, so the consumer's tolerance is asserted rather than assumed;
  · the resting-state and success branches are unaffected (`null` in, the resting sentence out; a landed summon still names its move).

Deliberately NOT in scope: renaming either field, and touching `index.html`.

WHY class-a: `plant/test/summon-view.selftest.mjs` exists and passes today; the taker adds assertions to it. BOUNDED PATHS: plant/summon-view.js, plant/test/summon-view.selftest.mjs. Priority 3 because the vision is explicit that page-and-game work outranks module hygiene this run — this is worth doing when someone is already in that file, not ahead of anything a visitor sees.
evidence: rejected: R2, and it is a contradiction inside the ticket rather than a missing gate. The scope says 'simplify line 99 to const rf = res.first' and calls the bare read 'deliberately the LESS forgiving option'. The gate section then says it must check that summonSentence 'produces the same string for a synthetic result carrying only first and for one carrying only refusal, so the consumer's tolerance is asse

beads.title: A knob with `parts` DERIVES its samples and refuses to be given them — requirement (a) enforced instead of asserted
beads.body:
The ticket describes `parts` as an extra descriptor alongside `samples`, and asks the gate to assert that the cartesian product of the parts equals `samples` as a set. I built it the other way round: `parts` REPLACES `samples`, the product is derived, and passing both throws at import naming the knob.

WHY. The failure the ticket names — 'a `parts` that offers fewer combinations than the domain silently removes settings the difficulty measure counted' — is only possible if the domain has two declarations. This tree has paid for that shape repeatedly and has it recorded: index.html's level-1 slider shipped `value="1000"` against `max="120"`, silently clamped by the browser, for weeks, because the opening setting had a home in the level literal and another in the markup. A check catches drift after it exists; one declaration means it cannot.

WHAT IT COSTS, stated plainly because it is the real trade: the assertion the ticket asked for becomes VACUOUS. 'The product of the parts equals samples' relates the module's output to itself once samples IS that product, and this ledger has the rule for that — an assertion that relates a function's outputs only to its other outputs measures the arithmetic between them, never the input set. So I did not write it. What the gate asserts instead is an expectation rebuilt INSIDE THE TEST FILE from a hand-typed double loop over 10..100, compared as a set of keys. That is strictly stronger: the vacuous version passes for a wrong compose, a swapped part order and a changed key function; the independent version fails all three. The product-order convention is additionally pinned as four literal samples (indices 0, 1, 91, 8280).

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT. A level whose declared domain is genuinely NOT a full cartesian product — some combinations illegal, a ragged grid. Then `parts` really would be a lossy presentation of a smaller `samples`, both would have to be declared, and the ticket's original check becomes the right one. Nothing like that exists today and I would not build for it speculatively; the reversal is one `if` in knob() plus the assertion the ticket asked for.

beads.title: `.map(compose)` would have silently corrupted the derived domain — map hands its callback three arguments
beads.body:
The natural way to build the product's settings is `product(...).map(compose)`. `Array.prototype.map` calls its callback with (element, index, array), so a `compose` that ever took a second parameter — a per-level options object, a formatter, anything — would silently receive the tuple's INDEX as that argument. It is `['1','2'].map(parseInt)` wearing a different hat, and the failure mode is worse than the classic: it does not throw and it does not produce obviously wrong values, it produces a DOMAIN. Every downstream number in this module (the win fraction, the play order, the pinned campaign order) is computed from that domain, so the corruption would surface as a difficulty curve that quietly changed.

The default compose here takes exactly one parameter, so nothing is wrong today. It is wrong the first time somebody writes a two-parameter compose, and at that point the bug is in a caller-supplied function and the evidence is in a line nobody is looking at. Written as `.map((t) => compose(t))` with a comment saying why, because the arity of a user-supplied callback is not something the module gets to assume.

General shape worth carrying: any place this codebase passes a CALLER'S function straight to map/filter/forEach/sort is a place the caller's arity is silently part of the contract. Wrapping costs one closure and removes the coupling entirely.

beads.title: Two selftest assertions in campaign.selftest.mjs use `.map(key)` with a caller-supplied key — same hazard, deliberately left alone
beads.body:
`new Set(samples.map(key))` inside knob(), and `new Set(k.samples.map(k.key))` in the gate, both hand a level-declared function straight to map. Today every `key` in the module takes one parameter (`String`, and level3's defensive object formatter), so both are correct.

I did NOT wrap these, and the reasoning is worth recording rather than the fix: the compose case had to be wrapped because compose is the thing this ticket introduced and its arity contract was being written for the first time. `key` has an established one-parameter contract across five existing levels and a passing gate; changing two call sites to defend against a hypothetical two-parameter key would be a drive-by edit to code the ticket did not name, in a file whose gate I cannot run. If a two-parameter `key` is ever wanted, the wrap is the same one-line change and this note says where.

beads.title: plant/CLAUDE.md's campaign paragraph is now half-stale, and it is outside this ticket's scope
beads.body:
plant/CLAUDE.md says the page carries 'a control built over `knob.samples` **by index** so an off-grid setting is unrepresentable'. That is still true for five of the six levels and is now incomplete for the sixth: LEVEL_3's control is built over `knob.parts`, one index slider per component, and the index-into-samples path is not what it uses. The 'off-grid is unrepresentable' claim survives intact — a part slider is still a position, and every combination of positions composes to a declared member — but a reader following that paragraph to understand the page will not find the branch the page actually takes for level 3.

Not fixed here: the ticket's SCOPE names four files and plant/CLAUDE.md is not one of them, and a diff outside the named paths fails containment and discards the whole turn. Proposed below rather than left in a comment, because this ledger's own lesson from the placement.mjs NaN fix is that prose describing a state the tree has left is a debt and a note in a comment is not a queue.

beads.title: Neither gate was run (no Bash) — recording only what is specific to THIS unrun turn, not the standing recommendation
beads.body:
The standing 'gate unverifiable in-turn' recommendation is in this ledger well past twenty times and recent turns agreed to stop restating it. What is worth one entry is that this turn's risk profile is unusual in one respect: it CHANGED THE SHAPE OF AN EXISTING DOMAIN that six other assertion blocks depend on, rather than adding a new file or a new block. The realistic failure was not 'my new assertion is wrong', it was 'I quietly reordered LEVEL_3's samples and the pinned win fraction, campaign order and slider semantics all moved with it'.

So the mitigation was aimed there. `product()` varies the LAST list fastest, which is byte-for-byte the order the `for a of as { for b of bs }` grid it replaced produced — traced by hand and then PINNED as four literal samples in the gate (index 0 = 10x10, 1 = 10x11, 91 = 11x10, 8280 = 100x100), so a future reimplementation that changes the convention fails loudly instead of shuffling the game. The opening setting's flat index was hand-computed twice by different routes (60*91 + 35 = 5495 from the ranges, and the odometer division backwards from 5495 giving [60, 35]) and both are asserted.

Two mechanical passes that need no shell were also run over the new test text, because arithmetic is not the only way an unrun file dies: every added string was checked for a backtick nested inside a template literal and for an ASCII apostrophe inside a single-quoted string (the typographic ’ is used throughout, matching house style), since either makes the file fail to PARSE and then not one assertion runs — a failure that reads like an unrelated typo. The one regex I reused verbatim from the file's existing line 131 (`['"`]...['"`]`) was chosen precisely because that form is already proven to parse in this file.

beads.title: Is two sliders actually better than one 8281-stop index slider, or did it just become two bad controls?
beads.body:
The whole premise of this ticket is that a single slider sweeping a 91x91 product lexicographically is the worst control on the page. That is obviously true as an argument and I cannot verify it as an experience, because I have no browser and this turn rendered nothing. Two things could be wrong and only a person can see either. (1) Ninety-one stops in a 15rem column is about 0.16rem per stop on desktop and much less on a phone — it may be that the miner slider is now ALSO unusable, just less spectacularly, and that the honest control for this level is a number input or a pair of coarse buttons rather than a range. (2) The two capacities interact through a min(), so a player who drags the miner up and sees nothing change is being told something true and confusing; the read-out shows each part's value but nothing shows WHICH of the two is currently binding, and I decided not to add that because it is level knowledge the page must not have. Not decidable from here, and I shipped the reversible version: parts is a presentation layer, and going back to one slider is deleting one field from the level's knob declaration.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com on a phone, play to the third level in the order (it is 'Two machines in a row'), and try to reach a winning setting from the opening 70/45 using only the two sliders.

WATCH FOR: Whether you can land on a specific number at all with a thumb, and whether it is ever obvious which of the two machines is the one holding you back.

SO THAT: If the sliders are fine, the next control work is the binding-machine hint and it belongs in campaign.mjs's verdict sentence, not in the page. If they are not, the fix is a control-shape descriptor (a part can declare it wants steppers or a number field) and that is the game-view.js extraction proposed above, done sooner and with one more field in the spec.

beads.title: Extract the campaign panel's control rendering into a testable module — the page now has THREE control shapes and only a regex watches them
beads.body:
index.html's campaign block now branches three ways on the shape of the knob: one slider per part, a button per setting, or a single index slider. That branch is real logic — it decides what a player can touch — and the only thing checking it is index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs reading the page as TEXT. A regex can see that `max="${p.samples.length - 1}"` is present; it cannot see that the right control was chosen, that a part slider opens at the position the game is actually on, or that the read-out under a part shows the member its position selects. That is exactly the gap that justified extracting summon-view.js out of this same page (lp-250e23), and it is the same page one panel over.

THE WORK: a `plant/game-view.js` exporting pure descriptors, no DOM — `controlSpec(knob, value)` returning `{ shape: 'parts'|'buttons'|'slider', controls: [{ name, max, at, label }] }` and `settingFrom(knob, spec, positions)` returning the setting a set of positions composes to. index.html then renders descriptors and reads events, exactly as it does for the summon panel. index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs is REWRITTEN (not deleted) to assert the relocation — absence of the branch in the page, presence in the module — which is this ledger's MOVE precedent and the only thing that makes a relocation reviewable.

WHY IT IS WORTH A TURN: the new gate can drive a real Campaign through all six levels and assert, for each, that the chosen shape matches the knob, that every control's `at` is in range, that composing the reported positions gives back exactly the setting the game holds, and that the label under each control is the member at that index. None of that is reachable today. It also closes the accessibility gap I left: the part `<label>` has no `for` and the input has no `id`, so clicking a part's label does not focus its slider — trivial to fix once the id is a descriptor field, fiddly and untestable while it is a template literal inside the page.

class-a + creates-gate. The named file must not exist at promotion, must exist and pass afterwards, and `node plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs` plus the rewritten wiring gate must both still pass.
evidence: rejected: R4, and secondarily R2. INDEPENDENCE: it rewrites the campaign block in plant/index.html and REWRITES plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs — the same two files, and in the gate's case the same file wholesale, that lp-6e4b6f edits. Two seats working those concurrently is not a merge conflict this loop resolves, it is one turn silently discarding the other; the ledger already records 'Every

beads.title: plant/CLAUDE.md still says the campaign control is built over knob.samples by index — LEVEL_3's is not, since lp-056d80
beads.body:
plant/CLAUDE.md's campaign paragraph describes the page as carrying 'a control built over `knob.samples` **by index**'. Since lp-056d80 that is true of five levels and not of LEVEL_3, whose knob declares `parts` and whose control is one index slider per component composed by the knob's own `compose`. The paragraph's load-bearing claim — that an off-grid setting is unrepresentable — is still exactly true and should be kept; what is missing is the branch, and the sentence a reader most needs: a knob with `parts` DERIVES its `samples` from the product and refuses to be given both, so `parts` is a presentation of the same finite domain and nothing about the win fraction or the play order moves when a knob gains one.

SCOPE: plant/CLAUDE.md only. Two or three sentences in the existing campaign section, plus a line in the 'two things to know before changing it' note.

WHAT THE GATE CAN AND CANNOT DO, said plainly because it is the honest half of this ticket: NO GATE CAN CHECK THAT PROSE IS TRUE. The named gates certify only that the described behaviour still holds — that `parts` still derives, still refuses a double declaration, and that the page still types no bound — so a wrong sentence would pass. This is a documentation ticket graded on no-regression, and anyone promoting it should know that rather than discover it. It is proposed at P2 for that reason. The alternative — leaving the file to drift — is what this ledger has recorded twice as a debt nothing collects (summon-session.mjs's header still describing a fixed NaN bug in the present tense), and prose that describes a tree the code has left is worse than no prose because it is trusted.

[turn 68 — done] Documentation-only edit to plant/CLAUDE.md, the single file the ticket scopes. Two changes. (1) The 'It now drives the page' paragraph said the page carries 'a control built over knob.samples by index'; that named one of three branches. It now reads 'built by index over the declared domain', followed by a new paragraph naming all three shapes and the rule that picks between them (index.html:333-338 picks on the shape of the KNOB, not on which level it is): a knob with `parts` gets one slider per component, a domain of eight or fewer gets a button per setting, anything else gets the single index slider. It states that all three emit a POSITION — which is what keeps the off-grid-unrepresentable claim, the load-bearing sentence the ticket asked be kept, true of every branch rather than only the slider — names LEVEL_3 as the `parts` case composed by the knob's own `compose`, and carries the sentence the ticket said a reader most needs: a knob with `parts` DERIVES its `samples` from the product and throws if given both, so `parts` is a presentation of one finite domain and nothing about the win fraction, the play order or move()'s membership test moves when a knob gains one. (2) One sentence added to the 'two things to know' note: for a `parts` knob the bounds the page reads are each part's own domain and `samples` is the derived product, so it is still one declaration in one place. Every claim was traced to source before writing: campaign.mjs:202-262 for the derive/refuse/positions behaviour, index.html:293-362 for the three branches and 394-414 for the button branch routing through choose(Number(at)) — a position — which is the one claim the ticket's framing did not cover. HONESTY ON THE GATE, which is the ticket's own stated caveat: I have no Bash and ran neither named gate. That matters less here than usual and I checked rather than assumed — `grep CLAUDE.md plant/test/` returns nothing, and this diff touches one .md file that no module imports, so neither gate's inputs changed. No gate can check that prose is TRUE; that half rests on the source tracing above, not on a green run.

beads.title: The existing gate already claimed requirement (a) — and got it by SEARCHING, which is the exact thing this ticket says is worthless
beads.body:
Before writing anything I grepped the bounded paths for the thing the ticket says is missing, which the ledger keeps recording as the cheap defence against a stale ticket. It is half-there, and the half that is there is the wrong half.

campaign.selftest.mjs §11 is headed 'a refusal the player caused, in ONE move, on every level (e)' and it looks exactly like requirement (a) delivered. Its move comes from:

    const losing = e.knob.samples.find((s) => !grade(e, s).ok);

That is an ORACLE choosing the move. The bound it reports is 1 because a function that can see every outcome needed one guess. It proves the domain contains a losing setting — which the win fractions, all strictly between 0 and 1, already proved — and it says nothing whatsoever about how far a player walks.

So the ticket was RIGHT that requirement (a) is uncovered, and it would have been easy to read §11 and conclude otherwise. The distinction is worth stating in general form because it is not obvious from the assertion text: A BOUND MEASURED BY A SEARCH IS A PROPERTY OF THE SEARCH, NOT OF THE THING SEARCHED. §11's '1' and this file's '1' are the same numeral and different claims — one says an answer exists, the other says a stranger walks into it.

I did NOT edit §11. It is not wrong, it is answering a weaker question honestly, and rewriting a passing gate to make room for a new one is how a turn breaks something it was not asked to touch. The new file says in its header which question each answers, so the next reader does not have to work it out.

The transferable check, and it cost one grep: when a ticket says a claim is uncovered, look for the assertion that LOOKS like it and ask what chose its inputs. An assertion whose fixture was selected by the oracle it is testing is decoration however strong its wording.

beads.title: FIVE OF SIX LEVELS OPEN ALREADY WON — the thirty-second bar is currently met by re-affirming the setting you were given
beads.body:
This fell out of pinning the blind bounds and it is the most significant thing this turn found. It is a fact about the GAME, not about the gate.

    level1  opens rate 120 -> achieved 51 of demand 50   FED
    level3  opens {70,45}  -> achieved 45 of demand 44   FED
    level4  opens rate 102 -> 30.6 and 71.4 of 30 and 70 FED
    level5  opens 0.30     -> exactly 30 and 70          FED
    level6  opens 0.40     -> exactly 24 and 60          FED
    level2  opens 'cheap'  -> 30 of 50                   BROKEN

Five of the six are in a winning state before the player touches anything. The only thing standing between a stranger and a completed level is Campaign's `won = ok && moves > 0` clause — and campaign.selftest.mjs §12 already pins that 'one move, EVEN TO THE SAME SETTING, is enough to win it'.

So the measured result of requirement (b) is that a blind player finishes the entire six-level campaign in SEVEN MOVES, five of which are 'nudge the control one notch and accept the level you were already given'. On level1 it is worse than a nudge: the opening sits at the TOP of its domain (index 110 of 111), so STEP_UP clamps and the winning move is literally re-selecting rate 120.

WHY THIS IS NOT A COMPLAINT ABOUT THE LEVELS. Each level's own header argues for its opening deliberately — 'opens feasible, barely' is LEVEL_1/3/4/5's stated texture, and the intended arc is that you BREAK it and then fix it. That is a legitimate design and the refusal really is one notch away on level5 and level6. The problem is that nothing REQUIRES the breaking. The win is available on arrival and the game hands it over for any input at all.

Measured against the vision's actual bar — 'an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for' — the refusal half is in excellent shape (this gate proves 1 move reaches it on all six) and the WIN half is hollow. Requirement (a) is genuinely satisfied; requirement (b) is satisfied on a technicality.

The fix is one clause and it is proposed below: require the winning value to DIFFER from knob.start, not merely that a move happened. It is satisfiable on every level today (119, {70,46}, 103, 0.31, 0.41, golden all win and all differ from the opening) except level1, where the opening is at the ceiling — and exposing that is the point rather than an obstacle.

beads.title: level3's 91x91 grid flattened into one index is NON-MONOTONE — the down-walk loses at move 2 and WINS AGAIN at move 36
beads.body:
level3's knob is `grid(intRange(10,100), intRange(10,100), (miner, smelter) => ({miner, smelter}))` — 8281 settings in one array, index = (miner-10)*91 + (smelter-10). The page builds its control over that array BY INDEX (index-campaign-wiring pins the slider maximum as samples.length - 1). So level3 ships one slider that moves two numbers.

Walking it down from the opening {70,45}:

    move  1  index 5494  {70,44}  min 44 >= 44   FED
    move  2  index 5493  {70,43}  min 43 <  44   REFUSED
    moves 3-35            {70,42} down to {70,10}  all REFUSED
    move 36  index 5459  {69,100} min 69 >= 44   FED AGAIN

5459 = 91*59 + 90, so it is miner 69, smelter 100 — the walk ran the smelter to its floor and WRAPPED into the previous miner row, where the smelter jumps from 10 back to 100. Every 91 notches it does this again.

TWO CONSEQUENCES, and the second is the one that matters.

1. FOR THE GATE: 'find the first refusal, then assume it stays refused' is false on this level, so the scan has to keep scanning. The re-entry at move 36 is asserted explicitly, which is what stops a later turn 'simplifying' the scan into a monotone one and having it still pass.

2. FOR THE PLAYER, and this is a real playability defect rather than a test detail: dragging level3's slider one notch to the left, thirty-five times, makes the factory worse and worse, and then on the thirty-sixth notch it abruptly works again — because a number the player cannot see jumped from 10 to 100. A control whose effect is discontinuous at invisible boundaries is not a puzzle, it is a lever with a trick in it. The two other multi-value ideas in this repo do not have this problem because they have one dimension.

Proposed below as its own bead: order level3's samples so the index is monotone in the outcome. The win FRACTION is a property of the set and does not change, so ORDER and the campaign order are untouched; what changes is that the slider becomes readable. It will require recomputing this file's level3 literals, which is correct — reshaping a control is a design decision and should cost a conversation with a test.

beads.title: Blindness is enforced by stringifying the policy and by pre-computing the plan, rather than by asserting it in prose
beads.body:
The ticket's central risk is stated plainly: 'a policy that SEARCHES the domain for a losing setting proves only that the domain contains one, which is already known.' A header paragraph promising the policies are blind is worth nothing — it is exactly the kind of claim that drifts away from the code, and this ledger already records the general shape (the gap is between the docstring and the assertions).

So blindness is checked two ways, both mechanical:

  1. §2 calls policy.toString() and fails on /\b(grade|verdict|feasible|deficits|achieved|margin|won|wins|ok)\b/. It also asserts policy.length <= 3, so a policy cannot have quietly been handed the Campaign.
  2. §3 computes each policy's first eight choices BEFORE any Campaign exists, plays them, recomputes, and asserts the plan is byte-identical. A plan that changed is a plan that was watching.

Neither is sufficient alone: (1) catches a policy that peeks, (2) catches a pure policy fed a sequence somebody else chose by grading.

WHAT I REJECTED. Asserting blindness by comparing the blind bound against the searched bound ("they differ, therefore no search") — that fails on the four levels where the two coincide at 1, so it would silently stop checking on exactly the levels where it is easiest to cheat.

THE CONTROL IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART. §2 is four NEGATIVE assertions over three short strings, and a negative passes for a broken matcher exactly as loudly as for clean code — a stray character in the alternation and all four print ticks while checking nothing. So a deliberately-cheating policy (CHEATING, defined and never driven) is stringified and the regex MUST catch it, and a second assertion checks it caught the word 'grade' specifically rather than something incidental.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: if a future policy legitimately needs a word on that list, widen the list at the same time as adding an assertion that the new policy's plan is still fixed in advance — do not delete the check, which is the one move that makes it stop meaning anything while still printing a tick.

beads.title: The wrong-direction CONTROL is split in two and the 5/1 split is pinned, because neither half can cover all six levels
beads.body:
The ticket asks for one control: 'a policy that moves one step in the WRONG direction must NOT find a win within the same bound, or the bound is not measuring anything.' Building it exposed that no single control covers the game, and the reason is the finding above — five levels open fed, one opens broken.

  §6, wrong direction for a REFUSAL: STEP_UP must find no refusal within the STEP_DOWN bound. Bites on level1, level3, level4, level5, level6. CANNOT bite on level2: level2 opens broken, so 'good' (one step up) also loses and neither direction is the wrong one.

  §7, wrong direction for a WIN: on level2, STEP_UP wins at move 2 and STEP_DOWN never wins in 200 moves (it is clamped on 'cheap'). CANNOT bite on the other five: they open fed, so one move in ANY direction wins and direction is unmeasurable.

The two are exact mirrors and between them every level is covered by at least one.

THE CHOICE I MADE, and it is the one worth recording: I pinned the exception as a TABLE (UP_AVOIDS_REFUSAL, one boolean per level) and asserted that exactly five of six are true, rather than skipping level2 or weakening §6 to 'at least one level avoids a refusal'. A skipped case is indistinguishable from a passing one from outside, and a control that has been quietly disarmed to bite on nothing still prints a full row of ticks. The table also fails if a level is ever retuned across the fed/broken line, which is a design change that should be noticed.

REJECTED: choosing the 'right' direction per level by grading both and taking whichever found the answer first. That is a search over a two-element set, and it would have made the direction claim circular — the wrong direction would be wrong by definition rather than by measurement.

beads.title: Two specific unrun-gate risks I engineered out, and the one I could not
beads.body:
No Bash this turn, so the file was never executed. The standing recommendation is in this ledger well past twenty times and recent turns agreed to stop restating it; I am not restating it. What is worth recording is what is SPECIFIC to this file, because its risk profile is neither pure arithmetic nor pure prose.

ENGINEERED OUT — 1. THE BLINDNESS REGEX FIRING ON A POLICY. §2 fails the gate if /\b(...|ok|won|margin|...)\b/ matches a policy's own source. A policy written with a parameter named `ok`, or a helper called `won`, would fail a gate about playthroughs for a reason that has nothing to do with playthroughs — a checker that fails correct work. So every policy was written to use only `samples`, `i0`, `k` and `Math`, and I traced each source string character by character against the alternation. `(samples, i0, k) => samples[Math.max(0, i0 - k)]` contains no listed word; nor does the clamped-up form; nor `(samples) => samples[0]`.

ENGINEERED OUT — 2. A SCAN THAT 'REACHES' A BOUND WITHOUT MOVING. `scan()` aborts on a refused move AND asserts `r.moves === k` on every step. Without the second check, a clamped policy whose value the game declined would sit still while the loop counted, and the bound would be reported as satisfied by a walk that never walked. This mattered concretely: two levels open at an end of their domain (level1 at the top, level2 at the bottom), so clamped repeats are the normal case here rather than an edge, and they are only legitimate because Campaign accepts a move to the same setting — which campaign.selftest.mjs §12 pins independently.

NOT CLOSED, and it is the only assertion I would look at first if the gate goes red: level3's re-entry at move 36. Every other literal is cross-checked against a boundary campaign.selftest.mjs already pins as passing (rate 50, 44x44, rate 100, 0.30, 0.40, golden). The 36 rests on my own index arithmetic alone — 5495 - 36 = 5459 = 91*59 + 90 -> {miner 69, smelter 100}, min 69 >= demand 44 — plus the claim that moves 3..35 stay in the miner-70 row (indices 5460..5492, smelter 10..42, all below 44). I believe it, and it is one derivation rather than a measurement.

The general half: for a gate built on INDEX arithmetic over a flattened domain, the risk is neither a wrong expected number nor a lexical slip — it is an off-by-one in the flattening, which produces a confidently wrong literal that reads perfectly. The defence available without a shell is to derive the same index twice by different routes (I used both (miner-10)*91+(smelter-10) forwards and 91*q+r backwards), and to pin `samples.length` and the opening index FIRST so a domain change fails with a message naming it rather than fifty move-count assertions later.

beads.title: Is a game a blind player finishes in seven moves too easy — or is the arc (break it, then fix it) doing the work a win state cannot?
beads.body:
This is the one question this turn could not settle by writing a check, and I want to be precise about why. The MEASUREMENTS are all now executable and pinned: a stranger reaches a refusal in one move on every level; five of six levels open in a winning state; a blind up-stepping player completes the whole campaign in seven moves, five of them nudges that accept a level already won.

What no gate can decide is whether that is bad. Two readings are both coherent. (1) A game you beat without understanding it is not a puzzle, and the win should require an actual change — that is the proposal I filed at P1. (2) The levels are DESIGNED to open fed and barely so ('opens feasible, barely' is the stated texture of four of them); the intended experience is that you break it, see the refusal, and put it back, and a win state that fires when you restore it is exactly right. Under reading (2) the seven-move completion is an artefact of a blind policy that never explores, not a description of what a person does.

I shipped the measurement rather than the opinion, and filed the fix as a proposal rather than doing it, because it changes a contract three gates assert and it is reversible only by a conversation.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com cold, play the campaign through once without reading anything, and time it. Do not try to be a good player.

WATCH FOR: Whether you ever deliberately BREAK a level to see what happens, or only push the control until the line turns green — and whether finishing a level felt like anything.

SO THAT: If you broke levels unprompted, the arc is doing the work and my P1 proposal should be dropped: the win state is fine and the next ticket is about making the refusal more legible. If you only pushed toward green and finishing felt like nothing, promote the proposal — require the winning setting to differ from the opening — and follow it with a bead moving level1's opening off the ceiling of its own domain, which is where that change bites first.

beads.title: A level must be WON by changing something: make `won` require a value different from the opening setting
beads.body:
Five of the six levels open in a winning state (level1 51/50, level3 45/44, level4 30.6 and 71.4 of 30 and 70, level5 exactly 30/70, level6 exactly 24/60); only level2 opens broken. The only thing that stops a stranger completing them by arriving is Campaign's `won = ok && moves > 0`, and campaign.selftest.mjs §12 pins that a move TO THE SAME SETTING satisfies it. plant/test/playthrough.selftest.mjs now measures the consequence: a blind player finishes the entire campaign in 7 moves, and on level1 the winning move is literally re-selecting the rate it opened on, because the opening sits at the top of the domain and the up-policy clamps.

The vision's bar is 'an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for'. The refusal half is in good shape — that gate proves one move reaches a refusal on all six levels. The win half is satisfied on a technicality.

THE CHANGE, and it is one clause: in campaign.mjs, `won` becomes `ok && moves > 0 && knob.key(value) !== knob.key(knob.start)` — the player must have moved to a setting that is not the one they were given. Keep `moves > 0` as well; a level entered, changed, and changed back is not a win either, and dropping the move count would make that pass.

WHY IT IS SATISFIABLE TODAY, checked before proposing: every level has a winning setting different from its opening — level1 rate 119, level3 {70,46}, level4 103, level5 0.31, level6 0.41, level2 golden. So no level becomes unwinnable.

WHAT IT WILL BREAK, said up front so it is not a surprise. (1) campaign.selftest.mjs §12 asserts 'one move — even to the same setting — is enough to win it'; that assertion is the OLD contract and must be inverted, with a new one proving a changed setting does win. (2) playthrough.selftest.mjs's UP_TO_WIN table changes: level1's STEP_UP clamps at the ceiling and would no longer win at all, which is the real finding here rather than an obstacle — either level1's opening moves off the top of its domain, or its win policy has to be STEP_DOWN. Whichever is chosen, say which in the body of the change. (3) index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs may assert the next button appears on `won`; the field is unchanged, only its rule.

GATE: `node plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs` and `node plant/test/playthrough.selftest.mjs`, both of which exist and pass today. This is class-a rather than creates-gate: no new file is needed, and the work is precisely that both existing gates must be brought to the new contract and still pass. Do NOT weaken an assertion to make them pass — §12's same-setting case must be REPLACED by its opposite, not deleted.

Deliberately NOT proposed as part of this: changing any level's opening numbers. Each level header argues for its own opening and that is a separate design conversation.

[turn 67 — done] Implemented the one-clause change and brought both gates to the new contract. campaign.mjs's verdict() now returns `won: v.ok && this.moves > 0 && knob.key(value) !== knob.key(knob.start)` — compared through the knob's own key because level3's setting is an object and copy() hands back a fresh one on every move, so identity would report 'changed' for the opening. campaign.selftest.mjs §12 has its old assertion INVERTED rather than deleted (a same-setting move is still accepted, still counts as a move, still leaves the factory fed, and is no longer a win), paired with the positive it needs to be non-vacuous (rate 119 wins), plus a move-back case (won un-sets, because it is the CURRENT setting that must differ) and a new per-level check that a winning setting exists which is NOT the opening one — the clause would make a level whose only winner is its opening a dead end, and 'the win fractions are comfortably above 1/n' is an argument, not a check. playthrough.selftest.mjs needed the larger edit: STEP_UP can no longer win level1 at all, because level1 opens at the TOP of its domain so every clamped move re-selects rate 120. UP_TO_WIN became WIN_POLICY + WIN_POLICY_NAME + MOVES_TO_WIN, with level1 on STEP_DOWN (rate 119 — scale = min(capacity 51, rate), so the depot's 50 is met down to rate 50) and the other five unchanged on STEP_UP; §7 and §8 read the policy per level, every win additionally asserts the final setting differs from the opening, and a new level1 CONTROL asserts STEP_UP is ACCEPTED for all 200 scan moves, FED the whole way, and never won — which is the sharpest statement of the new rule anywhere in the suite and goes red if the clause is dropped. The campaign total is unchanged at 7 blind moves; what changed is that all seven are now real changes. I also corrected plant/CLAUDE.md's `won is ok && moves > 0` sentence. NOT RUN: this turn had Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep and no Bash, so neither gate was executed — every literal was hand-traced (see the learnings for the two I would look at first). One consequence I did NOT fix and am proposing instead: on a fed-but-unchanged level the page now shows the ✓ 'Everything is fed' sentence with the next button hidden and no explanation, which reads as a broken button.

beads.title: level3's 8281-setting grid is flattened so its slider wraps: order the samples monotonically in outcome
beads.body:
level3's knob is `grid(intRange(10,100), intRange(10,100), (miner, smelter) => ({miner, smelter}))`, and the page builds its control over that array BY INDEX (index-campaign-wiring pins the slider maximum as samples.length - 1). So one slider moves two numbers, and the flattening is row-major in miner: index = (miner-10)*91 + (smelter-10).

Measured and now pinned in plant/test/playthrough.selftest.mjs §5: walking the control down from the opening {70,45} refuses at move 2 ({70,43}), stays refused for thirty-three more notches as the smelter runs to its floor, and then at move 36 SUCCEEDS AGAIN — index 5459 is {miner 69, smelter 100}, because the walk wrapped into the previous miner row and the smelter jumped from 10 back to 100. It does this every 91 notches.

For a player this is a lever with a trick in it: drag left, the factory gets worse and worse, then abruptly works, because a number they cannot see jumped. A control whose effect is discontinuous at invisible boundaries is not a puzzle.

THE CHANGE: order level3's samples so the index is monotone in the outcome — sort by min(miner, smelter) ascending, ties by miner then smelter, so dragging right never makes the factory worse. The winning region becomes a contiguous suffix of the domain.

WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE, and it is why this is cheap: winFraction is a count over a SET and is order-independent, so WIN_FRACTION.level3 stays 3249/8281, ORDER stays level1, level4, level3, level2, level5, level6, and no other level is touched. campaign.selftest.mjs §5's four boundary assertions are all `grade(e, {miner, smelter})` calls that name their setting explicitly rather than by index, so they are unaffected too.

WHAT MUST CHANGE WITH IT: playthrough.selftest.mjs's OPENING.level3 (5495) and DOWN_TO_REFUSAL.level3 (2) are index claims and will move; and its §5 assertion that the down-walk WINS AGAIN at move 36 must be REPLACED by its opposite — that the walk is monotone, i.e. once refused it stays refused for the rest of the domain. That inversion is the whole point of the ticket and is the assertion that proves the fix landed. Deleting it instead of inverting it is the one move that would make this change unverifiable.

GATE: `node plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs` and `node plant/test/playthrough.selftest.mjs`, both existing and passing today. class-a, no new file.

AN ALTERNATIVE I CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: giving level3 two controls. That needs a second knob shape in campaign.mjs and a second control in the page, which is a much larger change touching the module contract every level shares — and it does not obviously beat one honest slider. If a later turn wants it, it is a separate bead and this one does not block it.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED ON A STALE PREMISE, and the prescribed change would break a live control rather than fix one. Two independent failures. (1) THE PREMISE IS NO LONGER TRUE. The ticket says level3's knob is `grid(intRange(10,100), intRange(10,100), ...)` and that the page builds one index slider over it. Since lp-056d80 the knob declares `parts` (campaign.mjs:318-321) and index.html:337-342 sets `slider.hid

beads.title: The new rule requires a CHANGE, not a FIX — and on level1 that is 71 different settings producing an identical verdict
beads.body:
Worth stating plainly because the ticket's framing invites the stronger reading, and the stronger reading is not what shipped.

`won` now requires the current setting to differ from `knob.start`. It does NOT require the player to have broken anything, to have seen a refusal, or to have improved anything. On level1 the winning move is any of the 71 rates from 50 to 120 — and for every rate at or above 51 the verdict is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the opening's, because scale = min(capacity 51, rate) and the capacity is what binds. So the player wins by dragging the slider one notch and producing exactly the same factory.

That is still strictly better than what it replaced. The old rule was satisfiable by a move to the setting you were already on — on level1, literally re-selecting the value the control opened at, because the opening sits at the ceiling and the up-policy clamps. A stranger could complete six levels without the control ever moving. Now the control has to move.

But measured against the vision's actual bar — 'an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for' — this closes the WIN half only up to 'acted on'. The 'got refused for' half is still unrequired, and the refusal is genuinely one move away on every level (playthrough §4 proves YANK_FLOOR is refused in 1 on all six), so it is available and not demanded.

THE NEXT RUNG, and it is a design decision rather than a bug: track whether the player has seen `ok === false` on this level, and require it for the win. That is a real state-machine change (one boolean in `_enter`, one line in `move`), it is gateable with the existing two files, and it is the version that matches the vision sentence word for word. It is also the version that can frustrate — a player who solves a level in one correct move is then told to go break it first — which is exactly the taste question a gate cannot settle. Proposed below and filed as an ask, rather than done here, because the ticket named one clause and this is a second one with a real cost attached.

beads.title: level5 and level6 open on the FIRST winning setting in their own domain — so an ascending sweep for a win now has to step over the opening
beads.body:
Both levels ship at the LOW EDGE of their winning window by deliberate design (level5.mjs: shareA in [0.30, 0.50], shipped 0.30; level6.mjs: shareA in [0.4, 0.5], shipped 0.4 — 'the same opens feasible, barely texture every prior level ships with'). Their knobs sweep 0.05..0.95 ascending. So the FIRST member of `samples` that feeds is exactly `knob.start`.

That matters for campaign.selftest.mjs §10, which finds a win by walking the whole domain and breaking on `verdict().won`. Under the old rule it broke at 0.30 and 0.40; under the new one those are not wins, and it carries on to 0.31 and 0.41 (both inside the window) and breaks there. `used` goes from 26 to 27 and from 36 to 37, and the assertion is `used <= samples.length`, so it still passes.

It passes BECAUSE §10 was written as a sweep of the whole domain rather than as 'find the first setting that feeds'. Had it been written the tidier way — break on `verdict().ok` — this change would have made it fail on two levels, and the failure would have read as 'level5 has no winning setting', which is false and is a full turn of misdiagnosis. I left the loop alone and added a comment at it saying why it must stay a sweep.

The general shape: a rule that adds a condition to a search's success predicate silently changes WHERE the search stops, and any assertion downstream that quietly depended on the old stopping point is a landmine. The defence is not a stronger assertion, it is checking every existing search whose predicate you just narrowed.

beads.title: This change makes the page's ✓ sentence and its next button disagree, and nothing on the page explains why
beads.body:
index.html line 386 is `next.hidden = !(v.won && !st.finished)`. The sentence beside it comes from campaign.mjs's `sentence(v)`, which branches on `v.ok` — the FACTORY's verdict — and says '✓ Everything is fed, with N% to spare'.

Those two now disagree in a state a player reaches by doing nothing: five of the six levels open fed, so the page shows a green tick saying everything works, and no way to continue, and no sentence anywhere saying 'you have not changed anything yet'. Before this change the disagreement was unreachable in practice (any move at all won). It is now the DEFAULT opening state of five levels out of six.

That is a worse first impression than the bug this ticket fixed, and it is on the one screen a stranger meets.

I did not fix it here and the reason is not timidity: `sentence()` deliberately speaks about the factory, and campaign.mjs's own header keeps `move().accepted` and `verdict().ok` apart as 'two senses of ok, kept apart on purpose because a renderer will meet both'. Folding the game's win state into the factory's sentence would collapse exactly the distinction that file was careful about. The right fix is in the renderer — the page already has `v.won` and can say 'the factory works — now change something and see what breaks' — and it belongs with index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs, which is neither of this ticket's gates. Proposed below at P1, because it changes what a visitor sees, which the vision says is the only thing that outranks everything else.

beads.title: level1's blind WIN policy became STEP_DOWN; level1's opening was left where it is
beads.body:
The ticket named the fork and asked whoever took it to say which way they went: 'either level1's opening moves off the top of its domain, or its win policy has to be STEP_DOWN'.

I took STEP_DOWN, for three reasons in descending order of weight.

1. The ticket's own closing paragraph says changing a level's opening numbers is deliberately NOT part of this work, because each level header argues for its own opening. LEVEL_1's is argued: the source rate is far above anything the smelter can consume so that CAPACITY is what binds, which is the lesson of the level. Moving the opening off the ceiling to make a test policy work is a design change made for a test's convenience.

2. Moving the opening would have invalidated four hand-derived literals in playthrough.selftest.mjs (OPENING.level1, DOWN_TO_REFUSAL.level1 = 71, the tightness case at move 70, and §1's 'level1 opens at the TOP of its domain, so STEP_UP clamps'), all of which are currently correct and none of which I can re-derive by running anything. Changing the policy invalidates one number and it stays 1.

3. It is the more informative outcome. A per-level policy table forces the file to SAY that level1 is the odd one out and why, and it made room for the level1 CONTROL — STEP_UP accepted 200 times, fed throughout, never won — which is now the clearest assertion of the new contract in the suite. A moved opening would have hidden the whole phenomenon.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: if level1's opening ever moves off the ceiling for a genuine design reason, WIN_POLICY.level1 should go back to STEP_UP and the level1 CONTROL block should be deleted rather than repaired — it is a statement about a clamped opening, and with the opening moved it would be asserting nothing.

beads.title: `moves > 0` was kept although it is now redundant — and the comment says so rather than pretending otherwise
beads.body:
The ticket asked for `won = ok && moves > 0 && value !== start` and justified keeping the move count with 'a level entered, changed, and changed back is not a win either, and dropping the move count would make that pass'.

That justification is wrong, and I kept the clause anyway. `this.value` only ever changes through an accepted `move()`, so a value differing from `start` already implies `moves > 0`; and the changed-back case is refused by the value comparison alone, since after changing back the CURRENT value IS the opening. The move count adds nothing to either case.

I kept it because it is free, because it states the intent independently of how `value` came to be set, and because a future `_enter()` that opened somewhere other than `knob.start` would need it. What I did NOT do is repeat the ticket's reasoning in the source: campaign.mjs's docstring says in as many words that the clause is redundant today and why it is there anyway.

A redundant clause with a false justification attached is worse than no clause: the next person to read it believes it is load-bearing and either preserves it for the wrong reason or removes the wrong one of the two. Saying 'this is redundant and here is why it stays' costs two lines and is the only version that survives someone auditing it.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: nothing about correctness. If someone wants the minimal expression, dropping `moves > 0` is safe TODAY and the docstring says which invariant makes it safe.

beads.title: 'No level became unwinnable' is checked in the gate, not thrown at import
beads.body:
The new clause introduces a failure mode the old one could not have: a level whose ONLY winning setting is its own opening becomes impossible to complete, and because `next()` does not require a win the player is not hard-stuck — but the campaign has a level nobody can beat and nothing says so.

campaign.mjs already throws at module load for the analogous contradiction (`start` not in the declared domain), with the reasoning 'the cheapest place to find out is import time', so the precedent pointed at a throw.

I put it in campaign.selftest.mjs §12 instead. A throw at import fails EVERY gate that imports campaign.mjs — index-campaign-wiring, playthrough, campaign — and takes the live page with it, for what is a design mistake rather than a corruption. And I could not run anything this turn: if my reading of any level's winning window were wrong, a throw would have converted one wrong literal into a whole-suite outage discovered downstream. deploy-plant runs the suite before publishing, so the gate catches it before anything ships, which is the property that actually matters here.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: if the check is ever wanted at import, it is three lines inside the existing win-fraction sweep (count a win at a key differing from start) and the gate assertion should then be kept as the thing that proves the throw fires.

beads.title: Neither gate was run — the two assertions I would look at first, and why the rest is safer than usual
beads.body:
No Bash this turn. The standing recommendation is in this ledger well past twenty times and recent turns agreed to stop restating it; I am not restating it. What is worth recording is which of MY assertions are load-bearing on arithmetic I could not execute, since most of this turn's numbers were inherited rather than derived.

SAFER THAN USUAL, and this is the unusual part: every move-count literal in playthrough.selftest.mjs except one was ALREADY PASSING before this turn and is untouched. DOMAIN, OPENING, OPENS_FED, DOWN_TO_REFUSAL, UP_AVOIDS_REFUSAL, the 71-notch bound, the level3 re-entry at move 36 — none of them is conditioned on `won` (a refusal never was), so §1, §4, §5 and §6 are byte-equivalent in behaviour to the version that passes today. The change is confined to the win half.

THE TWO I WOULD LOOK AT FIRST:

1. MOVES_TO_WIN.level1 === 1 under STEP_DOWN. This is the only genuinely new number. It rests on scale = min(capacity 51, rate): at rate 119 the smelter is capacity-bound at 51 against a demand of 50, exactly as at the opening rate of 120. Cross-check that makes me confident: §5 already pins, and passes today, that STEP_DOWN from 120 does not reach a refusal until move 71 (rate 49), and that at move 70 (rate 50) the level is still FED. Move 1 being fed is implied by an assertion the file already makes.

2. The five per-level 'the winning setting is NOT the opening one' assertions in §7. Each needs the policy's first winning setting to differ from `start`, which is trivially true for a strictly-stepping policy — EXCEPT where it clamps, which is precisely level1 (handled by the policy swap) and level2 (which steps up off its floor and so does move). I traced level3 by index (5495 -> 5496 = 91*60 + 36 -> miner 70, smelter 46, min 46 >= demand 44) rather than trusting the shape.

LEXICAL PASS, run because a parse error kills every assertion and reads like an unrelated typo: no added string contains a backtick nested inside a template literal, and no added single-quoted string contains an ASCII apostrophe (the em dash and the typographic forms used in prose are safe). New block scopes in §7 and §8 were checked for brace balance by re-reading the region rather than by eye at write time — `down` and `won` are declared in two sibling blocks in §7 and do not collide.

beads.title: Is 'you must change something' enough, or must a level be BROKEN before it can be won?
beads.body:
lp-000596 made a win require a setting different from the one the player was handed. It deliberately did not require the player to have caused a failure first, because that is a second clause with a real cost and the vision's bar mentions both halves ('an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for').

What I cannot settle from here is how the weaker rule FEELS. It is measurably better than what it replaced — the control now has to move — but on level1 any of 71 settings wins and most produce a factory identical to the opening, so the required action can be arbitrary. The stronger rule (proposed as a follow-up) makes the game teach itself, and can also feel like being made to jump through a hoop after you have already understood the puzzle. Both are one clause; neither is decidable by a gate, because both pass every check the suite can express.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, play the first two levels without reading anything, and stop the moment you feel you have finished a level.

WATCH FOR: Whether you MOVE the control before pressing next, or hunt for a next button that is not there yet — and whether, on a level that opens already working, you ever discover what makes it fail.

SO THAT: If you moved the control naturally and still learned what breaks it, the current rule is enough and the follow-up should be dropped. If you sat on a green tick looking for a next button, the renderer proposal is the urgent one. If you finished both levels without ever seeing a failure, promote the stronger rule — that is the vision's bar going unmet with every gate passing.

beads.title: The page must SAY why the next button is missing — a fed level with the button hidden reads as broken
beads.body:
Consequence of lp-000596, and it lands on the one screen a stranger meets. index.html renders `next.hidden = !(v.won && !st.finished)` beside a sentence built from `v.ok`. Five of the six levels open ALREADY FED, so the opening state of most of the game is now: a green tick reading '✓ Everything is fed, with N% to spare', and no next button, and nothing anywhere saying why. Before lp-000596 that state was unreachable in practice because any move at all won; it is now the default. A player who has been told they succeeded and given no way forward concludes the page is broken, not that they have not played yet. That is a worse first impression than the hole lp-000596 closed. THE CHANGE: when `v.ok && !v.won && st.moves >= 0`, the page shows a line telling the player the factory works and that they have not changed anything yet — something like 'the factory already works; move the control and find out what breaks it'. The page must NOT compute that condition itself: `v.won` and `v.ok` both already come back from `verdict()`, so the branch is `v.ok && !v.won`, two fields the controller already returns. No new decision in an event handler. DELIBERATELY NOT in campaign.mjs's `sentence()`: that function speaks about the FACTORY, and campaign.mjs's header keeps `move().accepted` and `verdict().ok` apart on purpose ('two senses of ok, kept apart because a renderer will meet both'). Folding the game's win state into the factory's sentence collapses exactly the distinction that file is careful about. This is renderer work. BOUNDED PATHS: plant/index.html, plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs. WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK, and a weaker check will not do. index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs already drives a real Campaign, so the assertion is behavioural rather than textual: build a Campaign, assert at zero moves that `v.ok === true && v.won === false` on ORDER[0] (the state in question is reachable), and assert the page's block contains a branch on `!v.won` alongside the `hidden` rule — a regex for the sentence's words alone would pass for a hardcoded string that never renders. It must ALSO assert the page does not compute the condition from `moves` or from a level id, which is the drift this whole wiring gate exists to prevent. P1 and it is vision item 1 — it changes what a visitor sees, and the vision says that outranks everything. [turn 70 — done] Added the missing sentence and the check that it is driven by the controller rather than by the page. plant/index.html gains one mount point (

), one CSS rule that deliberately sets no `display` so the UA's [hidden] rule is unopposed, and five lines in paint(): `const untouched = v.ok && !v.won`, hide/show from it, and the sentence 'The factory already works. Move the control and find out what breaks it.' The condition is exactly the two fields verdict() already returns — no move count, no level id, no second oracle call — and the words stay out of campaign.mjs's sentence(), which speaks about the factory, per the ticket. plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs gains section (9b) with three legs, each covering a hole in the other two: (i) the state is REACHABLE, driven on a real Campaign — ORDER[0] opens ok:true/won:false — plus a CONTROL that one accepted move to a winning setting leaves the state while `ok` stays true (without that control every other assertion is satisfied by a page that shows the line whenever the factory works); (ii) the page's condition is CAPTURED from the block and read, asserted to be exactly `v.ok && !v.won` and to name no level id — a substring search for '!v.won' would pass for a page that also consulted st.moves, and st.moves is two lines below in the progress line, so 'the block never mentions moves' could not have been the check; (iii) the mount point exists, ships hidden, is driven by that one condition, and its sentence is checked against campaign.mjs's own BANNED and asserted to CLEAR rather than linger. HONESTLY: I had no Bash, so neither the gate nor the suite was executed and the page was never rendered in a browser. Every regex was hand-traced character by character against the exact bytes written (including the greedy [^;]+ capture stopping at the first semicolon, and `untouched\s*\?` skipping the two earlier occurrences of the identifier that are not followed by '?'), and the added block was checked against every pre-existing assertion in the same gate — sections (3),(4),(5),(6),(7) — for a forbidden literal, a level id or a banned call. The added script text contains no digits at all, which is what makes the section-(5) bound check safe. The four other gates that read index.html as text were checked too and none of them constrains what I added.

beads.title: A level should be won by FIXING it, not merely by changing it: require the player to have seen a refusal
beads.body:
lp-000596 closed half of the vision's bar. The bar is 'an intention they formed, acted on, AND GOT REFUSED FOR'. `won` now requires a setting that differs from the opening — the 'acted on' half — and requires nothing about the refusal.

The gap is measurable rather than rhetorical. On level1 every one of the 71 rates from 50 to 120 wins, and for every rate at or above 51 the verdict is byte-identical to the opening's, because scale = min(capacity 51, rate) and the capacity binds. So the player wins by nudging the slider and producing exactly the same factory. Five of the six levels open fed, so on five of six the winning move can be an arbitrary one.

THE CHANGE, and it is small: Campaign tracks whether `verdict().ok === false` has been true on the CURRENT level since it was entered. One field cleared in `_enter()`, set in `move()` (or computed in `verdict()` and latched), and added to the `won` conjunction. `won` becomes: the factory works, the setting is not the one you were given, and you have seen it fail at least once here.

WHY IT IS SATISFIABLE ON EVERY LEVEL TODAY, checked before proposing: plant/test/playthrough.selftest.mjs §4 already proves, and passes, that YANK_FLOOR — dragging the control to the bottom of its own range — is REFUSED in exactly one move on all six levels. So 'break it, then fix it' is at most two moves everywhere, and the blind campaign bound goes from 7 to at most 13.

WHAT IT WILL BREAK, said up front. (1) playthrough.selftest.mjs's MOVES_TO_WIN table: every entry grows by the moves needed to see a refusal first, and the blind policies must be composed (yank to the floor, then step to a winner) rather than being a single monotone walk — that is the real work of this ticket and it is where its risk is. (2) MOVES_TO_FINISH_THE_GAME changes and must be recomputed, not adjusted until green. (3) campaign.selftest.mjs §12's 'a move to a DIFFERENT winning setting IS a win' becomes false as written and must gain a preceding refusal, with the no-refusal case inverted into a new assertion — the same replace-do-not-delete discipline lp-000596 used.

THE HONEST RISK, and it is why this is proposed rather than done: it can frustrate. A player who reads the level correctly and fixes it in one move is told to go break it first, which is a worse feeling than the problem it solves. That is a taste judgement no gate can settle and an ask has been filed alongside this. If it turns out badly it is one clause to remove, which is the cheap-to-reverse property the vision asks for when nobody is available to decide.

BOUNDED PATHS: plant/campaign.mjs, plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs, plant/test/playthrough.selftest.mjs.
evidence: rejected: R3 and R4, and the honest risk the ticket names is worse than it costs it. R3/BOUNDED PATHS: it changes what `won` MEANS, and plant/index.html:386 reads v.won to decide whether the next button exists — but plant/index.html is not in its bounded paths. So the ticket ships a live behaviour change to a public page it is forbidden to touch: after it, a player who moves straight to a winning setting is

beads.title: The drift was two branches wide, not one — the ticket named LEVEL_3 and missed LEVEL_2's button control, which is ALSO not the index slider
beads.body:
lp-b27cc4 was written from the recorded finding that plant/CLAUDE.md's 'a control built over knob.samples by index' stopped covering LEVEL_3 when lp-056d80 gave it `parts`. That is right, and reading index.html rather than trusting the ticket showed the paragraph was short by TWO branches, not one.

`buildControl()` (index.html:328-362) picks between three shapes, and its own comment says it picks on the SHAPE OF THE KNOB rather than on which level it is:

    multi     = !!k.parts                              -> one slider per component  (LEVEL_3)
    discrete  = !multi && k.samples.length <= 8        -> one button per setting    (LEVEL_2, 3 options)
    otherwise -> the single index slider                                            (LEVELS 1, 4, 5, 6)

So 'the index slider' describes four of six levels, not five.

THE PART WORTH KEEPING is that the paragraph's LOAD-BEARING claim survived all three anyway, and it survived for a reason that is invisible from the button markup. A button renders as `data-i="${j}"` and the click handler does `choose(Number(at))`, where `choose(at)` is `game.move(knobOf().samples[at])` — so a button is a position into `samples` exactly as a slider stop is. The part sliders likewise emit positions and are composed by the knob's own `compose`. Off-grid is unrepresentable on every branch.

That is why the fix was to widen the sentence ('built by index over the declared domain') and add the branches underneath, rather than to qualify the claim. A reader who had assumed 'by index' meant 'there is a slider' would have been wrong about the mechanism while right about the guarantee — and the guarantee is the thing the paragraph exists to state.

THE TRANSFERABLE HALF, and this ledger has the shape from other directions: a ticket authored from a finding inherits the finding's SAMPLE, not its census. The finding was about LEVEL_3 because LEVEL_3 was the level that changed; nobody had gone back and enumerated the branches. Reading the dispatching function once, rather than the one level the ticket named, cost one Read and changed the correction from partial to complete.

beads.title: The same paragraph carried a SECOND stale sentence, in the future tense, describing work that had already landed
beads.body:
The 'two things to know before changing it' note said: 'the follow-up that wires the page must take its control bounds *from here* instead of keeping a second copy.'

That follow-up is lp-6c88fb, and it landed — the same file says so eight lines further down ('It now drives the page (lp-6c88fb)'). So one paragraph told a reader the wiring was outstanding while its neighbour told them it was done, and the two had been sitting next to each other unnoticed.

A future-tense sentence is a particularly durable kind of stale prose and it is worth naming as its own category. A present-tense sentence that goes wrong ('legalSeed ACCEPTS a NaN point') at least reads as a claim someone might check. An instruction to a future turn reads as a to-do, and a to-do that has been done looks exactly like a to-do that has not — there is no internal contradiction for a reader to notice, only a redundant task somebody might redundantly perform. Corrected to the present tense in the same edit, since the ticket's scope was this file and the sentence is in the very note it asked me to extend.

This is the third instance in this ledger of prose describing a tree the code has left (summon-session.mjs's NaN header, summon-view.js's `first`/`refusal` header, and now two sentences in plant/CLAUDE.md). All three were found by an agent reading the file for another reason. None was found by a check, because no check exists — which is what the proposal below is for.

beads.title: Widened the existing sentence rather than qualifying it, and added the branches as a new paragraph rather than a clause
beads.body:
Two ways to fix 'a control built over knob.samples by index'. QUALIFY it — 'by index (except LEVEL_3)' — which is the smaller diff and the one the ticket's phrasing suggests. Or WIDEN it to 'built by index over the declared domain' and put the branch taxonomy in a paragraph of its own.

I took the second, for a reason that is about what the sentence is FOR. 'By index' in that paragraph is not describing a widget; it is stating the guarantee that an off-grid setting is unrepresentable, which is the sentence the ticket explicitly asked be kept. Hanging an exception off it implies the guarantee has one, and it does not — the parts sliders and the buttons are both positions, so the guarantee is total. A qualification would have made a true and total claim read as a leaky one, which is a worse outcome than the staleness it fixed.

What I rejected beyond that: mentioning ALL_AT_ONCE's value of 8 as a page constant to be kept in step with anything. It is not a domain bound, it is a layout judgement the page is explicitly allowed to make ('the page's ONE judgement about a control, and it is about SIZE rather than about which level it is'), and documenting it as a coupling would invite someone to move it into the module where it does not belong. I wrote 'eight or fewer' as a description of current behaviour instead.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a fourth control shape whose emitted value is NOT a position — a free text entry, a continuous drag that rounds. At that point the guarantee really would have an exception, the widened sentence would become the false one, and the honest form is to say which branches carry it. Nothing in the tree suggests that today; every branch routes through `choose()` or `compose()`.

beads.title: A gate that every backticked identifier in plant/CLAUDE.md exists in plant/ — catches the symbol half of prose drift, and says out loud that it cannot catch the rest
beads.body:
plant/CLAUDE.md is the file a turn reads first, and it has now drifted three times that this ledger records (summon-session.mjs's NaN paragraph, summon-view.js's first/refusal paragraph, and two sentences in the campaign section fixed by lp-b27cc4). Every one was found by an agent reading the file for an unrelated reason. Nothing collects this debt, and the ledger has twice recorded that a note in a comment is not a queue.

NO GATE CAN CHECK THAT PROSE IS TRUE and this proposal does not claim to. It checks a strict subset that is nonetheless the commonest way a paragraph rots: THE SYMBOLS IT NAMES STOP EXISTING. A paragraph describing `withShareA` after a rename, or `reformPocketAll` after a deletion, is wrong in a way a machine can see.

WHAT THE GATE DOES. Read plant/CLAUDE.md. Extract every single-backtick span. Keep only the ones that look like a code identifier — matching /^[A-Za-z_$][\w$.]*(\(\))?$/ or ending in a source extension (.mjs/.js/.html/.json) — and discard prose in backticks, shell fragments, and anything with a space. For a FILE token, assert the path exists under plant/ (resolving a bare name like `campaign.mjs` against plant/ and plant/test/ and plant/levels/). For an IDENTIFIER token, assert the string occurs somewhere in plant/**/*.{mjs,js,html} — a grep, deliberately, not a parse: the claim is 'this name is still in the tree', which is the weakest useful claim and the only one that cannot produce false failures on a name that is real but reached by an unusual route.

WHY THE WEAK VERSION IS THE RIGHT ONE. A checker that fails correct work is worse than no checker, and this ledger has that lesson from a verifier that failed correct geometry by exactly the yaw angle. A stricter gate — 'every named export in the doc is actually exported' — would go red for a documented internal helper, for a name mentioned historically ('it once returned `first`'), and for the doc's own deliberate references to foam/, which the loop cannot read. Each of those is a legitimate sentence. So the gate must also carry an explicit ALLOW list in the test file, with a comment per entry saying why the token is not expected to resolve, and the historical-mention case is exactly what that list is for.

CONTROLS THE GATE MUST CARRY, because a file of only negative assertions passes trivially when its extractor breaks: assert the token list is non-empty and above a floor (the file names dozens of modules today); assert that a deliberately fabricated token — a literal `noSuchSymbolInPlant` appended to the scanned text in a test-local copy of the string, never to the file itself — IS caught; and assert the file-vs-identifier classifier puts at least one token in each bucket. Without the fabricated-token control, a regex that matches nothing passes every assertion in the file.

WHAT IT WILL NOT CATCH, and this belongs in the file's own header so nobody over-trusts it: a sentence that names only real symbols and describes behaviour they no longer have. That is precisely the drift lp-b27cc4 fixed — `knob.samples` and 'by index' were both real, and the sentence was still incomplete. This gate would not have caught it. It is worth building anyway because it catches a different and cheaper class for free, forever, and because 'the doc names a function that no longer exists' is the version most likely to send a future turn down a dead end.

SCOPE: plant/test/doc-symbols.selftest.mjs only, plus the allow list inside it. No source file changes. Proposed at P2 because it changes nothing a visitor sees, per the vision's standing rule that non-page work does not go above item 1.
evidence: rejected: R6, and a concrete cost the ticket does not price. Everything matching plant/test/*.selftest.mjs is run by loop-work's whole-suite check AND by deploy-plant before it publishes — plant/CLAUDE.md itself says so, in the paragraph explaining why tools/ is deliberately not test/. So this proposal puts a PROSE checker on the path that publishes the game: a rename anywhere in plant/ now fails an unrelat

beads.title: The gate failed twice on a hand-derived fixture literal that reads perfectly — four of a cube's seven seeds inherit the centre's x, and nobody noticed
beads.body:
THE DEFECT. §10's hull block asserted that a cube summoned at [0.5, 18.9, 38] is blamed on seeds [0, 2] — "the centre and the -x neighbour", which is what the comment above it said and what anyone would say. The real answer is [0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

WHY THE OBVIOUS ANSWER IS WRONG. A cube's neighbours sit at exactly ±2r along ONE axis each (q = 1 for a unit axis normal, so the anisotropic metric cannot move them). So of the seven seeds, only indices 1 and 2 have a different x from the centre. The +y, -y, +z and -z neighbours all carry x = 0.5 UNCHANGED — and x = 0.5 is precisely what put the centre outside the x >= 1 wall. Six seeds out of hull, not two, and the only one inside is index 1 (+x, x = 3.7).

WHY IT SURVIVED TWO TURNS. Turn 1 wrote, in its own recorded finding, that the fixture is "a cube centred at x=0.5, whose centre and -x neighbour are both outside the wall WHILE ITS OTHER FIVE SEEDS ARE WHEREVER THE FOAM LEFT THEM". That sentence is the bug in one clause: the other five seeds are not wherever anything left them, they are at a fixed offset from a centre that is out of bounds, and four of them inherit the offending coordinate exactly. Turn 2 then re-derived turn 1's four STATED fixture claims from the sources — carefully, and correctly — but this claim was not among the four it listed, so the re-derivation walked straight past it. A verification pass scoped to the claims a previous turn wrote down cannot find the claim it did not write down.

THE TRANSFERABLE SHAPE, and it is sharper than "check your arithmetic". When a fixture point is chosen to violate a constraint, ASK WHICH OF ITS DERIVED POINTS INHERIT THE VIOLATING COORDINATE. A constellation is not a cloud of independent positions; it is one centre plus fixed offsets, and an offset that is zero on the violated axis propagates the violation verbatim. The intuition that fails here is thinking of "the shape" as spread out in all directions — it is, but not on every axis at once, and the axis-aligned solid is the one where that is least visible. This is the cube trap the whole project already knows about (`solids.mjs`'s 22° warning: a cube survives because axis-aligned normals are the only ones the metric cannot rotate) arriving from a completely different direction: the cube is again the solid whose special structure makes the wrong general answer look right.

FIXED WITH MORE THAN THE CORRECTED NUMBER. The expected set is now recomputed inside the test from `pocket.W/H/D` against the constellation the fixture really built — an independent route that touches neither `hullViolation` nor `legalSeed` — and the corrected literal is kept alongside it. The recomputation catches a wrong expectation; the literal catches a moved fixture. Neither alone would have caught both, and it was the first kind that cost two turns.

beads.title: The section had no proper-subset control, so 'blame the whole shape' would have passed — and on this fixture that is one seed away from true
beads.body:
Every assertion in the hull block compared two verbs' blamed sets to each other and to a literal. None of them asserted that anything was NOT blamed.

That matters more here than it usually does. The fixture blames SIX OF SEVEN seeds. An implementation that simply blamed the entire constellation whenever the centre is out of hull — which is a plausible shortcut, and arguably a defensible product decision — differs from the correct answer by exactly one element, and would have passed the old assertion trivially once the literal was corrected to a six-element set. The check would have read as thorough and measured nothing about attribution.

So the block now asserts that index 1 is inside the wall AND that neither verb names it. That is what makes the blamed set a proper subset and the whole section a claim about attribution rather than about refusal.

The control is written as a RELATION (`x > 1 && x < W - 1`) rather than as `x === 3.7`. The value is 0.5 + 2r = 0.5 + 3.2 and I believe it is bit-exactly 3.7 in doubles, but a gate that fails correct work on a rounding argument is worse than no gate, and the property under test is "inside the wall", not "equal to a number I computed".

GENERAL FORM, and this ledger has it from several directions already: a test that only ever asserts membership cannot distinguish a discriminating classifier from one that says yes to everything. The cheap fix is always the same — assert one thing that must be EXCLUDED — and it is cheapest to add at the moment you are already staring at the set.

beads.title: Made the set-comparison sorts numeric even though the cube fixture cannot tell the difference
beads.body:
`[...new Set(...)].sort()` with no comparator sorts LEXICOGRAPHICALLY. For a 7-seed cube the indices are 0..6, single digits, so lexicographic and numeric order coincide and no cube fixture can ever expose the difference.

They diverge at 10. A dodecahedron is 13 seeds and an icosahedron 21, and both are first-class members of `SOLID_NAMES`.
