Print the tightest pair and its gap in the failure detail. Then the existing preview/place equality assertion is guarded by its own precondition rather than by a paragraph in a comment, and a future turn that retunes TINY gets a failure that names the real reason — 'a pair sits 0.004 from the threshold, the two verbs may disagree by rounding' — instead of a mysterious set mismatch.

WHY class-a AND NOT creates-gate: `plant/test/summon-view.selftest.mjs` exists and passes; this adds a control to it and changes no module. WHY IT IS NOT DECORATION: it can fail. Set TINY to a value where a pair lands on 1.5 and it goes red, which is exactly when the equality assertion below it stops being sound.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED ON PRIORITY, not on craft — and the craft here is real, so read this reason rather than reproposing it unchanged. The reasoning is careful and the turn that wrote it did genuine work: recomputing the tiny-cube pair table at r=0.4 and finding the SAME COUNT of refused pairs but a DIFFERENT ten, with the tightest at 1.4314 against MIN_SEED_GAP, is exactly the kind of thing that silently inv

beads.title: The ticket's own mitigation does not solve the false positive it names — a setext heading underline IS a whole line of seven equals
beads.body:
The ticket specifies /^(<<<<<<< |=======$|>>>>>>> )/ and justifies the whole-line anchoring on the bare-equals form like this: 'a markdown horizontal rule is a run of = or - under a heading and ======= alone is a legal one, so the bare-equals form must be matched as a WHOLE LINE only'.

The premise is right and the conclusion does not follow. A setext heading underline is EXACTLY a whole line of = characters:

    A heading
    =======

So whole-line matching does not remove that false positive — it is precisely the case whole-line matching MATCHES. What whole-line matching removes is the different and easier case of `=======text`, i.e. a run welded to prose. The ticket conflated the two, and a check built to its letter would go red on any plant/ document that used a setext heading with a seven-character underline. The ticket also says, correctly, that 'a marker check that cries wolf on ordinary markdown gets deleted' — so the defect would have been terminal for the check rather than cosmetic.

THE FIX COSTS NOTHING AND LOSES NO DETECTION: flag a bare whole-line `=======` only when an unclosed `<<<<<<< ` sits above it. A lone run of equals with no `<<<<<<<` before it and no `>>>>>>>` after it is not a conflict; it is a rule or a heading underline. A real conflict always has all three markers, so the condition can never suppress a true positive. The two angle-bracket markers have no legitimate markdown meaning whatsoever and stay unconditional.

The pair of controls is what makes this a rule rather than a weakening: a bare `=======` under a heading must NOT fire, and the identical line inside an open conflict MUST fire. Either one alone is satisfied by 'never match a bare equals at all', which is a strictly weaker check that looks the same from the outside.

THE TRANSFERABLE HALF, and it is not about markdown: when a spec names a false positive AND names the mitigation, check that the mitigation actually covers the case. The two arrive together and read as one thought, so the mitigation inherits the credibility of the observation. Here the observation was correct, specific, and the fix attached to it addressed a neighbouring case.

beads.title: Exempting fenced code blocks opens a hole that passes every other assertion in the file — the control is 'a marker AFTER a closed fence still fires'
beads.body:
The ticket requires a control that the check does not fire on 'a fenced code block containing a diff example'. Taken at its weakest that is satisfied trivially: `--- a/x`, `+++ b/x` and `@@ -1 +1 @@` match no marker pattern, so a fence exemption is not needed to pass it and the control proves nothing.

I implemented a real fence exemption anyway, because the alternative is worse than it looks: a document explaining conflict markers has to QUOTE them, and it will quote them inside a fence. Without the exemption, documenting the hazard trips the check that exists to catch it — and this ticket's own bead body quotes three markers verbatim. A check that forbids its own documentation gets an exception carved into it by the next turn, badly.

THE HOLE THE EXEMPTION OPENS, and it is the classic one for any stateful skip: an implementation that treats the first fence opener as 'ignore everything after this' passes the walk assertion, the mid-sentence control, the setext control, the positive control on a bare synthetic conflict, AND the fenced-block control. Five of the six sections. It fails only on a fixture with a real marker AFTER a closed fence, which is the one nobody writes because it feels redundant.

So that fixture is in, plus two more guarding the same state machine: a DANGLING fence (an opener with no closer) exempts nothing at all, so the tail of a file whose fence balance a conflict broke is still scanned; and a `~~~` does not close a ``` , so a mismatched pair leaves the region unclosed and therefore scanned. The dangling-fence rule is the conservative direction on purpose — the residual it leaves is a conflict wholly inside a properly balanced fence, which is stated in the file header rather than left to be discovered.

GENERAL SHAPE, and this ledger has it from several directions: when a check gains an EXEMPTION, the assertion that matters is not that the exempt thing is exempt. It is that the exemption ENDS. Every 'skip this region' rule can be implemented as 'skip the rest of the input' and no positive fixture inside the region can tell the two apart.

beads.title: Took the OTHER side's first sentence, not HEAD's, and kept HEAD's `won` paragraph as instructed
beads.body:
The ticket says to keep HEAD's `won` paragraph verbatim and splice in the other side's `parts` sentence. It says nothing about the sentence the two sides SHARE and differ on, which is the opening one about where the page gets its control bounds:

  HEAD:  '...and the follow-up that wires the page MUST TAKE its control bounds
          *from here* instead of keeping a second copy.'
  other: '...and the page TAKES its control bounds *from here* rather than
          keeping a second copy. For a knob with `parts` the bounds the page
          reads are each part's own domain and `samples` is the derived
          product, so that is still one declaration in one place.'

I took the other side's, and the `parts` sentence came with it as one unit.

WHY: HEAD's is future tense about work that has already landed. The wiring is lp-6c88fb, and plant/CLAUDE.md says so itself eight lines below the conflict ('It now drives the page (lp-6c88fb)'). So HEAD's side leaves one paragraph telling a reader the wiring is outstanding while its neighbour says it is done. The ledger already records this exact sentence as stale and records why the future-tense form is the durable kind of doc rot: a present-tense claim that goes wrong reads as something checkable, whereas an instruction to a future turn that has been carried out looks exactly like one that has not, so there is no internal contradiction for a reader to notice.

WHAT I REJECTED: keeping HEAD's sentence verbatim on a literal reading of 'keep HEAD's paragraph'. That would have re-committed a sentence the ledger already flagged, in the file whose accuracy is this ticket's entire justification.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: if the page ever stops reading its bounds from campaign.mjs, the present-tense claim becomes false and the sentence needs rewriting — but so would HEAD's, and index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs would go red first. No content was lost either way: HEAD's `won` paragraph is present verbatim, and the other side's shorter, now-incomplete `won` sentence was the only text dropped, which is what the ticket asked for.

beads.title: Did not match diff3's `|||||||` base marker, and it costs no detection
beads.body:
A diff3-style merge writes four marker kinds: `<<<<<<< `, `||||||| ` (the common ancestor), `=======` and `>>>>>>> `. The ticket names three. I implemented three.

The reason is not deference: a diff3 conflict STILL writes the other three, so every diff3 conflict is already caught — by the opening marker alone, before the base marker is ever reached. Adding a fourth pattern buys literally zero additional detection.

Against that zero: a pattern anchored on a run of pipe characters is one unlucky markdown table away from crying wolf, in a file format whose tables are made of pipes. This document is full of them. The ticket is explicit that a check which cries wolf gets deleted, and I am not willing to spend that risk on a pattern with no marginal value.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: nothing I can foresee. If a merge tool ever emitted a base marker WITHOUT the other three it would slip through, but no three-way merge format does that — the base section is delimited by the opening marker above it by construction.

beads.title: Building the marker literals with repeat(7) removed the one hand-error class an unrun gate could not survive
beads.body:
This gate is a check FOR a literal string, written by a turn that cannot execute it. The dominant risk is therefore not arithmetic (there is none) and not a stale expectation (the fixtures are synthetic) — it is miscounting a run of identical characters. Seven angle brackets typed by hand, in eleven separate places across the fixtures and the predicate, with no compiler and no test run to notice that one of them has six.

And the failure would have been silent in the passing direction. A predicate looking for six `<` still matches a real seven-`<` marker as a prefix, so §4 keeps passing; a FIXTURE built with six would fail its own positive control, which is at least loud. The dangerous combination is a predicate with the wrong count and fixtures with the same wrong count — every assertion agrees, and the gate cannot see a real conflict.

So nothing is typed. `const LT = '<'.repeat(7)` once, and every fixture and every branch of the predicate is composed from it. The count now exists in exactly one place and cannot disagree with itself. It also makes the source readable: no line of this .mjs file begins with a marker, which matters because a line starting with `<<<<<<<` in a JavaScript source is itself a syntax error unless it happens to be inside a string.

THE TRANSFERABLE HALF: when a gate's subject is a literal token, DERIVE the token once rather than typing it at each site. The usual argument for that is maintenance; the argument here is stronger and different — a hand-typed repeated character is the one defect a suite of self-consistent fixtures is structurally unable to detect, because the fixtures and the predicate are wrong together.

beads.title: Neither file was run — the two things that could have gone wrong here are lexical and stateful, not numerical
beads.body:
The standing 'gate unverifiable in-turn' recommendation is in this ledger well past twenty times and recent turns agreed to stop restating it. I am not restating it. What is worth one entry is that this file's risk profile has NO arithmetic in it at all, so the ~25 prior instances that reason about whether a hand-computed number is right do not transfer, and the two failure modes that DO apply are the ones a turn without a shell can actually check.

1. LEXICAL — a parse error kills every assertion and reads like an unrelated typo. Checked deliberately: the only nested template literal is the `ok()` detail clause, copied verbatim from index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs where it is already proven to parse. No prose string contains an ASCII apostrophe. The fixture strings that contain backticks (the fence lines, and the CLAUDE.md excerpt carrying `parts` in inline code) are SINGLE-quoted, where a backtick is an ordinary character. The one regex containing a backtick, /^ {0,3}(`{3,}|~{3,})/, is a regex literal, where a backtick is likewise ordinary.

2. STATEFUL — the fence tracker is the only state in the file, and a stateful skip that never un-skips passes almost everything. That is covered by three fixtures rather than by reading the code twice: a marker after a CLOSED fence, a DANGLING fence, and a mismatched ~~~ against a ```. Each targets one branch of the tracker.

Every fixture was then hand-traced line by line — index, fence state, open state, expected hit line numbers — against the exact strings the file builds, not against a description of them. The traces agree with every asserted count (3, 3, 0, 2, 0, 3, 3, 3).

What I could NOT do is confirm the directory walk against a real filesystem. `markdownFiles(join(here, '..'))` finds one file today, and §1 asserts that the list is non-empty and contains CLAUDE.md by name precisely because the realistic way this check silently stops working is a walk that comes back empty. If anything in this gate goes red, that is the assertion to read first — it fails with the list it actually found.

beads.title: Assert that every plant/ path plant/CLAUDE.md NAMES actually exists — the decidable slice of doc rot, next to the conflict check
beads.body:
plant/CLAUDE.md is the orientation document every turn reads, and this ledger records FOUR separate instances of its prose (or a module header's) describing a tree the code has left: summon-session.mjs's NaN paragraph, summon-view.js's first/refusal paragraph, two sentences in plant/CLAUDE.md itself, and the merge conflict lp-ad6c32 just resolved. Every one was found by an agent reading the file for an unrelated reason. None was found by a check.

'Does this paragraph still describe the code' is undecidable and must stay out of scope — lp-ad6c32's body says so explicitly and it is right. But there is a DECIDABLE SLICE of exactly the same family, with the same perfect-detection property that made the conflict check worth building: a path either exists or it does not.

plant/CLAUDE.md names roughly twenty files in inline code — `production.mjs`, `placement.mjs`, `level.mjs`, `pocketLevel.mjs`, `foamworld.js`, `campaign.mjs`, `summon-view.js`, `levels/level2.mjs`, `test/production.selftest.mjs`, `test/multi-insert.selftest.mjs`, `test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs`, `tools/loop-brief.mjs` and more. If any of those is renamed, moved or deleted, the document keeps naming it and nothing notices. That is the single most likely way this file goes wrong next, because a rename is a mechanical edit nobody thinks of as a documentation change.

SCOPE (bounded paths): plant/test/docs.selftest.mjs only. It is the natural home — same file, same family of check, and it already walks the .md files and has the fence machinery.

WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK, and a weaker version is not worth building:

  (a) Extract every inline-code span from every .md under plant/ that LOOKS LIKE A PATH INTO THIS TREE, and assert the file exists. The extraction must be CONSERVATIVE and the ticket lives or dies on this: only a span matching something like /^[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+\.(mjs|js|html|json|md)$/ counts, so `won`, `ok && moves > 0`, `Domain=.mino.mobi` and `FACTORIO.md` §2 are not mistaken for paths. Spans naming a path OUTSIDE plant/ (../docs/LOOP-SPRINTS.md, ../foam/FACTORIO.md) must be skipped explicitly rather than resolved, because this gate must not go red when a file elsewhere in the repo moves — that is somebody else's blast radius.

  (b) Resolve each candidate relative to plant/, and ALSO accept a bare basename that matches exactly one file in the tree, because the document writes `test/production.selftest.mjs` in some places and `production.mjs` in others.

  (c) A POSITIVE CONTROL, for the same reason lp-ad6c32 needed one: the whole check is a negation over an extracted list, so an extractor that returns nothing passes silently. Run the extractor over a synthetic document naming a file that does not exist and assert it FIRES; run it over one naming a real file and assert it does not. Assert the extracted list from the REAL document is non-empty and contains at least one known name.

  (d) A CRY-WOLF CONTROL, which is the assertion that decides whether anyone keeps this: the extractor must be shown NOT to fire on the inline-code spans in plant/CLAUDE.md today that are not paths. Pin a handful of real ones from the file (`won`, `parts`, `knob.start`, `blame:'caller'`, `plant/**`) as must-not-match. A check that reports twelve false positives on the day it lands gets deleted, and correctly.

CLASS: class-a. The gate file plant/test/docs.selftest.mjs EXISTS after lp-ad6c32 and passes today, so this is certified against an existing gate — the new assertions are added to it and the whole suite must still pass. Not creates-gate: nothing new is being created.

DELIBERATELY OUT OF SCOPE: checking that the PROSE about a file is accurate, checking that every file is mentioned (the reverse direction, which would fire on every internal helper and is pure noise), and any link checking outside plant/.
evidence: rejected: REJECTED ON ITS OWN CRY-WOLF CRITERION, which it states and then fails. The ticket says 'a check that reports twelve false positives on the day it lands gets deleted, and correctly' — so I ran its stated extractor spec against plant/CLAUDE.md as it stands. The regex /^[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+\.(mjs|js|html|json|md)$/ plus 'skip spans naming a path OUTSIDE plant/ (../docs/..., ../foam/...)' fires on AT LEA

beads.title: Applied INTRO's COUNT rule to LINES too, which cost a reword of both sentences — uniform rule beats a per-string human exemption
beads.body:
The ticket said LINES must be held to INTRO's two rules (one sentence, no BANNED word) and to its count rule 'if it survives review'. That conditional is the whole judgement call, and it bites: 'That was the last one — there is nothing after it.' contains 'one' at a word boundary and FAILS the count rule.

THE CASE FOR EXEMPTING IT IS GENUINELY GOOD. INTRO's count rule exists because ORDER is COMPUTED, so a sentence counting levels can expire on an import with nothing to catch it. LINES.finished renders only when st.finished has latched — a state that is true by construction at the end of ORDER however the levels are reordered — so 'the last one' cannot expire. On the merits, the exemption is correct.

I APPLIED THE RULE ANYWAY, and the reason is the rule's own stated justification, which I think settles it. campaign.mjs's INTRO comment says the count rule is 'DELIBERATELY STRICTER THAN ITS OWN JUSTIFICATION' precisely because NO REGEX CAN TELL a count that expires from one that does not. Exempting LINES.finished because I personally checked that this particular count is state-guarded is EXACTLY the per-string human judgement the rule was written to avoid making — and it would leave the rule off for every line added to LINES afterwards, by whoever reads 'LINES is exempt' and stops there. Fail closed, the same call this repo's blast-radius checker and class taxonomy already make.

WHAT IT COST, stated plainly because it changes what a visitor reads:
  'The factory already works. Move the control and find out what breaks it.'
    -> 'The factory already works — move the control and find out what breaks it.'  (also required: it was TWO sentences)
  'That was the last one — there is nothing after it.'
    -> 'That was the last level — there is nothing after it.'
Neither is worse prose and the first change was mandatory anyway.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: delete the two `LINES.${name} counts nothing` assertions from §2c. It is one line and the module's own docstring says so, so a later turn that disagrees can undo this without archaeology. The one-sentence and banned-word rules are NOT reversible in the same cheap way and I would not reverse them.

beads.title: The ticket's own headline assertion is not runnable — there is no DOM — and what replaces it is STRONGER, not a workaround
beads.body:
The ticket says 'the assertion that BITES is one line, `nudge.textContent === LINES.untouched`'. That line cannot exist: index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs reads index.html as TEXT in node. There is no element, no textContent, no browser.

It would have been easy to treat that as a shortfall and settle for something weaker. It is the opposite, and the reasoning is worth keeping because the same substitution is available to any wiring gate in this tree.

A DOM assertion `nudge.textContent === LINES.untouched` compares TWO STRINGS AT RUNTIME. It passes iff they happen to be equal, and a page that hardcoded a byte-identical copy of the sentence would pass it. What the page does now is render `LINES.untouched` BY REFERENCE — so equality does not need asserting, it holds by construction, and the only way to break it is to stop reading the export. So the assertions that carry the ticket are:

  · the reference render is present, in full, including the `: ''` clearing arm;
  · NO quoted string appears in that ternary at all (`!/untouched\s*\?\s*['\"`]/`), which catches a DIFFERENT sentence being hardcoded — something `includes` cannot see;
  · `!html.includes(LINES.untouched)` — the words have LEFT the page, derived from the export rather than retyped, so a renamed sentence is covered the day it lands.

The third is the ledger's standing MOVE rule (absence at the source, presence at the destination) and it is the one that makes the diff reviewable. Together they are strictly stronger than the runtime equality the ticket asked for, because they forbid the page from OWNING a sentence rather than merely requiring it to own the same one.

TRANSFERABLE: when a ticket names a runtime equality that the harness cannot reach, check whether the code can be restructured so the equality is unnecessary. 'Rendered by reference' is not a weaker proxy for 'equal at runtime' — it is the property that makes runtime equality unfalsifiable, and it is checkable from a text gate.

beads.title: Two sections applying the same four prose rules would have been two copies — and the copy I was about to make carried a FALSE claim I inherited
beads.body:
§2b (INTRO) declared COUNT_WORDS and countRe inside its own block. Adding §2c (LINES) for the same four rules meant either a second copy or a hoist. I hoisted, and turned the three inline predicates into named functions (ONE_SENTENCE, bannedIn, levelIdIn, countRe) at module scope, so both sections and all their controls run the SAME code. Two declarations of one rule is the exact drift this file exists to catch, one file over — and a drifted copy fails in the direction that prints ticks, because every one of these rules is used as a NEGATIVE assertion.

THE PART WORTH RECORDING is what fell out of moving the comment rather than copying it. §2b's note read:

    Word boundaries on purpose: "everything" must not read as "ten".

That is FALSE, in both halves. 'everything' (e-v-e-r-y-t-h-i-n-g) contains no 'ten'. The control underneath it tests `!countRe.test('everything downstream is stone.')`, and the word that actually needs the boundary is STONE, which does contain 'one'. The assertion was correct and load-bearing the whole time; the sentence explaining it was wrong, and had been sitting next to it unread.

I nearly propagated it. My first draft of §2c's control comment copied the claim verbatim and then embellished it ('and "control", which both of these lines use, is the word that would break first') — also false, since 'control' contains no count word either. I caught both only by spelling the words out letter by letter, which is a thing you do for a hand-verified assertion and do not normally do for a comment.

TWO THINGS TRANSFER. (1) A comment justifying a check is not checked by anything, so it rots in place while the check stays green — this repo has the shape recorded three times for prose describing code, and this is the smaller, commoner version: prose describing a TEST. (2) RELOCATING a comment is the cheapest moment to audit it, because you have to read it to move it. Copying is what lets it survive unread. Corrected at the new home, with a note saying what it used to claim so nobody 'restores' it.

beads.title: The wiring gate lost four assertions and gained six — what was removed, and why removing it was the point rather than collateral
beads.body:
A turn that edits the gates grading it is the shape this ledger warns about, so here is the removal, itemised, since 'I updated some tests' is not reviewable.

DELETED from §(9b), all four operating on a regex-extracted quoted string:
  · 'there is a sentence, and it is the page's own'  (!!match)
  · 'it is a sentence, not a paragraph'              (20 < len < 200)
  · 'it does not say "<w>"' for each BANNED word
  · 'it is CLEARED when the state does not hold'     (`? '...' : ''`)

The first three are properties the string has ON ITS OWN. The ticket's argument — and the ledger's, recorded for §(8) and the intro — is that they pass for a sentence about a completely different game. They were the strongest thing available while the page owned the words, and they became unsatisfiable the moment it stopped, because there is no quoted string left to extract. That is the MOVE precedent working as designed: the old location's guard is not damage to repair, it is the artefact that proves the relocation happened, so it was rewritten to assert ABSENCE at the source.

The fourth is the only one that was doing work independent of ownership, and it was NOT dropped — it is now `/LINES\.untouched\s*:\s*''/`, asserting the same clearing arm against the new render.

The prose rules those three enforced were not lost either; they moved to campaign.selftest.mjs §2c, where they run against the EXPORT rather than against whatever the page happened to quote — which is a stronger place for them, since the export is the single owner and the page can no longer disagree.

NET: §(9b) is four assertions lighter and five heavier, §(9c) is entirely new (the finished suffix previously had NO check of any kind — nothing asserted it existed, let alone that it said anything), and §2c adds twenty-odd. Nothing that was checking a real property stopped being checked.

beads.title: Neither gate was run — the two assertions I would look at first, and the one class of failure hand-tracing genuinely does close
beads.body:
No Bash. The standing recommendation is in this ledger past twenty-five times and recent turns agreed to stop restating it; I am not restating it. What is worth an entry is which of MY assertions could go red for a reason unrelated to the code, since this turn's risk is textual rather than arithmetic — there is not one number in the diff.

WOULD LOOK AT FIRST, in order:

1. `!/untouched\s*\?\s*['\"`]/.test(block)`. This is a NEGATION over the whole campaign block, so it fails if ANY occurrence of 'untouched' is followed by '?' and a quote. There are four occurrences and I traced each: line 405 is inside a comment where 'untouched' is followed immediately by a BACKTICK (not '?'), 407 by ' = ', 408 by ';', 409 by ' ? L'. None matches. If this goes red the cause is a fifth occurrence somebody added, not the rule.

2. `/st\.finished[\s\S]{0,80}?LINES\.finished/`. A bounded-distance match across a line break; I counted the gap as ~20 characters. Reformatting that ternary onto one line or across four keeps it well inside 80, but this is the one assertion whose truth depends on LAYOUT rather than on content, which makes it the fragile one. The assertion beside it (`\$\{v\.line\}\s*\$\{LINES\.finished\}`) is layout-independent and carries the same claim, so a red here with a green there means 'reformatted', not 'broken'.

WHAT HAND-TRACING ACTUALLY CLOSED, and this is the useful half: the lexical pass found nothing, and I ran it anyway because a parse error kills every assertion and reads like an unrelated typo. Checked: no backtick nested inside a template literal anywhere added; no ASCII apostrophe inside a single-quoted string (both LINES values are apostrophe-free, which was luck, and both test controls were written that way deliberately); countRe carries no /g flag despite being used for ~12 separate .test() calls across two sections — a sticky lastIndex there would make alternate calls return false, which is the ONE defect in this diff that would have produced a confidently wrong PASS rather than a red gate. Also confirmed the backtick inside `['\"`]` is a legal regex-literal class character (it is; only ']', '\\' and line terminators are special there).

The predicates themselves I evaluated by hand against both strings letter by letter, which is how the two false comments in the other finding were caught. That is a form of checking that scales badly and does work.

beads.title: Wire #gameIntro to campaign.mjs's INTRO — the third and last hand-typed sentence on the campaign panel, and the module's words must win
beads.body:
COMPLETES THE ASYMMETRY lp-3302ee deliberately left open. index.html's `

` is now the ONLY text on the campaign panel that campaign.mjs does not own: level titles and blurbs are asserted ABSENT from the page (index-campaign-wiring §4 checks `!block.includes(e.blurb)`), and after lp-3302ee both game-state sentences are rendered by reference. The intro alone is still typed into the markup. WHY IT MATTERS AND NOT AS TIDINESS. §(8) asserts the intro exists, is under 400 chars, and contains no BANNED word. The ledger records exactly what that cannot catch: 'it checks a property of the text, never that it is the RIGHT text… it would pass for an intro describing a completely different game.' The assertion that bites is `intro.trim() === INTRO.blurb`, and it is only available once the page reads the module. INTRO has existed, fully specified and gated, since lp-ffddc7 — nothing renders it. THE ORDERING CONSTRAINT, which is the whole reason this is a separate ticket and not a line in lp-3302ee. The two texts DISAGREE and the module must win: page: 'A little factory that has to feed everything it promised. Each level gives you one setting to move; get nothing short and the next one opens.' INTRO.blurb: 'Each puzzle is a small factory that is not quite working, and you get a single control — move it until everything downstream gets what it asked for.' The shipped page wording is TWO sentences and says 'one setting' and 'level' — it violates INTRO's one-sentence rule, its count rule AND (arguably) its level-naming rule, all three of which campaign.selftest.mjs §2b already enforces on INTRO and passes. So a turn that wires this by copying the PAGE's words into the module goes red in campaign.selftest.mjs and will be tempted to relax §2b. That is the failure mode to forbid in the body: the module's words are correct and already gated, the page's words change, and §2b is not to be touched. lp-3302ee hit the identical fork for LINES and resolved it the same way, at the cost of rewording both lines. SCOPE (bounded paths): plant/index.html, plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs. campaign.mjs should need NO change — INTRO is already correct, already frozen, already gated. If it turns out to need one, that is a signal the wording decision is being made in the wrong direction. WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK, and it must be a REPLACEMENT rather than an addition, or the ticket has bought nothing: · §(8)'s property checks (non-empty, <400 chars, no BANNED word) are REPLACED by identity: the page renders `INTRO.title` and `INTRO.blurb` by reference, and the extracted `#gameIntro` text equals INTRO.blurb. The property checks live on in campaign.selftest.mjs §2b against the export, which is the stronger home for them. · the DEPARTURE half, per this tree's standing rule for relocation work: `!html.includes()` derived from nothing hand-typed — assert instead that the markup's #gameIntro element is EMPTY in source (filled at paint time), and that no BANNED-free-but-page-owned paragraph is left behind. `!html.includes(INTRO.blurb)` is NOT the right check here (the page must contain it after render, but not in source), so assert the element ships empty and the block writes it from the export. · the page imports INTRO from ./campaign.mjs, matching how it already imports LINES. BOTH GATES EXIST AND PASS TODAY, so this is class-a with no new file. It changes what a visitor reads on the first screen, which is vision item 1's territory. [turn 90 — done] Wired #gameIntro to campaign.mjs's INTRO. plant/index.html: the hand-typed two-sentence paragraph is deleted, `

` now ships EMPTY, a new `

` ships empty beside it, the campaign block imports INTRO alongside Campaign/entryOf/LINES, and two lines at the block's startup write `INTRO.title` and `INTRO.blurb` by reference (once, not in paint() — the first screen does not change). The module's words won and the page's changed, exactly as the ticket required; campaign.mjs and campaign.selftest.mjs are UNTOUCHED. Section (8) of index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs was REPLACED rather than extended: the three property checks (non-empty, <400 chars, no BANNED word) are gone — they live on in campaign.selftest.mjs against the export — and in their place are the import, both mounts asserted empty in source, both by-reference assignments, a negative that no first-screen text is quoted into either assignment, the departure (neither INTRO.title nor INTRO.blurb appears in the page source, derived from the export not hand-copied), and a control that those two needles are substantial so the negations are not vacuous. BANNED is no longer imported by that file (it was used nowhere else). NOT VERIFIED BY EXECUTION: no Bash this turn, so neither gate was run. Every regex was hand-traced character by character against the exact bytes I wrote (traces in the findings), the two departure checks were confirmed by grepping index.html for all three candidate strings (no matches), and I checked the four other gates that read index.html as text — index-summon-wiring's Campaign-import regex and index-level4/5/6's html assertions are all unaffected, and campaign.selftest.mjs does not read the page at all.

beads.title: The page shows a green tick and no way forward on five of six opening screens — the nudge line exists but the ✓ sentence still contradicts it
beads.body:
RECORDED IN THE LEDGER AND STILL UNFIXED, and lp-3302ee moved the words without touching the contradiction they sit in. Worth a ticket because it is on the one screen a stranger meets.

THE STATE. Five of the six levels open ALREADY FED (level1 51 against demand 50, level3 45 against 44, level4 30.6/71.4 against 30/70, level5 exactly 30/70, level6 exactly 24/60). So on arrival `verdict()` returns `ok: true, won: false`, and the page renders campaign.mjs's own `sentence(v)`:

    ✓ Everything is fed, with 2% to spare (tight).

…beside a next button that index.html correctly hides (`!(v.won && !st.finished)`). Read cold, a green tick with no way forward is a broken page. lp-6e4b6f added the nudge line underneath ('The factory already works — move the control and find out what breaks it.') which explains it, and the tick still SAYS THE LEVEL IS DONE two lines above.

WHAT MAKES THIS NOT A ONE-LINE FIX, and why it is a ticket rather than a drive-by. The obvious repair is to branch `sentence()` on `won`. That is WRONG and lp-3302ee's ticket text explains why: sentence() speaks about the FACTORY, and campaign.mjs's header keeps `move().accepted` and `verdict().ok` apart on purpose ('two senses of ok, kept apart because a renderer will meet both'). Folding the game's win state into the factory's sentence destroys exactly the distinction the module is careful about — the same argument that made LINES a sibling export rather than a branch in sentence().

THE SHAPE THAT PRESERVES IT: the ✓ glyph and the word 'fed' are the factory's; whether this counts as DONE is the game's. So the page should render the factory sentence WITHOUT a completion glyph when `ok && !won`, or LINES should gain a third line that replaces rather than supplements. Both are module-owned text changes plus a render branch, and both are gateable by the pair of gates that already exist. Deciding between them is a taste call the turn should make and record; the ledger's standing guidance is to pick the option that is easier to reverse.

SCOPE (bounded paths): plant/campaign.mjs, plant/index.html, plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs, plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs.

WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK:
  · campaign.selftest.mjs: `sentence()` (or whatever replaces the glyph decision) is driven at BOTH `ok && !won` and `ok && won` on a real Campaign, and the two outputs must DIFFER — a single-state fixture cannot test a conjunction, which is the hole §(9b) of the wiring gate already had to close with a second fixture one move away.
  · index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs: the page branches on the same two fields it already has and computes nothing new (no move count, no level id, no second verdict), and any new text is module-owned and asserted absent from the page, per the rule lp-3302ee established for LINES.
  · CONTROL, and it is the one that makes the section non-vacuous: a fixture in the `!ok` state must be unchanged by this work — the failure sentence is the factory's and has nothing to do with winning.

BOTH GATES EXIST AND PASS TODAY: class-a, no new file. This changes what a visitor sees on the opening screen of five of six levels, which is vision item 1.

[turn 87 — done] Split the completion MARK off the factory's words in campaign.mjs, so the opening screen of five of six levels no longer shows a green tick beside a hidden next button. `plain(v)` now returns the verdict's words unmarked; `sentence(v)` is `MARK + ' ' + plain(v)`; `verdict()` returns both as `line` and `plain`; and the page renders `plain` when `v.ok && !v.won` and `line` otherwise, reusing the ONE `untouched` condition it already computed for the nudge line. Neither function looks at `won`, so the ok/won distinction the module's header is careful about is intact — the GAME picks the form, the FACTORY writes the words. Verified by hand that `line` is BYTE-IDENTICAL in all three branches after the refactor (the old literals were '✗ ' + body, '✓ ' + body), which is why playthrough.selftest.mjs, campaign.selftest §10/§11 and the wiring gate's `${v.line} ${LINES.finished}` composition are all untouched — I chose this shape partly for that. Added campaign.selftest §14 (the module contract: MARK's key set, line === mark + plain, and a two-state fixture one move apart) and index-campaign-wiring §(9d) (the page PICKS rather than composes: the branch captured and read, exactly one `untouched` derivation, exactly one game.verdict() call, and no mark glyph anywhere in the block, checked against MARK rather than a retyped character). HONESTLY: NEITHER GATE WAS RUN — this turn had Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep and no Bash. Every regex was traced against the exact bytes I wrote, every existing assertion in both gates was re-read against the new source (§(9b)'s `^v\.ok\s*&&\s*!\s*v\.won$` still captures the moved declaration verbatim; §(9c)'s `${v.line} ${LINES.finished}` is deliberately unchanged), and the level1 fixture numbers were hand-computed. The page was never rendered in a browser.

beads.title: A session refusal's field set depends on the VERB, not just the reason — `ok` is on every preview refusal and on no place refusal, and `role` is preview-only
beads.body:
Writing the ten exact key sets out turned up two irregularities in the same family as the two lp-53afb4 found one layer down, and neither was written anywhere.

1. `ok: false` IS ON EVERY PREVIEW REFUSAL AND ON NO PLACE REFUSAL. `legalSeed` returns `{ ok: false, reason, ... }` and `legalSummon`'s `self` push sets it too, so every refusal arriving through `preview` carries it. The kernel sets it on the RESULT (`refuse()` returns `{ ok: false, pocket: null, ... }`) and never on the individual refusal objects inside `refusals[]` — checked at all five push sites in `reformPocketAll` plus the `empty` and `closure`/`nav` ones. `_attribute` copies and adds; it does not invent an `ok`.

   So a caller writing `if (rf.ok === false)` is CORRECT ON ONE VERB AND WRONG ON THE OTHER. It works today only because `undefined` is falsy too, i.e. every ordinary truthiness form (`if (!rf.ok)`, `rf.ok ? ... : ...`) accidentally agrees. The strict form, which is the one a careful reader reaches for precisely because the field is a boolean, is the one that breaks — and it breaks silently, treating every place refusal as though it had not been refused.

2. `role` (`'centre'` / `'neighbour'`) IS ON PREVIEW `hull` AND `seed` ONLY. Not on preview `self` — `legalSummon` deliberately omits it because a pair has no single role, which lp-53afb4 already recorded — and not on ANY place refusal, because the kernel has no notion of a constellation and `_attribute` does not invent one. A renderer saying 'the centre of the cube is in rock' works on a highlight and renders `undefined` on the summon the player actually attempted, which is the exact failure shape the `summonSeed`/`point` divergence had.

Note what makes (2) fixable and (1) arguable. `role` IS derivable on the place path: `place()` hands `reformPocketAll` exactly `con.seeds` in order, so `summonSeed === 0` is the centre by construction — the same argument that licensed the `summonSeed` copy. `ok` is not obviously worth adding, because the honest reading is that a refusal object is a refusal and `ok` on it was always redundant; the defensible fix is the other direction, dropping it from the preview path. Both are proposed below; neither was done here, because the ticket says pin the shapes and a turn that changes the shapes it was sent to pin has graded itself.

THE TRANSFERABLE HALF, and it is why the ticket was right to demand exact sets: a PRESENCE check on the fields you expect can never find these. Nobody looks for `ok` on a place refusal, so nobody discovers it is missing, and nobody looks for `role` either. The irregularity is only visible when the four shapes are put side by side — which is what `Object.keys(r).sort().join(',')` forces and what no amount of `typeof rf.gap === 'number'` ever will.

beads.title: An added-key control is the obvious one and the COPY control is the one that bites — it is the only one that proves the comparator is not identity
beads.body:
The ticket asks for 'at least one CONTROL proving the comparator can see a difference — a spread-with-an-extra-key must not compare equal'. That is necessary and it is the weaker of the two controls that section needs.

Every assertion in §11 is `kset(x) === literal`. The failure mode the ticket names is a comparator stuck on a constant, and the extra-key control closes it. The failure mode it does NOT name is a comparator that is accidentally about the OBJECT rather than about its fields — one that compared identity, or memoised on the object, or (the realistic version) that a later refactor turns into `refusalsEqual(a, b)` doing something structural. Against any of those, `kset({ ...sample })` and `kset(sample)` must be EQUAL, and the extra-key control says nothing about it: two different objects with different key sets are distinguished by identity comparison too.

So the pair is: a spread copy compares EQUAL, a spread-plus-one compares UNEQUAL. Together they pin that the function is a pure function of the key set and nothing else. I added a third — a spread-minus-`blame` compares unequal — which is weaker than the other two and cheap, and its real job is to state that the assertion is bidirectional, since 'fails when a field is ADDED as well as when one is removed' is the entire reason the ticket exists.

GENERAL SHAPE: when a section's assertions all have the form `f(x) === literal`, the controls needed are not one but two, and they point in opposite directions — something that must differ, and something that must NOT. Only the second one rules out a comparator that is over-sensitive, and an over-sensitive comparator is the version that fails correct work, which this repo has already recorded as worse than no checker.

beads.title: Wrote the field-list table into the MODULE header too, not only into the gate
beads.body:
The ticket names two bounded paths and describes work in only one of them. I edited both, and the reasoning is the ticket's own premise turned round.

The WHY paragraph says the drift is likelier here than one layer down because `_attribute` ADDS fields, 'and nothing asserts what that union is'. True — and nothing STATES it either. `placement.mjs`'s docstring names its per-reason shapes and `placement.selftest.mjs` §8 pins them, and that pairing is exactly what made lp-53afb4 able to find the `metric`/`role` irregularities: a claim to check the assertions against. `summon-session.mjs` had a long, careful header about `summonSeed` and `first`/`refusal` and no field list at all, so §11's ten literals would have been the only statement of the contract anywhere — assertions with nothing to disagree with.

The ledger's most-repeated lesson about this file family is that the gap that matters is BETWEEN THE DOCSTRING AND THE ASSERTIONS (lp-c46a0c, and the `legalSummon` 'every refusal carries summonSeed' sentence that the metric refusal falsified). A gate with no stated promise beside it cannot exhibit that gap; it can only be right. So the header now carries the table, the three irregularities, and the two reasons that are unreachable by construction, and it names §11 as what pins them.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: if a reviewer judges that a table in a comment is a second copy that will drift from the literals in the gate. That is a real objection and the honest answer is that it will drift the same way any docstring does — the mitigation is that they sit one grep apart and that the gate fails loudly, not that the duplication is free. I judged a stated-and-checked contract better than a checked-but-unstated one; the reverse call is to delete the table and leave §11's literals as the sole statement.

WHAT I DID NOT DO, deliberately: I did not fix either irregularity. `role` is genuinely derivable on the place path (`summonSeed === 0` is the centre by construction) and `ok` could be made uniform in either direction. A turn sent to PIN a set of shapes that then changes those shapes has written both sides of its own gate, which is the specific cheat this ledger warns about. Both are proposed below against this same, now-stronger gate.

beads.title: The three unreachable reasons were handled three DIFFERENT ways, and only one of them is honest as a skip
beads.body:
§11 has to say something about `closure`, `nav`, `empty` and `metric`, none of which any fixture can guarantee. Treating them uniformly would have been wrong — they are unreachable for three different reasons and each admits a different strength of claim.

  · `closure` / `nav` — NOT DECIDABLE BEFORE THE REBUILD. They may occur on some fixture and not on this one, and nothing can force them. Synthesised through `_attribute` with a hand-written raw refusal, exactly as §10 already does for the no-index exemption. This is the weakest of the three, and it is the best available: the raw shape (`{ reason, points }`) is a two-field object read straight off `reformPocketAll` line 953, so the only thing being trusted is that I transcribed two field names.

  · `empty` — UNREACHABLE FROM THE SESSION BUT TRIVIALLY REACHABLE FROM THE KERNEL, because `place()` always hands over a non-empty constellation. So the RAW refusal is taken from a real `reformPocketAll(S.pocket, [])` call and only the `_attribute` step is synthetic. That is strictly stronger than hand-writing `{ reason: 'empty' }`, and it costs one line. Worth doing wherever it is available: a synthetic fixture that could have been a real one is a transcription risk taken for no reason.

  · `metric` — UNREACHABLE BY CONSTRUCTION, which is a different kind of statement entirely and the only one that can be asserted rather than narrated. The ticket asks to 'say so out loud rather than skipping quietly'. Saying so is a comment; PROVING it is asserting the construction — `preview`'s `con.aniso === pocket.opts.aniso` — because that identity is precisely why `legalSummon`'s mismatch branch cannot fire. Plus the negative, that no refusal on either verb's fixture has `reason === 'metric'`.

THE TRANSFERABLE RULE: 'this case cannot occur here' is not one claim, it is three, and they are worth different amounts. If it cannot occur BY CONSTRUCTION, assert the construction — that is a real check and it goes red if the construction is ever weakened. If it cannot occur BY FIXTURE LUCK, synthesise, and say which part of the synthesis is trusted. If a neighbouring layer can produce it cheaply, get it from there rather than typing it. A section that treats all three as 'skipped' throws away two claims it could have made.

beads.title: Give a place-path per-seed refusal its `role`, the same way it was given its `summonSeed`
evidence: rejected: REJECTED ON TWO GROUNDS, and the first is a concrete defect rather than a priority call. (1) THE TICKET'S OWN ACCEPTANCE CRITERION IS WRONG, and following it fails the gate. The body says 'the two place literals ... GAIN role and nothing else' and quotes exactly two: `at,axis,blame,clamped,depth,limit,point,reason,summonSeed,value,wall` (summon-session.selftest.mjs:869, place 'hull') and `at,blame

beads.title: Pin the exact key set of every refusal record `level.mjs` and `pocketLevel.mjs` emit — the third and fourth producers of refusal-shaped objects, neither with a field list anywhere
evidence: rejected: REJECTED as the third consecutive proposal of one shape, aimed at the two modules with the fewest readers in the tree. I grepped for importers: `level.mjs` and `pocketLevel.mjs` are imported by their own selftests and by nothing else. Not index.html, not campaign.mjs, not level-view.js, not summon-view.js. A field list is worth pinning because a CALLER branches on it — that is the entire argument

beads.title: The ticket asked for two contradictory gate assertions — I took the later one (ships EMPTY), because a DOM equality is both unreachable here and weaker than what replaces it
beads.body:
lp-ef6599's gate requirements contain a contradiction that has to be resolved before anything can be written:

  · 'the extracted #gameIntro text equals INTRO.blurb'
  · '...assert the element ships EMPTY and the block writes it from the export'

Those cannot both hold. An element that ships empty extracts as the empty string.

I took the second, for three reasons and only the first is about the ticket. (1) It is the later, more considered paragraph — it arrives after the ticket has just talked itself out of `!html.includes(INTRO.blurb)`, so it is the sentence written with the problem in view. (2) The first is not reachable: index-campaign-wiring reads index.html as TEXT in node. There is no element and no textContent. (3) The ledger already settled the general question for lp-3302ee's LINES: 'rendered by reference is not a weaker proxy for equal at runtime — it is the property that makes runtime equality unfalsifiable.' A DOM assertion compares two strings and passes for a page that hardcoded a byte-identical copy; a by-reference render cannot be unequal.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a DOM harness (jsdom or a headless browser) arriving in plant/test/. At that point the runtime equality becomes available and is worth adding — but as an ADDITION, not a replacement, because it would still not forbid the page from owning a sentence.

The general shape, and it is worth more than this instance: when a ticket names a runtime equality its harness cannot reach, the question is not 'what is the closest available proxy' but 'can the code be restructured so the equality is unnecessary'. Here it could, and the restructure is the deliverable rather than a workaround for it.

beads.title:
Added a second mount for INTRO.title rather than repurposing

Plant

— the masthead is a product name, not game copy
beads.body:
The ticket requires the page to render INTRO.title AND INTRO.blurb by reference. The page had exactly one candidate heading, `

Plant

`, and INTRO.title is 'Get everything fed'. Two options: (a) fill the existing h1 from INTRO.title — the product name disappears from the page; (b) add `

` between the h1 and the intro paragraph. I took (b). 'Plant' is the site's name and is not game copy: it is not subject to INTRO's prose rules, it does not go stale when a level is retuned, and no gate anywhere asserts it (I grepped all 8 test files that read index.html — none mentions h1 or the masthead). Deleting it to satisfy a ticket about the intro sentence would be a drive-by change to something the ticket did not name. (b) also matches campaign.mjs's own stated intent for the field names: 'a LEVELS entry's (title, blurb) on purpose, so the page can render the intro screen and a level screen with the same two lines.' A title mount beside a blurb mount mirrors gameTitle/gameBlurb exactly, which is the shape the module was written for. COST, stated plainly: the first screen now carries three headings in a row — 'Plant', 'Get everything fed', then the level's own title. That may read as clutter and I cannot judge it without a browser; it is the ask below. WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: one line. `$('gameIntroTitle').textContent = INTRO.title` becomes `$('gameHeading')...` or the h2 is deleted and the h1 filled instead — the gate's two title assertions would need their id changed and nothing else. That reversibility is why I chose the additive option: per vision.md's standing rule, when it is a matter of taste, pick the option that is easier to reverse.

beads.title: Removing the last consumer of BANNED from the wiring gate opens an attractive wrong repair: a block-wide sweep would fail on the block's own comments
beads.body:
§(8) was the only place index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs used BANNED, so wiring the intro to the module leaves that import unused. The obvious instinct is to keep the coverage by widening the check — sweep the whole campaign block for banned vocabulary instead of just the intro paragraph.

THAT CHECK CANNOT PASS, and it fails for a reason that has nothing to do with what a visitor reads. The block's own comments discuss the design in exactly the vocabulary BANNED forbids: 'its own call to the oracle', 'The page never grades a network', 'no second verdict'. BANNED exists to keep words like 'oracle' and 'feasibility' off the SCREEN; a text gate cannot tell a rendered string from a comment, so a block-wide sweep would go red on prose that is doing its job. It would then be relaxed or deleted, and this tree already records that a checker which fails correct work is worse than no checker.

So I removed BANNED from the import and left a comment at the import site saying both halves: where the rule went (campaign.selftest.mjs §2b, against the export, which is the stronger home because the export is the single owner) and that the sweep is not the replacement and must not be added.

THE TRANSFERABLE HALF: when a relocation makes a check vacuous at the old site, the danger is not the lost coverage — it is that the next reader tries to restore it by widening the SUBJECT. A property that was meaningful about one rendered string is usually meaningless about the file that renders it, because the file also contains the reasoning. Say so at the import, where the unused symbol is the thing that prompts the question.

beads.title: Eight gates read index.html and only one touches #gameIntro — checked first, because the last page-relocation ticket was rejected for breaking four it never named
beads.body:
The ledger records lp-250e23 being rejected because it 'breaks a passing gate it never names', and that the rejection itself UNDERCOUNTED — four gates read index.html as text, not one. That cost a whole ticket cycle.

So before editing anything I grepped for every test file reading index.html: summon-view, index-summon-wiring, level-view, campaign, index-campaign-wiring, and index-level4/5/6-wiring — eight. Then grepped all of them for the things this change touches: `gameIntro`, `BANNED`, `h1`, `sub"`. Only index-campaign-wiring matches, at §(6)'s id list and §(8).

Why this change is genuinely narrow, unlike that one: it DELETES no mount and RENAMES nothing. §(6)'s `id="gameIntro"` presence check still passes (the element is still there, just empty), and `id="gameIntro"` does not falsely match the new `id="gameIntroTitle"` because the closing quote is part of the pattern. index-summon-wiring finds its block positionally from `indexOf('import { SummonSession')` to end of file, and everything I touched is far above that anchor.

The check cost two greps and it is the difference between a ticket that lands and a ticket that is rejected for collateral nobody enumerated. Worth doing on any change to index.html, permanently — the page is read as text by eight independent gates and none of them declares itself in the page.

beads.title: The four new negations needed a control, because `!html.includes(undefined)` passes
beads.body:
Six of §(8)'s assertions after this change are negations: no quoted string written into either mount, and INTRO's two strings absent from the page source. A negation passes silently over an empty or missing subject, and there are two independent ways that happens here.

(1) A mis-sliced `block` — already covered, the marker section pins `block.length > 400`.

(2) AN INTRO FIELD THAT CAME BACK UNDEFINED. This one is specific and nastier than it looks: `html.includes(undefined)` does not throw. It coerces the argument to the string 'undefined', searches for that, and finds nothing — so `!html.includes(INTRO.blurb)` returns TRUE and prints a tick for an INTRO whose blurb does not exist. The two `includes` assertions are exactly the ones that would be satisfied by the export vanishing, which is the opposite of what they are for.

So the section ends with a control asserting both fields are non-empty strings. It is three lines and it is what makes the four negations claims rather than tautologies.

Note that campaign.selftest.mjs §2b already asserts INTRO's fields are non-empty. That is not a reason to omit it here: this gate must not depend on another gate having run, and the assertion is about whether THIS FILE's negations have a subject, which is a different claim from whether INTRO is well-formed. A negation and its control belong in the same section or the pairing is invisible.

beads.title: Neither gate was run — what is specific to this unrun turn is that there is no arithmetic in it at all, only regex-against-bytes
beads.body:
The standing 'gate unverifiable in-turn' recommendation is in this ledger well past twenty-five times and recent turns agreed to stop restating it. I am not restating it. What is worth one entry is that this turn's risk profile has NO numbers in it whatsoever, so the many prior instances that reason about whether a hand-computed value is right do not transfer. Three things could have gone wrong and each was checked mechanically:

1. REGEX AGAINST BYTES. Every new pattern was traced character-by-character against the exact lines I wrote, AFTER re-reading them from disk rather than against my intention. The one worth naming: `/\$\('gameIntro'\)\.textContent\s*=\s*INTRO\.blurb\s*;/` must not be confused by the neighbouring `gameIntroTitle` line — it is not, because the closing quote is inside the pattern, so `gameIntro'` cannot match `gameIntroT`. Same reasoning protects §(6)'s existing `id="gameIntro"` check.

2. LEXICAL. A parse error kills every assertion and reads like an unrelated typo. No backtick nested inside a template literal was added; no ASCII apostrophe inside a single-quoted string (the typographic form is used in prose, matching house style); the two regexes containing a bare backtick inside `['\"`]` are regex literals, where a backtick is an ordinary class character — and line 352 of this same file already ships that exact form and passes, which is why I reused it rather than inventing an escape.

3. REGEX STATE. No /g flag on anything used with .test(), so no lastIndex can persist between calls. This is the only defect in the diff that would have produced a confidently wrong PASS rather than a red gate.

WHAT REMAINS GENUINELY UNCHECKED and is not closable without a browser: that the two mounts paint, and that three stacked headings on the first screen read acceptably. The first is mechanical and near-certain; the second is taste and is the ask.

beads.title: Does the first screen now carry one heading too many?
beads.body:
The page opens with three headings stacked before any control: 'Plant' (the h1 masthead, hand-typed and legitimately so), 'Get everything fed' (INTRO.title, new this turn), then the current level's own title from the module — e.g. 'Ore to gears'. Plus INTRO's sentence and the level's blurb between them.

I cannot settle this from here and it is not a gate question. Every machine-checkable property holds: the words are the module's, they are one sentence, they use no banned vocabulary, they name no level. Whether a stranger reads three headings as orientation or as throat-clearing before the game is a judgement about a rendered page, and this turn has no browser and no person.

I chose the additive shape deliberately because it is the cheapest to reverse — see the decision in this outbox. The alternative is to fill the h1 from INTRO.title and drop 'Plant' from the page, which is one line in index.html plus an id change in two assertions.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com on a phone and on a laptop. Read from the top without scrolling.

WATCH FOR: Whether you reach the control within a few seconds, or whether the second heading makes you skim past the level's own title. Also whether losing the word 'Plant' from the page would cost anything you care about.

SO THAT: If it reads as clutter I fill the h1 from INTRO.title and delete the h2 — the game's heading becomes the page's heading, one line plus two assertion ids. If it reads fine I leave it and the shape is settled for whatever the first screen becomes next. If the answer is that the whole intro should be hidden once a level is entered, that is a different and larger ticket about the first screen being a screen rather than a paragraph above one, and I would file it against the campaign panel rather than against INTRO.

beads.title: Give the summon block explicit BEGIN/END markers, so its gate stops depending on where the block sits in the page
beads.body:
index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs finds the code it grades POSITIONALLY — `html.indexOf('import { SummonSession')` to end of file — and its own closing note admits the dependency. index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs does not: it anchors on `// CAMPAIGN BLOCK BEGIN` / `// CAMPAIGN BLOCK END` and says why, in a header paragraph that is worth copying verbatim: 'Restructuring the page around a positional anchor can fail a gate that is entirely correct, and a checker that fails correct work is worse than no checker.'

This is not hypothetical for this page. The ledger records that lp-a59b0f's gate found the summon block positionally and that MOVING the summon panel above the constellation inspector would have put the inspector's own solid picker and its 1.5/2.2 defaults on the wrong side of the delimiter, failing negative assertions that were correct. The page is under active first-screen work (vision item 1), so it will be reordered again.

SCOPE: plant/index.html (add two comment markers around the summon block), plant/test/index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs (slice between them instead of from indexOf to EOF; update the header note that admits the positional dependency).

WHAT THE GATE MUST STILL DO, and this is the part that makes it a real ticket rather than a tidy-up: EVERY existing assertion must keep its wording and its intent, changing only how `block` is obtained. The negative assertions are the ones at risk — 'no solid name hand-typed in the block', 'no placement threshold re-typed' — because a marker placed too narrowly silently shrinks the subject and every negation then passes for free. So the change must also assert the slice is non-trivial (`block.length > N`), exactly as the campaign gate's marker section does, or the relocation weakens the gate while looking like a refactor.

CLASS-A: `node plant/test/index-summon-wiring.selftest.mjs` exists and passes today, and this ticket must leave it passing.

beads.title: plant/CLAUDE.md still describes the first screen as page-owned prose — record that every word on it now comes from campaign.mjs
beads.body:
plant/CLAUDE.md's `index.html` paragraph describes the campaign panel in detail (one level at a time, the control built by index, the three control shapes) and says nothing about who owns the first screen's WORDS. That was accurate when written and is now the last undocumented half of a three-ticket sequence: · lp-ffddc7 wrote INTRO into campaign.mjs, fully gated, and nothing rendered it; · lp-3302ee moved the two game-state sentences into LINES and rendered them by reference; · lp-ef6599 (this turn) did the same for INTRO, so the campaign panel now contains NO hand-typed copy at all — level titles and blurbs were already asserted absent, both state sentences are LINES, and the intro is INTRO. The only hand-typed visible text left above the game is the `

Plant

` masthead, which is a product name rather than game copy. WHY IT IS WORTH A TICKET RATHER THAN A COMMENT. This tree has four recorded instances of prose that outlived the code it described (summon-session.mjs's NaN header, summon-view.js's first/refusal header, and two sentences in this very file, one of them in the future tense describing work that had already landed). Every one was found by an agent reading the file for an unrelated reason. plant/CLAUDE.md is the file every turn reads FIRST to orient itself, so a gap there costs more than a gap anywhere else — and the specific risk here is a future turn 'fixing' the first screen by typing a better sentence into the markup, which is precisely the failure mode the last three tickets were spent closing. SCOPE: plant/CLAUDE.md only. HONEST ABOUT THE GATE, because this is the weak part and the proposal should not pretend otherwise: `node plant/test/docs.selftest.mjs` exists and passes, but it only walks the markdown for unresolved merge conflicts — it is explicitly NOT a documentation linter and its own header says it must not grow into one, because 'does this paragraph still describe the code' is undecidable. So the gate proves the edit does not corrupt the file; it cannot prove the paragraph is right. A human or a reviewing turn reading the diff is the only real check, and that is the correct trade for a documentation ticket rather than a reason to skip it.

beads.title: INTRO.title had no mount point anywhere — the ticket asked the page to render it and the element did not exist
beads.body:
The ticket says the gate must check that 'the page renders `INTRO.title` and `INTRO.blurb` by reference'. It is written as if both were already on screen and only the sentence needed rewiring. Only the sentence had an element. `INTRO` has carried a `title` ('Get everything fed') since lp-ffddc7, and campaign.mjs's own header explains why — 'the field names are a LEVELS entry's (`title`, `blurb`) on purpose, so the page can render the intro screen and a level screen with the same two lines'. The level screen does exactly that, with `#gameTitle` and `#gameBlurb`. The intro screen had `#gameIntro` and nothing else. So half of a deliberately symmetric export has been unrendered since it was written, and the ticket inherited the blind spot. The obvious candidate for the missing mount is the existing `

Plant

`, and it is the wrong one. That heading is the SURFACE's name — this page is plant.minomobi.com and also carries the constellation inspector below the game — while INTRO.title is what the GAME asks of you. Putting the game's headline in the page's only h1 would have made the inspector a section of a document titled 'Get everything fed'. So a new `

` was added. Worth noting for whoever reads the diff: this is the one part of this ticket that is a DESIGN addition rather than a relocation, and it is why the diff touches the markup above the campaign panel as well as inside it. THE TRANSFERABLE HALF: when a ticket says 'render X and Y by reference', check that there is somewhere to render each of them. A wiring ticket authored from a finding about ONE field will describe the export as though every field were symmetric with it, and the sibling field is exactly the thing nobody has looked at — because if anyone had, it would already be on screen.

beads.title: `!html.includes(INTRO.blurb)` is the departure check AND would be the wrong arrival check — a render-by-reference move inverts the usual rule
beads.body:
This tree's standing rule for relocation work is absence at the source, presence at the destination. For a move of CODE that is straightforward. For a move of WORDS into a module the page renders by reference, the two halves land in different artefacts and the naive form of each is wrong. The arrival cannot be `html.includes(INTRO.blurb)`: the page contains the sentence only after paint, and never in source. Asserting it would forbid the very thing the ticket asks for. The ticket says so explicitly and it is worth restating because the instinct is strong — a text gate's usual move is 'the words are there'. So the arrival is two claims instead of one: the mount ships EMPTY in source (`

`), and the block ASSIGNS from the export (`$('gameIntro').textContent = INTRO.blurb`). Neither alone is sufficient — an empty element with no assignment is a blank first screen, and an assignment into an element that ships with words is two owners. And the departure IS `!html.includes(INTRO.blurb)`, which is the same expression the arrival could not use, pointed the other way. It also catches more than it looks: because the needle comes from the export, a page that kept its OLD paragraph fails on the empty-mount check rather than on this one, and a page that hand-copies the NEW wording fails on this one. The two together leave no room for a second copy of either string. The control that matters: both departure checks are negations over a needle from another module, so a degenerate needle would make them meaningless (`html.includes('')` is true for every file, so an empty needle fails CLOSED — but a one-character one would almost certainly be present and also fail closed, and a reader should not have to work that out). §(8) asserts the needles' lengths and says why in a comment.

beads.title: Two prose passages now justify a live RULE with a page that no longer exists — and one of them is inside the gate that enforces it
beads.body:
campaign.mjs's INTRO docstring and campaign.selftest.mjs §2b both defend the count rule by pointing at the page's hand-typed intro:

  campaign.mjs:104-109  "index.html's own hand-typed intro — 'Each level gives you one setting to move' — would fail this check, which is the honest way to say what it costs"
  campaign.selftest.mjs:55-58  "index.html's own hand-typed intro would fail this. If you are here because a sentence you like was rejected, reword the sentence…"

As of this turn there is no hand-typed intro. The sentence quoted in campaign.mjs is deleted from the page, so the example is now a claim about a string that exists nowhere.

WHY THIS INSTANCE IS WORSE THAN THE THREE ALREADY IN THE LEDGER (summon-session.mjs's NaN header, summon-view.js's `first`/`refusal` header, plant/CLAUDE.md's two sentences). Those were DESCRIPTIONS that went stale. These two are JUSTIFICATIONS for a rule that is still enforced, and one of them sits in the gate file next to the assertion, addressed to the next person whose sentence the rule rejects. A stale description misinforms; a stale justification invites the reader to conclude the rule was aimed at a problem that has been solved and can be deleted. The count rule is exactly the sort of assertion that gets 'tidied' by whoever it next inconveniences, and its own defence now reads as obsolete.

The fix is small and it is a REWORDING, not a deletion — the example is still the clearest illustration of what the rule costs, it just needs the past tense and the reason it is no longer in the page. Both files are outside this ticket's bounded paths (the ticket says campaign.mjs needing a change would be a signal the wording decision was going the wrong way, which it was not), so this is proposed rather than done. Filed as a proposal rather than a comment because this ledger's own lesson is that a note in a comment is not a queue.

beads.title: A Grep result showed `/` where the source has `//` — SECOND observed instance, and this time I knew to check
beads.body:
Grepping campaign.selftest.mjs returned:

    164-  / string and asserting things it is like: short enough, no banned word. That

A single forward slash beginning a line inside a comment block. If real, that line would be a syntax error, campaign.selftest.mjs would not parse, and one of this ticket's two gates would die with a message about a comment — an extremely attractive explanation to file, especially for a turn that cannot run anything.

It is not real. `Read` on the same line shows `//`. The tool rendering dropped a character.

The ledger already records this exact false positive from a different file (foam/foamworld.js's `// NaN also lands here`), with the rule: never file a lexical or syntactic defect on the strength of a search tool's rendering; confirm the bytes with a direct read first. This is the second sighting, in a different file, in a different session — so it is a reproducible property of the tooling rather than a one-off glitch, and it lands specifically on `//` at the start of a rendered continuation line, which is the most common shape in this codebase's heavily-commented test files.

Worth escalating from 'a rule I follow' to 'a rule with a known frequency': anyone grepping .mjs files here will hit this, it always looks like a fatal parse error, and it always appears while you are hunting for one.

beads.title:
INTRO.title gets a new `

` and `

Plant

` stays
beads.body:
CHOSEN: add an empty h2 between the h1 and the intro paragraph, filled from INTRO.title.

REJECTED — render INTRO.title into the existing `<h1>`. It is the smaller diff and it is wrong: the h1 names the SURFACE (plant.minomobi.com, which also serves the constellation inspector below the game), and INTRO.title names the GAME's objective. Retitling the page 'Get everything fed' would make the inspector a subsection of the game's headline, and it discards the only place the surface's own name appears on screen.

REJECTED — fold the title into the intro paragraph (e.g. a `<strong>` inside it). That would break the extraction the gate needs and, worse, make the paragraph hold two exports, so a future check on either has to parse the other out.

REJECTED — do not render INTRO.title at all, and gate only the sentence. That is the minimum that satisfies the ticket's headline assertion, and it leaves half a deliberately symmetric export unused with nothing saying so — the state that produced this finding in the first place.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a person looking at the page and finding two headings above the level panel too heavy. It is one line of markup and one line of script to remove, and the gate's two title assertions come out with them; nothing else depends on the element. Styled inline (`font-size:1.15rem`) rather than by a new CSS rule, deliberately, so removing it leaves no orphaned selector — this tree already has a recorded case of an id-keyed rule outliving the elements it was written for.

beads.title: Neither gate was run — the two regexes I would look at first, and the one hazard I engineered out
beads.body:
No Bash. The standing recommendation is in this ledger well past twenty-five times and recent turns agreed to stop restating it; I am not restating it. What is worth an entry is which of MY assertions could go red for a reason unrelated to the code, because this diff contains no arithmetic at all — the risks here are lexical and regex-shaped. WOULD LOOK AT FIRST: 1. `/]*id="gameIntroTitle"[^>]*><\/h2>/`. This is the only assertion about an element that did not exist before this turn, so there is no adjacent proven case to lean on. Traced against the exact bytes: `

` — `]*` takes ` `, the id literal matches, `[^>]*` takes the style attribute (which contains no `>`), then `><\/h2>`. Holds. The companion hazard is that `id="gameIntroTitle"` CONTAINS `id="gameIntro` as a prefix; section (6)'s existing loop builds `id="gameIntro"` WITH the closing quote, so it does not match the new element and still matches the paragraph. Checked explicitly because a false match there would have been silent. 2. `/st\.finished[\s\S]{0,80}?LINES\.finished/` — not mine, but my edit inserted lines into the same block, and a bounded-distance regex is the one kind that layout can break. It spans lines 382-384 and my insertion is at 445, well after it. Unaffected. ENGINEERED OUT — A STANDALONE DIGIT IN THE CAMPAIGN BLOCK. Section (5) derives a forbidden set of control-bound literals from `LEVELS` at run time and tests each against the block with `(?

beads.title: The page owns no prose — assert it as ONE invariant instead of three sentence-by-sentence checks
beads.body:
WHAT IS TRUE NOW AND IS NOT ASSERTED AS A RULE. After lp-3302ee and lp-ef6599, every word on the campaign panel is a campaign.mjs export rendered by reference: the level title and blurb, the two game-state lines, and the first screen's title and sentence. index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs checks that ONE SENTENCE AT A TIME — a per-string assertion for each of the five, each added by the turn that moved that string.

So the fourth sentence somebody types into the page is not caught. Nothing asserts the INVARIANT; five assertions assert five instances of it, and a sixth mount point with a hardcoded paragraph in it passes every one.

THE CHECK, and it is available from a text gate without a browser. Inside the campaign block, every assignment to a `.textContent` or `.innerHTML` must have a right-hand side that is either an export reference, a template literal composed only of module values, or the empty string — never a quoted run of English. Concretely: extract every `textContent =` / `innerHTML =` right-hand side in the block, and fail any whose value contains a quoted string of more than ~3 words. The existing per-string checks stay (they name WHICH export goes WHERE, which the invariant cannot), so this is an addition, not a replacement.

WHY IT IS WORTH A TICKET RATHER THAN A HABIT. The ledger records the underlying hole three times in three different words: 'it checks a property of the text, never that it is the RIGHT text', 'a check that cannot fail is indistinguishable from a check that passes', and the MOVE precedent about absence at the source. Each time the fix was applied to the one string in front of the turn. This is the general form, and it is the cheap moment to write it — right after the last hand-typed string left the page, so the check passes on arrival and every future one is caught on the day it lands.

THE PART THAT NEEDS CARE, stated so the turn does not weaken it: the block legitimately contains short quoted strings — `'next level'`, `'finish'`, `'lvl-verdict '`, class names, ids, `''`. A word-count threshold is a heuristic and a heuristic that cries wolf gets deleted. Two controls are required: a hand-written right-hand side of a real sentence MUST be caught, and every string the block ships today MUST NOT be.
