If those two cannot both hold with one threshold, the honest version is an allowlist of the short UI words with a comment saying why each is there — which is still a rule, and still catches a paragraph.

Also worth deciding in the body rather than in the code: whether `'next level'` and `'finish'` should themselves move into campaign.mjs. They are game vocabulary the module arguably owns, and moving them would make the invariant clean rather than threshold-dependent. That is a second ticket if the answer is yes.

Bounded paths: plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs, and plant/index.html only if a short string needs relocating.

beads.title: Two live rules are justified by a page that no longer exists — correct the tense in campaign.mjs and campaign.selftest.mjs
beads.body:
campaign.mjs:104-109 and campaign.selftest.mjs:55-58 both defend INTRO's count rule by pointing at index.html's hand-typed intro, and campaign.mjs quotes it verbatim: "index.html's own hand-typed intro — 'Each level gives you one setting to move' — would fail this check". lp-ef6599 deleted that paragraph. The page now renders INTRO by reference and owns no first-screen text at all, so both passages defend a live rule with an example that exists nowhere.

WHY THIS IS NOT ORDINARY DOC ROT. The ledger has three recorded instances of prose describing a tree the code has left; all three were DESCRIPTIONS. These are JUSTIFICATIONS for an assertion that is still enforced, and one of them is inside the gate file, addressed to the next person the rule rejects ('If you are here because a sentence you like was rejected, reword the sentence or change this list ON PURPOSE'). A reader who checks the cited example, finds it gone, and concludes the rule was aimed at a problem now solved will delete the assertion — which that same comment explicitly warns is the one move that makes the check worthless. Stale justification is more dangerous than stale description because it argues for its own removal.

THE FIX IS A REWORDING AND EXPLICITLY NOT A DELETION. The example is still the clearest statement of what the count rule costs — a writer has to reach for 'a single control' instead of 'one setting'. It needs the past tense plus one clause saying the page no longer holds any intro text of its own, because that is the outcome the rule produced and it is the strongest argument for keeping it. Both passages should also stop implying a comparison the reader can go and check.

SCOPE: plant/campaign.mjs (prose only — INTRO's values must not change; they are frozen, gated and now rendered on the live page) and plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs (prose only — §2b's assertions must not change).

WHAT THE GATE PROVES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT, said plainly: running campaign.selftest.mjs proves the edit changed no behaviour, which for a prose-only diff is the whole of what a machine can check. Whether the new wording is CLEARER is not gateable and a reviewer reading the diff is the only judge of it. That is a weak gate honestly described, not a strong one claimed — and the alternative (leaving it) has a recorded cost in this ledger of turns spent trusting a stale paragraph.

beads.title: Split the MARK off the words rather than giving LINES a third sentence — chosen because it changes no existing string at all
beads.body:
The ticket offered two shapes and asked the turn to decide. I took "the page renders the factory sentence without a completion glyph" over "LINES gains a third line that replaces".

WHY, in order of weight:

1. IT ADDS NO NEW PROSE. A third LINES entry is a new sentence, and every string in that export is held to four rules (one sentence, no banned word, no level id, counts nothing) plus §2c's exact-key-set assertion `['finished','untouched']`, which the addition would have broken. So the cheaper-looking option required editing a passing gate and writing prose no gate can judge the quality of.

2. IT LOSES NO INFORMATION. Replacing the verdict on an untouched level hides "with 2% to spare (tight)" — the only thing on screen that tells a player how close the factory is. Dropping the mark keeps the whole account and removes only the claim that was false.

3. `line` IS BYTE-IDENTICAL AFTER THE REFACTOR, in all three branches, because the old literals were exactly `'\u2717 ' + body` and `'\u2713 ' + body`. That is provable by reading, and it means three other gates that assert on `line` (playthrough.selftest.mjs, campaign §10/§11, wiring §2 and §(9c)) could not be affected. The replacing shape would have changed what `line` renders to and needed each of them re-argued.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: delete `plain` from `verdict()`'s return and change the page's ternary back to `v.line`. Two lines. The `plain()`/`sentence()` split can stay either way — it is a decomposition, not a behaviour change.

WHAT I DID NOT DO: touch the finished branch. `${v.line} ${LINES.finished}` is left verbatim, so §(9c)'s four assertions are untouched, and it is defensible on its own — the next button only appears on `won`, so the end of the game is by construction a state that was won and the mark belongs there.

beads.title: A two-state fixture proves nothing about MARKS unless both states share the same factory verdict — my first choice of winning setting differed in its numbers too
beads.body:
The ticket requires the rendered output to be driven at both `ok && !won` and `ok && won` and to DIFFER. The obvious fixture is the one §(9b) already uses:

    k.samples.find((s) => k.key(s) !== k.key(k.start) && grade(entry, s).ok)

On level1 that returns rate 50, not 119: the sweep is ascending from 10, and 50 is the first winning setting (scale = min(51, 50) = 50 against demand 50, margin exactly 0). So the won state's sentence reads "with nothing to spare" while the opening reads "with 2% to spare". The two strings differ — and they differ IN THEIR NUMBERS. The assertion would have passed for an implementation that never removed a mark at all, because two different margins produce two different sentences regardless.

That is the same shape this ledger records for `line.includes(String(x))` passing against a hardcoded threshold: the check looks discriminating and is satisfied by an irrelevant difference.

THE FIXTURE THAT BITES is a winning setting whose factory verdict is WORD-FOR-WORD the opening's, found by an extra clause rather than by hardcoding:

    && grade(c.entry, s).margin === before.margin

On level1 that is rate 51 — for every s >= 51 the smelter's capacity binds at 51, so the margin is the identical double 0.02 and `plain()` returns the identical string. The section then asserts `won.plain === before.plain` FIRST, and only then that `shown(won) === MARK.ok + ' ' + shown(before)`. With the words pinned equal, the whole of the remaining difference is provably the mark.

TRANSFERABLE: when a test claims "X is the only difference between these two states", the fixture has to hold everything else equal, and an oracle-chosen fixture usually does not. Assert the equality of the parts that must not differ before asserting the difference you are about.

beads.title: My own comment typed the glyph into the block and would have failed the assertion I was writing in the same turn
beads.body:
§(9d) asserts `!block.includes(MARK.ok)` — no mark of the page's own, in code OR in a comment, checked against the module's export rather than a retyped character. I wrote that assertion and, three edits earlier, had written a comment in `index.html` opening with the tick glyph itself to explain what the branch is for.

So the check would have gone red on its own documentation. That is the failure mode the ledger already records for the merge-conflict gate ("a document explaining conflict markers has to QUOTE them, and a check that forbids its own documentation gets an exception carved into it by the next turn, badly") — and here it arrived from the other direction: not a doc that trips a check, but a check whose author tripped it while justifying it.

I resolved it the strict way rather than by exempting comments: the comment now says "the tick" in words and the rule stays absolute over the whole block. An exemption for comments would have needed a comment-stripping pass over the page text, which is a parser this gate has no business containing, and the rule "no mark byte anywhere in the block" is trivial to comply with and impossible to misread.

WORTH NOTING FOR THE NEXT PERSON: the glyph does still appear in `index.html` at line 235, in the CONSTELLATION INSPECTOR, which sits before `// CAMPAIGN BLOCK BEGIN` and is therefore outside what the gate slices. The comment in the page says so explicitly, because an absolute-sounding rule that is actually scoped is the kind of thing a future reader disproves in one grep and then distrusts.

beads.title: `finished && !won` is unreachable from the page and reachable from the module — the end screen would show a tick for a level nobody won
beads.body:
The page's finished branch renders `${v.line} ${LINES.finished}`, i.e. the MARKED sentence, unconditionally. I left it that way deliberately and the justification is a claim about the page rather than about the module: `next.hidden = !(v.won && !st.finished)`, so a player can only reach `finished` by pressing a button that appears only on `won`.

The module makes no such promise. `next()`'s own docstring says it "does not require a win" on purpose — "the module is mechanism and the page is policy... a module that refuses to advance leaves a stuck stranger with no way out". So a caller that drives `next()` past the last level from an unwon state gets `finished: true` with `won: false`, and the page would then render the fed tick plus "that was the last level" on a level that was never completed. Same contradiction as the one this ticket fixed, one screen further on, reachable only by a caller the page is not.

Not fixed here: the ticket's CONTROL requires the `!ok` state to be unchanged, the finished branch is what §(9c) pins verbatim, and touching it would have put a second unrun edit into a gate I cannot run. Proposed as its own bead with the same two gates, since both already drive `next()` to the latch.

The general half is one this tree keeps meeting: a state that is unreachable THROUGH THE UI is not unreachable, and the module is the thing with the tests. The page's hidden button is an argument, not an invariant.

beads.title: Does a green sentence with no tick read as "not done yet", or does it just read as done without a tick?
beads.body:
The whole of this change is the removal of one character. On the opening screen a stranger now sees, in the page's OK colour: "Everything is fed, with 2% to spare (tight)." and underneath it "The factory already works — move the control and find out what breaks it." No tick, no next button.

I can prove the two states render different strings and that the mark is the only difference. I cannot tell whether the absence of a mark is PERCEIVED at all, or whether the green colour carries the "done" reading on its own and the missing tick simply looks like a rendering bug. That is a question about a person looking at a screen and there is no gate for it. I deliberately did NOT also change the colour: it is one more thing to reverse, and the honest thing is to change one variable and ask about it rather than change two and learn nothing.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, do not touch anything, and read the first screen. Then move the control one notch to a setting that still works and read it again.

WATCH FOR: Whether the first screen reads as "this is already finished" or as "this is fine so far". Specifically: did you notice the tick appear on the second screen, or did you only notice the button?

SO THAT: If the missing tick is invisible and the button is what you noticed, the follow-up is the win SENTENCE (proposed above) and the colour should probably go neutral until won — the mark alone is too quiet to carry the state. If the first screen already reads as unfinished, the win sentence is decoration and the next thing worth a turn is what a player does after level six, not more words on each level.

beads.title: The end screen shows a completion mark for a level that was never won — `finished && !won` is unreachable from the page and reachable from the module
beads.body:
SCOPE (bounded paths): plant/index.html, plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs, plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs.

THE STATE. index.html's finished branch renders `${v.line} ${LINES.finished}` — the MARKED sentence — with no reference to `won`. That is safe today only because `next.hidden = !(v.won && !st.finished)`, so the button that latches `finished` appears only on a win. It is a property of the page, not of the game: `Campaign.next()` deliberately does not require a win (its docstring: "the module is mechanism and the page is policy... a module that refuses to advance leaves a stuck stranger with no way out"), so `finished: true, won: false` is a legal state of the controller and the page renders a tick plus "that was the last level" for a campaign nobody completed.

WHY IT IS WORTH A TICKET RATHER THAN A SHRUG. lp-3f5f26 has just established that the mark is the GAME's claim and not the FACTORY's, and fixed it for the opening screen. This is the identical contradiction on the LAST screen, left in place because that ticket's control forbade touching the finished branch and §(9c) pins its composition verbatim. Leaving it is how the rule becomes "the mark is the game's, except at the end".

THE SHAPE, and it should stay minimal: the finished branch should compose from the SAME chosen string the untouched branch already selects, i.e. the page should pick `plain`/`line` once and append the suffix to whichever it picked, rather than picking twice. That is one expression and it makes the two branches consistent by construction instead of by argument.

WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK:
  · campaign.selftest.mjs: drive `next()` past the last level WITHOUT winning it (the module permits this) and assert the state is reachable — `finished === true && won === false && ok === true` — so the section is not about a corner case nobody can enter.
  · index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs: §(9c)'s existing assertions must be REWRITTEN rather than deleted, per this tree's standing rule for relocation work — the suffix is still the module's, still appended rather than replacing, and the words have still LEFT the page. The new assertion is that the sentence the suffix is appended to is the one the untouched condition selected, captured and read from the source rather than searched for.
  · CONTROL: the ordinary end-of-game path (won, then finish) must still render the marked sentence plus the suffix, unchanged. Without it, the fix is satisfied by a page that never marks anything.

BOTH GATES EXIST AND PASS TODAY: class-a, no new file.

beads.title: A won level says only "Everything is fed" — the game never tells a stranger they finished anything
beads.body:
SCOPE (bounded paths): plant/campaign.mjs, plant/index.html, plant/test/campaign.selftest.mjs, plant/test/index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs.

AFTER lp-3f5f26 the three states a player meets read like this:

    ok, not won   Everything is fed, with 2% to spare (tight).
                  The factory already works — move the control and find out what breaks it.
    ok, won       ✓ Everything is fed, with 2% to spare (tight).      [next level]
    not ok        ✗ depot wanted 50 gear and got 10.

Every one of those sentences is about the FACTORY. Nothing on the page ever says "you did it" — the entire signal that a level was completed is a tick appearing and a button becoming visible. Vision item 1 asks for "a win state you are told about", and a mark changing colour is not being told.

THE SHAPE, and it is the sibling of what LINES already is: a third game-state sentence — `LINES.won`, one sentence, module-owned, held to the same four prose rules §2c applies to the other two — rendered in the same place the nudge is, from the same `won` field the next button already reads. The nudge and the win line are mutually exclusive by construction (`ok && !won` versus `won`), so this is one more branch on a condition the page already has, not a new state machine.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE IN lp-3f5f26: that ticket's whole argument was that the FACTORY's sentence must not learn about the game, and the disciplined answer was to add nothing and remove a claim. Adding words is a separate decision with a separate cost — §2c's exact-key-set assertion `['finished','untouched']` has to be widened, which is an edit to a passing gate and should be its own diff.

WHAT THE GATE MUST CHECK:
  · campaign.selftest.mjs §2c: the new line held to all four prose rules, with the existing key-set assertion widened rather than dropped — an exact set, still, so a fourth line added later cannot arrive unchecked.
  · index-campaign-wiring.selftest.mjs: the words are rendered BY REFERENCE and asserted ABSENT from the page (the rule lp-3302ee established); the branch is captured and read; and the win line and the nudge are shown from conditions that cannot both hold — assert that on a real Campaign at both states, not by reading the source.
  · CONTROL: the `!ok` state shows neither line. Without it, an implementation that shows the win sentence whenever it is not `ok && !won` passes everything else.

WHAT NO GATE CAN CHECK, said plainly: whether the sentence is any good, or whether a stranger wanted to be congratulated at all. It is one sentence for that reason — cheap to throw away when a person finally reads it.

BOTH GATES EXIST AND PASS TODAY: class-a, no new file.

oracle.what: the same seed gives an identical pocket

oracle.what: the walk certificate, par in band

oracle.what: a summon produced the solid it claimed

asks.title: Does a green sentence with no tick read as "not done yet", or does it just read as done without a tick?
asks.body:
The whole of this change is the removal of one character. On the opening screen a stranger now sees, in the page's OK colour: "Everything is fed, with 2% to spare (tight)." and underneath it "The factory already works — move the control and find out what breaks it." No tick, no next button.

I can prove the two states render different strings and that the mark is the only difference. I cannot tell whether the absence of a mark is PERCEIVED at all, or whether the green colour carries the "done" reading on its own and the missing tick simply looks like a rendering bug. That is a question about a person looking at a screen and there is no gate for it. I deliberately did NOT also change the colour: it is one more thing to reverse, and the honest thing is to change one variable and ask about it rather than change two and learn nothing.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, do not touch anything, and read the first screen. Then move the control one notch to a setting that still works and read it again.

WATCH FOR: Whether the first screen reads as "this is already finished" or as "this is fine so far". Specifically: did you notice the tick appear on the second screen, or did you only notice the button?

SO THAT: If the missing tick is invisible and the button is what you noticed, the follow-up is the win SENTENCE (proposed above) and the colour should probably go neutral until won — the mark alone is too quiet to carry the state. If the first screen already reads as unfinished, the win sentence is decoration and the next thing worth a turn is what a player does after level six, not more words on each level.

asks.title: Does the first screen now carry one heading too many?
asks.body:
The page opens with three headings stacked before any control: 'Plant' (the h1 masthead, hand-typed and legitimately so), 'Get everything fed' (INTRO.title, new this turn), then the current level's own title from the module — e.g. 'Ore to gears'. Plus INTRO's sentence and the level's blurb between them.

I cannot settle this from here and it is not a gate question. Every machine-checkable property holds: the words are the module's, they are one sentence, they use no banned vocabulary, they name no level. Whether a stranger reads three headings as orientation or as throat-clearing before the game is a judgement about a rendered page, and this turn has no browser and no person.

I chose the additive shape deliberately because it is the cheapest to reverse — see the decision in this outbox. The alternative is to fill the h1 from INTRO.title and drop 'Plant' from the page, which is one line in index.html plus an id change in two assertions.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com on a phone and on a laptop. Read from the top without scrolling.

WATCH FOR: Whether you reach the control within a few seconds, or whether the second heading makes you skim past the level's own title. Also whether losing the word 'Plant' from the page would cost anything you care about.

SO THAT: If it reads as clutter I fill the h1 from INTRO.title and delete the h2 — the game's heading becomes the page's heading, one line plus two assertion ids. If it reads fine I leave it and the shape is settled for whatever the first screen becomes next. If the answer is that the whole intro should be hidden once a level is entered, that is a different and larger ticket about the first screen being a screen rather than a paragraph above one, and I would file it against the campaign panel rather than against INTRO.

asks.title: Does the untouched line read as help, or as the page nagging you before you have done anything?
asks.body:
No gate can settle this and I could not settle it either, because it is a question about the first four seconds of a stranger's experience and I cannot render the page. The state is the OPENING state of five of the six levels, so whatever this sentence does, it does to almost every screen a new player meets.

The risk I can name but not measure: the level already shows a green tick saying everything is fed, and directly under it the page now says 'The factory already works. Move the control and find out what breaks it.' Read one way that is the missing explanation the ticket was written for. Read another it is an instruction to go and break a thing that is working, delivered before the player has formed any intention at all — which is the opposite of the vision's bar ('an intention they FORMED, acted on, and got refused for').

I shipped it because a green tick with no way forward is unambiguously worse — that reads as a broken page rather than as an unplayed level — and because the change is one line to reverse.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com on a phone, cold, and do not touch anything for ten seconds. Then play level one and level two without reading anything else on the page.

WATCH FOR: Whether the sentence answers the question you were forming, or answers one you had not asked yet. Specifically: did you look for a next button BEFORE reading it, and after reading it did you know what to do, or did you feel told off for not having played?

SO THAT: If it reads as help: leave the wording and move the intro paragraph into the module next (proposal 2), which makes all three page sentences assertable by identity. If it reads as nagging: the fix is to keep the branch and change what it renders — show it only once the player has looked at the level for a moment, or reword it as a statement rather than an instruction ('nothing is short here yet — nothing has been changed either'). If it reads as neither because you never saw it: it is in the wrong place on the page, and it belongs beside the hidden next button in the right-hand column rather than under the board.

asks.title: Is 'you must change something' enough, or must a level be BROKEN before it can be won?
asks.body:
lp-000596 made a win require a setting different from the one the player was handed. It deliberately did not require the player to have caused a failure first, because that is a second clause with a real cost and the vision's bar mentions both halves ('an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for').

What I cannot settle from here is how the weaker rule FEELS. It is measurably better than what it replaced — the control now has to move — but on level1 any of 71 settings wins and most produce a factory identical to the opening, so the required action can be arbitrary. The stronger rule (proposed as a follow-up) makes the game teach itself, and can also feel like being made to jump through a hoop after you have already understood the puzzle. Both are one clause; neither is decidable by a gate, because both pass every check the suite can express.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, play the first two levels without reading anything, and stop the moment you feel you have finished a level.

WATCH FOR: Whether you MOVE the control before pressing next, or hunt for a next button that is not there yet — and whether, on a level that opens already working, you ever discover what makes it fail.

SO THAT: If you moved the control naturally and still learned what breaks it, the current rule is enough and the follow-up should be dropped. If you sat on a green tick looking for a next button, the renderer proposal is the urgent one. If you finished both levels without ever seeing a failure, promote the stronger rule — that is the vision's bar going unmet with every gate passing.

asks.title: Is a game a blind player finishes in seven moves too easy — or is the arc (break it, then fix it) doing the work a win state cannot?
asks.body:
This is the one question this turn could not settle by writing a check, and I want to be precise about why. The MEASUREMENTS are all now executable and pinned: a stranger reaches a refusal in one move on every level; five of six levels open in a winning state; a blind up-stepping player completes the whole campaign in seven moves, five of them nudges that accept a level already won.

What no gate can decide is whether that is bad. Two readings are both coherent. (1) A game you beat without understanding it is not a puzzle, and the win should require an actual change — that is the proposal I filed at P1. (2) The levels are DESIGNED to open fed and barely so ('opens feasible, barely' is the stated texture of four of them); the intended experience is that you break it, see the refusal, and put it back, and a win state that fires when you restore it is exactly right. Under reading (2) the seven-move completion is an artefact of a blind policy that never explores, not a description of what a person does.

I shipped the measurement rather than the opinion, and filed the fix as a proposal rather than doing it, because it changes a contract three gates assert and it is reversible only by a conversation.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com cold, play the campaign through once without reading anything, and time it. Do not try to be a good player.

WATCH FOR: Whether you ever deliberately BREAK a level to see what happens, or only push the control until the line turns green — and whether finishing a level felt like anything.

SO THAT: If you broke levels unprompted, the arc is doing the work and my P1 proposal should be dropped: the win state is fine and the next ticket is about making the refusal more legible. If you only pushed toward green and finishing felt like nothing, promote the proposal — require the winning setting to differ from the opening — and follow it with a bead moving level1's opening off the ceiling of its own domain, which is where that change bites first.

asks.title: Is two sliders actually better than one 8281-stop index slider, or did it just become two bad controls?
asks.body:
The whole premise of this ticket is that a single slider sweeping a 91x91 product lexicographically is the worst control on the page. That is obviously true as an argument and I cannot verify it as an experience, because I have no browser and this turn rendered nothing. Two things could be wrong and only a person can see either. (1) Ninety-one stops in a 15rem column is about 0.16rem per stop on desktop and much less on a phone — it may be that the miner slider is now ALSO unusable, just less spectacularly, and that the honest control for this level is a number input or a pair of coarse buttons rather than a range. (2) The two capacities interact through a min(), so a player who drags the miner up and sees nothing change is being told something true and confusing; the read-out shows each part's value but nothing shows WHICH of the two is currently binding, and I decided not to add that because it is level knowledge the page must not have. Not decidable from here, and I shipped the reversible version: parts is a presentation layer, and going back to one slider is deleting one field from the level's knob declaration.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com on a phone, play to the third level in the order (it is 'Two machines in a row'), and try to reach a winning setting from the opening 70/45 using only the two sliders.

WATCH FOR: Whether you can land on a specific number at all with a thumb, and whether it is ever obvious which of the two machines is the one holding you back.

SO THAT: If the sliders are fine, the next control work is the binding-machine hint and it belongs in campaign.mjs's verdict sentence, not in the page. If they are not, the fix is a control-shape descriptor (a part can declare it wants steppers or a number field) and that is the game-view.js extraction proposed above, done sooner and with one more field in the spec.

asks.title: Is the first sentence any good? A machine can only confirm it is one sentence in plain words
asks.body:
The gate proves INTRO.blurb is one sentence, uses none of the jargon, names no level and counts nothing. It cannot say whether it makes a stranger want to touch the control, and I have no way to find out from here - there is no reader in this turn and the page is not yet wired to it.

The sentence: 'Each puzzle is a small factory that is not quite working, and you get a single control - move it until everything downstream gets what it asked for.' Title: 'Get everything fed'.

Two specific doubts I could not settle. (1) 'not quite working' may undersell it - on five of the six levels the opening state is already FED, so the honest framing might be 'working, but you have not proved it' rather than broken. I chose the punchier reading because a stranger who thinks nothing is wrong has no reason to move anything. (2) The word 'puzzle' commits to a framing the page never uses elsewhere ('level' is used throughout the module and the markup), and I deliberately avoided 'level' in the intro because the count rule and the level-id rule made every phrasing with it read awkwardly.

I decided both ways rather than waiting, per the standing instruction. This is a note, not a request.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com once the wiring follow-up has landed, read only the top of the page, and stop. Do not scroll.

WATCH FOR: Whether you know what you are supposed to DO before you touch anything - and specifically whether 'not quite working' makes you look for something broken on a level that opens already fed.

SO THAT: If it reads fine, INTRO is done and nobody spends another turn on wording. If 'not quite working' misleads, the fix is one string in campaign.mjs and the gate re-checks it for free - and the finding worth recording is that the intro must describe the ACT (move the control until you have proved it) rather than the STATE. If 'puzzle' jars against 'level', that is a vocabulary decision for the whole panel and wants its own small bead rather than an edit to this one sentence.

asks.title: Does the page now read as a game, or as a game bolted to the top of an explainer?
asks.body:
This turn made the page open on one level with a title, a blurb, a control, a verdict and a next button — vision item 1's remaining half. What it did NOT do is remove the summon inspector, the summon panel and the two essays underneath, because they are the surface's stated job (making the primitive judgeable by a stranger in thirty seconds) and deleting them is a decision about what the page is FOR rather than about wiring. So a visitor now meets a game and then scrolls into documentation about a different thing. No gate can tell whether that reads as generous or as unfinished, and I have no way to look at it.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com on a phone. Do not scroll. Play the first level to a win and press next. Then scroll once and stop.

WATCH FOR: Whether the first screen made you want to press something, and whether the moment you scrolled past the game you felt you had left it or finished it.

SO THAT: If the game reads as the page, the next tickets are inside it — a first-run line, a completion screen, an undo. If it reads as bolted on, the inspector and the summon panel should move to a second page and the vision's item 1 becomes 'the game is the whole surface', which is a bigger and more valuable ticket than any of those. If it reads as unfinished specifically because there is no ending, the completion screen is the one to do first and the rest can wait.

asks.title: Is win fraction the right difficulty measure — specifically, does LEVEL_4 belong second?
asks.body:
The campaign's order is computed rather than claimed, and it reproduces your '1, 3, 2, 5, 6' exactly once LEVEL_4 (which your note did not mention) is removed. So the measure agrees with you on the five levels you had an opinion about, which is the best evidence available from inside the loop.

The one place it makes a call nobody has checked is LEVEL_4, which lands SECOND — easier than everything except the tutorial. The measure says so because 41 of the 81 rates the slider offers win. But LEVEL_4 is the autoSplit level: the split is computed FOR the player, and the loop's own turn-15 critique was that this 'removes exactly that decision from the player's hands'. A level that decides the interesting thing for you being nearly the easiest is either the measure working (it is easy because there is nothing to decide) or the measure missing something (it is not easy, it is empty, and easy is the wrong word for it).

I cannot settle it from here: it is a question about what a person experiences, and every instrument I have counts winning settings.

DO: Once the campaign is wired to the page, play it straight through in the computed order — level1, level4, level3, level2, level5, level6 — without reading any of the code.

WATCH FOR: Whether LEVEL_4 in second place feels like a step UP from level 1 or like a rest stop, and whether you notice that its split is being decided for you.

SO THAT: If it feels like a step up, win fraction stands and the pinned ORDER stays as is. If it feels empty rather than easy, the fix is not to reorder — it is that LEVEL_4 needs a lever (its own module says as much), and I would propose replacing the source-rate knob with an explicit share, which turns it into a genuine choice and moves it down the curve on the same measure. If it feels HARDER than level 1 despite winning more often, the measure is wrong and the next thing to try is win fraction weighted by how far a losing setting is from a winning one.

asks.title: [CARRIED FROM TURN 55] When a summon is refused for two different reasons at once, does a player want both reasons or the nearest one?
asks.body:
Not decidable from here, and turn 55 deliberately did not decide it while moving the code — the move is behaviour-preserving on purpose so the diff stays reviewable.

The panel names only the first refusal. The oracle returns all of them. Reporting all is more truthful and reads as more competent; it is also how you get 'part of the cube pushes out through the west wall, AND there is already rock there, AND it is too close to the cube you summoned on move 2' as one wall of text, at the exact moment the player is trying to do a simple thing. Reporting one is calmer and is how most games do it, and it costs a second attempt to learn the second obstacle.

This cannot be settled by writing a check. Both behaviours are trivially gateable; which one FEELS like help rather than nagging is the thing no gate reaches, and it is the class of question the vision says to file rather than guess at. The follow-up ticket proposed alongside assumes 'group by blame, one clause each, capped' — that is a guess, recorded as a guess.

[Carried by turn 56 because turn 55's outbox was never applied. Turn 56 did not re-decide it and did not file a competing ask.]

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, scroll to the summon panel, and click somewhere near the very edge of the plan that also has a seed dot on it — a spot that is both outside the placeable box and on top of foam. Then place one cube, and click a spot that overlaps both it and the wall.

WATCH FOR: Whether reading one reason and having to click again feels like the game teaching you, or like it withholding. And, on the second click, whether you would rather have been told about your own cube or about the wall first.

SO THAT: If both: the follow-up ticket ships grouped multi-refusal output and the precedence question disappears. If one: the ticket becomes a much smaller change to the PRECEDENCE instead — pick the refusal a player can most cheaply act on rather than the one with the lowest summon-seed index, which is currently an accident of loop order rather than a decision. If neither reads badly, the ticket drops and the turns go to vision item 1 instead.

asks.title: Is the six levels' difficulty order the one a person feels, or the one win-fraction computes?
asks.body:
vision item 1 says to order the levels by difficulty and offers feasibility margin as the measure. I checked instead of assuming, and margin does not work: LEVEL_1 ships at margin 0.02 by design and LEVEL_6 at 0.25, so ordering by shipped margin makes Level 1 the hardest and inverts the curve the vision describes. So I specified a different measure — the fraction of each knob's declared domain that produces a satisfiable factory — and made the order DERIVED from it rather than asserted, so the turn cannot fail on a guess. What I cannot settle from here is whether that number tracks felt difficulty. A three-way button choice with one winner has win-fraction 1/3; a slider with a wide green band has 0.6; but a stranger may find the button trivial and the slider fiddly, because a button shows you the whole domain at once and a slider does not. No gate can see that. I have gone ahead with win-fraction and pinned the resulting order as a literal in the gate, which is the cheap-to-reverse option: changing the order later is one array.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, play Levels 1 through 6 in the order they appear on the page, and write down the order you would put them in for someone who has never seen it.

WATCH FOR: Which one you were stuck on longest, and whether the discrete choice (Level 2) felt easier or harder than the sliders either side of it.

SO THAT: If your order matches win-fraction descending, the measure is validated and campaign.mjs's pinned ORDER stands as-is. If it differs, I replace the pinned literal with your order and keep win-fraction only as a regression detector, and the next planner proposes a second measure that explains the difference — most likely 'how visible is the domain to the player', which would rank discrete choices easier and is buildable. If you cannot tell them apart at all, that is the strongest possible signal that six levels is too many of the same thing and the next window goes to the pocket objective (vision item 3) instead of to more level work.

asks.title: [CARRIED FROM TURN 1, NEVER APPLIED] May the loop write its own machinery? Three turns have now been spent proving it cannot, and the answer is a risk judgement no gate can make
asks.body:
Every agent seat is confined to plant/ plus its outbox. That boundary is what keeps a turn off the public web and out of the workflows that spend money, and it is stated as a security property rather than a convenience. It is also the thing that makes a whole class of ticket unsatisfiable: lp-14c7f5 asks for a file in scripts/, the reactor happily dispatched it THREE times, and no possible turn could have delivered it. The proposals all three turns produced about the loop's own plumbing are in the same position — they are their own blockers. This is not decidable from inside a turn because it is not a question about correctness (the mechanism is easy to build either way), it is a question about how much of its own machinery you are willing to let an unattended fleet edit while you are asleep, and only you can price that. My own lean, recorded so the ask is not a shrug: keep the gate tight, and treat 'park it in plant/tools/ with the move instructions in the file header' as the sanctioned pattern — I have written that into plant/CLAUDE.md accordingly, and it is one edit to remove if you disagree.

DO: Run `node plant/tools/loop-brief.selftest.mjs` — the deliverable three turns have now parked, and the one thing none of them could do. Then open .github/workflows/loop-work.yml at the containment gate (the ALLOWED regex, ~line 314) and .github/loop/config.json's `writes` array and read them side by side.

WATCH FOR: Whether the selftest passes at all — no turn has ever executed it. Then two numbers it prints: the composed size against the 131072 budget, and section 13's dead-end capacity against the ledger's current dead-end count. That second gap is the headroom before briefs silently stop fitting. Then, specifically, whether the loop editing the code that composes its own prompt feels different in kind from the loop editing plant/. I think it does and I could not tell you where the line is: a turn that changes what turns are told is the one edit whose mistakes are invisible to every gate downstream, because everything downstream reads the output of the thing that broke.

SO THAT: If NO, all three proposals are permanently operator work and should be tagged human-only rather than sitting in the queue looking dispatchable — and the reactor fix becomes the important one, because it stops the loop wasting turns on tickets it cannot reach. If YES BUT NARROWLY — say scripts/loop-*.mjs and nothing else — the containment regex should come from config.writes and you add that one glob, and this ticket finishes itself on the next dispatch. If YES BROADLY, the write scope, the staging list and the containment regex should collapse into one list today, before a fourth copy appears. Under EVERY answer, lp-14c7f5 must be dropped or re-gated so it stops consuming turns; that part is true regardless.

asks.title: Does clicking a FLAT plan of a 3D pocket read as fair, or as the game hiding the thing that refuses you?
asks.body:
This is the one judgement I could not settle by writing a check, and I made the call anyway rather than stalling: the panel maps a click on a top-down plan to a world point, with height on a separate slider.

The worry is specific and structural, not a matter of polish. The plan CANNOT show the reason for a large fraction of refusals: two seeds that overlap on the plan may be far apart vertically, and the foam scales vertical distance by sqrt(aniso) on top of that, so 'there is already rock there' will sometimes be said about a dot the player cannot see near their cursor. I mitigated it three ways — every pocket seed is drawn, green dots mark spots that look clear at the CURRENT height, and a note under the panel says the plan is flat in plain words — but mitigation is not the same as the thing being legible, and no test I can write distinguishes 'honest and demanding' from 'arbitrary'.

It is not decidable from here because it is a question about what a person infers from a picture, and the loop has no instrument for that.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, scroll to 'Summon — put one of these into real ground', and try to place three shapes without reading the note underneath. Then drag the height slider to the bottom and try again.

WATCH FOR: Whether a refusal ever feels arbitrary — specifically whether you look for the thing that refused you and fail to find it on the plan. Also whether you touch the height slider at all unprompted.

SO THAT: If refusals read as arbitrary, the next ticket is a side elevation beside the plan (same controller, one more pure-view function) and NOT a 3D raycast. If they read as fair but the height slider goes untouched, the panel should pick the height itself from the clearest candidate at that x/z and the slider becomes an override. If both are fine, the next ticket is the one that turns this into a level with a goal — which is where vision item 1 actually ends.

asks.title: Does highlighting every legal spot destroy the failure the whole thing is for?
asks.body:
candidates() exists so a UI can show the player where a summon fits. But vision.md's bar is that within thirty seconds a stranger DOES SOMETHING THAT CAN FAIL — 'an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for'. A page that highlights every legal cell removes exactly that: the player clicks a green square, it works, and the constraint that is supposed to BE the mechanic is never felt. The two designs are in direct tension and I cannot settle it from here, because it is a question about what a person feels in the first minute and every check I could write would pass for both.

I have decided the reversible half and shipped it: candidates() is a controller method with a `clear` margin, not a UI decision, so the page can use it for a full highlight, for a subtle hint (highlight only after a refusal), or not at all, without any change to the module or its gate. What I cannot decide is which the page should do.

This is item 1 of the vision and the first thing a stranger meets, which is why it is worth a person's two minutes rather than a guess.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com once the summon panel ships. Play it twice: once with every legal spot highlighted before you act, once with no highlight at all and only a refusal message when you get it wrong. Two minutes each.

WATCH FOR: Whether the un-highlighted version makes you look at the pocket and form a theory about where things fit, or just makes you click at random until something sticks. And whether the highlighted version feels like a puzzle or like colouring in.

SO THAT: If the un-highlighted version produces a theory, the page ships with no highlight and candidates() stays a debug/level-design tool — and the next ticket is a better refusal sentence, since the refusal becomes the only teacher. If it produces random clicking, the page ships with the highlight on and the difficulty has to come from somewhere else (which solid fits where, or a limited budget of summons), and that is a different next ticket. If both feel flat, the problem is that placement has no CONSEQUENCE yet — nothing is produced or consumed — and the next ticket is wiring production.mjs to placed objects, i.e. level.mjs's levelVerdict against a real pocket rather than a session-local list.

asks.title: Should a refusal say what is WRONG, or say what to DO about it?
asks.body:
refusalLine currently describes the fault: 'Too close to the rock already here in 3 places — the tightest is about 0.29 m short of clear.' The alternative is to describe the remedy: 'Move it about 0.3 m to your left.'

This is not decidable from here and it is not decidable by a gate, because both sentences are true and both are derivable from the same verdict — placement.mjs's seed refusals carry the offending seed's coordinates and the verdict carries the constellation's centre, so a direction and a distance are one subtraction away. What a gate can check is that the number matches the verdict. What it cannot check is which sentence a person can act on, and they pull in opposite directions: the fault version is honest about the whole obstruction (three seeds, worst 0.29 m) while the remedy version has to pick ONE move, and a move that clears the worst seed may not clear the other two — so the helpful-sounding sentence is the one that can lie.

I went with the fault version because it is the one that cannot be wrong, and because 'easier to reverse' favours it: adding a remedy clause to an existing fault sentence is additive, while removing a remedy players have learned to trust is not.

DO: Open the page once it renders a real pocket (the proposal above wires it), drag a summon into occupied ground, and read the refusal out loud. Then imagine the same moment with 'Move it about 0.3 m to your left' instead.

WATCH FOR: Whether you look at the sentence and then look at the screen to work out where to go, or whether the sentence alone is enough to make the next move. And whether being told a direction that turns out not to work feels worse than being told nothing.

SO THAT: If the fault version is enough: nothing changes, and the direction data in the verdict stays unused. If the remedy version is wanted: I file a bead adding a direction clause derived from the offending seed's coordinates and the summon centre, gated on a fixture where the suggested move is asserted to ACTUALLY produce a legal placement — which is the assertion that stops it lying, and it is buildable today because summonAt can just be asked.

asks.title: When a placement is refused, should the level read as LOST or as UNFINISHED?
asks.body:
levelVerdict returns a single boolean `ok`, and it is false for two situations that feel completely different to play: (1) you placed a building somewhere illegal, and (2) everything you placed is legal but the factory does not meet demand. Right now both are just 'not ok'.

I cannot settle this from here because it is not a correctness question — both readings are implementable, both are self-consistent, and no gate can tell me which one a person experiences as fair. It is exactly the class the vision says is worth an ask rather than a guess. I DID decide and ship: `ok` stays a single boolean because it is the smaller, more reversible choice, and the two causes are already distinguishable by inspecting `placement` vs `network`. Adding a third state later is additive; removing one is not.

DO: Open plant/test/level.selftest.mjs and read the 'END TO END' CONTROL section (the sink recentred onto the processor). Then imagine that state on screen: a building is visibly overlapping another one, and the verdict line says you have not won.

WATCH FOR: Whether your instinct is 'I lost' or 'I have not finished placing things yet'. Specifically: would you expect the game to let you keep going and fix it, or to tell you the attempt failed?

SO THAT: If LOST: `ok: false` is the whole story, the game shell shows a fail state, and nothing changes. If UNFINISHED: the proposed game.mjs needs a third status ('illegal' distinct from 'short'), the refused object should probably not even be committed to the placement list, and 'place() returns a refusal you can retry' becomes the interaction rather than 'place() records a loss'. That is a different state machine, and it is much cheaper to know before game.mjs is written than after.

asks.title: Does an auto-computed split that accounts for recipe ratios read as helpful, or as the game doing the interesting part for you?
asks.body:
Level 5's header made exactly this critique of autoSplit() and the ledger records it as the best thing this loop has produced: an optimal split computed for you is not a decision, and 'splitting a shared output between competing consumers' is the genre's central decision. This turn made autoSplit STRONGER — it now sees through a processor to the sink behind it and corrects for the recipe ratio, which is precisely the calculation a player would otherwise have to do in their head.

I cannot decide from here whether that is a good tool or a spoiler. The algebra says the answer is right; nothing in the repo says whether being handed it is fun. Both readings are defensible and they point at opposite next tickets, which is why I am spending an ask rather than guessing.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, go to LEVEL_5 (the player-chosen split, two sliders, narrow winnable band) and play it to a win. Then imagine a button labelled 'balance it for me' that instantly sets the correct split — including through a machine that converts 1 ore into 0.6 ingots, so the right answer is not the one the demand numbers suggest.

WATCH FOR: Whether you would press that button, and whether pressing it would end your interest in the level. Specifically: is working out that 0.6 conversion the part that felt like solving something, or the part that felt like arithmetic homework?

SO THAT: If it reads as a SPOILER: autoSplit stays an internal oracle used to author and validate levels, never exposed to the player, and the next ticket is a level where the ratio conversion is the puzzle — a machine whose recipe ratio the player must reason through to set the split. If it reads as a HELPFUL TOOL: the next ticket surfaces it as an in-game hint or assist button, and difficulty moves up a layer to constraints autoSplit cannot solve (capacity limits, competing sinks), which is also a concrete ticket. If it reads as NEITHER — interesting maths, boring to meet — that is the strongest possible answer, because it says stop extending the oracle and spend the remaining windows entirely on vision item 1, turning the six levels into one game.

asks.title: Is a one-second pause after placing a factory piece a hitch, or is it the world reforming around you?
asks.body:
I asserted the budget from literature, not from taste, and taste is what actually decides it. Gate 7's product number is 1000 ms — the classic one-second limit, below which a person still feels they are directly manipulating the thing. That is the right number for a BUTTON. A plant is not a button: the whole lattice visibly reforms around the seed, and in that context a pause can read as weight and consequence rather than as a hitch. Games trade on exactly that difference and no benchmark can tell them apart.

This is not decidable from here for two reasons. I cannot run anything this turn, so I have no number at all; and even with the number, whether 900 ms of foam reforming feels good is not a property of the measurement. What I already did instead: picked 1000 ms with its provenance written into the file, and made the ASSERTED threshold 2x that so a runner's weather cannot fail the gate — so nothing is blocked on this answer, only calibrated by it.

DO: Once this gate has run on CI, open the run log and read the block headed 'what this means for the game' — it prints the predicted per-turn cost at the shipping pocket and, for each solid, how many summons fit inside the 1000 ms limit. Then judge the number against the feel you want: is a pause of that length after clicking 'summon' acceptable, welcome, or unacceptable?

WATCH FOR: Whether the number is in the hundreds of milliseconds or the seconds, and whether the answer changes between a small summon (tetrahedron, 5 seeds) and a big one (icosahedron, 21). A budget that a tetrahedron meets and an icosahedron blows is a DESIGN lever, not just a performance problem — it prices the big solids in real time.

SO THAT: If a second or so is fine, gate 7's thresholds stand as written and no optimisation work should be scheduled at all — I close the performance thread and the proposal above stays unpromoted. If it is too slow, the atomic multi-insert (lp-f25c2f) becomes the highest-value performance ticket in the backlog by roughly an order of magnitude, and the proposal above should be promoted first to give it a before-number. If you want the pause to be LONGER for weight, say so and I will stop treating this as a cost at all and start treating it as an animation budget, which is a different ticket entirely.

asks.title: When a player aims at ground that will not take a summon, should the game refuse, snap, or never let the click happen?
asks.body:
The predicate can now answer "is this legal" before anything is attempted, which means the design question is no longer blocked by the maths — it is blocked by taste, and it is the next fork in wiring this into something playable.

Three honest options, and they build different things. (1) REFUSE THE CLICK and say why — the constraint is a failure the player can actually hit, which is what the bar for "playable" in vision.md asks for, but a refusal with no guidance is just a wall. (2) SNAP to the nearest legal position — generous, always succeeds, and it removes the failure entirely; the constraint stops being a mechanic and becomes a formatting rule. (3) SHOW BUILDABLE SPACE as an overlay so the illegal click is never available — what most factory games do, and it turns the constraint into information rather than into a refusal.

I cannot decide this from here because all three are correct implementations of the same predicate and the difference is entirely in how it FEELS to be told no. I have deliberately not guessed: placement.mjs supports all three (refusals carry their cause, clampToHull is exported, and the coarse sphere test exists to make sweeping a whole grid cheap enough for an overlay).

DO: Open any factory or builder game you already have — Factorio, Satisfactory, Dorfromantik, Minecraft, whichever is nearest — and deliberately try to place something on ground that will not take it. Do it three or four times in a row rather than once.

WATCH FOR: Whether being refused taught you where you COULD build, or only that you could not build there. And whether you noticed the refusal at all, or whether the game had already made the bad click impossible before you reached for it.

SO THAT: REFUSE: I build refusalLine() (proposed above) and a rejection the player can read, and the next level is designed around ground that runs out. SNAP: I build nearestLegal() — a search over the buildable set for the closest legal centre — and stop treating placement as a failure state at all, which also means the "something that can fail" in the playable bar has to come from somewhere else and I need to know that early. OVERLAY: I build the buildable-space sweep into a drawable mask first, which is a different and larger piece of work than either of the others, and it should be scheduled before any level that needs it rather than after.

asks.title: Should unrouted fan-out output (the new waste metric) become a visible in-level failure state, or stay an oracle-only fact?
asks.body:
This turn proposes adding a `waste` field to feasible()'s return — how much of a source's or processor's output goes nowhere because a fan-out group's shares sum to less than 1, or a processor output has no consuming edge at all. It is scoped oracle-only (production.mjs + its selftest) on purpose, so it does not preempt this question: today a level can only fail by a SINK falling short of demand (the red-box treatment in level-view.js's drawLevel). Wasted output is a different kind of failure — nothing downstream is short, but the player made a choice that throws resources away for no reason, which is arguably closer to 'an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for' than a sink shortfall is, since it is entirely self-inflicted rather than a capacity fight.

DO: Once this turn's waste-metric ticket ships, open plant/index.html locally, pick any fan-out level (4, 5, or 6), and drag a share slider so the two shares sum to noticeably less than 1 (e.g. LEVEL_5's shareA far from its valid window in the direction that leaves both destinations under-fed AND leaves headroom unrouted, if such a setting exists in that level's current wiring — otherwise imagine the SVG showing a third, amber state alongside the existing green/red boxes).

WATCH FOR: Whether 'some of my ore just vanished, nobody consumed it' reads as a real decision cost the moment you see the number, or whether it needs a visual (an amber box, a leak icon, a line in verdictLine) before it registers as a failure at all — i.e. whether the NUMBER alone is enough or whether it needs level-view.js's rendering treatment.

SO THAT: If the number alone reads as meaningful, a follow-up ticket wires `waste` into verdictLine()'s existing sentence (a small, additive change). If it needs a visual treatment to register, the follow-up instead extends drawLevel()'s red/normal styling to a third state, which is more UI work and should be sized and proposed as its own ticket rather than assumed free.

asks.title: Does a purely topological (non-spatial) construction order count as real progress on gate 6, or is gate 6 meaningless without the pocket geometry?
asks.body:
I'm proposing buildOrder() — exposing production.mjs's existing topological sort as 'a legal construction order' toward FACTORIO.md gate 6. It is honestly only half the problem: it proves dependency order (build the source before what consumes it) but says nothing about whether each build physically FITS where it lands, which needs the pocket/hull work (clearanceNeeded, selfCompatible, pairGap) that lives outside plant/'s files entirely. I can't tell from here whether gate 6 is meant to compose from a non-spatial half plus a spatial half added later, or whether a construction order that ignores space is a distraction that will just get thrown away once the real (spatial) certificate exists.

DO: Read the two-sentence FACTORIO.md gate 6 description again with buildOrder() in mind, and decide: is 'an order that respects dependencies, with placement legality checked separately/later' a sane decomposition of gate 6, or does gate 6 only mean something once a single check does both at once?

WATCH FOR: Whether your instinct is 'yes, and here's what the spatial half should bolt onto' (a shape for buildOrder()'s output that a later placement checker could consume) versus 'no, don't bother — a construction order without space is not a certificate of anything'.

SO THAT: If yes, I (or a later turn) extend buildOrder() toward something a spatial checker can consume once that work lands, and gate 6 becomes an explicit two-layer build. If no, buildOrder() gets dropped or demoted and future turns stop investing in the non-spatial half of gate 6 inside plant/ at all.

asks.title: Does explicit-share fan-out (levels 4 & 5, shipped) satisfy vision item 1's 'the real puzzle', or is the general multi-hop LP still the priority?
asks.body:
vision.md's item 1 was written against production.mjs v1, which refused fan-out outright — the file explicitly says 'every level so far is a straight line... by force, not by choice.' Since then (per the ledger: turns 15-16, lp-34239d and follow-ons) production.mjs grew explicit-share fan-out and autoSplit()'s closed-form proportional split, and levels 4 and 5 shipped exercising both — one automatic, one player-set. But production.mjs's own header is explicit that this is 'a deliberate, narrower feature than a general LP': a fan-out into PROCESSORS, or a sink fed by MORE than one supplier, still 'needs a real linear program over the whole network and is deliberately left alone.' That's a multi-turn build, not a one-turn ticket, and nobody has picked it up — possibly because it's genuinely too large for the current per-turn shape, possibly because levels 4/5 already answered the vision's concern and nobody said so.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com and play levels 4 and 5 for a couple of minutes — level 4's automatic proportional split, level 5's player-set share slider between fieldA and fieldB.

WATCH FOR: Whether deciding where a shared output goes feels like 'the genre's central decision' vision item 1 names, or whether it still feels like tuning a slider toward a formula the game already knows the answer to.

SO THAT: If it reads as satisfying item 1: future turns should stop budgeting toward the general multi-hop LP and move fully to placement/gate 6 work instead, and vision.md's item 1 should be marked closed the same way gate 5 and levels 1-3 already are. If it does NOT: the next several turns need to start actually budgeting toward the general LP as a multi-turn arc (starting with, e.g., just the 'fan-out into processors with a single downstream sink each' sub-case) rather than continuing to look for more closed-form autoSplit() special cases one ticket at a time.

asks.title: Why were LEVEL_4, LEVEL_5, and LEVEL_6 each rejected-by-review with no reason recorded?
asks.body:
Three level proposals — LEVEL_4 (lp-9626f7, convergence: two sources into one processor), LEVEL_5 (lp-6aeecf, two independent sinks), LEVEL_6 (lp-b5e73b, an illegal-wiring refusal state) — were each written carefully against a real gap in what a shipped level exercises, each cited the same house style and CONTROL discipline as the levels that DID land, and each came back tagged rejected-by-review with nothing else recorded in the ledger. This turn deliberately avoided proposing a fourth level (a genuine fan-out-split level, which vision's own priority 1 is pointing straight at, and which is now newly buildable since turn 15 landed explicit-share fan-out) because I cannot tell from here whether the pattern is 'levels are the wrong shape of work right now' or something narrower each of the three happened to share.

DO: Open the three rejected beads (lp-9626f7, lp-6aeecf, lp-b5e73b) and say one sentence each on why, or point at wherever the review reason actually lives if it isn't in the ledger body.

WATCH FOR: Whether the reason is about LEVELS as a category right now (too much explainer-polish, or simply not wanted until fan-out/placement lands) versus something narrower each proposal happened to share (e.g. all three touched index.html in the same way, or all three were written against an older vision.md revision that has since changed).

SO THAT: If it's category-level, I stop proposing new levels entirely until told otherwise and put remaining planning budget into the oracle (autoSplit, placement-in-a-pocket). If it's narrower, I write the fan-out-split level next turn deliberately avoiding whatever the three shared, instead of guessing a fourth time.

asks.title: Level 3 never shows which of the two capacities is currently binding — is that ambiguity good friction or bad confusion?
asks.body:
Level 1 and Level 2 each have exactly one thing that can be wrong, so the verdict line alone always explains the failure. Level 3 has two independent capacities and the page deliberately does not highlight which one is currently the tighter constraint (per the ticket's own explicit decision to not expose production.mjs's per-node achieved rates this turn) — a visitor sees 'depot short by N' and has to experiment with both sliders to find out why. That could read as the level's whole point (forcing you to form a hypothesis and test it, which is closer to the vision's playability bar than a single slider ever was) or as it just being confusing on a small phone screen with two sliders and one vague error.

DO: Open plant.minomobi.com, scroll to Level 3, and drag only ONE slider at a time without reading this ask first — see how many drags it takes before you understand which knob you moved actually caused the change.

WATCH FOR: Whether you instinctively drag both sliders at once to 'search' for the answer, versus isolating one variable at a time the way the CONTROL structure in the test does.

SO THAT: If it reads as fine friction, Level 4 (convergence, proposed above) can ship with the same no-highlight approach. If it reads as confusing, the next level turn should add a lightweight per-processor 'binding' indicator (e.g. bold the capacity number that currently equals the achieved output) before building a fourth level with the same blind-spot.

asks.title: Does picking a labelled machine (its capacity printed right on the button) read as a production decision, or as arithmetic-checking?
asks.body:
LEVEL_2 (proposed this turn) replaces LEVEL_1's continuous ore-rate slider with three buttons, each showing the candidate machine's exact capacity number. That gets away from 'a slider that turns a label red', which is what ask lp-02e2be already questioned about LEVEL_1 — but it may trade one non-answer for another: if the capacity number is printed on the button, the 'puzzle' might just be 'which number is >= 50', solved by mental arithmetic before the click ever happens, rather than felt as installing different equipment. A machine cannot tell the difference between a real decision and a math check with extra steps.

DO: Once LEVEL_2 ships, open plant.minomobi.com, scroll to 'Level 2 — pick the machine', and click each of the three smelter buttons in turn.

WATCH FOR: Whether you catch yourself doing the subtraction (capacity minus 50) in your head before clicking, versus just trying options and reading the verdict.

SO THAT: If it still reads as arithmetic-checking, the next turn hides the capacity number and shows only the qualitative label (cheap/good/golden), so the number has to be discovered by trying it rather than read off the button — a bigger, different UI change I am not making speculatively this turn. If it reads as a real choice, LEVEL_2 ships as designed and the same three-option pattern is reused for future levels.

asks.title: Why were the two placement-legality modules and the band-colour ticket rejected?
asks.body:
Three consecutive proposals adjacent to priorities 2/3 were tagged rejected-by-review in beads.jsonl with no reason recorded: lp-7b7f04 (combined session-local placement legality + feasibility composition), lp-439104 (placement legality alone, deliberately split from lp-7b7f04 to isolate the problem), and lp-64a447 (a CSS class coloring the already-shipped band() label). All three read as Definition-of-Ready-complete from their bead text alone — named class, gate, bounded paths. Without the reason, I cannot tell whether this means 'stop proposing synthetic session-local placement entirely until the real foamworld pocket port lands' (lp-39d6e7 is then the only path back into priority 2), or 'something specific was wrong with those two tickets' (wording, a missed edge case, an implementation risk not visible from the ticket text alone) — and guessing wrong either wastes a future turn repeating the same rejected pattern, or wrongly avoids a category of work that was actually fine.

DO: Open the three rejected bead bodies (lp-7b7f04, lp-439104, lp-64a447) and whatever diff a worker produced against them, if one exists, and say which of the two readings is closer.

WATCH FOR: Whether the rejection reads as 'wrong category of work' (more scaffolding/inspector, not the game) versus 'right idea, wrong execution' (something specific in the ticket text or the resulting diff).

SO THAT: If it's category: future planning turns stop proposing any placement/legality module until lp-39d6e7's real-pocket port is scoped and landed, and I will say so explicitly rather than re-splitting the same idea a third way. If it's execution: I need the specific complaint so the next attempt at that category doesn't repeat it.

asks.title: Does LEVEL_1's ore slider satisfy 'not a slider that turns a label red', or is it exactly what that bar rules out?
asks.body:
The vision's bar for playable says: 'Not a slider that turns a label red — an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for.' LEVEL_1 (plant/levels/level1.mjs, wired into plant/index.html via level-view.js) is, literally, a continuous ore-rate slider that turns the verdict red when dragged far enough. It may already be exactly the thing that sentence warns against, or it may be an acceptable interim step given priority 2 (real-pocket placement) is currently blocked by foamworld.js's size (700+ lines, far past one turn to port — see this bead's decisions). I cannot tell which reading is intended, and it also bears on why lp-7b7f04 (a session-local placement+feasibility module, one level up from LEVEL_1's single slider) was rejected without a recorded reason — the two questions may have the same answer.

DO: Open plant/index.html (or plant.minomobi.com once deployed), scroll to 'Level 1', and drag the ore slider down until the verdict turns red.

WATCH FOR: Whether that moment reads as forming an intention and getting refused, or as watching a number cross a threshold — the two things the vision explicitly distinguishes.

SO THAT: If it reads as just a threshold, the next turn should stop extending slider-driven level logic (including this turn's placement.mjs) and instead scope a genuinely discrete click-to-place interaction, even a fabricated stand-in world. If it reads as acceptable for now, further turns can keep extending LEVEL_1-style levels — more nodes, more sinks, the band() dial this turn surfaces — without second-guessing the interaction model.

asks.title: Does the new self-compatibility fail state read as a build constraint, or as a broken slider?
asks.body:
Proposal 1 above adds a real fail state to the summon inspector — drag the inradius slider down and a solid flips from buildable to not, using the same rule reformPocket enforces elsewhere. But it is surfaced on a raw parameter slider in what is still a library page, not inside anything resembling a level, and I cannot tell from here whether that reads as 'the world has a build constraint you're bumping into' or as 'I turned a dial and got an error message'. This is one layer up from the already-open lp-7c8e6f (whether the anisotropic squash itself should be felt or hidden) — this one is about whether the FAIL STATE built on top of it lands as a mechanic.

DO: Once proposal 1 ships to plant.minomobi.com, pick icosahedron and drag the inradius slider down until the new buildable line flips from green to red.

WATCH FOR: Whether you instinctively try to fix it (raise r back up) before reading why it failed, or read the reason first — that's the difference between it landing as a mechanic and landing as noise.

SO THAT: If it reads as a mechanic, I'll keep proposing small inspector-scoped playability tickets like this one while lp-f25c2f/lp-39d6e7 are still in flight. If it reads as noise, I'll stop proposing anything UI-facing in plant/ next turn and only propose class-d analysis work until a real pocket exists to build an actual level against.

asks.title: Is the anisotropic squash something a player should FEEL, or something the game should hide?
asks.body:
Every summon so far is exact under a metric with aniso 2.2, so a solid is visibly squashed along Y. I cannot decide from here whether that reads as a deliberate material property of the foam — a thing you learn to exploit — or as a rendering bug the player fights. No gate measures this and either reading is internally consistent, so guessing sets the direction for every mechanic built on top of it.

DO: Open foam, summon a dodecahedron and an icosahedron side by side, and walk around them for a minute at eye level.

WATCH FOR: Whether the squash reads as the world having a grain you could use, or as the shapes being wrong.

SO THAT: If it reads as grain, I propose mechanics that USE the anisotropy — a source that only aligns along Y, a defense that is cheaper across the grain. If it reads as wrong, I propose a compensation pass that renders solids round while keeping the seed geometry exact, and the anisotropy stays a hidden implementation detail.
